fields.title: Coram Deo
fields.subtitle: Living every day before the face of God
fields.description: Coram Deo is Latin for “before the face of God.” This teaching book for every Christian, from new believers to those who have walked with God for decades, shows how all of life is lived in His presence: knowing Father, Son and Holy Spirit; meeting Him daily in the Word, prayer and the morning watch; becoming like Christ; marriage, family, work and church; and mission, stewardship and the hope of glory. Each chapter tells the story of a man or woman of God and ends with questions and a step for the week.
fields.about_html:
Every one of us lives before someone’s face: parents, employers, neighbours, the crowd. The Reformers had a phrase for a different way to live: coram Deo, “before the face of God.” This book is about that face, and what it means to live every day in His presence. It is not about earning God’s favour. We walk with Him because, in Christ, He has already accepted us.

The book moves in five parts. “Foundations” asks who God is: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. “Walking with God” begins with love and shows how we meet Him daily, in His Word, in prayer, in the morning watch, in abiding in Christ and in the spiritual disciplines. “Becoming Like Christ” covers discipleship, the Sermon on the Mount, faith, holiness, the healing of the soul, spiritual warfare and suffering. “Living as God’s People” turns to marriage and singleness, children, work, the Church, its ministries and gifts, and serving one another. “Living for God’s Purposes” looks to the Great Commission, stewardship, finishing well and the new heavens and new earth.

Each chapter opens with Scripture, teaches from the Bible, tells the story of one man or woman of God, from Augustine of North Africa and Martin Luther to George Müller, Amy Carmichael, Andrew Murray and Festo Kivengere of Uganda, and ends with questions for reflection and one practical step for the week ahead. Where faithful Christians differ, the book sets out the main views fairly; an appendix explains how to hold firm on the essentials and extend grace on the rest. Scripture is quoted from the Open Word Bible (OWB), Balanced edition, which is dedicated to the public domain.

qa.question: What does Coram Deo mean?
qa.answer: It is Latin for “before the face of God,” a phrase the Reformers used for living first before God rather than before people. The book takes it as its central idea: every part of life, from the morning watch to work, family, church and mission, is lived in God’s presence.

qa.question: Who is Coram Deo written for?
qa.answer: For every Christian: new believers taking their first steps, believers who hold the right beliefs but feel far from God or have grown dry, and those who have walked with God for decades and want to finish well. It was written with the fast-growing churches of Africa, Asia and Latin America in mind.

qa.question: How is each chapter laid out?
qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a key Scripture, teaches from the Bible with several passages woven through it, tells in depth the story of one man or woman of God from church history, and ends with questions for reflection and one practical step to take in the week ahead.

qa.question: Which men and women of God does Coram Deo tell about?
qa.answer: Witnesses from every century and continent: Augustine, Athanasius and Cyprian of North Africa, Polycarp, Martin Luther, Brother Lawrence, Susanna and John Wesley, George Müller, Hudson Taylor, Andrew Murray, Pandita Ramabai, Sadhu Sundar Singh, Bakht Singh, Watchman Nee, Wang Mingdao, Toyohiko Kagawa, Corrie ten Boom and Alexander Mackay of Uganda, among others. Many of their own books are free to read here in full.

qa.question: How does the book handle questions on which Christians disagree?
qa.answer: Where faithful Christians differ, on baptism in the Spirit, the gifts of the Spirit or the Sabbath for example, it presents the main positions fairly and then lands on the common ground all share. Where it takes a view of its own it says so plainly, and the Appendix explains how to tell primary beliefs from secondary and tertiary ones.

qa.question: Which Bible translation does it use?
qa.answer: Every Scripture is quoted from the Open Word Bible (OWB), Balanced edition, a new translation from the Hebrew and Greek that is dedicated to the public domain.

fields.title: Introduction: Before the Face of God
fields.body_html:
“My heart says to You what You have said: ‘Seek My face.’ So I will seek Your face, LORD.”

— Psalm 27:8 (OWB)

The hall in the German city of Worms was packed and hot. It was April 1521. At one end sat the most powerful man in Europe, the young Emperor Charles V, surrounded by princes, bishops and the envoys of the Pope. Torches were lit as the evening came on. On a table lay a pile of books. In front of the table stood a monk in a plain black habit, Martin Luther, a teacher of the Bible from the small town of Wittenberg.

The question put to him was simple. Were these books his? And would he take back what he had written in them?

Every face in that room was turned towards him. The emperor could have him outlawed. The Church could hand him over to be burned, as it had burned others before him. Many in the crowd wanted him to fail, and some wanted him dead. Luther had asked for a night to think. He had spent it in prayer. Now he gave his answer: unless he was shown from Scripture and plain reason that he was wrong, he could not take back what he had written. His conscience, he said, was held captive by the Word of God. To go against conscience was neither right nor safe. Then he asked God to help him.

What gave a frightened monk the courage to stand there? Luther had learned to ask one question above every other. Not, “What will these faces think of me?” but, “How do I stand before the face of God?”

Living before faces

You will probably never stand before an emperor. But you know what it is to live before faces.

Every one of us lives before someone’s face. We dress, speak and work with an eye on how others see us: our parents, our employers, our neighbours, our church, the crowd. A student lies awake before results day, imagining her father’s face. A young man takes a loan he cannot afford so that his wedding will look as fine as his cousin’s. A pastor measures his worth by the size of last Sunday’s crowd. A mother hides her tears from the women at the well, because a believer is supposed to be strong. Much of our worry comes from this. We long to be approved, and we fear being exposed.

Today the faces never go home. They follow us on the phone in our pocket, counting who has seen us, who has liked us, who has passed us by. We can spend a whole life performing for an audience that is never satisfied.

The Reformers of the sixteenth century had a phrase for a different way to live: coram Deo, “before the face of God.” Luther set it against living coram hominibus, “before people.” The question that matters most is not what others think of us, but how we stand before the One who sees everything, knows everything, and loves us still.

That is what this book is about. It is not mainly about religion, rules or even good habits. It is about a face, the face of God, and what it means to live every day in His presence.

The story of God’s face

Read the Bible from beginning to end, and you will find that it tells the story of God’s face.

In the beginning, the man and the woman walked with God in the garden. Nothing stood between them. Then sin entered, and the first thing they did was hide.

“Then they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden at the breezy time of the day, and the man and his wife hid from the LORD God among the trees of the garden.” (Genesis 3:8)

In Hebrew, they hid “from the face of the LORD God.” We have been hiding ever since: behind busyness, behind achievement, behind religion, behind shame. Yet notice who moves first. It is not the man who goes looking for God. It is God who comes looking for the man: “But the LORD God called to the man, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9). God has been asking that question ever since.

God never stopped seeking. Out of all the nations He drew near to one people, and to one man among them. “The LORD would speak with Moses face to face, the way a person talks with a friend” (Exodus 33:11). Moses wanted more. “Please, let me see Your glory” (Exodus 33:18), he prayed, and God showed him as much as a sinful man could bear.

God also gave His priests a blessing to speak over His people every day. It is a blessing about His face:

“May the LORD bless you and watch over you. May the LORD make His face shine toward you and show you favor. May the LORD lift up His face to look on you and grant you peace.” (Numbers 6:24-26)

Think about what that means. When a father’s face lights up as his child walks into the room, the child knows he is welcome. When a face turns away, he knows he is not. God wanted His people to know, morning by morning, that His face was turned toward them in favour.

David knew it. When enemies surrounded him, he did not first ask God for an army. He answered God’s invitation: “You have said, ‘Seek My face.’ So I will seek Your face, LORD” (Psalm 27:8).

Then, in the fullness of time, the face of God appeared among us. A baby was born in Bethlehem, and the eternal Son of God had a human face that could be seen and touched. “No one has ever seen God. The one and only Son, who is Himself God and is close beside the Father, has made Him known” (John 1:18). When Philip asked Jesus to show them the Father, Jesus answered, “To have seen Me is to have seen the Father” (John 14:9). Paul puts it this way:

“For the God who said, ‘Out of darkness light will shine,’ is the one who shone in our hearts, to bring the light of the knowledge of God’s glory, the glory seen in the face of Christ.” (2 Corinthians 4:6)

On the cross that face was struck, spat upon and crowned with thorns. Jesus took our hiding and our shame so that the hiding could end. Now, because of His blood, we are invited to come near: “So let us approach with hearts that are true, fully sure in our faith” (Hebrews 10:22). Through the Spirit, we are changed as we look at Him: “But all of us, our faces uncovered, look upon the Lord’s glory as in a mirror, and we are being changed into the same image we see, from glory to ever greater glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

And the story ends where it began, only better. In the last chapter of the Bible, God’s servants are in the city of God, and “they will look upon His face, and His name will be written on their foreheads” (Revelation 22:4). The garden was lost by hiding from His face. The city is entered by seeing it.

Created to know Him

You were made for this. Jesus said, “And eternal life is this: that they know You, the only true God, and the one You sent, Jesus Christ” (John 17:3). Not to know about Him. To know Him.

That difference matters. You can know a great deal about the president of your country: where he was born, what he believes, what he did last week. That does not mean he knows you, or would let you into his house. Many people know a great deal about God. They can recite the creed and argue about doctrine. But eternal life is not a set of facts in the head. It is a relationship with a Person.

God Himself says that this is the one thing worth boasting about:

“The wise must not boast about their wisdom, the strong must not boast about their strength, and the rich must not boast about their wealth. Instead, whoever boasts should boast of this: that they understand and know Me, that I am the LORD, who acts with loyal love, justice and righteousness on the earth.” (Jeremiah 9:23-24)

We only see ourselves rightly in the light of God’s face, and we only rest when we have found Him. John Calvin began his great teaching book by saying that true wisdom comes down to two things, the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves. More than a thousand years earlier, Augustine of North Africa looked back on his restless youth and confessed that God had made us for Himself, and that our hearts are restless until they rest in Him. You will hear both men in their own words in Chapter 2.

Why this book

Many Christians believe the right things but feel far from God. Some came to faith with great joy and have slowly grown dry. Others love God sincerely but have never been shown how to walk with Him day by day, or how faith reaches into marriage, work, money, suffering and church life. They have a Sunday faith and a Monday life, and the two hardly meet.

And many new believers in the fast-growing churches of Africa, Asia and Latin America have been given a Bible but few tools to help them grow. Some have been taught a gospel of quick blessing that leaves them confused when trouble comes. Others have been given long lists of rules, but never told that God wants them, not only their obedience.

This book is for all of them. It is for the new believer taking first steps, and for the one who has walked with God for fifty years and wants to finish well. It is written to be simple enough for the first and deep enough for the second.

The journey ahead

The book moves in five parts.

Part One, Foundations, asks who God is: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Everything depends on knowing whose face we seek. We will see how we are brought into relationship with Him through the cross of Christ and the gift of the Spirit.

Part Two, Walking with God, begins with love, the heart of everything, and then shows how we meet God daily: in His Word, in prayer, in the morning watch, in abiding in Christ and in the spiritual disciplines.

Part Three, Becoming Like Christ, explores how God makes us like His Son: discipleship, the life of the Kingdom in the Sermon on the Mount, faith, holiness, the healing of the soul, spiritual warfare and suffering.

Part Four, Living as God’s People, turns to our life together: marriage and singleness, raising children, work, the Church and its ministries, spiritual gifts and serving one another.

Part Five, Living for God’s Purposes, looks outward and forward: the Great Commission, stewardship, finishing well, and the hope of judgment, paradise and the new heavens and new earth. A final chapter gathers it all together.

Along the way you will meet men and women from every century and continent who learned to live before the face of God. You will meet Augustine and Athanasius of North Africa, and Polycarp, who would not deny his King. You will meet Luther and Calvin, Brother Lawrence in his kitchen and George Müller with his orphans. You will meet Hudson Taylor in China and Amy Carmichael in India, Andrew Murray in South Africa, and Festo Kivengere of Uganda, who learned to forgive the men who killed his friends. Each of them discovered that the presence of God is not a distant ideal but a daily reality. Many of their own books are in the Ochorus library, and you can read them in full.

How to read this book

Each chapter follows the same pattern. It opens with a passage of Scripture. It teaches from the Bible, quoting it often, so that you hear God’s voice and not only ours. It tells in some depth the story of one man or woman who lived what the chapter teaches. And it ends with questions for reflection and one practical step to take in the week ahead.

Read it with your Bible open. Look up the verses. Underline what speaks to you. Read it alone if you must, but better still, read it with others: with your husband or wife, with a friend, with a small group or a class of new believers. A chapter a week will carry a group through the book in about seven months.

Where faithful Christians disagree, this book says so honestly. On questions such as baptism in the Spirit, the gifts of the Spirit or the Sabbath, you will find the main views set out fairly, and then the common ground that all share. Where the book takes a view of its own, it says so plainly. The Appendix explains how to tell the beliefs that define the Christian faith from those where believers may differ, so that we can hold firm on the first and be gracious on the rest.

Do not rush. This is not a book to finish, but a life to begin.

Grace first

One more thing must be said before we begin, because everything else rests on it.

None of this is about earning God’s favour. You do not walk with God so that He will accept you; you walk with Him because, in Christ, He already has. “So now that we have been declared righteous by faith, we are at peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1).

That is why living before God’s face is not a burden but a release. The faces of the crowd are never satisfied. They praise us one day and forget us the next. But the face that matters most has already turned toward us in Christ, and it shines with welcome. Luther could stand before the emperor because he had first stood before God, a sinner forgiven and accepted. When you know how you stand with God, you are free from the tyranny of every other face.

The practices in these pages, reading the Word, praying, keeping the morning watch, fasting, serving, giving, are not ladders to climb into His presence. They are doors He has already opened, and He is waiting on the other side.

So come. Seek His face. And may the LORD make His face shine toward you.

Questions for reflection

  • Whose faces do you live before most? Whose approval do you find yourself seeking, and whose disapproval do you fear?
  • Read Genesis 3:8-9. In what ways do people hide from God today? In what ways have you hidden from Him?
  • What is the difference between knowing about God and knowing Him (John 17:3)? Which describes you better right now?
  • Which part of this book’s journey do you most need, and why?
  • Why does it matter that we walk with God because we are already accepted, and not in order to be accepted?

A step for this week

Each morning this week, before you look at your phone or speak to anyone, read Psalm 27:8 and pray it back to God in your own words: “Lord, You have said, ‘Seek My face.’ Today I will seek Your face.” Then, once during the day, when you notice yourself worrying about what someone thinks of you, stop and remind yourself quietly, “I am living before the face of God, and in Christ His face is turned toward me.”

study_questions.question: How is the Bible the story of God's face?
study_questions.answer: In Eden the man and woman hid "from the LORD God among the trees of the garden" (Genesis 3:8), yet God came seeking them. He spoke with Moses "face to face, the way a person talks with a friend" (Exodus 33:11), gave the priestly blessing "May the LORD make His face shine toward you" (Numbers 6:25), and finally showed His glory "in the face of Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6). The story ends with God's servants in the city of God: "they will look upon His face" (Revelation 22:4).

Practices such as Bible reading, prayer and fasting are not ladders to climb into His presence but doors He has already opened.

fields.title: Almighty God, Our Father
fields.body_html:
“The LORD is the God of all ages, the maker of the earth to its farthest edges. He does not tire or wear out, and His understanding is beyond all searching.”

— Isaiah 40:28 (OWB)

If we are going to live before the face of God, we need to know whose face it is. A child who is frightened of a strict father will hide from him. A child who knows her father is good will run to him. The same is true of us. How we picture God shapes how we pray, how we work, how we face trouble and how we treat other people.

A. W. Tozer, the American pastor, once wrote that what comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us. That is a bold claim, but it is true. If we think God is distant, we will stop praying. If we think He is harsh, we will serve Him out of fear. If we think He is small, we will trust Him only with small things. But if we come to know Him as He truly is, everything begins to change.

So this book begins where the Bible begins: with God Himself. In this chapter we will look at who God is, the names by which He makes Himself known, what He is like, and why He made us. In the next two chapters we will meet the Son and the Holy Spirit. Together these three chapters form the foundation for everything else, because all of the Christian life is a response to the God who has first shown us His face.

The God who simply is

The Bible’s first sentence does not argue for God. It simply announces Him: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). Before there was a sun, a sea, a mountain or a single human being, God was already there. He did not begin. He has no birthday. Moses prayed, “from the endless past to the endless future You are God” (Psalm 90:2).

This is what Christians mean when they say that God is eternal and self-existent. Everything else in the universe depends on something outside itself. A tree needs soil, rain and sunlight. A child needs parents, food and care. Even the stars burn for a time and then fade. But God depends on nothing. Nobody made Him, nobody keeps Him alive, and nobody can add to Him or take from Him.

When God called Moses at the burning bush, Moses asked what name he should give to the people of Israel. God answered, “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14). It is a mysterious name, but it tells us something wonderful. God does not say “I was” or “I will become”. He simply is. He is always present, always Himself, always full of life.

Think of what this means for an ordinary day. The God who meets you in the morning is not tired from yesterday. Isaiah says He “does not tire or wear out” (Isaiah 40:28). Mothers grow weary. Farmers grow weary. Pastors grow weary. God does not. When you come to Him at the end of a long day in the market or the office, you are not troubling Him. He is not running low.

The names that reveal Him

In the Bible, a name is more than a label. It tells you something about the person. God has given us several names for Himself, and each one opens a window onto His character.

Elohim is the name we meet in Genesis 1:1. It is the general Hebrew word for God, and it speaks of His strength and greatness as the Creator of all things. The God of the Bible is not one god among many local spirits. He is the maker of heaven and earth.

Yahweh is God’s personal, covenant name, the name He gave to Moses at the bush. It is linked to the words “I AM”. Many English Bibles, including the one quoted in this book, print it as “the LORD” in capital letters. When you see LORD written that way, remember that you are reading God’s own personal name. He is not a nameless force. He is someone who can be known and called upon.

El Shaddai means God Almighty. When Abram was ninety-nine years old and still waiting for the son God had promised, God appeared to him and said, “I am God Almighty. Live your life before Me and be wholehearted” (Genesis 17:1). Notice those words: live your life before Me. Here, at the very start of God’s story with His people, is the idea of this book. The Almighty God calls us to live in His presence, before His face.

Abba is an Aramaic word, the language Jesus spoke at home. It is the warm word a child uses for a father. Jesus used it when He prayed, and astonishingly He gives the same word to us. Paul writes, “You received the Spirit of adoption as children, and in the Spirit we call out, ‘Abba, Father!’” (Romans 8:15). The eternal I AM, the Almighty, the Creator of the stars, invites us to call Him Father. That is why this chapter is called “Almighty God, Our Father”. He is both. If we forget that He is Almighty, we will make Him small. If we forget that He is our Father, we will keep Him far away.

What God is like

Theologians use a set of words to describe the attributes of God, the qualities that belong to Him by nature. Some of these words sound difficult, but each one carries comfort for daily life.

Holiness. God is holy. That means He is utterly pure and utterly different from us. In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw a vision of God on His throne, and the angels around Him were crying, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies! All that fills the earth is His glory” (Isaiah 6:3). Isaiah did not feel proud to be there. He cried, “Woe to me! I am finished” (Isaiah 6:5). The closer we come to God, the more we see our own sin. Yet that same chapter shows God cleansing Isaiah and sending him out. Holiness is not God’s way of keeping us out. It is the fire that makes us clean.

Sovereignty. God rules over all things. Nothing happens outside His knowledge or beyond His control. Presidents, armies, droughts and diseases are not the final word. God is.

Omnipotence. This long word simply means that God is all-powerful. He can do everything that is consistent with His own good character. Nothing is too hard for Him.

Omniscience. God knows everything. David prayed, “LORD, You have looked deep into me, and You know me. Whether I sit down or get up, You know it; even from far away You grasp what I am thinking” (Psalm 139:1-2). That can be frightening if we are hiding something. But it is also deeply comforting. God knows the worry you have not told anyone. He knows the prayer you could not put into words. You never have to explain yourself to Him from the beginning.

Omnipresence. God is everywhere. David goes on, “Where could I go to get away from Your Spirit? Where could I run to escape Your presence?” (Psalm 139:7). Whether you are in a crowded city bus, a village hut, a hospital ward or a prison cell, God is there. This is the ground beneath the whole idea of coram Deo. We do not have to travel to find God’s face. We are already before it.

Immutability. God does not change. “I am the LORD, and I do not change” (Malachi 3:6). People change their minds. Governments change their laws. Prices in the market change every week. But God’s character and promises stay the same. The God who kept His word to Abraham will keep His word to you.

What God’s heart is like

Knowing God’s power is not enough. We also need to know His heart. The devil believes that God is powerful, but he does not trust Him. What we need to see is that God’s power is joined to perfect goodness.

When Moses asked to see God’s glory, God passed in front of him and proclaimed His own name: “The LORD, the LORD, a God of tender compassion and grace, slow to grow angry, rich in faithful love and in truth” (Exodus 34:6). This is God’s own description of Himself, and the rest of the Old Testament quotes it again and again. It tells us that He is:

  • Loving. John puts it in four short words: “God is love” (1 John 4:8). Love is not just something God does. It is who He is.
  • Faithful. He keeps His promises, even when we fail to keep ours.
  • Just. The same passage says He “will never acquit the guilty” (Exodus 34:7). God takes wrong seriously. He is not indifferent to the widow cheated of her land or the child who is abused.
  • Merciful. He does not give us what our sins deserve.
  • Good. Everything He does is right and kind, even when we cannot yet see how.
  • Patient. He is “slow to grow angry”. Think of how long He has waited for you, and how often He has given you another chance.

Some people find it hard to put God’s justice and His love together. But a judge who did not care about evil would not be loving. And a God who only punished, with no mercy, would leave us without hope. In the next chapter we will see how God’s justice and His love meet perfectly at the cross of Jesus Christ.

In the fourteenth century, in the English city of Norwich, a woman we know as Julian lay so ill that she and those around her expected her to die. During that illness she received a series of visions of God’s love, and after she recovered she spent many years living as an anchoress, a woman set apart for prayer in a small room attached to a church. She thought about those visions for the rest of her life. In one of them she saw something very small:

“Also in this He shewed me a little thing, the quantity of an hazel-nut, in the palm of my hand; and it was as round as a ball. I looked thereupon with eye of my understanding, and thought: What may this be? And it was answered generally thus: it is all that is made.”

Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love

She wondered how something so small and fragile could last. The answer came: “It lasteth, and ever shall [last] for that God loveth it.” Julian understood that the whole universe is held in being by the love of God. Years later, when she asked what the meaning of all her visions had been, she wrote that the answer was simple: “Love was His meaning.”

God the Creator

God’s greatness and goodness are not hidden. He has written them across the sky. “The heavens tell over and over how glorious God is; the vault of the sky makes known what His hands have made” (Psalm 19:1). A herdsman watching the stars over the savannah, a fisherman on a quiet lake at dawn, a child staring at an ant carrying a crumb: all of them are looking at the handiwork of God.

Paul says that creation makes God known so clearly that no one can claim ignorance: “what cannot be seen of God, His everlasting power and divine nature, has been in plain view, understood from the things He made” (Romans 1:20). Every sunrise is a sermon.

But the high point of creation is not the stars or the mountains. It is us. “So God created human beings in His image. In the image of God He created them; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). Of all the creatures God made, only human beings bear His image. That means we were made to reflect Him, to represent Him on earth, to rule the world with care on His behalf, and above all to know Him and be known by Him.

This has two great consequences. First, every human being has dignity. The street child, the elderly widow, the refugee, the person of another tribe or nation, the unborn child: each one bears God’s image. We cannot despise any of them without despising the One whose image they carry. Second, we were made for relationship. A fish was made for water. A bird was made for the air. You were made for God. Nothing else will fully satisfy you, because nothing else is the thing you were made for.

A restless heart finds its home

No one in the history of the Church has shown this more clearly than Augustine, the African bishop. He was born in AD 354 in Thagaste, a town in the Roman province of North Africa, in what is now Algeria. His mother, Monica, was a Christian who prayed for him constantly. His father was not a believer until near the end of his life.

Augustine was brilliant. He studied in Carthage, became a teacher of rhetoric, the art of public speaking, and rose to a respected post in the Italian city of Milan. But his heart was never at peace. He chased pleasure, lived with a woman he did not marry, followed one philosophy after another, and longed for fame. Each of these promised to satisfy him, and each one left him emptier than before. Later he looked back and wrote to God: “Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee.”

In the summer of 386, in a garden in Milan, the struggle came to a head. Augustine knew that the Christian faith was true, but he could not let go of his old life. He kept putting it off until tomorrow. Weeping under a fig tree, he heard what sounded like a child’s voice from a nearby house, chanting, “Take up and read; Take up and read.” He picked up the letters of Paul, opened them, and read the first words his eyes fell on, the call to put away drunkenness and immorality and to put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:13-14). In that moment, he later said, the darkness of doubt fled away. The next Easter he was baptised in Milan. A few years later he returned to Africa, and in time he became bishop of Hippo, a port city on the coast of what is now Algeria, where he served for over thirty years until his death in 430.

Augustine wrote many books, but the best loved is his Confessions, a long prayer in which he tells God the story of his life. Near its very beginning he writes the words for which he is most remembered:

“Thou awakest us to delight in Thy praise; for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.”

Augustine, Confessions

That sentence has travelled through sixteen centuries and across every continent because it describes every human being. The businessman with a full bank account and an empty heart is restless. The young woman who has moved to the city in search of a better life and finds only loneliness is restless. The religious person who keeps every rule but has never met God is restless. We were made for God, and until we rest in Him we will keep searching.

Augustine also shows us why the knowledge of God matters so much. He did not simply learn facts about God. He came to know God Himself, and that changed everything: his desires, his friendships, his use of his gifts and his whole life’s work. More than a thousand years later the Reformer John Calvin opened his great book, the Institutes of the Christian Religion, in the same spirit:

“Our wisdom, in so far as it ought to be deemed true and solid Wisdom, consists almost entirely of two parts: the knowledge of God and of ourselves.”

John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion

Calvin meant that the two belong together. When we see God as He is, we see ourselves truly: small, sinful, dependent, and yet loved. And when we honestly face our own need, we are driven back to God.

Why it matters

Some people think that learning about God’s attributes is only for scholars. But right knowledge of God shapes the whole of life. It shapes three things in particular.

It shapes our worship. We praise what we admire. When we see God’s holiness, power, wisdom and love, praise rises naturally. A church that sings without thinking about who God is will soon grow cold. A church that knows God will worship Him with both joy and awe.

It shapes our trust. When the rains fail, when the business collapses, when the doctor brings bad news, what we believe about God is tested. If God is sovereign, good and unchanging, then we can trust Him even when we do not understand Him. A small God produces anxious people. A great and loving God produces people who can sleep in a storm.

It shapes our obedience. We obey people we respect and trust. If God is holy, we will take sin seriously. If God is our loving Father, we will obey Him not as slaves afraid of punishment but as children who want to please the One who loves them.

God Himself tells us where real pride and joy should be found. Not in wisdom, strength or wealth, but in this: “whoever boasts should boast of this: that they understand and know Me, that I am the LORD, who acts with loyal love, justice and righteousness on the earth” (Jeremiah 9:24). The greatest thing a person can say is not “I am rich” or “I am clever” but “I know God”.

Living before the face of the Father

All of this brings us back to the central idea of this book. To live coram Deo, before the face of God, is not to live under the eye of a stern inspector. It is to live in the presence of the Almighty God who is also our Father. He sees everything, so we do not need to pretend. He is everywhere, so we are never alone. He is all-powerful, so nothing is beyond His help. He is holy, so we can trust Him to make us clean. And He is love, so we can come to Him without fear.

Picture a small child playing in a field while her father works nearby. She runs, falls, gets up, picks flowers, and every few minutes she looks up to make sure he is still there. He always is. She plays with freedom because she knows his eye is on her. That is the life God offers us: work, rest, family, trouble and joy, all lived under the loving gaze of our Father.

But there is a problem. We have seen that God is holy, and we are not. Like Adam and Eve in the garden, we have hidden from His face. How can sinful people come near a holy God and call Him Father? That is the question of the next chapter, where we meet Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, who came to bring us home.

Questions for reflection

  • Before reading this chapter, what came into your mind when you thought about God? Has anything in that picture changed?
  • Which of God’s names (Elohim, Yahweh, El Shaddai, Abba) means the most to you right now, and why?
  • Which attribute of God do you find most comforting? Which do you find most challenging?
  • Read Psalm 139:1-12 slowly. How does it feel to be known so completely by God?
  • Augustine said our hearts are restless until they rest in God. Where have you looked for rest apart from Him?
  • How might knowing God more truly change the way you work, worry or treat other people this week?

A step for this week

Each morning this week, before you check your phone or begin your work, read one part of Psalm 139 (verses 1-6 on the first day, 7-12 on the second, 13-18 on the third, and so on, beginning again when you reach the end). Choose one phrase that describes God and write it on a small piece of paper. Carry it with you through the day, in your pocket, on your desk or beside the cooking pot. Whenever you see it, pause for a few seconds and say to God, “You are here, and You are my Father.” At the end of the week, notice how often you remembered that you were living before His face.

study_questions.question: What does it mean that God is both Almighty and our Father?
study_questions.answer: God is eternal and self-existent, the great I AM who said, "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14), and He is God Almighty, El Shaddai. Yet through the Spirit He invites us to call Him Abba, the warm word a child uses for a father: "You received the Spirit of adoption as children, and in the Spirit we call out, 'Abba, Father!'" (Romans 8:15). If we forget that He is Almighty we make Him small; if we forget that He is our Father we keep Him far away.

study_questions.question: What are the main attributes of God?
study_questions.answer: The Bible shows that God is holy, sovereign, all-powerful (omnipotent), all-knowing (omniscient), everywhere present (omnipresent) and unchanging (immutable). He says, "I am the LORD, and I do not change" (Malachi 3:6). His character is love, faithfulness, justice, mercy, goodness and patience, as He proclaimed to Moses: "The LORD, the LORD, a God of tender compassion and grace, slow to grow angry, rich in faithful love and in truth" (Exodus 34:6).

study_questions.question: Why does knowing God correctly matter for everyday life?
study_questions.answer: Right knowledge of God shapes our worship, our trust and our obedience. A small God produces anxious people, while a great and loving God lets us trust Him even when we do not understand. God Himself says the one who boasts should boast "that they understand and know Me, that I am the LORD, who acts with loyal love, justice and righteousness on the earth" (Jeremiah 9:24). As Augustine discovered, we were made for God, and our hearts stay restless until they rest in Him.

fields.title: Jesus Christ, Our Redeemer
fields.body_html:
“For God’s love for the world was such that He gave His one and only Son, so that everyone who believes in Him may not perish but have eternal life.”

— John 3:16 (OWB)

In Chapter 2 we saw that God is holy, almighty and good, and that He made us to know Him as our Father. But we also saw the problem. We are not holy. Like the first man and woman in the garden, we have hidden from God’s face. How can people like us come near to a God like Him?

The answer is not a method or a set of rules. It is a person: Jesus Christ. In Him the face of God has come close to us, and through Him we are brought home. This chapter tells the story of how that happened, and what it means for you today.

Made for the garden

The Bible’s story begins in a garden. God placed the man and the woman in Eden, gave them good work to do, and walked with them. There was no shame, no fear and no distance. They lived openly before the face of God, and it was a joy, not a burden.

This is what we were made for. Not merely to exist, or to work, or to be religious, but to live in friendship with God. Every longing you have ever felt for a home where you are fully known and fully loved is an echo of Eden.

The fall: hiding from His face

Then everything went wrong. The serpent tempted the woman to doubt God’s word and God’s goodness. She ate the fruit God had forbidden, gave some to her husband, and he ate too. Notice what happened next: “Then they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden at the breezy time of the day, and the man and his wife hid from the LORD God among the trees of the garden” (Genesis 3:8).

The people who had walked with God now hid from Him. When God called, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9), Adam answered, “I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid” (Genesis 3:10). Fear, shame and blame entered the world. Adam blamed the woman. The woman blamed the serpent. Relationships with God, with one another and with the earth itself were broken.

This is what the Bible calls sin. Sin is not just breaking rules. It is turning away from God’s face to go our own way. Isaiah puts it simply: “Every one of us has wandered off like sheep; we have each turned aside down our own path” (Isaiah 53:6). We see the results everywhere: in broken marriages, corrupt governments, tribal hatred, greed in the market, and the quiet selfishness of our own hearts. Worst of all, sin separates us from God, the source of life. Death came into the world with it (Romans 5:12).

The promise of a Redeemer

Yet even in that dark moment, God made a promise. Speaking to the serpent, He said that a child of the woman would one day crush it: “He will strike your head, and you will strike his heel” (Genesis 3:15). Christians have long seen this as the first announcement of the gospel. One day a Redeemer would come from the human family, and in defeating the enemy He would Himself be wounded.

The rest of the Old Testament builds on that promise. God called Abraham and promised that through his family all nations would be blessed. He rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt through the blood of the Passover lamb. He promised David a son whose kingdom would never end. Isaiah spoke of a child called Immanuel, a name that means God with us (Isaiah 7:14). And Isaiah described a suffering Servant who would carry the sins of others: “it was for our rebellions that He was pierced through, for our guilt that He was crushed. On Him fell the discipline that won our peace, and His welts have brought us healing” (Isaiah 53:5).

For centuries God’s people waited. Then, “when the time God had set was complete, God sent out His Son” (Galatians 4:4).

The Word became flesh

John’s Gospel opens with words that echo Genesis: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The Word is the eternal Son of God, the second person of the Trinity. He did not begin to exist in Bethlehem. He has always been with the Father, sharing His glory. Then John writes the most astonishing sentence ever written: “The Word became flesh and made His home among us” (John 1:14).

This is what Christians call the incarnation, which means “coming in the flesh”. God the Son became a real human being. He was born as a baby, learned to walk and talk, worked with His hands as a builder, grew tired and hungry, wept at a friend’s grave and felt the pain of nails.

Paul describes this in his letter to the Philippians. Christ, “being in the form of God, did not treat being equal with God as something to exploit for Himself. Rather, He emptied Himself, taking on the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6-7). What did He empty Himself of? Not His deity. He never stopped being God. He laid aside the privileges and glory of heaven, and chose the life of a servant. He was fully God and fully man, at the same time, in one person.

Why does this matter? Because only one who is truly God can save us, and only one who is truly human can stand in our place. If Jesus were only a good man, He could not carry the sins of the world. If He were only God dressed up as a man, He could not die our death. He is both, and so He is the bridge between God and us.

Born of a virgin, the sinless second Adam

The Bible tells us how the Son came into the world. The angel Gabriel was sent to a young woman in Nazareth named Mary. When she asked how she could have a child when she had never been with a man, the angel answered, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will cover you with its shadow. So the child to be born will be holy, and will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Matthew sees in this the fulfilment of Isaiah’s promise: “See, the virgin will become pregnant and have a son, and people will call Him Immanuel” (Matthew 1:23).

Paul helps us see why this matters. He compares Adam and Christ. Adam was the head of the human race, and through him sin and death spread to all. Christ came as the head of a new humanity: “For the disobedience of one man made the many sinners, and in the same way the obedience of the one will make the many righteous” (Romans 5:19). Paul even calls Jesus “the last Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:45). Where the first Adam fell, the second Adam stood firm.

So Jesus was fully human, yet without sin. The letter to the Hebrews says He “has been put to the test in every way, as we are, but without sinning” (Hebrews 4:15). He knows what temptation feels like. He knows hunger, loneliness, betrayal and grief. But He never once turned from His Father’s face.

Christians have explained the link between the virgin birth and Jesus’ sinlessness in slightly different ways. Some point to the absence of a human father: Jesus did not come into the world simply as one more child in Adam’s line. Others put the weight on the Holy Spirit’s sanctifying work in His conception, the Spirit coming upon Mary so that the child would be holy. Both views agree on what matters most. Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of Mary, truly one of us and yet free from sin, so that He could be the Saviour we need.

Athanasius: standing for the Son

In the fourth century, the Church faced a crisis over exactly this question: who is Jesus? A popular teacher in Alexandria, Egypt, named Arius taught that the Son of God was a created being, very great but not truly God. His ideas spread quickly. They were even said to have been put into simple songs that sailors, traders and dock workers sang around the Mediterranean.

Standing against him was a young man from the same city, Athanasius. Born around the end of the third century, he grew up in Alexandria, one of the great cities of Africa, and served as an assistant to its bishop, Alexander. In 325 he went with Alexander to the Council of Nicaea, where church leaders from across the empire confessed that the Son is truly God, of one being with the Father. A few years later Athanasius himself became bishop of Alexandria.

The struggle was far from over. Emperors changed their minds, and powerful men took Arius’s side. Athanasius was driven from his city into exile five times. He spent years hiding, travelling and writing, sometimes sheltered by the desert monks of Egypt. People came to speak of “Athanasius against the world”. He would not give way, because he knew that if Jesus is not truly God, then we are not truly saved.

Athanasius wrote a short book, On the Incarnation, that is still read today. In it he explained why the eternal Word took a human body. Humanity had turned from God and was sliding into ruin and death. The Word came, not because He had been far away, for He fills all creation, but to show His loving-kindness and to rescue us. He used a picture everyone in his day could understand:

“And like as when a great king has entered into some large city and taken up his abode in one of the houses there, such city is at all events held worthy of high honour, nor does any enemy or bandit any longer descend upon it and subject it; but, on the contrary, it is thought entitled to all care, because of the king’s having taken up his residence in a single house there: so, too, has it been with the Monarch of all.”

Athanasius, On the Incarnation

Imagine a poor neighbourhood where a king comes to live. The thieves stay away. The roads are repaired. Everyone in that place is honoured because the king lives among them. Athanasius said that is what happened when the Son of God took on our humanity. He came to live in our “city”, and the enemy’s hold over us was broken.

Athanasius died in 373, back in Alexandria. Within a few years, at the Council of Constantinople in 381, the Church reaffirmed the faith he had defended. When you recite the Nicene Creed, or simply confess that Jesus is Lord and God, you are standing where this African bishop stood.

The cross: He took our place

Jesus lived a perfect life, taught with authority, healed the sick and welcomed sinners. Then He went willingly to the cross. Why?

The Bible’s answer is that He died in our place. “Christ had never known sin, yet for our sake God made Him to be sin, so that, united with Him, we might become God’s righteousness” (2 Corinthians 5:21). This is called substitution: Jesus stood where we should have stood and received what we deserved. It is also called atonement, which means making us “at one” with God again by dealing with our sin. “Christ died for our sins, in keeping with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3).

Remember from Chapter 2 that God is both just and loving. At the cross both are fully shown. God did not pretend that sin did not matter. The price was paid in full. But He paid it Himself, in the person of His Son. “But God proves how much He loves us: Christ died for us when we were still sinners” (Romans 5:8). Not when we were good. When we were still sinners.

In the eleventh century, Anselm, an Italian-born monk who became archbishop of Canterbury in England, wrote a book called Cur Deus Homo, which means “Why God Became Man”. In it he and his student Boso talk through why only Jesus could save us. Humanity owed a debt to God that only a human being ought to pay, yet only God was able to pay it. Anselm concludes:

“If it be necessary, therefore, as it appears, that the heavenly kingdom be made up of men, and this cannot be effected unless the aforesaid satisfaction be made, which none but God can make and none but man ought to make, it is necessary for the God-man to make it.”

Anselm of Canterbury, Proslogium, Monologium and Cur Deus Homo

Here again we see why the incarnation and the cross belong together. The Son became man so that He could die for us.

Risen and ascended

The story does not end at the tomb. On the third day, God raised Jesus from the dead. “But as it is, Christ has been raised from the dead: He is the firstfruits of those who have died” (1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstfruits are the first part of the harvest, the promise that the rest is coming. Because Jesus rose, all who belong to Him will rise too.

The resurrection is God’s public declaration that the price has been paid and that sin and death have been defeated. Forty days later Jesus ascended to heaven, where He reigns at the Father’s right hand. God has “freely given Him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). One day every knee will bow to Him.

How to receive Him

All this is wonderful news, but news must be received. Jesus began His preaching with these words: “Repent, and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15).

Repentance means turning around. It is more than feeling sorry. It means turning away from sin and from running our own lives, and turning towards God.

Faith means trusting Christ alone. Not Christ plus our good works, our church attendance or our family background. Faith is like stepping into a boat: you stop trusting your own swimming and put your whole weight on the boat. Paul writes, “If you declare with your lips that Jesus is Lord, and in your heart believe that God raised Him from the dead, then you will be saved” (Romans 10:9). And he makes clear that salvation is a gift: “For it is by this grace that you have been saved, through faith. None of this comes from you; it is God’s gift” (Ephesians 2:8).

When we believe, God does three great things for us:

  • Justification. God declares us righteous, not because we are good, but because Christ’s righteousness is counted as ours.
  • Regeneration. The Holy Spirit gives us new life. Jesus called this being “born from above” (John 3:7), and we will look at it more in Chapter 4.
  • Union with Christ. We are joined to Jesus, so that what is His becomes ours.

Martin Luther, the German Reformer, rediscovered the joy of justification by faith after years of trying to earn God’s favour as a monk. In his small book Concerning Christian Liberty he described union with Christ as a marriage, in which the bride and bridegroom share everything:

“Christ is full of grace, life, and salvation; the soul is full of sin, death, and condemnation. Let faith step in, and then sin, death, and hell will belong to Christ, and grace, life, and salvation to the soul.”

Martin Luther, First Principles of the Reformation

If you have never received Christ, you can do so now. Tell God honestly that you have sinned and turned from His face. Thank Him that Jesus died for you and rose again. Ask Him to forgive you, and put your trust in Jesus as your Saviour and Lord. Then tell another Christian, and find a church where you can grow.

If you have trusted Christ, you can be sure you belong to Him. John wrote his letter “so that you may know that you have eternal life—you who believe in the name of the Son of God” (1 John 5:13). Your assurance rests not on your feelings, which change, but on God’s promise, which does not.

Adopted into God’s family

Salvation is not only rescue from something. It is welcome into something. “But to all who received Him, who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). God does not merely forgive us and send us away. He brings us into His family.

In the Roman world, an adopted son received his new father’s name and full rights as heir. Paul uses that picture: “So you are no longer a slave but a child, and if you are a child, then you are also an heir, made so by God” (Galatians 4:7). Many people carry wounds from their earthly fathers, from absence, harshness or neglect. In Christ, you have a Father who will never leave you.

This also changes who we belong to. “You were bought, and a price was paid for you. So bring glory to God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20). Your body, time, money, gifts and relationships are no longer simply your own. You belong to the One who paid for you with His own blood. That is not a heavy chain. It is the deepest security a person can know.

Think about what this means for daily life coram Deo. You no longer stand before God’s face as a criminal before a judge, or as a servant afraid of his master. You stand as a beloved child before a Father. You can wake each morning, go to work, sit with your family and face trouble knowing that you are accepted, forgiven and loved.

Sent out as His family

Before Jesus returned to the Father, He gathered His followers and gave them a task: “Go, then, and make disciples of all the nations: baptize them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teach them to keep everything I have commanded you. And remember this: I Myself am with you every day, until the close of the age” (Matthew 28:19-20).

The family of God is not a closed club. The redeemed are sent to bring others home. From a small group in Jerusalem, the good news has travelled to every continent, and today some of the fastest-growing churches in the world are in Africa, Asia and Latin America.

But Jesus also knew that His followers could not do this in their own strength. So He told them to wait for the gift His Father had promised. That gift is the Holy Spirit, and He is the subject of Chapter 4.

Questions for reflection

  • Adam and Eve hid from God after they sinned. In what ways do people, including you, still hide from God today?
  • Why does it matter that Jesus is both fully God and fully man? What would we lose if He were only one or the other?
  • Athanasius would not give way even when emperors and church leaders were against him. What truths about Jesus are under pressure where you live?
  • Read 2 Corinthians 5:21 slowly. Put it into your own words, using “I” and “me”.
  • Have you repented and put your trust in Christ alone? If so, what gives you assurance?
  • How might knowing that you are an adopted child of God change the way you think about yourself this week?

A step for this week

Write out your own short testimony, no more than one page, in three parts: what your life was like before you knew Christ (or, if you grew up in the faith, when the gospel became real to you), how you came to trust Him, and what difference He makes now. Use simple words, as if you were telling a neighbour over a cup of tea. Then, before the week ends, read it aloud to one other Christian, and thank God together for bringing you out of hiding and into His family.

study_questions.question: Why did Jesus have to be both fully God and fully man?
study_questions.answer: Only one who is truly God can save us, and only one who is truly human can stand in our place. The eternal Word "became flesh and made His home among us" (John 1:14); He emptied Himself of His privileges, not His deity. As Anselm put it, the debt of sin is one that none but God can pay and none but man ought to pay, so it was necessary for the God-man to pay it.

study_questions.question: What happened on the cross, according to the Bible?
study_questions.answer: Jesus died in our place, taking the penalty our sins deserved and making us at one with God again. "Christ had never known sin, yet for our sake God made Him to be sin, so that, united with Him, we might become God's righteousness" (2 Corinthians 5:21). At the cross God's justice and love meet: "But God proves how much He loves us: Christ died for us when we were still sinners" (Romans 5:8).

study_questions.question: How do I receive Jesus Christ and know that I am saved?
study_questions.answer: Jesus called people to "Repent, and believe in the gospel" (Mark 1:15): turn from sin and trust Christ alone, not your own good works. "If you declare with your lips that Jesus is Lord, and in your heart believe that God raised Him from the dead, then you will be saved" (Romans 10:9). Your assurance rests on God's promise, not your feelings, for John wrote "so that you may know that you have eternal life" (1 John 5:13).

fields.title: The Holy Spirit, Our Helper
fields.body_html:
“I will ask the Father, and in answer He will give you another Advocate, who will be with you forever.”

— John 14:16 (OWB)

Chapter 3 ended on a mountain in Galilee. The risen Jesus gave His followers an enormous task: to make disciples of all the nations. Think of who they were. Fishermen, a former tax collector, a handful of ordinary men and women who had run away on the night of His arrest. How could people like that carry the gospel to the ends of the earth?

Jesus did not expect them to do it alone. Before He ascended, “He charged them not to go away from Jerusalem but to wait there for what the Father had promised” (Acts 1:4). Then He told them what that promise was: “But when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, you will receive power, and you will bear witness to Me in Jerusalem, through all Judea and Samaria, and out to the farthest end of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

This chapter is about that promise. We have met God the Father, who made us for Himself, and God the Son, who came to bring us home. Now we meet God the Holy Spirit, who lives within us and makes the presence of God a daily reality. If coram Deo means living before the face of God, the Holy Spirit is the One who brings that face near.

Who the Holy Spirit is

Many Christians are less sure about the Holy Spirit than about the Father and the Son. Some think of Him as a power, like electricity, or a feeling that comes in a lively church service. But the Bible shows that the Holy Spirit is a person, and that He is fully God.

He is a person. Jesus never called the Spirit “it”. He said, “the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father is going to send in My name, is the one who will teach you everything and remind you of all I have said to you” (John 14:26). Only a person can teach and remind. The Spirit also speaks, guides, prays for us and chooses how to give His gifts. He can even be hurt: “do not grieve God’s Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 4:30). You cannot grieve a force. You can only grieve someone who loves you.

The word Jesus used, translated “Advocate” in our Bible and “Helper” or “Comforter” in others, describes someone called alongside to help: a friend who stands beside you, speaks up for you and strengthens you. Jesus said the Spirit would be “another” Advocate. In other words, the Spirit would be to the disciples what Jesus Himself had been: a constant companion and guide.

He is fully God. When Ananias lied about the money from a field he had sold, Peter asked him, “why did Satan fill your heart, to make you lie to the Holy Spirit” (Acts 5:3). A moment later he said, “It is not human beings you have lied to, but God” (Acts 5:4). Lying to the Spirit is lying to God. The Spirit shares the work of God: He was present at creation, He gives life, He knows the deep things of God. That is why Jesus commanded us to baptise “into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). One name, three persons. This is the mystery of the Trinity, and the Holy Spirit is fully part of it.

The American evangelist D. L. Moody, whom we will meet properly later in this chapter, pressed this point on his hearers in his little book Secret Power:

“I want to call attention to this fact that whenever Christ spoke of the Holy Ghost He spoke of Him as a person, not a mere influence; and if we want to honor the Holy Ghost, let us bear in mind that He is one of the Trinity, a personality of the Godhead.”

D. L. Moody, Secret Power

What the Spirit does

The Bible describes many works of the Spirit. Four are especially important at the start of the Christian life.

He convicts. Jesus said that when the Spirit came, “He will show the world to be in the wrong about sin, about righteousness and about judgment” (John 16:8). No preacher can make a person see their need of Christ. Only the Spirit can open blind eyes. When a hard-hearted neighbour suddenly begins to ask about God, or a sermon you have heard many times pierces your heart, that is the Spirit at work.

He gives new birth. Jesus told Nicodemus, “unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, they cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). We saw in Chapter 3 that when we believe, God gives us new life. The Spirit is the One who does it. Paul says God “saved us through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).

He dwells within. The Spirit does not visit believers now and then. He makes His home in them. “If anyone lacks the Spirit of Christ, that person is not His” (Romans 8:9). Every true Christian, however young in the faith or weak they feel, has the Holy Spirit living within.

He seals. Paul writes, “you believed; and in Him you were sealed with the Holy Spirit God had promised. The Spirit is the down payment on our inheritance” (Ephesians 1:13-14). In the ancient world a seal on a letter or a sack of grain showed who owned it and kept it safe. A down payment, like a deposit on a piece of land, is a guarantee that the full payment will follow. The Spirit within you is God’s mark of ownership and His promise that He will bring you all the way home.

Spirit, soul and body

How does the Spirit of God relate to us on the inside? Here Christians have found different ways of describing the same truth.

Watchman Nee was one of the most influential Chinese Christian leaders of the twentieth century. Born in 1903, he came to faith in Fuzhou in 1920, around the age of seventeen, during meetings led by the evangelist Dora Yu. He went on to plant many churches across China and wrote books that are still read in many languages, including The Spiritual Man and The Normal Christian Life. After the Communist government came to power he was arrested in 1952, and he spent the last twenty years of his life in prison and labour camps, where he died in 1972.

Nee taught that a human being has three parts. The body relates to the physical world. The soul, which includes the mind, emotions and will, relates to ourselves and others. The spirit is the deepest part of us, the part made to relate to God. He drew this from verses like Paul’s prayer: “may your spirit, soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:23). When we are born again, Nee said, the Holy Spirit comes to dwell in our human spirit and join with it. Paul writes, “anyone who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with Him” (1 Corinthians 6:17), and “The Spirit Himself joins our own spirit in testifying that we are God’s children” (Romans 8:16). From that inner place, the Spirit then works outward, renewing our soul and finally our body.

Many theologians see it differently. They believe the Bible describes two parts rather than three: a body and an inner self, which Scripture sometimes calls the soul and sometimes the spirit, using the words almost interchangeably. Faithful Christians hold both views. This book offers Nee’s three-part picture as a helpful lens rather than a test of faith, and we will return to it in Chapter 15 when we think about the healing of the soul. What both views agree on is the main thing: God’s Spirit lives in the deepest part of every believer.

Nee loved to remind Christians how great a treasure they carry:

“Has it really come home to you that wherever you go, you carry with you the Holy Spirit of God? You do not just carry your Bible with you, or even much good teaching about God, but God Himself.”

Watchman Nee, The Normal Christian Life

Baptism in the Spirit: three views

Few subjects have caused more discussion among Christians than the baptism in the Holy Spirit. Jesus promised it: “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit before many days have passed” (Acts 1:5). But what is it, and when does it happen? Here are the three main views, presented as fairly as we can.

At conversion. Many evangelical, Reformed and Baptist Christians believe that baptism in the Spirit happens once, when a person first believes. They point to Paul: “all of us were baptized in one Spirit into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). Paul says “all of us”, not only some. On this view every Christian has already been baptised in the Spirit, and later experiences of power are better described as being filled again.

As a later experience. Pentecostal Christians, and many in the older Holiness tradition, believe the baptism in the Spirit is a distinct experience, usually after conversion, which gives power for witness and service. They point to the disciples, who already believed in Jesus before Pentecost, and to the believers in Samaria and Ephesus, who received the Spirit in a fresh way after they had come to faith (Acts 8 and Acts 19). Many Pentecostals also teach that speaking in tongues usually accompanies this experience.

Both. Many others, including many in charismatic and renewal movements, hold a middle view. They believe the Spirit is fully given at conversion, but that believers may also have later, powerful experiences of the Spirit coming upon them, sometimes called a release or overflow of the Spirit already within. Moody himself spoke this way. In Secret Power he wrote, “The Holy Spirit dwelling in us, is one thing; I think this is clearly brought out in Scripture; and the Holy Spirit upon us for service, is another thing.”

These are real differences, and they matter to those who hold them. They are explained further in the Appendix. But it is important to notice how much all three views share.

The common ground: keep on being filled

Every tradition agrees on this: every believer needs to be continually filled with the Spirit and to rely on Him for everything. Paul writes, “Do not get drunk on wine, for that is reckless, wasteful living. Instead, let the Spirit fill you” (Ephesians 5:18). The form of the command in Paul’s language suggests something ongoing: keep on being filled. It is not a single event to look back on but a daily dependence.

We see this in the book of Acts. The disciples were filled with the Spirit at Pentecost. A few weeks later, after praying together under threat of persecution, “every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit, and they went on proclaiming God’s word fearlessly” (Acts 4:31). The same people, filled again.

Moody put it in a homely picture:

“The fact is, we are leaky vessels, and we have to keep right under the fountain all the time to keep full of Christ, and so have a fresh supply.”

D. L. Moody, Secret Power

Think of a clay water pot with a small crack. It may be full in the morning, but by evening it is half empty. The answer is not to throw it away, but to keep returning it to the well. So whatever view you hold on the baptism in the Spirit, the daily need is the same: come back to the fountain, ask to be filled, and depend on Him.

D. L. Moody: a man filled for service

Dwight Lyman Moody was born in 1837 in Northfield, Massachusetts. His father died when he was a small child, and the family was poor. He left school early, and as a young man he worked in his uncle’s shoe shop in Boston. There, in 1855, his Sunday school teacher, Edward Kimball, came into the shop and spoke to him about Christ, and Moody gave his life to the Lord.

Moody moved to Chicago, where he sold shoes successfully but soon poured his energy into reaching poor children. His Sunday school grew to many hundreds. He became known as a tireless worker, and later as a popular preacher. Yet by 1871 he knew something was missing. Two women in his meetings told him that they were praying for him to receive the power of the Spirit. At first he did not see why he needed it. Before long he became hungry. He began to pray with them, crying out to God for power.

In October 1871 the Great Chicago Fire destroyed much of the city, including Moody’s church and his home. Soon afterwards, while he was in New York raising money to rebuild, the answer came. Walking along a street in the city, Moody was overwhelmed by a sense of God’s presence and love, so strong that he went to a friend’s house to be alone with God. He spoke of it only rarely afterwards, but he said that from then on, though he preached the same sermons, far more people came to Christ.

In 1873 Moody sailed for Britain with the singer Ira Sankey, and for two years they held meetings that drew enormous crowds in Scotland, Ireland and England. Back in America he preached to many thousands more, and he founded schools in Northfield and a Bible institute in Chicago to train ordinary men and women for ministry. He died in 1899.

Moody never became a scholar, and he never claimed to be anything special. That is exactly the point. The Spirit took an uneducated shoe salesman and made him a witness to two continents. What He did for Moody, in his own way and measure, He longs to do for every believer who will depend on Him.

Empowered to live a holy life

The Spirit’s power is not only for preaching to crowds. It is first of all for living a holy life in an ordinary home, workplace and village.

Every Christian knows the struggle Paul describes: “For the flesh sets its desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). The “flesh” here does not mean our physical bodies. It means our old, self-centred nature, which pulls us towards anger, lust, jealousy and pride. We cannot defeat it by willpower alone. But Paul gives a promise: “walk by the Spirit, and you will never carry out what the flesh desires” (Galatians 5:16). And again: “if by the Spirit you keep putting the body’s practices to death, you will live” (Romans 8:13).

As the Spirit works in us, He produces fruit: “the fruit the Spirit produces is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23). Notice that it is fruit, not a list of achievements. A mango tree does not strain to produce mangoes. It stays rooted, receives rain and sunshine, and the fruit grows in season. In the same way, as we stay close to God, the Spirit grows Christlike character in us. We will see more of this in Chapter 9 and Chapter 14.

Empowered for the Great Commission

The Spirit also empowers us to witness. On the day of Pentecost the believers were gathered in one place when “a sound came out of heaven, like a mighty wind sweeping through” (Acts 2:2). Then “Every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in other languages as the Spirit gave them the words to say” (Acts 2:4). That same day Peter, who had denied Jesus only weeks before, preached boldly, and about three thousand people believed.

This fulfilled the promise of the prophet Joel, that God would “pour out My Spirit upon all people” (Joel 2:28): sons and daughters, young and old, servants and masters. The Spirit is not reserved for pastors and missionaries. He is given to the market trader, the nurse, the student and the grandmother alike.

The Spirit also gives gifts to every believer for the good of the Church and its mission. “Gifts are given out in different ways, but it is the same Spirit who gives them” (1 Corinthians 12:4). Some receive wisdom, some faith, some gifts of healing, some prophecy, some tongues and their interpretation. “Each person is given a way in which the Spirit is openly at work, and it is given for the good of all” (1 Corinthians 12:7). We will look at the gifts more fully in Chapter 23. For now, it is enough to know that you have been equipped. The Spirit who sent the apostles out to the ends of the earth also sends you across the street, into your office and into your family with good news.

Walking in step with the Spirit

How, then, do we live with the Spirit day by day? Paul gives a beautiful picture: “Since our life comes from the Spirit, let us also follow the Spirit’s lead in each step we take” (Galatians 5:25). Think of walking beside a friend on a long road. You match your pace to theirs. You listen when they speak. You turn when they turn.

Walking with the Spirit is like that. It means beginning the day by asking Him to fill you. It means listening for His quiet prompting: to apologise, to give, to speak to someone, or to keep silent. It means confessing sin quickly when you grieve Him, rather than letting distance grow. It means depending on Him in small things, like a hard conversation or a difficult task at work, and not only in great crises. This is what it means to live coram Deo in practice: the Spirit within us makes God’s face near in every hour.

And the first fruit the Spirit grows in us is love. Paul names it at the head of the list, and Jesus called love the mark by which the world would recognise His disciples. That is where Part Two of this book begins, in Chapter 5.

Questions for reflection

  • Before reading this chapter, did you think of the Holy Spirit more as a person or as a power? What difference does it make that He is a person who can be grieved?
  • Which of the Spirit’s works (convicting, giving new birth, dwelling within, sealing) are you most thankful for today?
  • How do you find Watchman Nee’s picture of spirit, soul and body helpful? Where do you see the Spirit renewing your mind, emotions or will?
  • What view of the baptism in the Spirit have you been taught? How does the common ground, being continually filled, apply to you whatever your view?
  • Moody said we are “leaky vessels”. What drains your spiritual strength, and how can you return to the fountain more often?
  • Which part of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23) do you most need Him to grow in you right now?

A step for this week

Each morning this week, before you leave your home or start your work, pray a simple prayer: “Holy Spirit, fill me today. Help me to walk in step with You.” Then choose one part of the fruit of the Spirit to focus on for that day (love on the first day, joy on the second, and so on through the list). In the evening, take five minutes to look back. Where did you sense the Spirit’s prompting? Where did you resist Him? Thank Him for His help, confess where you fell short, and ask to be filled again tomorrow.

study_questions.question: Is the Holy Spirit a person or a force?
study_questions.answer: The Holy Spirit is a person and fully God, not an impersonal power. Jesus spoke of Him as "the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father is going to send in My name" who "will teach you everything" (John 14:26), and Scripture warns, "do not grieve God's Holy Spirit" (Ephesians 4:30). You cannot grieve a force; you can only grieve someone who loves you. When Ananias lied to the Spirit, Peter said, "It is not human beings you have lied to, but God" (Acts 5:4).

study_questions.question: What are the different views on the baptism in the Holy Spirit?
study_questions.answer: Some Christians believe it happens once at conversion, since "all of us were baptized in one Spirit into one body" (1 Corinthians 12:13). Others, including Pentecostals, see it as a distinct later experience of power for witness, and many hold that the Spirit is fully given at conversion but may later come upon believers in fresh power. All agree on the common ground: every believer needs to keep on being filled, as Paul commands, "let the Spirit fill you" (Ephesians 5:18).

study_questions.question: How can I walk with the Holy Spirit every day?
study_questions.answer: Walking with the Spirit means asking Him to fill you each day, listening for His prompting, confessing sin quickly and depending on Him in small things as well as great. Paul writes, "Since our life comes from the Spirit, let us also follow the Spirit's lead in each step we take" (Galatians 5:25). As we stay close to Him, He grows His fruit in us: "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control" (Galatians 5:22-23).

fields.title: Love: The Mark of a Christian
fields.body_html:
“I am giving you a new commandment: love one another. In the same way that I have loved you, you too must love one another.”

— John 13:34 (OWB)

In the first three chapters we met the God whose face we seek: the Father who made us for Himself, the Son who came to bring us home, and the Holy Spirit who lives within us. Now we begin Part Two of this book, which asks how we walk with this God day by day. In the coming chapters we will look at Scripture, prayer, the morning watch, abiding in Christ and the spiritual disciplines.

But before any of those, we must speak about love. This order is deliberate. If we begin with practices, we may turn them into a new set of rules: read this much, pray this long, fast this often. Many sincere Christians have done exactly that, and they have grown tired, proud or discouraged. If we begin with love, everything else finds its proper place.

Why love comes first

One day a teacher of the law asked Jesus which commandment was the greatest. It was a test, and the scholars of the day had long debated the answer.
