Jesus replied without hesitation: “‘Love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind.’ This command is the great one, the first of all. A second command is of the same kind: ‘Love your neighbor as you love yourself.’ The whole of the law, and the prophets as well, hangs on these two commands” (Matthew 22:37-40).

Picture a coat hanging on a hook. Take away the hook and the coat falls to the floor. Jesus says that the whole of God’s law hangs on love. Every command about worship, honesty, purity, generosity and justice is a way of loving God or loving people. Without love, obedience becomes a heap of rules lying on the ground.

The same is true of the habits we will explore in the next chapters. Reading the Bible, praying, rising early to meet God, fasting and serving are not ways of earning God’s love. We already have it, as we saw in Chapter 3. They are ways of loving God back and of receiving more of His love. A husband who spends time with his wife is not paying for the right to be married. He is enjoying the marriage. So it is with us and God.

Paul makes the same point in his famous chapter on love. “I may be able to prophesy, and know every mystery and everything there is to know; I may have all the faith there is, enough to move mountains; but if I do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2). Great gifts, deep knowledge and impressive faith count for nothing without love. And when everything else passes away, love remains: “three things last: faith, hope and love. And of these three, the greatest is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13).

God’s love is the source of ours

Where does this love come from? Not from inside us. Our natural love is weak, selfish and easily worn out. We love those who love us, and we grow cold towards those who hurt us. The love God asks for must come from God Himself.

John writes, “This is where love is found: not in our having loved God, but in His loving us and sending His Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 4:10). And then, in one short sentence: “We love because He loved us first” (1 John 4:19).

Think of the moon. It has no light of its own. It shines only because it reflects the sun. When the earth comes between them, the moon goes dark. We are like that. We can only love as we stand in the light of God’s love for us. When we drift away from Him, our love grows dim. When we return to Him, it shines again.

This is why living coram Deo, before the face of God, is the key to a life of love. The more we know His face turned towards us in kindness, the more His love flows through us. Paul says, “through the Spirit His love has flooded our hearts” (Romans 5:5). The Holy Spirit, whom we met in Chapter 4, is the One who pours God’s love into us, and love is the first fruit He grows.

Loving God with all we are

The greatest commandment goes back to the words every Jewish family recited daily: “Hear, Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. You are to love the LORD your God with your whole heart, with your whole being, and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:4-5).

Notice the word “whole”. God does not ask for a portion of our love, like a tax collector taking his share. He asks for all of it: heart, soul, mind and strength. That means our feelings and desires, our thoughts and beliefs, our energy and abilities. It means loving God on Sunday morning and on Monday at work, in the field and in the kitchen, when we are happy and when we are grieving.

This does not mean we must stop loving our families, our friends or our homeland. It means God takes first place, and all our other loves are ordered under Him. When God is first, our other loves become healthier, not weaker. A man who loves God above all will love his wife better, not less.

In the twelfth century a French monk named Bernard, abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux, was asked a simple question by a church leader in Rome: why should we love God, and how much? He answered in a little book called On Loving God:

“I should say that God Himself is the motive of our love to Him, and that the measure of due love is to be without measure.”

Bernard of Clairvaux, On Loving God

Bernard went on to describe how love grows, step by step. At first, he said, a person loves only himself. Then, discovering that he cannot manage without God’s help, he begins to love God, but for his own sake. Over time, as he keeps coming to God in his need, he begins to taste God’s goodness and love Him for God’s own sake. At the highest step, which Bernard thought was rarely reached in this life, a person even loves himself only for God’s sake. Whatever we think of his stages, Bernard’s point is clear and freeing: you do not have to begin with perfect love. You can begin where you are, even with mixed motives, and God will grow your love as you keep coming to Him.

Loving our neighbour, our family and the Church

Jesus joined the second command to the first: love your neighbour as yourself. John shows us why they cannot be separated: “If someone says, ‘I love God,’ but hates a brother or sister, that person is a liar. For anyone who does not love a brother or sister, whom they have seen, is not able to love God, whom they have not seen” (1 John 4:20).

Who is my neighbour? Jesus answered that question with the story of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37). Your neighbour is anyone God places in your path who needs your help, whatever their tribe, language, religion or social standing.

Love begins at home. It is often easier to be kind to strangers than to the people we live with. The husband who is patient with customers but harsh with his wife, the mother who serves the church but shouts at her children, the young person who is polite to friends but rude to parents: each needs to hear that love starts in the house. Paul’s description of love is a good mirror for family life: “Love is patient; love is kind. Love does not envy, does not show off, is not puffed up. It does not behave shamefully, it does not look for its own advantage, it does not lose its temper, and it does not keep a tally of wrongs” (1 Corinthians 13:4-5).

Love must also mark the Church. On the night before He died, Jesus gave His disciples a new commandment, and then added: “If you have love for one another, everyone will know by this that you are My disciples” (John 13:35). Not our buildings, our programmes, our music or even our doctrine, important as these are. Our love for one another is the sign the world is meant to see. When churches split over pride, when believers of different tribes or classes will not eat together, when gossip runs through the congregation, the world sees something else.

Paul tells us how to dress for life together: “So put on, like clothing, a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience” (Colossians 3:12). Then he adds, “Over all of these put on love, which binds everything together and makes it complete” (Colossians 3:14). Love is like the belt that holds all the other garments in place.

Forgiveness and reconciliation

Nowhere is love tested more than when we have been hurt. Anyone who lives with other people will be wronged: by a spouse, a parent, a business partner, a church leader, a neighbour. What then?

The Bible’s command is clear: “Be patient with one another’s faults, and when someone has a grievance against another, forgive. The Lord has forgiven you freely; you must do the same” (Colossians 3:13). The reason we forgive is that we have been forgiven. We owed God a debt we could never pay, and He cancelled it at the cross. How can we refuse to cancel the far smaller debts others owe us?

It helps to be clear about what forgiveness is and is not. Forgiveness does not mean pretending the wrong did not happen, or that it did not matter. It does not mean that there are no consequences, or that we must immediately trust someone who has abused that trust. It means releasing the person from our desire for revenge and handing the matter to God, the just Judge. Reconciliation, the restoring of the relationship, is the goal wherever it is possible, but it needs both sides. Paul says, “If it can be done, and so far as it lies with you, keep peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18). We do our part, and we leave the rest to God.

Corrie ten Boom: the hand she could not lift

Few people have shown the cost and power of forgiveness more clearly than Corrie ten Boom. She was born in the Netherlands in 1892 and grew up in the town of Haarlem, above her father’s watch shop. The ten Booms were a warm, praying family who opened their home to anyone in need.

During the Second World War, when Germany occupied the Netherlands, the family hid Jewish people and members of the resistance in their house, including in a small secret room behind a false wall in Corrie’s bedroom. In February 1944 they were betrayed and arrested. Corrie’s elderly father died in prison within days. Corrie and her sister Betsie were eventually sent to Ravensbrück, a women’s concentration camp in Germany. There, amid cold, hunger and cruelty, the sisters held secret Bible readings and prayed with other prisoners. Betsie grew weaker and died in the camp in December 1944. Shortly afterwards Corrie was released.

After the war Corrie travelled widely, telling people that God’s love is deeper than the deepest pit of suffering, and that He forgives all who come to Him. In 1947, after speaking at a church in Munich in Germany, she was approached by a man she recognised. He had been one of the guards at Ravensbrück, where her sister had died. He did not remember her, but he told her that he had since become a Christian and knew God had forgiven him for the cruel things he had done. Now he wanted to hear forgiveness from one of the women who had suffered there. He held out his hand.

Corrie later wrote that she stood frozen. She had preached forgiveness to others, yet she could not lift her own hand. Memories of Betsie’s suffering came flooding back. She knew that she must forgive, and she knew that she could not do it in her own strength. So she prayed silently, asking Jesus to help her. Woodenly, almost mechanically, she put out her hand and took his. As she did, she said, a warmth seemed to flow through her, and she found herself forgiving him from her heart. She later said that she had never known God’s love so intensely as in that moment.

Corrie’s story teaches us something vital. Forgiveness does not always begin with a feeling. Often it begins with an act of obedience, made in weakness, trusting God to supply the love we lack. When she could not love, God loved through her. “We love because He loved us first” (1 John 4:19).

Loving our enemies

Jesus goes further still. Forgiving a friend who has hurt us is hard enough. But He says, “love your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you, so that you will be children of your Father in heaven. He makes His sun rise on evil people and good people alike, and He sends rain on those who do right and those who do wrong” (Matthew 5:44-45).

This is the love that marks God’s children. Anyone can love people who love them back. “If you love the people who love you, what reward is there in that?” (Matthew 5:46). But when we bless those who curse us, we look like our Father, who gives sun and rain even to those who reject Him. And we look like Jesus, who prayed for the soldiers nailing Him to the cross: “Father, forgive them. They do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

In Korea, a pastor named Son Yang-won lived out this command in a way that still moves people today. He served for years among people with leprosy in a colony in the south of the country, caring for those whom others shunned. Under Japanese colonial rule he was imprisoned for refusing to bow at Shinto shrines. Then, in 1948, during a violent uprising, his two eldest sons, both young Christians, were shot dead by a young man caught up in the rebellion. When the killer was captured and about to be executed, Pastor Son pleaded for his life. He then took the young man into his family as his own son, and led him towards Christ. Two years later, during the Korean War, Son Yang-won himself was killed by soldiers of the invading army. Many Korean Christians remember him as a man whose love for enemies came straight from the cross.

Most of us will never face such a test. But we all have people we find hard to love: a rival at work, a neighbour who wronged us, someone from a group that has hurt our people, a relative who betrayed us. Loving them does not mean approving of what they did. It means wanting God’s good for them, praying for them, refusing revenge and doing them good when we can. This is only possible as we live close to the God who loved us when we were His enemies (Romans 5:8).

From love to communion

There is one more thing to say about love. Love always wants to be near the one it loves. A young man in love does not need to be told to spend time with the woman he hopes to marry. He looks for every chance. A mother whose child has moved to a distant city waits eagerly for a phone call.

So it is with God. When we truly love Him, we want to hear Him and be with Him. Jesus promised this: “Whoever loves Me will be loved by My Father; I in turn will love them and show Myself to them” (John 14:21). And again: “Anyone who loves Me will keep My word. My Father will love them, and We will come to them and make Our dwelling place with them” (John 14:23).

Notice how love, obedience and communion are woven together. Those who love Jesus keep His word. Those who keep His word find the Father and the Son making their home with them. This is the life of coram Deo at its warmest: not a servant standing nervously before a master, but a friend sitting at a table with the One who loves him.

How does God speak to those who love Him? First and above all, through His Word, the Scriptures. That is where Chapter 6 begins. If love is the heart of our life with God, the Bible is the place where we most clearly hear the voice of the One we love.

Questions for reflection

  • Why do you think Jesus put love before every other command? How does that change the way you think about Bible reading, prayer and other spiritual habits?
  • “We love because He loved us first” (1 John 4:19). When have you most clearly experienced God’s love for you?
  • Bernard of Clairvaux said that we can begin loving God even with mixed motives. Where are you on that journey?
  • Read 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 and put your own name in place of the word “love”. Which phrases are hardest to say honestly?
  • Is there someone you need to forgive, or someone you need to ask for forgiveness? What would be the first step?
  • Who is an “enemy” in your life, someone you find hard to love? How could you pray for them this week?

A step for this week

Choose one person you find hard to love: a family member, a colleague, a neighbour or someone in your church. Each day this week, pray for that person by name, asking God to bless them in a specific way. Then, before the week ends, do one concrete act of kindness for them, such as a greeting, a small gift, a helping hand or a word of thanks. If there is a wrong between you that needs forgiving, ask God for the strength Corrie ten Boom asked for, and take the first step you can, even if your feelings have not yet caught up.

study_questions.question: What is the greatest commandment in the Bible?
study_questions.answer: Jesus said the first and greatest command is to love the Lord your God "with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind" (Matthew 22:37), and the second is to love your neighbour as yourself. The whole law hangs on these two. That is why Bible reading, prayer and the other disciplines are ways of loving God and receiving His love, never duties to earn it.

study_questions.question: How can I love others when I do not feel loving?
study_questions.answer: Our love comes from God's love, not from inside us: "We love because He loved us first" (1 John 4:19), and "through the Spirit His love has flooded our hearts" (Romans 5:5). Like the moon reflecting the sun, we love as we stay in the light of His love. Corrie ten Boom found that forgiveness often begins as an act of obedience made in weakness, trusting God to supply the love we lack.

study_questions.question: What does the Bible say about forgiving those who hurt us?
study_questions.answer: We forgive because we have been forgiven: "The Lord has forgiven you freely; you must do the same" (Colossians 3:13). Forgiveness does not pretend the wrong did not matter or require us to trust an abuser immediately; it releases our desire for revenge and hands the matter to God. Reconciliation is the goal where possible: "If it can be done, and so far as it lies with you, keep peace with everyone" (Romans 12:18).

fields.title: The Word of God: Hearing Him Speak
fields.body_html:
“All Scripture is breathed out by God and is useful for teaching, for rebuking, for correcting and for training in righteousness, so that the one who belongs to God may be fully capable, equipped for every good work.”

— 2 Timothy 3:16–17 (OWB)

Think of a young man who has gone to the city to find work, leaving behind the woman he hopes to marry. A letter arrives from her. He reads it on the bus, again at lunch, and once more before he sleeps. He notices every word. Why? Because he loves the one who wrote it, and through the letter he hears her voice.

In Chapter 5 we saw that love is the heart of the Christian life. Those who love God want to hear Him. Jesus said, “Anyone who loves Me will keep My word. My Father will love them, and We will come to them and make Our dwelling place with them” (John 14:23). Love listens. And the place where God has chosen to speak most clearly, most surely and most often is His written Word, the Bible.

To live coram Deo, before the face of God, is not to live before a silent face. The God whose face we seek is a God who speaks. This chapter is about learning to hear Him: reading the Bible, studying it, turning it over in our hearts, storing it in our memories and, above all, doing what it says.

God speaks

The first thing the Bible tells us about God’s activity is that He spoke. “God said, ‘Let there be light’,” and there was light. The God who made the world by His word has not fallen silent. He spoke through the prophets, and finally He spoke through His Son. And He made sure that what He said would be written down and kept for us.

Paul tells Timothy that “all Scripture is breathed out by God” (2 Timothy 3:16). The words did not simply come from good and wise people thinking about God. They came from God Himself, breathed out the way we breathe out words when we speak. Peter says the same: “no prophecy ever came because a human being willed it; rather, people spoke from God as the Holy Spirit bore them along” (2 Peter 1:21). The human writers were real people, with their own languages, styles and situations. Yet the Holy Spirit carried them along, the way the wind carries a sailing boat, so that what they wrote is truly God’s Word.

This is why the Bible is our sure standard for faith and for life. Preachers, traditions, dreams and feelings must all be measured against it, as the believers in Berea knew. They “went through the Scriptures day after day to check whether what Paul said was true” (Acts 17:11). If even the apostle Paul’s preaching was checked against the Bible, so must everything else be.

And this Word is not a dead letter. “For the word of God is alive and at work, and it has a keener edge than any two-edged sword. It reaches right in, cutting through soul and spirit, through joints and marrow, and it weighs the thoughts and purposes of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12). You may open it on an ordinary morning and find a familiar verse speaking straight to the worry you carried to bed. That is the living God speaking through His living Word.

The whole story

Many Christians know parts of the Bible well but have never seen how it fits together. It is not a random collection of sayings. It is one great story, told across many centuries and many books, with one great Hero.

It begins with creation: a good world, with man and woman made in God’s image to walk with Him. Then comes the fall: sin enters, the hiding begins, and death follows. The story narrows to Abraham’s family, through whom God promises to bless all nations, and follows Israel through slavery and rescue, kings and prophets, exile and return. All the while the promise grows: a King is coming, a Servant who will suffer, a new covenant written on the heart.

Then the promise is kept. Jesus Christ is born, lives, dies for our sins and rises again. He pours out the Holy Spirit and sends His Church to every nation. And the story looks forward to its ending, which is really a new beginning: a new heaven and a new earth where God’s people will see His face.

After His resurrection, Jesus walked with two discouraged disciples on the road to Emmaus. “Then, starting with Moses and going on through all the prophets, He explained to them what was written about Himself in every part of the Scriptures” (Luke 24:27). Later He told the apostles, “whatever the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms have written about Me must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). Jesus is the centre of the whole Bible. The Old Testament points forward to Him; the New Testament tells of Him and flows out from Him. When you read any part of Scripture, it is always worth asking, “How does this part of the story lead me to Christ?”

Jesus also warned the religious leaders of His day: “You pore over the Scriptures, since you think that eternal life is to be found in them; and they are the ones that testify about Me. But you do not want to come to Me so that you can have life” (John 5:39–40). It is possible to know the Bible well and miss the One it is about. We read the Bible not to collect facts but to meet a Person.

Reading: the whole Bible, for relationship

The first step in hearing God is simply to read His Word, regularly and widely. A healthy body needs a balanced plate, not one favourite dish; a healthy Christian needs the whole counsel of God, not only favourite verses.

George Müller, the German-born pastor who cared for many thousands of orphans in Bristol, England, without ever asking anyone but God for money, was a man soaked in Scripture. He read the Bible through many times in his long life. In Answers to Prayer he gave this advice:

“It is of immense importance for the understanding of the word of God, to read it in course, so that we may read every day a portion of the Old and a portion of the New Testament, going on where we previously left off.”

George Müller, Answers to Prayer

He went on to warn that “there are many believers, I fear, in our day, who have not read even once through the whole of the Scriptures; and yet in a few months, by reading only a few chapters every day they might accomplish it.” That is still true. Reading three or four chapters a day takes about twenty minutes and brings you through the whole Bible in a year.

Here are some simple ways to begin:

  • A gospel first. If you are new to the Bible, start with Mark or Luke, a chapter a day.
  • Old and New together. Read a chapter or two from the Old Testament and one from the New each day, as Müller advised, keeping a bookmark in each.
  • A yearly plan. Simple plans take you through the whole Bible in a year. If that feels too much, take two.
  • Listening. If reading is hard for you, listen to the Bible read aloud. For much of history God’s people have heard Scripture more than they have read it.

Above all, read for relationship, not just information. Before you begin, ask God to speak: “Take the veil from my eyes, so that I may see the wonders in Your instruction” (Psalm 119:18). As you read, notice what it shows you about God: His character, His promises, His ways. Read as the young man read his letter, listening for the voice of the One who wrote it.

Pandita Ramabai: a Bible for her people

Ramabai was born in 1858 into a high-caste Brahmin family. Her father, a Sanskrit scholar, did something unusual for his time: he taught his wife and daughter the sacred Sanskrit texts. The family lived as wandering pilgrims, and when famine struck in the 1870s, Ramabai lost her father, her mother and her sister. She and her brother walked thousands of miles across India, reciting scripture in temples to earn a living. In Calcutta, scholars were so impressed by her learning that they gave her the titles “Pandita” and “Sarasvati,” honours almost never given to a woman.

Yet her learning did not give her peace. She married, and within two years her husband died, leaving her a widow with a baby daughter, Manorama. She had seen how harshly widows were treated, and longed to help them. Through Christian friends she came into contact with the Bible, and in 1883, in England, she was baptised.

But Ramabai later wrote that for years she had found the Christian religion without truly finding Christ. It was through reading the Scriptures for herself that she came to see that she was a sinner in need of a Saviour, and that Jesus Christ had died for her. The Word that had been a subject of study became the voice of a Friend.

Back in India she opened homes for widows and abandoned girls, and later founded the Mukti Mission at Kedgaon, near Pune. Mukti means salvation or freedom. During terrible famines she took in hundreds of starving girls and women. They learned to read, to work, and to know the Lord. In 1905 a deep revival of prayer and repentance swept through Mukti, as girls and women gathered around the Word and cried out to God.

Then Ramabai set herself a task that would fill the last years of her life. She wanted the people of her own Marathi-speaking region, including the poor village women she loved, to have the whole Bible in language they could understand. So, already a scholar of Sanskrit and other languages, she learned Hebrew and Greek so that she could translate from the original texts. She finished the work shortly before she died in 1922, not long after the death of her beloved daughter.

Why would a woman who had lost so much give her last strength to translating a book? Because she had found in it the voice of the living God, and could not bear for her people to go without it. If she gave her final years so that others could read God’s Word, how can we leave our own Bibles closed?

Studying: seeing what is there

Reading is like walking through a field. Studying is like stopping to dig. Both are good. But some treasures lie below the surface.

Of the scribe Ezra we read, “Ezra had set his heart to study the law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and rulings in Israel” (Ezra 7:10). Notice the order: study, then practise, then teach. Ezra’s study was not mere curiosity. It was the first step to obedience.

R. A. Torrey, the American Bible teacher and evangelist, wrote a great deal about how to study the Bible. In How to Succeed in the Christian Life he put it bluntly:

“The one who neglects his Bible is bound to make a failure of the Christian life. The one who studies his Bible in the right spirit and by a true method is bound to make a success of the Christian life.”

R. A. Torrey, How to Succeed in the Christian Life

In the same chapter Torrey recalls a saying of his friend D. L. Moody: “In prayer we talk to God. In Bible study, God talks to us, and we had better let God do most of the talking.”

A simple and time-tested method has three steps.

  1. Observation: what does it say? Read the passage slowly, more than once. Who is speaking, and to whom? Which words are repeated? Many mistakes come from not seeing what is actually on the page.
  2. Interpretation: what does it mean? Ask what the writer meant for his first readers. Pay attention to the context: the verses before and after, the book it belongs to, and where it sits in the whole story. Notice the kind of writing it is: a psalm is poetry, a proverb gives wise general patterns rather than promises for every case, a parable is a story with a point. Read each in its own way.
  3. Application: what does it mean for me? Only after the first two steps do we ask how this truth should change what we believe, how we feel and what we do today.

One more key is to let Scripture interpret Scripture. God does not contradict Himself. When one verse is hard to understand, look at what the rest of the Bible says on the same subject. Clearer passages shed light on harder ones, and this guards us from building a teaching on one verse taken out of its place.

You do not need to be a scholar. A Bible, a notebook and an honest heart will take you a long way, and studying with others keeps us from strange ideas.

Meditating: turning it over in the heart

Bible reading can be fast. Meditation is slow. Meditation in the Bible does not mean emptying the mind. It means filling it with God’s Word and turning that Word over and over, the way a cow chews the cud, until its goodness is drawn out and becomes part of us.

God told Joshua, as he took up the leadership of Israel, “Keep this book of the law always on your lips, and reflect on it by day and by night, so that you take care to do all that is written in it. Then you will bring your ways to a good end, and then you will act wisely and succeed” (Joshua 1:8). The very first psalm paints the picture of a person whose delight is in God’s instruction: “they recite it quietly to themselves day and night. That person is like a tree set out beside channels of water, which bears its fruit when its season comes, and whose leaves never dry up” (Psalm 1:2–3).

Anyone who has farmed in a dry land knows the difference between a tree beside a stream and a tree on the open hillside. In the dry season one withers; the other stays green. Meditation sends our roots down into the Word, so that when dry seasons come we still have water.

How do we meditate? Take a short passage, even one verse. Read it slowly several times, perhaps aloud, stressing a different word each time. Ask, “Lord, what are You saying to me here?” Then carry the verse with you through the day. The psalmist says, “How I love Your instruction! I turn it over in my mind all day long” (Psalm 119:97).

Memorising: the Word hidden in the heart

“Deep in my heart I have kept Your word safe, so that I will not sin against You” (Psalm 119:11). When we memorise Scripture, we carry it with us into places where we cannot open a book: a hospital bed, a long journey, a sleepless night, a moment of sudden temptation.

Jesus showed us the power of this. After forty days of fasting in the wilderness, He was tempted by the devil (Matthew 4:1–11). Each time, He answered with Scripture He knew by heart, all of it from the book of Deuteronomy. When tempted to turn stones into bread, He answered, “No one lives on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). When offered the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship, He answered from Scripture again: “You must worship the Lord your God and serve no one but Him” (Matthew 4:10). The Son of God fought temptation with the sword of the Spirit. How much more do we need it?

Memorising is easier than many people think. Choose one verse a week, write it on a small card, and read it aloud several times a day. Review old verses as you add new ones. In a year you will carry more than fifty passages in your heart.

Hearing and doing

All of this, reading, studying, meditating and memorising, has one aim. It is not that we become clever. It is that we become obedient, and through obedience, more like Christ.

James writes, “Be people who carry out the word, not just people who hear it. Otherwise you are fooling yourselves. Anyone who hears the word but does not carry it out is like a man studying his own face in a mirror. He looks himself over, goes away, and at once forgets what he looked like” (James 1:22–24). Imagine seeing a smear of dirt on your face in the mirror and walking out without washing it off. That is reading the Bible and changing nothing.

“But whoever looks closely into the perfect law of freedom and stays with it, not hearing and then forgetting but doing the work, will be blessed in what they do” (James 1:25). The blessing is not in the hearing alone. It is in the doing.

So when you finish reading, ask a simple question: “What is one thing God wants me to believe, or do, or stop doing, because of what I have read today?” Then do it. Perhaps it is to forgive someone, to speak more gently to your children, or to be honest in your business. Obedience is how the Word moves from the page into your life.

This is living coram Deo with an open Bible: not standing over Scripture as its judges, but sitting under it as listeners, ready to obey.

From the Word to prayer

George Müller learned one more lesson from the Bible that changed his whole life with God, and it leads us straight into Chapter 7.

For years Müller had begun each day by trying to pray as soon as he was dressed, and often his mind wandered. Then, in 1841, he saw something new. He described it in his journal, later published as The Life of Trust:

“I saw more clearly than ever that the first great and primary business to which I ought to attend every day was, to have my soul happy in the Lord.”

George Müller, The Life of Trust

So he changed the order. Instead of beginning with prayer, he began with the Bible, reading slowly and meditating on each verse, asking only for a few words of blessing first. And he discovered that, after a few minutes of meditation, his soul was “led to confession, or to thanksgiving, or to intercession, or to supplication; so that, though I did not, as it were, give myself to prayer, but to meditation, yet it turned almost immediately more or less into prayer.”

That is the pattern of a true conversation. God speaks first; we answer. The Word stirs us, and our hearts respond in praise, confession and requests. Prayer that grows out of Scripture rests on what God has said.

The Bible is God’s letter to His children. But He wants us to answer, and to talk with Him face to face. That is where we turn next.

Questions for reflection

  • How would you describe your relationship with the Bible right now: a duty, a struggle, a delight, or something else? Why?
  • Jesus is the centre of the whole Bible (Luke 24:27). How might that change the way you read the Old Testament?
  • What can you learn from Pandita Ramabai’s love for God’s Word and her work to bring it to her people?
  • Which of the three steps of study (observation, interpretation, application) do you most often skip? What happens when you do?
  • Think of a time when a verse you remembered helped you in a moment of temptation or fear. What happened?
  • What is one thing God has said to you through His Word recently that you have not yet done?

A step for this week

Choose one of the Gospels and read one chapter each day this week, using Müller’s pattern. Before you read, ask God in a sentence to speak to you. Read slowly, stopping at any verse that catches your attention, and turn it over in your mind. Write down one sentence about what the chapter shows you about Jesus and one thing you will do because of it. Then turn what you have read into a short prayer. Choose one verse from the week, write it on a card, and carry it with you until you can say it by heart.

study_questions.question: Is the Bible really the Word of God?
study_questions.answer: Yes. Paul writes that "all Scripture is breathed out by God" (2 Timothy 3:16), and Peter says that "people spoke from God as the Holy Spirit bore them along" (2 Peter 1:21). The human writers were real people, but the Spirit carried them along so that what they wrote is truly God's Word. That is why the Bible is the sure standard by which every teaching, tradition and feeling is measured.

study_questions.question: How should a Christian study the Bible?
study_questions.answer: A simple, time-tested method has three steps: observation (what does it say?), interpretation (what did it mean for its first readers, in its context and kind of writing?) and application (what does it mean for me today?). Let Scripture interpret Scripture, so that clearer passages shed light on harder ones. Like Ezra, who "set his heart to study the law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach" it (Ezra 7:10), we study in order to obey.

study_questions.question: What is the difference between reading, meditating on and memorising Scripture?
study_questions.answer: Reading takes us through the whole Bible regularly, ideally a portion of the Old and New Testaments each day. Meditating means turning a short passage over slowly until it shapes our thoughts, like the person in Psalm 1 who recites God's instruction "quietly to themselves day and night" (Psalm 1:2). Memorising stores the Word in the heart for moments of temptation, as Jesus answered the devil with Scripture he knew by heart (Matthew 4:1–11).

fields.title: Prayer: Talking and Listening to God
fields.body_html:
“But when you pray, go into an inner room, shut the door, and pray to your Father who is there in secret. Your Father sees what is hidden, and He will repay you.”

— Matthew 6:6 (OWB)

A small child does not need lessons before speaking to her father. She runs to him with a scraped knee, a drawing, a question, a complaint. She does not choose her words carefully. She simply talks, because he is her father and she knows he is listening.

In Chapter 6 we learned that God speaks to us through His Word. Prayer is our answer. He speaks first; we respond. George Müller found that when he began the day by meditating on Scripture, his reading turned almost by itself into confession, thanksgiving and requests. That is the natural shape of prayer: a conversation in which God has the first word and we reply as His children.

To live coram Deo is to live before a face that is turned towards us. Prayer is how we speak to that face, and how we learn to hear it speak back.

What prayer is

Prayer is not a ritual to perform or a spell to get results. It is not a speech for others to admire. Jesus warned against praying “at the street corners where others can see them” (Matthew 6:5). He also warned against piling up empty words, as if God could be worn down by length: “do not keep piling up empty words as the pagans do. They think they will be heard because they say so much” (Matthew 6:7). Then He added something wonderful: “Your Father already knows what you need before you ask Him” (Matthew 6:8).

If God already knows, why pray at all? Because prayer is not mainly about giving God information. It is about relationship. A husband may know his wife is tired, but he still wants her to tell him about her day. Prayer is the way we share our life with God and receive His life in return.

So prayer can be very simple and very honest. “People, rely on Him in every season; empty your hearts out before Him. God is our shelter” (Psalm 62:8). Empty your heart. Tell Him your fear about the harvest, your anger at your employer, your worry about your son, your joy at a birth. Nothing is too small and nothing is too large.

Paul gives the same invitation, with a promise attached: “Do not worry about anything. Instead, in everything, bring your requests to God through prayer and petition, with thanksgiving. And God’s peace, which is beyond all our understanding, will stand guard over your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:6–7). The picture is of a soldier on guard at the gate. When we hand our worries to God, His peace stands at the door of our hearts.

The Lord’s Prayer as a model

The disciples watched Jesus pray, and it made them want to pray too. “Lord, teach us how to pray,” one of them asked (Luke 11:1). Jesus answered with the prayer we call the Lord’s Prayer. It is good to pray these words as they stand, as Christians all over the world have done for two thousand years. It is also a pattern, a frame on which to hang our own prayers.

“Our Father in heaven, may Your name be kept holy. May Your kingdom come. May Your will be done on earth, as it is done in heaven. Give us today the bread we need. Forgive us what we owe You, as we too have forgiven those who owe us. And do not lead us into testing, but rescue us from the evil one” (Matthew 6:9–13).

Notice its shape.

  1. “Our Father in heaven.” Prayer begins with relationship. He is our Father, near and loving, and He is in heaven, great and powerful.
  2. “May Your name be kept holy. May Your kingdom come. May Your will be done.” Before we ask for anything for ourselves, we put God first: His honour, His rule, His purposes.
  3. “Give us today the bread we need.” Then we bring our daily needs, simply, one day at a time.
  4. “Forgive us ... as we too have forgiven.” We confess our sins and let go of others’ sins against us.
  5. “Rescue us from the evil one.” We ask for protection in the spiritual battle.

You can pray through the Lord’s Prayer slowly, line by line, filling in each part with your own words. When you reach “Give us today the bread we need,” name the needs of your household. When you reach “as we too have forgiven,” name the person you find hard to forgive.

Kinds of prayer

The Bible shows many kinds of prayer. Five are especially helpful to remember.

  • Adoration is praising God for who He is. “Bless the LORD, my soul; let all that is deep within me bless His holy name” (Psalm 103:1). Adoration lifts our eyes from our problems to our God.
  • Confession is agreeing with God about our sin and receiving His forgiveness. David prayed, “God, create a pure heart for me, and make my spirit new and steady inside me” (Psalm 51:10).
  • Thanksgiving is thanking God for what He has done. “Whatever happens, give thanks; this is what God wants for you in Christ Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).
  • Supplication is asking God for our own needs, as Jesus invites us to do.
  • Intercession is praying for others. “... pray for each other, so that you may be healed. When a righteous person prays, that prayer is at work, and it can do a great deal” (James 5:16).

A healthy prayer life has room for all five. If we only ask, our prayers become a shopping list. If we only praise, we forget that God wants to meet our needs. Many believers find it helpful to move through these kinds of prayer in turn, especially in a longer time of prayer.

Praying Scripture

One of the best teachers of prayer is the Bible itself. The Psalms were Israel’s prayer book, and they have been the Church’s ever since. They give us words for every season: joy and grief, fear and trust, anger and repentance. When you do not know how to pray, open the Psalms and pray them as your own.

You can do the same with other passages. Paul’s prayers for the churches are rich models (Ephesians 1 and 3, Philippians 1, Colossians 1). Turn his words into prayers for your family and church: “Lord, let my children’s love overflow more and more.” The promises of Scripture can also be turned into prayer. When you read, “The sheep that belong to Me listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me” (John 10:27), you might pray, “Lord, You know me. Help me to hear Your voice today and follow You.”

Praying Scripture keeps our prayers in line with God’s will, stretches them beyond our own small concerns, and gives words to the heart when it has none.

Praying Hyde

Few people have shown the power of persevering prayer more clearly than John Hyde, the American missionary whom many in India came to call “Praying Hyde.”

Hyde was born in 1865 in Illinois, the son of a Presbyterian minister. He sailed for India in 1892 to serve in the Punjab, in the north-west of the country. His start was not impressive. He was hard of hearing, and he found learning the local languages slow work. He was a quiet man, not a natural public speaker.

But Hyde learned to pray. He came to believe that the missionary task was first of all a spiritual battle, to be fought on his knees before it was fought in the villages. He gave himself to prayer with a seriousness that astonished those around him, often praying late into the night and sometimes through whole nights. He would pray for people by name, for hours, carrying them before God until he had peace.

In 1904 Hyde and others formed the Punjab Prayer Union, a fellowship of believers who committed themselves to pray for revival in India. That same year a convention for Christian workers began at Sialkot. While the meetings went on, Hyde and a few companions gave themselves to prayer in a room set apart for it, sometimes for days at a time. Many testified that God moved powerfully in those gatherings, with deep repentance among believers and many coming to faith in Christ. The Sialkot conventions continued for years, and Hyde’s prayer was woven through them.

Those who knew him say that he prayed specifically and persistently for people to come to Christ, asking God for definite numbers of souls and holding on until he saw them. His praying cost him. His health broke down, and he left India in 1911. He died in America the following year, aged only forty-six.

What can an ordinary believer learn from such a man? Most of us will not pray through the night. But Hyde shows us that prayer is real work, perhaps the most important work, and that God answers the persistent prayers of ordinary people. He was not gifted in the ways the world admires. He simply took God at His word, and went to Him again and again. “When a righteous person prays, that prayer is at work, and it can do a great deal” (James 5:16).

Listening prayer

Prayer is not only talking. It is also listening. The boy Samuel, sleeping near the ark of God, heard his name called in the night. When he finally understood that it was the Lord, he answered, “Speak, for Your servant is listening” (1 Samuel 3:10). That is a good prayer for any of us.

Elijah, worn out and afraid, met God on the mountain. The Lord was not in the mighty wind, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire, but in “a faint sound, thin as silence” (1 Kings 19:12). God often speaks quietly. If our prayer is all speaking and no stillness, we may miss Him.

God speaks above all through Scripture, and that is where we should expect to hear Him first. But Christians also testify that the Spirit brings a verse to mind, lays a person on their heart, gives a sense of peace or unease about a decision, or prompts them to act. How should we treat such impressions?

With openness and with care. Paul writes, “Do not smother the Spirit; do not look down on prophecy. Test everything; keep hold of what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21). John adds, “do not believe just any spirit; test the spirits to find out whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1). We should neither dismiss every inner prompting nor accept every one as God’s voice. Our own desires and fears can easily sound like God. Here are four simple tests.

  1. Scripture. God never contradicts His written Word. An impression that leads away from what the Bible teaches is not from Him.
  2. Conscience. Does it lead towards holiness, love and humility, or towards pride, fear or sin?
  3. Wise counsel. What do mature believers who know you and know the Bible say? God’s guidance is usually confirmed in the community of His people.
  4. Fruit. Over time, does it bear good fruit: love, peace, faithfulness and the building up of others?

Listening prayer is not a special gift for a few. It is part of the relationship every child of God may enjoy. Jesus said His sheep listen to His voice (John 10:27). We learn that voice the way a child learns a parent’s voice: by spending time together, and above all by knowing what He has already said.

Persevering prayer and unanswered prayer

Jesus told His disciples “a parable about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). A poor widow kept coming to an unjust judge, demanding justice, until he gave in just to be rid of her. If even a bad judge yields to persistence, Jesus said, “surely God will give justice to the people He has chosen, when they call out to Him day and night” (Luke 18:7). In Luke 11 He told of a man who knocks on his friend’s door at midnight and keeps on knocking until he gets the bread he needs. Then He said, “ask, and God will give to you; search, and you will find; knock, and God will open the door for you” (Luke 11:9).

But what about prayers that seem to go unanswered? Every honest Christian knows them. A sick child who did not recover. A marriage that broke. A job that never came. Here we must be gentle and truthful.

Sometimes God says “wait.” Andrew Murray, the South African pastor, wrote about this in With Christ in the School of Prayer:

“Let us learn to give God time. God needs time with us.”

Andrew Murray, With Christ in the School of Prayer

Sometimes God says “no,” because He has something better. Paul begged the Lord three times to remove his “thorn in the flesh.” The answer was not the removal he asked for, but a deeper gift: “My grace is enough for you, for power comes to its fullness in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Even Jesus, in Gethsemane, prayed, “Father, if You are willing, remove this cup from Me. Yet let Your will be done, not Mine” (Luke 22:42). The cup was not removed, and through that unanswered request the world was saved.

And sometimes we simply do not know why. In those times we hold on to what we do know: that God is our Father, that He is good, and that He hears. “Here is the boldness we have in coming to Him: whenever we ask for something in line with His will, He listens to us” (1 John 5:14). Unanswered prayer is not unheard prayer. Keep praying. Keep trusting. Tell Him honestly how you feel, as the psalmists did. He can bear your questions.

Praying in the Spirit

We do not pray alone. “The Spirit also lends a hand in our weakness. What we should pray for, and how, we do not know. But the Spirit Himself pleads on our behalf, with groans that no words carry” (Romans 8:26). When we are too tired, too confused or too grieved to find words, the Holy Spirit prays within us and for us.

Paul tells us to “pray in the Spirit at every opportunity, with every kind of prayer and request” (Ephesians 6:18), and Jude urges believers to keep “praying in the Holy Spirit” (Jude 1:20). Christians understand this phrase in somewhat different ways. Many Pentecostal and charismatic believers include in it praying in tongues, a gift discussed further in Chapter 23. Others understand it more generally. But all agree on the heart of it: true prayer is not our own effort to reach God. It is led, prompted and empowered by the Spirit who lives in us. So whatever our tradition, we can begin every prayer by asking, “Holy Spirit, teach me to pray.”

Practical patterns of prayer

How can we build a life of prayer? Here are some simple patterns that believers across the centuries have found helpful.

Short prayers through the day. When the Persian king asked Nehemiah what he wanted, “I prayed to the God of heaven, and I said to the king” (Nehemiah 2:4–5). There was no time for a long prayer, only a quick lifting of the heart. You can do the same: a word of thanks when the bus arrives, a cry for help before a hard conversation, a blessing over a sleeping child. “Never stop praying” (1 Thessalonians 5:17) does not mean being on our knees all day. It means a heart that keeps turning towards God.

Set times of prayer. Daniel “got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had always done” (Daniel 6:10), three times a day, even when it put his life in danger. Regular times give our prayer a backbone. Chapter 8 will look closely at one of the most important: the morning.

Longer seasons of prayer. Before choosing His twelve apostles, Jesus “stayed up all night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12). From time to time, before big decisions or in times of need, set aside a longer time: half a day, an evening, a night with others.

Praying through a list. Intercession is easier when we are organised. Keep a list of people and needs. You might pray for your family every day, and give each day of the week a different focus: church leaders on Monday, neighbours and colleagues on Tuesday, missionaries on Wednesday, the nation on Thursday, and so on.

A prayer journal. Write down what you ask and the date. Later, write down how God answered. George Müller kept careful records of his requests and the answers he received, and they became a great encouragement to his faith. A journal helps us to remember, to give thanks, and to see God’s faithfulness over the years.

The most important pattern is simply to begin. A short prayer, prayed honestly today, is worth more than a long prayer you plan to pray someday.

Questions for reflection

  • How does it change your prayer to think of it as answering God, who has already spoken in His Word?
  • Which part of the Lord’s Prayer do you find easiest to pray, and which hardest? Why?
  • Of adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication and intercession, which do you most often leave out?
  • What strikes you most about John Hyde’s life? What might persistence in prayer look like for you?
  • Have you had an inner impression you believed was from God? How might the four tests have helped you?
  • Is there an unanswered prayer that has discouraged you? What would it mean to keep bringing it honestly to God?

A step for this week

Each day this week, pray slowly through the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13), pausing after each line to add your own words: praise for who God is, the needs of your household, the sins you need to confess, the people you need to forgive. Then start a simple prayer list in a notebook with five people you will pray for each day, writing the date beside each request. At the end of the week, read over your list and thank God for anything you have seen Him do.

study_questions.question: How do I pray using the Lord's Prayer as a model?
study_questions.answer: Pray it slowly, line by line, adding your own words. It begins with relationship ("Our Father in heaven"), puts God's name, kingdom and will first, then brings daily needs ("Give us today the bread we need"), confession and forgiveness, and a request for protection from the evil one (Matthew 6:9–13). It is both a prayer to pray as it stands and a frame for our own prayers.

study_questions.question: How can I tell if an impression in prayer is from God?
study_questions.answer: Treat impressions with openness and care: "Test everything; keep hold of what is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Weigh them against Scripture, since God never contradicts His written Word; against conscience; against the counsel of mature believers; and by the fruit they bear over time. God speaks above all through the Bible, so knowing what He has already said is the best way to recognise His voice.

study_questions.question: Why does God not answer some prayers?
study_questions.answer: Sometimes God says "wait," and as Andrew Murray wrote, we must "learn to give God time." Sometimes He says "no" because He has something better, as Paul learned when the Lord told him, "My grace is enough for you" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Even when we do not know why, we hold on to God's goodness: "whenever we ask for something in line with His will, He listens to us" (1 John 5:14). Unanswered prayer is not unheard prayer.

fields.title: The Morning Watch
fields.body_html:
“LORD, at daybreak You hear my voice. At daybreak I set everything out before You and keep watch.”

— Psalm 5:3 (OWB)

Long before the sun rises over the market town, the traders are awake. They load the vegetables, sweep the stalls and lay out the goods before the first customers arrive. The farmer is up too, walking to the field in the cool grey light, because the work done before the heat of the day sets the pattern for everything that follows. Ask either of them why they rise so early, and they will tell you: the first hours decide the day.

In Chapter 6 we learned to hear God in His Word. In Chapter 7 we learned to speak with Him in prayer. The morning watch brings these two together into a daily meeting with God, a set time at the start of each day when we come before His face, listen to Him, speak with Him, and give Him the day ahead.

The phrase “morning watch” has a long history. Watchmen on the city walls kept watch through the night and looked for the dawn. David wrote, “At daybreak I set everything out before You and keep watch” (Psalm 5:3). He laid his day before God like a trader laying out goods, and then looked up, expecting God to act.

Jesus rose early

The best reason for a morning watch is that Jesus kept one. Mark describes a full and exhausting day in Capernaum. Jesus taught in the synagogue, cast out an evil spirit, healed Peter’s mother-in-law, and then, as evening fell, the whole town crowded at the door with their sick, and He healed many. Then we read: “Long before daylight, He got up and went out. He went off to a lonely place and spent time there in prayer” (Mark 1:35).

Think of that. After the busiest day, when He might have slept late, Jesus rose before dawn to be alone with His Father. When the disciples found Him and said that everyone was looking for Him, He already knew what to do next. Time with the Father had set His direction.

This was not a single event but a pattern. Luke tells us that Jesus “kept slipping away to places in the wilderness to pray” (Luke 5:16). The prophet Isaiah, speaking of the Lord’s Servant, had foretold the same thing: “Each morning He rouses me; He rouses my ear to listen as a learner listens” (Isaiah 50:4). The Son of God lived in perfect fellowship with the Father, and yet He still sought time alone with Him at the start of the day. If He needed it, how much more do we?

Why the first hour matters

There is nothing magical about the morning. God hears prayer at noon and at midnight. Some believers, such as nurses on night shifts or parents of newborn babies, will need to find their quiet time at other hours, and God meets them there. Yet there are good reasons why so many of God’s people across the centuries have given Him the first part of the day.

The morning sets the day’s direction. Before the phone rings, before the news, before the demands of work and family, our minds are fresh. What fills them first tends to shape what follows. E. M. Bounds, the American Methodist preacher who wrote much about prayer, put it strongly in Power Through Prayer:

“The men who have done the most for God in this world have been early on their knees. He who fritters away the early morning, its opportunity and freshness, in other pursuits than seeking God will make poor headway seeking him the rest of the day.”

E. M. Bounds, Power Through Prayer

The morning is a first-fruits offering. In the Old Testament, God’s people gave Him the first of their harvest as a sign that all of it belonged to Him. Giving God the first moments of the day says the same thing about our time: this day is Yours.

The morning is when mercy is new. “It is by the LORD’s loyal love that we have not been wiped out, for His mercies have not failed. They are new each morning; how great is Your faithfulness!” (Lamentations 3:22–23). Whatever failures yesterday held, the morning is a fresh start. In the wilderness the Israelites gathered manna “morning after morning” (Exodus 16:21); yesterday’s manna would not feed them today. So too we need fresh grace for each new day.

The morning is when we ask for guidance. “Each morning let me hear of Your loyal love, since You are the one I rely on. Teach me which road to walk, for my whole being reaches up to You” (Psalm 143:8). It is wiser to ask for directions before the journey than after we are lost.

The morning is a time for joy. Moses prayed, “Fill us with Your loyal love at daybreak, and we will shout for joy and rejoice as long as we live” (Psalm 90:14). A heart filled with God’s love in the morning carries that joy into the market, the office and the kitchen. Many of us wake already anxious, our minds racing through the problems of the day. The morning watch lets God’s love speak first, before our fears do.

Susanna Wesley: a prayer closet in a crowded house

If anyone had an excuse not to keep a quiet time with God, it was Susanna Wesley.

She was born in London in 1669, one of the youngest of a very large family; her father, Samuel Annesley, was a well-known Puritan minister. She married Samuel Wesley, a clergyman, and the couple spent most of their married life in the rectory at Epworth, a small town in Lincolnshire, England. Susanna gave birth to nineteen children. Many died as babies or in childhood, a grief that came again and again. Money was always short. Her husband was often away, sometimes in debt, and once even in prison for debt. In 1709 the rectory burned to the ground in the night. The family barely escaped, and young John, aged five, was rescued from an upstairs window moments before the roof fell in.

Through all this, Susanna ran the household and taught the children herself. She held a home school for six hours a day. She made time each week to speak alone with each child about their soul. She wrote out lessons and explanations of the faith for them. Two of those children, John and Charles Wesley, grew up to be leaders of the great eighteenth-century revival, John as a preacher and Charles as the writer of thousands of hymns.

Where did such a woman find time for God? She made it. She kept regular times of private devotion, morning and evening, and guarded them carefully. Family tradition tells a lovely story about how she did it in a crowded house with no room of her own. When she needed to be alone with God, she would sit down and pull her apron over her head. The children knew what it meant: Mother is praying, and must not be disturbed. Under that apron, in the middle of the noise, she had her inner room.

Her letters show how much she valued this habit. To her eldest son Samuel, away at school, she wrote:

“Begin and end the day with Him who is the Alpha and Omega, and if you really experience what it is to love God, you will redeem all the time you can for His more immediate service.”

Susanna Wesley, quoted in Susanna Wesley

In another letter to him she described the true Christian as one who, “in the morning or evening, or any other time when occasion is offered,” will “be cheerfully disposed to retire from the world, that he may offer to his Creator his sacrifice of prayer and praise, and will account it his happiness, as well as his duty, so to do.”

Notice the words “happiness, as well as his duty.” Susanna was a disciplined woman, but her devotion was not grim. Time with God was her joy. And her example speaks to every busy mother, every worker with long hours, every student in a crowded room. You may not have a quiet house. You may not have a room of your own. But you can have an apron, a corner, a bench, a walk to work. Jesus said, “go into an inner room, shut the door, and pray to your Father who is there in secret” (Matthew 6:6). The inner room may be very small. What matters is that the door is shut to everything else for a while, and open to God.

What a morning watch looks like

There is no single correct way to keep a morning watch. But most believers find that it includes five simple elements.

  1. Stillness. Begin by being quiet before God. “Stop, and acknowledge that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). Take a few slow breaths. Let the noise in your mind settle. Remind yourself that you are before His face.
  2. Worship. Turn your heart towards God with praise and thanks. A psalm, a hymn or a simple sentence of adoration will do.
  3. Scripture. Read a passage of the Bible slowly, as we learned in Chapter 6. Listen for what God is saying.
  4. Prayer. Let the Word turn into prayer, as George Müller found. Confess, give thanks, bring your needs, pray for others, and lay the coming day before God.
  5. Listening. Before you rise, wait a little. Ask, “Lord, is there anything You want to say to me?” Write down anything that comes to mind, and test it as we learned in Chapter 7.

Some like to remember it as a conversation: God speaks in His Word, we answer in prayer, and we listen again.

Worship: beginning the day with God

Worship deserves a special word. Many of us begin our prayer time with a list of requests, as though we had rushed into a king’s court shouting our needs without bowing first. The psalmist shows a better way.

“Raise a glad shout to the LORD, all the earth! Serve the LORD and be glad doing it; come before Him with ringing cries of joy. Be sure of this: the LORD is God! He is the one who made us, and we belong to Him” (Psalm 100:1–3). “Come through His gates giving thanks, into His courtyards with praise” (Psalm 100:4). Thanksgiving is the gate; praise is the courtyard. We enter God’s presence by remembering who He is and what He has done.

Morning worship has three movements: adoration, praising God for who He is; thanksgiving, thanking Him for what He has done, including the gift of a new day; and surrender, giving ourselves and the day back to Him. You might simply say, “Lord, this day is Yours. My time, my work, my words and my family are Yours. Use me as You wish.”

That surrender is the bridge between private worship and the rest of life. Paul writes, “I appeal to you by the mercies of God: offer your bodies to God as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to Him. That is your reasonable worship” (Romans 12:1). Worship does not end when we close our Bibles. It continues as we sing with God’s people on the Lord’s Day, and it continues in everyday obedience: in honest work, patient parenting, kind words and faithful service. The morning watch is where the living sacrifice is laid on the altar for the day.

Practical help

Time. Choose a time you can keep. For most people this means getting up a little earlier, which usually means going to bed a little earlier. Start small. Fifteen minutes kept faithfully is better than an hour attempted once and then abandoned. As the habit grows, the time often grows with it.

Place. Find a place where you can be undisturbed: a chair in the corner, a bench outside, the kitchen before others wake. Some keep their Bible, notebook and pen there, ready each morning. Having a place helps the habit.

A simple structure. Use the five elements above, or something like this: two minutes of stillness, three minutes of worship, ten minutes of Scripture and prayer, and a moment of listening. Follow a reading plan so you do not waste time wondering what to read.

When it feels dry. Every believer has mornings when the Bible seems flat and prayer feels like talking to the ceiling. Do not be alarmed. Feelings come and go; God’s presence does not. The psalmist knew this. “God, You are my God, and I search hard for You. My whole self thirsts for You; my body aches for You in a dry and worn-out land with no water” (Psalm 63:1). Dryness itself can become a prayer.

Hudson Taylor, the pioneer missionary to inland China, knew such mornings. He tells in Separation and Service of a night spent in a wicked town in the province of Cheh-kiang, where his heart was oppressed and could find no relief. He woke the next morning “much cast down, and feeling spiritually hungry and thirsty indeed.” His regular reading that day was Numbers 7, a long chapter of repeated lists of offerings. He was tempted to skip it for something more comforting. But he decided to keep to his plan, praying God to bless him even through Numbers 7. “I fear there was not much faith in the prayer,” he wrote, “but oh! how abundantly it was answered, and what a feast God gave me!” The chapter he had dreaded became one of the most precious in the Bible to him.

The lesson is simple. Keep coming. On dry mornings, read anyway, pray anyway, and leave the results to God. Faithfulness in the ordinary days prepares us for the feasts.

With others. The morning watch is personal, but it need not be lonely. Husbands and wives can share a few minutes of Scripture and prayer before the day begins. Parents can gather children for a short reading and prayer at breakfast, as Susanna Wesley had her children read a psalm and a chapter of the Bible each morning. Some friends agree to read the same passage each day and share by message what God showed them. Shared habits are easier to keep, and they teach the next generation that a day begins with God.

When you miss a day. You will. Illness, travel, a crying baby or a late night will interrupt the pattern. Do not give up, and do not punish yourself. Simply begin again the next morning. His mercies are new each morning, and that includes the morning after you missed.

Grace, not legalism

Here we must be careful. The morning watch is a gift, not a law. It is an invitation from a Father who wants to meet His children, not a rule to earn His approval. God does not love you more on the days you keep it, or less on the days you miss it. In Christ you are already accepted.

Hudson Taylor urged believers to treasure this time. In Union and Communion he wrote:

“There is no time so profitably spent as the early hour given to JESUS only. Do we give sufficient attention to this hour? If possible, it should be redeemed; nothing can make up for it.”

Hudson Taylor, Union and Communion

Notice his words “if possible.” Taylor was not laying a burden on anyone. He was pointing to a treasure. When the morning watch becomes a box to tick, it loses its life. When it becomes a meeting with the One we love, it becomes the best part of the day.

Andrew Murray, the South African pastor, reminds us of its true purpose. In The Inner Chamber he warns against treating the quiet time as the goal in itself:

“The morning watch must not be regarded as an end in itself. It is not sufficient that it gives us a blessed time for prayer and Bible study, and so brings us a certain measure of refreshment and help. It is to serve as a means to an end. And that end is to secure the presence of Christ for the whole day.”

Andrew Murray, The Inner Chamber

That is the heart of the matter. We do not meet God in the morning so that we can leave Him there and go about our business alone. We meet Him in the morning so that we can walk with Him all day. The morning watch is the door into a day lived coram Deo, before His face, from the first hour to the last.

How do we carry His presence from the quiet of the morning into the noise of the day? Jesus answers that question with a picture of a vine and its branches, and that is where Chapter 9 will take us.

Questions for reflection

  • What usually fills the first minutes of your day? How does that shape the rest of it?
  • Jesus rose early to pray after His busiest day (Mark 1:35). What does that teach you about your own need for time with God?
  • Susanna Wesley found her inner room under an apron. Where could your inner room be?
  • Which of the five elements (stillness, worship, Scripture, prayer, listening) do you most need to add to your time with God?
  • How do you respond to dry mornings? What can you learn from Hudson Taylor’s experience with Numbers 7?
  • Does the morning watch feel to you more like a gift or a rule? Why?

A step for this week

Set your alarm fifteen minutes earlier for the next six days, and choose one place where you will meet God each morning. Each day, follow this simple pattern: one minute of stillness, praying “Lord, here I am before Your face”; a few minutes of worship, reading aloud Psalm 100 or another psalm of praise; a chapter of Scripture, read slowly; and prayer that grows out of it, ending with a sentence of surrender such as “This day is Yours.” Write one line in a notebook each morning about what God showed you. If you miss a day, simply begin again the next.

study_questions.question: What is the morning watch?
study_questions.answer: The morning watch is a set time at the start of each day to meet God, bringing together hearing Him in His Word and speaking with Him in prayer. David wrote, "At daybreak I set everything out before You and keep watch" (Psalm 5:3). Jesus Himself rose "long before daylight" to pray in a lonely place (Mark 1:35).

study_questions.question: What should I do in a daily quiet time with God?
study_questions.answer: Most believers find five simple elements helpful: stillness ("Stop, and acknowledge that I am God," Psalm 46:10), worship, reading Scripture slowly, prayer that grows out of what you read, and a moment of listening. Worship begins with adoration and thanksgiving and ends in surrender, offering yourself as "a living sacrifice" for the day (Romans 12:1). Fifteen minutes kept faithfully is better than an hour attempted once and abandoned.

study_questions.question: Is it a sin to miss my morning devotions?
study_questions.answer: No. The morning watch is a gift and an invitation, not a law, and God does not love you more on the days you keep it or less on the days you miss it. Simply begin again the next morning, because God's mercies "are new each morning" (Lamentations 3:23). As Andrew Murray wrote, its real aim is not the quiet time itself but "to secure the presence of Christ for the whole day."

fields.title: Abiding in the Vine
fields.body_html:
“Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. A branch cannot bear fruit by itself; it must remain in the vine. In the same way, you cannot bear fruit unless you remain in Me. I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever remains in Me, with Me remaining in them, is the one who bears much fruit, because you can do nothing apart from Me.”

— John 15:4–5 (OWB)

Cut a branch from a vine and lay it on the ground. For a little while it looks the same as the others: the same green leaves, the same shape. But it is already dying. It has no root of its own. By the end of the day its leaves droop; within a week it is dry. It did nothing wrong. It simply stopped being joined to the vine.

On the night before He died, Jesus took this ordinary picture from the vineyards of Israel and used it to describe the deepest secret of the Christian life. We are branches. He is the vine. Our life, our strength and our fruitfulness all depend on one thing: remaining joined to Him.

The anchor of Part Two

John 15 gathers together everything we have learned so far in Part Two. In Chapter 5 we saw that love is the mark of a Christian; here Jesus says, “Remain in My love” (John 15:9). In Chapter 6 we learned to hear God in His Word; here Jesus speaks of “My words” remaining in us (John 15:7). In Chapter 7 we learned to pray; here Jesus promises, “ask for whatever you want, and it will be done for you” (John 15:7). In Chapter 8 we learned to meet God each morning; here we learn how to carry that meeting into every hour of the day.

The picture has three parts. “I am the true vine, and My Father is the vine grower” (John 15:1). Jesus is the vine, the source of life. We are the branches, joined to Him and carrying His life into the world. And the Father is the gardener, who tends the vine with skill and care. The whole Trinity is at work here: the Son gives life, the Father tends, and, as Jesus teaches in the chapters around this one, the Spirit lives within us to make Christ’s presence real.

What it means to remain

Older English Bibles use the word abide, and many Christians still speak of “abiding in Christ.” The Open Word Bible uses the plainer word remain. Both mean the same thing: to stay, to dwell, to make your home. A branch does not visit the vine now and then. It stays joined, day and night, in every season.

Notice that Jesus does not say, “Become joined to Me,” as if we had to work our way in. If you belong to Christ, you are already in Him. The Father has joined you to the vine by grace, through faith. Jesus says, “Remain.” Stay where you have been placed. Keep drawing your life from Him.

Andrew Murray, the South African pastor whose books on the inner life have been loved for well over a century, wrote that many believers trust Christ for pardon yet have hardly realised the closeness He offers. In Abide in Christ he puts the promise simply: “only abiding in Jesus gives rest in Him.”

How, then, do we remain? John 15:7 gives a beautiful answer: “If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask for whatever you want, and it will be done for you.” Here the Word and prayer are joined together. His words remain in us when we read, meditate on and memorise Scripture, as we learned in Chapter 6. And when His words fill us, our prayers begin to match His will, so that we can ask with confidence, as we saw in Chapter 7.

Jesus adds a third thread: love and obedience. “You will remain in My love if you keep My commandments, just as I have kept the commandments My Father gave Me and remain in His love” (John 15:10). Remaining is not a feeling. It is a life of trusting, listening, praying and obeying. Elsewhere He said, “Anyone who loves Me will keep My word. My Father will love them, and We will come to them and make Our dwelling place with them” (John 14:23). When we remain in Him, God makes His home in us.

Pruning: when the gardener cuts

“He takes away any branch in Me that bears no fruit, and He prunes clean every branch that does bear fruit, so that it will bear more fruit” (John 15:2). These are some of the most comforting and most uncomfortable words in the chapter.

Anyone who has grown grapes, coffee or tea knows that a plant left alone grows long, leafy shoots that use up its strength and bear little fruit. So the gardener takes his knife and cuts. To a watching child it looks cruel. Healthy green growth falls to the ground. But the gardener knows what he is doing. Next season there will be more fruit, not less.

Andrew Murray lived in Wellington in the Cape, surrounded by vineyards, and watched the vine growers at work. In The True Vine he noticed something surprising about pruning:

“It is not the removal of weeds or thorns, or anything from without that may hinder the growth. No; it is the cutting off of the long shoots of the previous year, the removal of something that comes from within, that has been produced by the life of the vine itself.”

Andrew Murray, The True Vine

God does not only cut away obvious sin from our lives. Sometimes He cuts away good things: a plan, a position, a comfort, even a ministry that has become too much our own. He does it so that the life of Christ in us will go into fruit rather than into leaves.

How does the Father prune? Murray points out that Jesus’ next words are, “Because of the word I have spoken to you, you are clean already” (John 15:3). The Word of God is the gardener’s first knife. In Murray’s own words, “it is the Word of God that is the knife.” As we read Scripture, the Spirit shows us what needs to go, and we let it go.

But God also uses hardship. Illness, loss, failure, disappointment and opposition can all become His pruning knife when they drive us back to His Word and closer to Christ. “At the time it is given, no discipline seems a matter for joy; it seems a matter for sorrow. But afterward it pays back those who have been trained by it with a harvest of peace: righteousness” (Hebrews 12:11). If you are going through a season of cutting, take heart. The knife is in the hand of the Father who loves you, and He cuts only branches that bear fruit, so that they will bear more.

Fruit that lasts

What is the fruit Jesus looks for? In John 15 He names at least three kinds.
