Love. “My commandment is this: love one another in the same way that I have loved you” (John 15:12). The first fruit of abiding is love, the mark of a Christian we explored in Chapter 5. Paul lists love first among “the fruit the Spirit produces,” followed by “joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Joy. “I have said this to you so that My joy will be in you and your joy will be complete” (John 15:11). Not the passing happiness of good circumstances, but the deep gladness of Christ Himself, which remains even in sorrow.

Answered prayer. “I appointed you for this: to go and bear fruit, and for your fruit to remain, so that the Father may give you whatever you ask Him in My name” (John 15:16). Prayer that grows out of abiding is prayer that God delights to answer.

Notice, too, that the fruit is for others. A vine does not eat its own grapes. The fruit of our lives feeds our families, our churches, our neighbours and the world. And it brings glory to God: “This is how My Father is glorified: that you bear much fruit and so prove to be My disciples” (John 15:8).

How do we bear such fruit? Not by straining. A branch does not grit its teeth to make grapes. It simply stays joined to the vine, and the sap does the rest. Hannah Whitall Smith, the American writer whose book on trusting God has helped many anxious believers, described those who grow well in Christ this way:

“Their Lord told them to abide in Him. He promised that if they did, they would bear much fruit. They focus only on abiding, which is their part. They leave the rest to their good Husbandman, who alone can manage it.”

Hannah Whitall Smith, The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life

“Apart from Me,” Jesus said, “you can do nothing” (John 15:5). That is not a threat. It is a relief. The burden of fruitfulness is not on us. Our part is to remain.

From servants to friends

Then Jesus says something astonishing. “I do not call you servants any longer, since a servant is not aware of what his master is doing. I have called you friends instead, because I have made known to you everything I heard from My Father” (John 15:15).

A servant does what he is told without knowing why. A friend is let into the master’s heart. Jesus, the eternal Son of God, calls His disciples friends. He shares His purposes with them. He laid down His life for them: “No one has a love greater than this: that someone lays down their life for their friends” (John 15:13).

This changes how we live before God’s face. We do not come to Him as nervous workers waiting for orders, but as friends who are glad to be with Him. Obedience remains: “You are My friends if you carry out what I command you” (John 15:14). But it is the obedience of friendship, freely given, not the obedience of fear. Abiding is friendship with Jesus, lived out all day long.

Brother Lawrence: God among the pots and pans

How do we carry that friendship from the quiet of the morning watch into a busy day? Few people have answered that question more simply than a kitchen worker in seventeenth-century Paris.

He was born Nicolas Herman, in the region of Lorraine in eastern France, around 1614. As a young man he served as a soldier. At about eighteen something happened that changed his life. He later told a friend that one winter he saw a tree stripped of its leaves. He thought about how, in a little while, the leaves would return, and then the flowers and the fruit. In that bare tree he saw the power and care of God, and a love for God was kindled in him that never left.

After some years, including a time as a footman, he entered a community of Carmelite brothers in Paris as a lay brother, taking the name Lawrence. He was not a priest or a scholar. He described himself, with good humour, as “a great awkward fellow who broke everything.” He was given work in the kitchen, a job he naturally disliked, and he served there for about fifteen years. Later he repaired sandals for the community. He died in 1691.

Yet people came from far away to speak with this humble cook. A church official named Joseph de Beaufort visited him, recorded their conversations, and after his death gathered these together with some of Lawrence’s letters. The little book became known as The Practice of the Presence of God, and it has been read by Christians of many traditions ever since.

Lawrence’s secret was simple. He resolved to live in a continual sense of God’s presence, talking with Him throughout the day as with a friend. When he began a task, he asked God for grace to do it well. When he finished, he thanked Him. When he failed, he confessed it simply and returned to God without despair. When his mind wandered, he gently brought it back. He believed, as Beaufort recorded, “that our sanctification did not depend upon changing our works, but in doing that for God’s sake, which we commonly do for our own.”

Those who watched him in the busiest hours of the kitchen saw a calm, unhurried man. Beaufort recorded his words:

“The time of business,” said he, “does not with me differ from the time of prayer; and in the noise and clatter of my kitchen, while several persons are at the same time calling for different things, I possess God in as great tranquility as if I were upon my knees at the blessed sacrament.”

Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God

He did not find this easy at first. In one letter he admitted that he “found no small pain in this exercise,” because his mind kept wandering. But he kept returning, again and again, and over the years it became the habit of his heart. He wrote to a friend in trouble that God “requires no great matters of us; a little remembrance of Him from time to time; a little adoration.” And he added, “It is not necessary for being with God to be always at church: we may make an oratory of our heart wherein to retire from time to time to converse with Him in meekness, humility and love.” An oratory is a small place of prayer. Lawrence carried his with him wherever he went.

Practising His presence through the day

Brother Lawrence shows us what abiding looks like on an ordinary weekday. It is the morning watch stretched across the whole day. Paul gives the same vision: “In everything you say and everything you do, act in the name of the Lord Jesus, and through Him give thanks to God the Father” (Colossians 3:17). David wrote, “I have placed the LORD in front of me at all times; since He is there at my right hand, I will never stumble” (Psalm 16:8).

Here are some simple ways to begin.

  • Begin each task with God. Before you start work, cook a meal, drive, study or open the shop, say a short sentence: “Lord, I do this with You and for You.”
  • Use ordinary moments as reminders. A ringing phone, a door, a church bell, a bus stop, washing your hands: let these become small signals to turn your heart to God for a moment.
  • Talk with Him as you go. Thank Him for small mercies. Ask for help with small problems. Tell Him what you see. You do not need special words.
  • Return without shame. You will forget Him for hours at a time, as everyone does at first. When you notice, do not scold yourself. Simply turn back, as Lawrence did, and say, “Here I am again, Lord.”
  • Close the day with Him. Before sleep, look back over the day with God. Thank Him for His presence, confess where you went your own way, and rest in His care.

The aim is not to think about God every second, which is impossible while we work. It is to live with a quiet awareness that He is near, as a child playing in the yard knows her mother is in the house.

Trusting Him in trials, decisions and disappointments

Abiding is tested when life is hard. When a child is sick, when a business fails, when we must make a difficult decision, when a hope collapses, the temptation is to stop remaining and start striving: to worry, to plan in our own strength, to pull away from the vine.

Scripture calls us back. “Trust the LORD with your whole heart, and do not rely on your own insight. Keep Him in mind in everything you do, and He will clear a straight road ahead of you” (Proverbs 3:5–6). In decisions, abiding means bringing the choice to God in prayer and in His Word, seeking wise counsel, and then stepping forward in trust, believing that He will guide us. In trials, it means staying close to Him when we do not understand, remembering that the gardener’s knife is in loving hands. In disappointments, it means pouring out our hearts honestly, as the psalmists did, and letting Him carry what we cannot.

“The mind that is held steady You guard in peace, unbroken peace, for it relies on You” (Isaiah 26:3). The branch does not have to understand the storm. It only has to hold on to the vine, or rather, be held by it.

This is the life of a disciple. “Anyone who claims to remain in Him ought to live in the same way that Jesus lived” (1 John 2:6). Jesus lived every moment in the presence of His Father. He invites us to do the same, through Him. In Chapter 10 we will look at the spiritual disciplines, the practices of grace that help us stay close to the vine through every season of life.

Questions for reflection

  • What would it look like for you to “remain” in Christ during an ordinary working day?
  • John 15:7 joins the Word and prayer. How are these connected in your own life with God?
  • Can you think of a season when God pruned something from your life? What fruit came from it, or might come from it?
  • Which kind of fruit, love, joy or answered prayer, do you most long to see in your life?
  • How does it change your relationship with Jesus to know that He calls you His friend?
  • What strikes you most about Brother Lawrence? What is one ordinary task you could begin to do “with God”?

A step for this week

Choose three ordinary moments that happen every day, for example starting work, sitting down to eat, and travelling home. Each time one of these moments comes this week, pause for a few seconds and speak to God in one simple sentence, such as “Lord, I am with You and You are with me,” or “Thank You for being here.” Before you sleep each night, look back and notice when you remembered Him and when you forgot, without blaming yourself. At the end of the week, read John 15:1–17 slowly and thank Jesus for calling you His friend.

study_questions.question: What does it mean to abide in Christ?
study_questions.answer: To abide, or as the Open Word Bible puts it, to remain, means to stay joined to Christ as a branch stays joined to a vine, drawing our life from Him. Jesus said, "Remain in Me, and I will remain in you" (John 15:4). We remain as His words fill us, as we pray, and as we keep His commandments in love (John 15:7, 10).

study_questions.question: What does pruning mean in John 15?
study_questions.answer: Jesus said the Father "prunes clean every branch that does bear fruit, so that it will bear more fruit" (John 15:2). God's first pruning knife is His Word, and He also uses hardship, illness, loss and disappointment when they drive us back to Him. It hurts at the time, but "afterward it pays back those who have been trained by it with a harvest of peace" (Hebrews 12:11).

study_questions.question: How can I practise the presence of God during a busy day?
study_questions.answer: Brother Lawrence, a cook in a Paris monastery, learned to talk with God through every task, saying that in the noise of his kitchen he possessed God as calmly as if he were on his knees. Begin each task with a short prayer, use ordinary moments as reminders, talk with God as you go, and return without shame when you forget. Paul puts it simply: "In everything you say and everything you do, act in the name of the Lord Jesus" (Colossians 3:17).

fields.title: The Spiritual Disciplines
fields.body_html:
“Train yourself in godliness. Physical training has some value, but godliness is valuable in every way, since it holds promise both for life now and for the life to come.”

— 1 Timothy 4:7–8 (OWB)

A young woman in Nairobi decides she will run the city marathon. On the first morning she runs as hard as she can, and after two kilometres she sits down by the road, chest burning, and decides she is simply not a runner. Her neighbour, who has run three marathons, tells her, “You cannot run forty-two kilometres by trying. You run it by training.” So she starts again, slowly, three mornings a week. Month by month her body becomes able to do what it could not do before. On race day she is not trying harder. She is a different runner, made ready by many small, quiet mornings.

Paul uses exactly this picture. He tells Timothy to “train yourself in godliness” (1 Timothy 4:7). In the last chapter we saw that the Christian life is not first about effort but about abiding in Christ, the true Vine (see Chapter 9). Branches do not strain to produce grapes. Yet the same Jesus who told us to remain in Him (John 15:4) also went often to lonely places to pray, fasted in the wilderness, and kept the rhythms of worship. Abiding has a shape. The spiritual disciplines are that shape: practices that put us before the face of God again and again.

Why disciplines matter: training, not trying

A spiritual discipline is a practice that we do, by God’s grace, to place ourselves where He can change us. It does not earn His love; in Christ we already have that. A discipline is like a farmer ploughing his field. He cannot make a single seed grow; only God gives life, rain and sun. But the farmer who never ploughs or weeds will have a poor harvest. He works with God, not instead of God.

The American teacher Dallas Willard spent much of his life explaining this. Many Christians, he observed, try to become like Jesus in the moment of crisis: patient when the boss insults them, kind when the child is screaming. And they fail, because they are trying to do by sudden effort what can only be done by training. Jesus’ public strength flowed from His hidden habits of solitude, prayer, fasting and Scripture. If we want to live as He lived, we must arrange our lives as He arranged His.

This is grace-filled effort. Paul writes as a runner:

“Every competitor holds back from many things in training. They accept this to win a wreath that soon withers; we, to win one that never decays.” (1 Corinthians 9:25)

Effort is not the enemy of grace; earning is. Peter says we must “put every effort into this: let your faith provide goodness, and goodness knowledge, knowledge self-control, self-control endurance, endurance godliness” (2 Peter 1:5–6). Grace is where we start and what carries us, but it does not make us passive.

Discipline is not always pleasant. “At the time it is given, no discipline seems a matter for joy; it seems a matter for sorrow. But afterward it pays back those who have been trained by it with a harvest of peace” (Hebrews 12:11). The first mornings of rising early may feel hard and dry. The harvest comes later.

The disciplines are often grouped in three families. The inward ones take place mainly in the heart: meditation, prayer, study and fasting. The outward ones shape how we live in the world: simplicity, solitude, silence and submission. The corporate ones we practise together: worship, confession, guidance and celebration. The Quaker writer Richard Foster made a grouping like this well known in Celebration of Discipline (1978), helping many Christians see these practices as the ordinary tools of God’s people.

The desert father: Antony of Egypt

To see a disciplined life, we travel to Egypt around the year 270. A young man named Antony, about eighteen or twenty, had lost his parents and been left land and the care of his younger sister. One day, walking to church, he was thinking about how the first Christians had sold their possessions for the needy. Athanasius, the great bishop of Alexandria who later wrote Antony’s life, tells what happened next:

“Pondering over these things he entered the church, and it happened the Gospel was being read, and he heard the Lord saying to the rich man, ‘If thou wouldest be perfect, go and sell that thou hast and give to the poor; and come follow Me and thou shalt have treasure in heaven.’”

Athanasius, The Life of Antony

Antony took the words as spoken to him. He gave his family’s land to the villagers, sold the rest of his goods and gave the money to the poor, keeping a little for his sister. Soon after, hearing the words “be not anxious for the morrow,” he gave away even that and placed his sister in the care of faithful Christian women.

What he did next is important. He did not rush off to be a hero. He went to learn from older believers living simple lives of prayer near the villages, watching each one carefully:

“He observed the graciousness of one; the unceasing prayer of another; he took knowledge of another’s freedom from anger and another’s loving-kindness; he gave heed to one as he watched, to another as he studied; one he admired for his endurance, another for his fasting and sleeping on the ground.”

Athanasius, The Life of Antony

He was not idle. “He worked, however, with his hands,” Athanasius writes, “and part he spent on bread and part he gave to the needy. And he was constant in prayer.” Later Antony went further into the desert, first to the tombs and then to an empty fort near the Nile, where he lived alone for about twenty years in prayer, fasting and the Scriptures. When his friends finally broke down the door, they expected a man wasted or broken. Instead they found him healthy, calm and warm: “neither fat, like a man without exercise, nor lean from fasting and striving with the demons.” His discipline had not destroyed him. It had made him whole.

The deserts of Egypt filled with men and women who wanted to learn the way of prayer, later known as the Desert Fathers and Mothers. Antony taught them that the battle for the heart is real, but God’s weapons are simple. “A good life and faith in God is a great weapon,” he told them, and he named the practices the enemy fears: “the fasting, the sleeplessness, the prayers, the meekness, the quietness, the contempt of money and vainglory, the humility, the love of the poor.” Fasting and prayer stand side by side with humility and love of the poor. The disciplines were never meant to make anyone proud.

Antony died around the year 356, near the age of one hundred and five. About thirty years later in Milan, a restless young teacher from North Africa heard the story of Antony from a visitor. That teacher was Augustine (see Chapter 2), and the story shook him deeply and played its part in his conversion. One Egyptian’s hidden, disciplined life helped to win one of the great teachers of the Church. Antony lived coram Deo, before the face of God, in the desert. God saw, and God used it.

You are probably not called to live in a desert. But Antony’s story teaches us three things. Disciplines begin with hearing God’s Word and obeying it. They are learned from others who are further along. And they are meant to make us more loving, not less.

The inward disciplines: fasting

Meditation on Scripture and the study of the Bible were taught in Chapter 6, and prayer in Chapters 7 and 8. Here we look closely at the inward discipline that many Christians today have never been taught: fasting.

What fasting is. In the Bible, to fast means to go without food, for a time, for a spiritual purpose. It is not a diet, nor a hunger strike to force God’s hand. It is turning from food, a good gift, to turn towards God with special focus.

Fasting in the Bible. Moses fasted on the mountain. David humbled himself with fasting when others were sick (Psalm 35:13). Ezra proclaimed a fast by the Ahava canal “so that we might humble ourselves before our God and ask Him for a safe journey” (Ezra 8:21). Jesus Himself “fasted forty days and forty nights” before His public ministry began (Matthew 4:2). The church at Antioch was worshipping and fasting when the Holy Spirit called Barnabas and Saul to their mission, and “after more fasting and prayer, they laid their hands on the two men and let them go” (Acts 13:3).

Most important of all, Jesus expected His followers to fast. He did not say if you fast, but when:

“When you fast, do not put on a sad face as the hypocrites do. They make their faces look gloomy so that others will see they are fasting. Truly I tell you, they have been paid in full. But when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face, so that no one but your Father, who is there in secret, will know that you are fasting.” (Matthew 6:16–18)

When people asked why His disciples did not fast, He answered that the wedding guests do not mourn while the bridegroom is with them, but “a time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them, and then they will fast” (Matthew 9:15). We live in that time now.

Its purposes. Scripture gives several reasons to fast: to humble ourselves before God, as Ezra did; to seek guidance, as the church at Antioch did; to express repentance; to strengthen prayer in times of great need; and to remind our bodies that we do not live by bread alone. Every pang of hunger becomes a bell calling us back to God.

John Wesley, who fasted regularly for most of his life, warned against making fasting everything or nothing:

“It is not all, nor yet is it nothing. It is not the end, but it is a precious means thereto; a means which God himself has ordained, and in which therefore, when it is duly used, he will surely give us his blessing.”

John Wesley, Sermons on Several Occasions

Its motives. Jesus’ warning in Matthew 6 is about motive: the danger is fasting to be seen or to win a prize from God. Through Isaiah, God rebuked people who fasted while oppressing their workers. The fast He chooses is to “loose the bonds that wickedness has tied” and to “break your bread with someone who is hungry” (Isaiah 58:6–7). A fast that leaves us proud or harsh has missed the point. Give away the money you would have spent on food, and your hunger becomes someone else’s meal.

Its forms. The Bible and the history of the Church show several kinds of fast:

  • A normal fast: going without all food, but drinking water. Most fasts in the Bible were of this kind, often from morning until evening.
  • A partial fast: going without certain foods, as Daniel and his friends ate only vegetables and water, or eating one simple meal in a day.
  • A longer fast: several days, rarely and with care.
  • A shared fast: a church or a family fasting together for a particular need, as the people did in the days of Ezra and Esther.

Many early Christians fasted on Wednesdays and Fridays until the afternoon. Wesley urged the same, telling those whose work or health would not allow it to fast “as often as thy strength will permit.”

Preparation. Do not begin with a long fast. Begin by missing one meal and spending that time with God, then perhaps try a day from one evening meal to the next. Decide beforehand what you are fasting for, and write it down. Plan your time of prayer and Scripture. Tell only those who need to know, such as your husband or wife, or whoever cooks for the household. End the fast with something small and simple.

Sensible health precautions. God gave us our bodies, and fasting must never harm them. Drink plenty of water during any fast. Some people should not go without food at all, or only with a doctor’s guidance: those with diabetes, those whose medicines must be taken with food, pregnant or nursing mothers, children, the frail elderly, and anyone who has struggled with an eating disorder. If you do heavy labour in the field or on a building site, a partial fast may be wiser. If you feel faint or very unwell, stop and eat. Others can fast from the phone, television, social media or a favourite food. The heart of fasting is the same: turning from something good to give more attention to God.

The outward disciplines: simplicity, solitude, silence and submission

Simplicity. Simplicity is the freedom of a heart that seeks one thing: the Kingdom first (see Chapter 12). Simplicity is not poverty. A businesswoman in Lagos can live simply, and a poor farmer can be eaten up by envy. It means owning things without letting them own us: buying what we need rather than what will impress, giving away what we do not use, and refusing debt to keep up with the neighbours.

Solitude. Jesus loved the crowds, but He also left them. “Yet He kept slipping away to places in the wilderness to pray” (Luke 5:16). When His disciples came back tired from their mission, He said to them, “Come away on your own, to a place without people, and get a little rest” (Mark 6:31). Solitude is not loneliness; it is being alone with God. For a mother of five in a small house it may be a walk to the borehole, prayed through step by step. For an office worker it may be lunch alone in the park with a Bible.

Silence. Silence goes with solitude. Many of us cannot be quiet for five minutes without reaching for the phone. Yet God says, “Stop, and acknowledge that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). Silence means stopping our own talking, out loud and inside, so that we can listen. The Imitation of Christ, traditionally credited to Thomas à Kempis, a fifteenth-century monk in the Netherlands, has helped believers for over five hundred years. It says:

“In silence and quiet the devout soul advances in virtue and learns the hidden truths of Scripture.”

Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ

Try it. Sit quietly for five minutes before you pray. At first your mind will run like a goat that has slipped its rope. Gently bring it back. In time the silence will become a place of meeting.

Submission. Submission is the discipline of laying down the need to have our own way. Paul writes, “And you will submit to one another in the reverent fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21). This does not mean putting up with abuse. It is freedom from the endless need to win every argument and to be first. Jesus, Lord of all, washed His disciples’ feet. When we yield in small things, such as letting a colleague’s plan go forward or listening before we answer, we learn His humility. Service is close kin to submission, and Chapter 24 will explore it fully.

The corporate disciplines: worship, confession, guidance and celebration

Some disciplines we cannot practise alone. As Antony learned from many older believers, so we grow best among God’s people.

Worship. Worship is the response of the whole person to the worth of God, and there is something special when His people gather. “Come, let us sing out with joy to the LORD and raise a glad shout to the Rock who saves us” (Psalm 95:1). The writer to the Hebrews urges us not to “walk away from our own gatherings, as some have made it their practice” (Hebrews 10:25). On the Sunday when we feel tired or discouraged, we go anyway, and often it is that very Sunday that God meets us.

Confession. James writes, “So make it your practice to confess your sins to each other and to pray for each other, so that you may be healed” (James 5:16). God forgives when we confess to Him, but there is special healing when we bring a hidden sin into the light before a trusted, mature believer, such as a wise pastor or an older friend. Sin loves the dark; confession opens the curtains. The East African Revival of the twentieth century was marked by this kind of honest walking in the light together.

Guidance. Sometimes God guides us through the counsel of the community. When the early Church faced a great question about Gentile believers, the leaders listened, prayed and searched the Scriptures together, and then wrote, “The Holy Spirit and we ourselves have decided” (Acts 15:28). Before a big decision, such as a marriage or a new business, invite two or three mature believers to pray with you and speak honestly.

Celebration. Joy is commanded: “Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: rejoice!” (Philippians 4:4). When Ezra read the Law and the people wept, Nehemiah told them to go and eat, drink and share with those who had nothing, “for the joy of the LORD is your stronghold” (Nehemiah 8:10). Without celebration the disciplines turn grey. A church that fasts must also feast.

Building a rhythm of life without legalism

Every good thing can be twisted. A discipline becomes legalism when we use it to measure ourselves against others, to feel proud, or to earn God’s favour, or when we load it onto others as a burden God never gave.

The answer is not to throw the disciplines away, but to hold them as gifts. A young climbing bean needs a frame, or it will sprawl on the ground and rot. The frame does not give the plant life, but it gives life a shape in which to flourish. A rhythm of life is a trellis for the soul.

It will look different for a farmer and a nurse, a student and a grandmother, but it might include:

  • Daily: a morning watch with Scripture and prayer (see Chapter 8), and moments of turning to God through the day.
  • Weekly: gathering with the church for worship, a time of rest, and perhaps a regular fast from one meal.
  • Monthly: a longer time of solitude, a half-day of prayer, or a fast day for a particular need.
  • Yearly: a time to review your life before God with a trusted friend.

Begin small. As Thomas à Kempis put it, “Habit is overcome by habit.” Choose one discipline you have neglected and practise it faithfully for a month before adding another.

When you fail, as you will, do not despair. Come back. Near the end of his life Antony urged the younger monks not to grow idle in their labours nor faint in their training. Grace meets us every morning. The disciplines are not a ladder to climb up to God. They are paths to the place where He has promised to meet us, before His face.

All of this belongs to a bigger calling. Jesus did not ask us to collect spiritual habits; He called us to follow Him. The disciplines are a disciple’s daily training, and Chapter 11 asks what it means to be one.

Questions for reflection

  • What is the difference between “trying” and “training” in the Christian life? Where have you been trying hard and failing?
  • What strikes you most about Antony’s story: his obedience to the Word, his learning from others, or his health and warmth after years of discipline? Why?
  • Have you ever fasted? Which form of fasting might be wise for you, given your health and work?
  • Which outward discipline do you most need at this stage of life: simplicity, solitude, silence or submission?
  • Who could you confess to, or ask for guidance from, among the believers around you?
  • How can you keep celebration alive so that your disciplines remain a joy rather than a burden?

A step for this week

Choose one day this week to fast from one meal, either breakfast or lunch, as your health allows. Write down beforehand one thing you are bringing to God. When the mealtime comes, spend that time reading Matthew 6:1–18 slowly and praying for the need you wrote down, and each time you feel hungry during the day, turn the hunger into a short prayer. Set aside the money you would have spent on that meal and give it to someone in need before the week is over.

study_questions.question: What are the spiritual disciplines and why do Christians practise them?
study_questions.answer: A spiritual discipline is a practice we do, by God's grace, to place ourselves where He can change us. It does not earn His love, which we already have in Christ; it is training rather than trying, like a farmer who ploughs while only God makes the seed grow. Paul tells Timothy to "train yourself in godliness" (1 Timothy 4:7), and Hebrews promises that discipline "pays back those who have been trained by it with a harvest of peace" (Hebrews 12:11).

study_questions.question: How should a Christian fast safely and with the right motives?
study_questions.answer: Biblical fasting is going without food for a time for a spiritual purpose: to humble ourselves, seek guidance, repent or strengthen prayer. Jesus taught that we should fast quietly, "so that no one but your Father, who is there in secret, will know that you are fasting" (Matthew 6:18). Begin by missing one meal, drink plenty of water, and do not fast without a doctor's guidance if you have diabetes, take medicines with food, are pregnant or nursing, are a child or frail, or have struggled with an eating disorder.

study_questions.question: How can I build a rhythm of spiritual disciplines without becoming legalistic?
study_questions.answer: A discipline becomes legalism when we use it to feel proud, to measure ourselves against others or to earn God's favour. Hold the disciplines as gifts, like a frame that gives a climbing plant a shape in which to grow, and build a simple daily, weekly, monthly and yearly rhythm. Begin small with one neglected discipline, keep celebration alive with "Rejoice in the Lord always" (Philippians 4:4), and when you fail, simply come back.

fields.title: What It Means to Be a Disciple
fields.body_html:
“Anyone who wants to come after Me must say no to themselves, pick up their cross every day, and keep following Me.”

— Luke 9:23 (OWB)

In many towns in Africa and Asia you can still see an apprentice at work. A boy of sixteen sits in a carpenter’s shed beside an older man. He does not attend lectures on carpentry. He watches how the master holds the plane, how he chooses the wood, how he measures twice before he cuts once. He sweeps the floor, fetches the nails, makes mistakes and starts again. He eats with the master and hears how he talks to customers. Over months and years, the way the master works slowly becomes his own way. One day a customer walks in and cannot tell whose table is whose.

That is the picture behind the word disciple. In the New Testament a disciple is a learner, a pupil, an apprentice. The word appears more than two hundred and fifty times in the Gospels and Acts. The word Christian appears only three times in the whole New Testament, and it was first a nickname: “It was in Antioch that the disciples first came to be called Christians” (Acts 11:26). People were disciples first. The name came later.

In the last chapter we looked at the spiritual disciplines (see Chapter 10). The two words share a root, and they belong together. Disciplines are the training; a disciple is the person being trained. But the heart of discipleship is not a set of habits. It is a Person. To be a disciple is to live every day with Jesus, before His face, learning from Him how to live.

The call to follow: more than belief

When Jesus called His first followers, He did not hand them a list of beliefs to sign. He walked along the shore of Galilee, found fishermen mending their nets, and said, “Come, follow Me... and I will make you fishers of people” (Matthew 4:19). They left their boats and went with Him.

Belief matters greatly. We are saved by grace through faith, and not by anything we do (see Chapter 3). But true faith is never merely agreeing with facts about Jesus. The demons believe that much. Saving faith is trust that attaches itself to Jesus and goes where He goes. It is like the difference between believing that a bus goes to Kampala and actually climbing aboard.

Jesus’ invitation is warm and gentle:

“Come to Me, all of you who are worn out with work and weighed down with burdens, and I will give you rest. Put My yoke on your necks and learn from Me, because I am gentle and My heart is humble.” (Matthew 11:28–29)

A yoke joins two oxen so that they plough together. A young ox was often yoked beside an older, steady one, and it learned by walking in step. Jesus does not send us out to plough alone. He invites us under His yoke, to walk beside Him and learn His pace. Discipleship is a whole-life apprenticeship to the gentlest and wisest Master who ever lived.

So the question is not only, “Do you believe in Jesus?” It is also, “Are you following Him? Are you learning from Him? Is your life slowly becoming like His?”

The cost of discipleship

Jesus never hid the cost. Large crowds were following Him on the road, and He turned and said something that must have shocked them:

“No one can be My disciple who comes to Me without hating their father and mother, their wife and children, their brothers and sisters, and even their own life. Unless a person carries their own cross and walks behind Me, they cannot be My disciple.” (Luke 14:26–27)

Jesus is not telling us to hate our families. He commands us to honour our parents and love our neighbours. He is speaking in the strong language of His culture, which compared loves by contrast. Next to our love for Him, every other love must look like hatred. He must come first, even before the people we love most and before our own life.

Then He told two short stories. A man who wants to build a tower first sits down and adds up the cost, or else he lays the foundation and cannot finish, and everyone laughs. A king going to war first sits down to see whether his ten thousand soldiers can face twenty thousand. Jesus concluded, “So it is with you: whoever does not let go of all that they have cannot be My disciple” (Luke 14:33).

Count the cost, Jesus says. Following Me will take everything.

In Luke 9 He names three parts of that cost. “Anyone who wants to come after Me must say no to themselves, pick up their cross every day, and keep following Me” (Luke 9:23).

  • Saying no to ourselves. This is surrender. It does not mean hating ourselves or pretending we have no needs. It means taking ourselves off the throne. My plans, my comfort and my reputation are no longer in charge.
  • Picking up our cross every day. In Jesus’ day, a man carrying a cross was walking to his death. He was not coming back. To take up the cross is to accept that following Jesus may cost us our status, our money, our friends, and for some, our lives. Notice the words every day. The cross is not one great moment; it is a daily choice.
  • Keeping on following. The cross is not the goal. Jesus is. We deny ourselves and take up the cross in order to walk behind Him.

And then the promise: “Anyone who sets out to save their own life will lose it. But anyone who loses their life because of Me will save it” (Luke 9:24). The way down is the way up. The life given away is the life truly found.

In the 1930s a young German pastor named Dietrich Bonhoeffer saw the churches of his country grow comfortable while a cruel government rose to power. Many Christians kept going to church and kept quiet. In his book, known in English as The Cost of Discipleship (1937), Bonhoeffer warned against what he called cheap grace: forgiveness preached without repentance, grace without the cross, Christianity without following Christ. Real grace, he said, is costly. It cost God the life of His Son, and it calls us to give our whole lives in return. It is grace because it gives us life; it is costly because it calls us to follow. Bonhoeffer trained young pastors in an underground seminary, joined the resistance to Hitler, and was arrested. He was executed in a concentration camp in April 1945, only weeks before the war in Europe ended. He did not simply write about the cost. He paid it.

The sadhu who followed: Sundar Singh

Few lives show both the cost and the joy of following Jesus as clearly as that of Sundar Singh of India.

He was born in 1889 in the village of Rampur in the Punjab, in northern India, into a wealthy Sikh family. His mother was a deeply devout woman. She would rise before daylight to read the holy books of her religion, and she taught her son that he must seek God before he ate breakfast. Sundar grew up hungry for God. He read the Hindu and Sikh scriptures late into the night and questioned his teachers, but none of them could give him the peace his heart longed for.

When he was fourteen, his mother died, and then his older brother. His grief turned to bitterness. He went to a mission school, but he hated Christianity. One day, in front of his father and others, he tore up a copy of the Gospels and burned it.

For two days afterwards he was miserable. On the third night, he rose at three in the morning, bathed, and prayed that if there was a God at all, He would show Himself. If no answer came by dawn, he had decided, he would lie down on the railway line in front of the early train. He prayed and waited. Then, he later wrote, a light filled the room, and in it he saw not one of the gods he expected, but the living Christ, who said to him, “Why do you persecute Me? See, I have died on the Cross for you and for the whole world.” Sundar fell on the ground before Him. In his own words:

“My heart was filled with inexpressible joy and peace, and my whole life was entirely changed. Then the old Sundar Singh died and a new Sundar Singh, to serve the Living Christ, was born.”

Sadhu Sundar Singh, With and Without Christ

Now he learned the cost. His family begged, threatened and punished him. When he would not turn back, he was cast out. On his sixteenth birthday, in 1905, he was baptised in an Anglican church in Simla. Soon after, he put on the saffron robe of a sadhu, a wandering holy man, so that he could carry the message of Jesus in a form that Indian people would understand. He owned almost nothing and walked from village to village preaching Christ.

One evening he returned to his father’s house. His father let him stay one night, but made him sit apart, as one who would pollute the family. He brought his son food, and gave him water by pouring it into his hands from a vessel held high above, as one would give water to an outcaste. Sundar wept. Yet he wrote that his heart was filled with peace, and he thanked his father both for his past love and even for this treatment, telling him that Christ had not forsaken him when he dishonoured Christ, and so he would not complain now. Then he slept under a tree in the fields.

On another night, after preaching until dark in a village near his old home, he lay hungry under a tree. He had eaten nothing all day. The tempter whispered that at home he had once had every comfort, and now he had nothing. Instead, joy rose in him so strongly that he began to sing, and he praised God until midnight. He wrote:

“When I had ease and comfort at home, I knew nothing of this wonderful peace. But now when all is gone I have found in Christ this peace, which the world can neither give nor take away.”

Sadhu Sundar Singh, With and Without Christ

Sundar Singh travelled across India and into the high, cold mountains of Tibet, where he faced great hardship and danger for his faith. In the early 1920s he was invited to speak in Europe, America and Australia, and crowds came to hear the simple man in the saffron robe. He warned Western Christians that he had met many who were Christians in name but had never known the living Christ. In 1929 he set out once more for Tibet and was never seen again.

Many years after his conversion, he wrote, his long prayer was answered and his father also turned to the Lord. Looking back on all he had lost, Sundar said that Jesus’ promise had proved true. Jesus said that anyone who has left home and family “because of Me and because of the gospel will receive a hundred times as much now, in this present time” (Mark 10:29–30), together with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come. Sundar’s comment was simple: “I have found not only a hundredfold, but a hundred times a hundredfold.” He also wrote about the cross in a way that only someone who had carried it could:

“Those who bear the cross know from experience that the cross bears them and takes them safely to their destiny.”

Sadhu Sundar Singh, Reality and Religion

Sundar Singh’s calling was his own. Not every disciple wears a saffron robe or walks into Tibet. But every disciple counts the same cost and finds the same treasure.

Learning from Jesus: His teaching, example and way of life

An apprentice learns in three ways: by listening to the master, by watching the master, and by sharing the master’s life. So it is with us.

His teaching. “If you remain in My word, you really are My disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will free you” (John 8:31–32). A disciple does not pick and choose among Jesus’ words. We sit under them, read them, memorise them and obey them. The next chapter will open up the greatest single block of His teaching, the Sermon on the Mount, which ends with the call to hear His words and put them into practice (see Chapter 12).

His example. After washing His disciples’ feet, Jesus said, “What I gave you was an example, so that you also would do as I have done for you” (John 13:15). We learn from how He treated people: the leper He touched, the woman at the well He spoke with, the children He welcomed, the enemies He forgave. In any situation we can ask, “If Jesus were living my life, in my house, at my job, how would He act here?”

His way of life. Jesus said, “Every disciple who is fully trained will become like the teacher” (Luke 6:40). The goal is not just to know what Jesus knew, but to become who He is: loving, truthful, humble, prayerful, brave. This is why the disciplines of Chapter 10 matter. Jesus slipped away to pray, fasted, knew the Scriptures deeply and kept the Sabbath rhythms. If we want His life, we take up His practices.

Discipleship is lifelong

No one graduates from following Jesus. The new believer who came to Christ last month is a disciple. So is the grandmother who has walked with Him for sixty years. Both are still learning.

Paul, after decades of faithful service, wrote:

“I do not mean that I already have all this, or that I have already been made perfect. But I keep pursuing it, trying to take hold of it, because Christ has taken hold of me.” (Philippians 3:12)

This brings both comfort and challenge. The comfort is that you do not have to be mature to begin. Jesus called fishermen, tax collectors and zealots who argued about who was greatest. He was patient with them, and He will be patient with you. The challenge is that we must never stop growing. Some Christians stop learning after the first few years. They know the songs and the language, but their character has not changed in a long time. A disciple keeps asking, “Lord, what do You want to teach me now?”

Discipleship also looks different in each season of life. For a young believer it may mean learning to pray and read the Bible. For a young couple it may mean following Jesus in marriage and money. For a worker it may mean honesty when everyone else is cutting corners. For an older saint it may mean faithfulness through illness and the quiet ministry of prayer. Each season brings new lessons and new ways to take up the cross.

Being discipled and discipling others

Jesus’ last command to His followers was about this very thing:

“Go, then, and make disciples of all the nations: baptize them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teach them to keep everything I have commanded you. And remember this: I Myself am with you every day, until the close of the age.” (Matthew 28:19–20)

Notice that Jesus did not tell us to make converts or fill buildings. He told us to make disciples, and He described how: baptise them, and teach them to obey. Evangelism is the doorway (see Chapter 25), but discipleship is the house.

Paul shows the same pattern. He wrote to Timothy, “What you heard from me before many witnesses, pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). Count the generations in that one verse: Paul, Timothy, trustworthy people, and others. Faith is passed from life to life, like a torch passed from runner to runner.

This means two things for every believer.

You need someone ahead of you. Everyone needs an older brother or sister in Christ who can pray with them, answer questions, and speak the truth in love. If you have no such person, ask God for one, then look around your church for someone whose walk with God you respect, and ask if you can meet with them. In the eighteenth century, John Wesley organised his converts into small “classes” of about a dozen people who met every week under a leader. Each person was asked, in love, how their soul was doing. These simple meetings helped turn crowds of new believers into steady disciples.

You need someone behind you. You do not have to be a pastor or a Bible teacher to help someone else follow Jesus. A mother teaching her children to pray is making disciples. A believer in the office who invites a younger colleague to read John’s Gospel over lunch is making disciples. A farmer who prays every week with the young man who works his land is making disciples. Paul said simply, “Take me as your model, just as I take Christ as mine” (1 Corinthians 11:1). Ask yourself: who could I help to take one step closer to Jesus?

Discipling others is not about having all the answers. It is about sharing your life. Jesus “appointed twelve to be with Him” (Mark 3:14) before He sent them to preach. Being with comes before being sent.

Before His face, every day

A disciple lives coram Deo, before the face of God, not only in church but at the market, in the kitchen and in the fields. Sundar Singh’s father turned his face away. But Sundar had seen another Face, glorious and loving, and that Face was enough. This is the secret of the cost of discipleship. We can let go of everything because we have found Someone better than everything.

Jesus once compared the Kingdom to a man who found treasure buried in a field. “Full of joy, he went and sold everything he owned and bought that field” (Matthew 13:44). The man was not sad to sell his goods. He was full of joy, because he knew what he was getting. That is discipleship: not a grim duty, but a joyful exchange.

In the next chapter we sit down at the Master’s feet on the mountainside and listen to His teaching about life in the Kingdom of God (see Chapter 12). There we will see what kind of people His disciples are becoming.

Questions for reflection

  • How would you describe the difference between believing facts about Jesus and following Him as a disciple?
  • Jesus told us to count the cost. What has following Him cost you so far? What might it cost you in the future?
  • What part of Sundar Singh’s story speaks to you most, and why?
  • In which area of your life is Jesus calling you to say no to yourself and take up your cross today?
  • Who has helped you to follow Jesus? Who is ahead of you now, and who is behind you?
  • What is one way your character has changed since you began to follow Christ, and where do you most want to grow next?

A step for this week

Think of one believer who is a little further along the road than you, and one who is a little behind you. This week, contact the first and ask whether you could meet, perhaps every two weeks, to pray together and talk about following Jesus. Then invite the second to read Luke 9:18–27 with you over a meal or a cup of tea, and talk together about what it means to take up the cross every day in your own homes, work and town.

study_questions.question: What does it mean to be a disciple of Jesus?
study_questions.answer: A disciple is a learner or apprentice who lives with Jesus and learns from Him how to live. It is more than believing facts about Him; it is trusting Him enough to follow, as when He called the fishermen: "Come, follow Me... and I will make you fishers of people" (Matthew 4:19). We learn from His teaching, His example and His way of life, because "every disciple who is fully trained will become like the teacher" (Luke 6:40).

study_questions.question: What is the cost of following Jesus?
study_questions.answer: Jesus never hid the cost. He said, "Anyone who wants to come after Me must say no to themselves, pick up their cross every day, and keep following Me" (Luke 9:23): surrender of our own rule, a daily willingness to lose status, comfort or even life, and steady following. Yet He also promised that "anyone who loses their life because of Me will save it" (Luke 9:24), and Sadhu Sundar Singh found in Christ a peace that the world could neither give nor take away.

study_questions.question: How do Christians make disciples of others?
study_questions.answer: Jesus commanded, "Go, then, and make disciples of all the nations" (Matthew 28:19), by baptising and teaching people to obey Him. Paul passed the faith on through generations: "pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well" (2 Timothy 2:2). Every believer needs someone further along to learn from and someone behind to help, and discipling is mainly about sharing your life, not having all the answers.

fields.title: Kingdom Life: The Sermon on the Mount
fields.body_html:
“Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up onto the mountain. He sat down, and His disciples came to Him. And He began to teach them: ‘Blessed are those who are poor in spirit: the kingdom of heaven is theirs.’”

— Matthew 5:1–3 (OWB)

When a new government comes to power, it often publishes a manifesto: a statement of what it stands for and how the country will be run. In Matthew 5 to 7, Jesus gives the manifesto of the Kingdom of God. He sits on a hillside in Galilee, as teachers did in His day, with His disciples close around Him and the crowds listening behind. What He says turns the world’s ideas of success, power and happiness upside down.

In the last chapter we saw that a disciple is an apprentice of Jesus (see Chapter 11). Here we sit at the Master’s feet and listen. The Sermon on the Mount is not a list of rules for earning heaven. It is a portrait of the life Jesus is creating in His people, a life lived openly before the face of the Father who “sees what is hidden” (Matthew 6:4). Augustine of North Africa, early in his ministry, wrote a whole commentary on these chapters and called them a perfect pattern for the Christian life. John Wesley preached thirteen sermons on them. He insisted that the sermon must be taken whole, because its parts are:

“all joined as the stones in an arch, of which you cannot take one away, without destroying the whole fabric.”

John Wesley, Sermons on Several Occasions

So let us walk through it, stone by stone.

The Beatitudes: the blessed life turned upside down

Jesus begins with blessing. Eight times He says blessed. The word means deeply happy, truly well off, approved by God. But listen to whom He calls blessed:

“Blessed are those who are poor in spirit: the kingdom of heaven is theirs. Blessed are those who mourn: they will be comforted. Blessed are the gentle: they will inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness: they will be satisfied.” (Matthew 5:3–6)

The world says, “Blessed are the rich, the confident, the strong, the ones who get their own way.” Jesus says the opposite. The poor in spirit are those who know they have nothing to offer God, and come to Him with empty hands. Wesley wrote that “the foundation of all is poverty of spirit.” Those who mourn grieve over sin and over the brokenness of the world. The gentle are not weak; they are strong people who have placed their strength under God’s control. Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness want God’s way more than food.

Then come the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers and the persecuted (Matthew 5:7–10). “Blessed are the pure in heart: they will see God” (Matthew 5:8). Here is the promise at the centre of this book: the face of God, seen by those whose hearts He has made clean.

Notice that these are not eight different kinds of Christian. They are eight sides of one character, the character of Jesus Himself. He was poor in spirit, mourned over Jerusalem, was gentle and humble, hungered to do His Father’s will, showed mercy, was pure, made peace and was persecuted. The Beatitudes describe what happens to anyone who walks closely with Him.

Salt and light: our influence in the world

Next Jesus tells His small band of followers who they are:

“You are the salt for the earth... You are the light of the world. A town built on a hilltop cannot be hidden.” (Matthew 5:13–14)

In a world without fridges, salt kept meat and fish from going bad. It also gave flavour. Light shows the way and drives out darkness. Christians are meant to hold back the decay of society and to show the way to God. But salt does nothing in the shaker, and a lamp under a basket helps no one. Jesus says, “Your light must shine where people can see it, so that they will see your good deeds and give glory to your Father in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Wesley understood this well. Some Christians in his day thought the holiest life was one hidden away from the world. He disagreed:

“Christianity is essentially a social religion; and that to turn it into a solitary religion, is indeed to destroy it.”

John Wesley, Sermons on Several Occasions

Salt and light mean honesty in the market when others cheat, kindness on the bus when others push, integrity in the government office when others take bribes. The goal is not our glory but our Father’s.

Jesus fulfils the law by taking it to the heart

Some people thought Jesus had come to throw away the Old Testament law. He corrected them at once: “I have not come to do away with them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). He then gave six examples, each setting what the people had heard beside His own words, But I tell you. Two of them show the pattern clearly.

Murder. The sixth commandment says, “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). Many people felt safe because they had never killed anyone. But Jesus said:

“You have heard what our ancestors were told: ‘Do not commit murder. Whoever commits murder must answer for it in court.’ But I tell you that anyone who is angry with a brother or sister will have to answer for it in court.” (Matthew 5:21–22)

Murder is not only the physical act. The anger that boils inside, and the contempt that calls another person empty-head or fool, break the same commandment in the heart. Murder begins there. Jesus goes to the root.

Adultery. The seventh commandment says, “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14). Again, many felt clean because they had never slept with another person’s wife or husband. Jesus said:

“You have heard the commandment, ‘Do not commit adultery.’ But I tell you, a man who looks at a woman with the aim of wanting her for himself has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” (Matthew 5:27–28)

Adultery is not only the physical act. Lust in the heart, nursed and enjoyed, is adultery too. In a world where images are a click away on every phone, these words are as urgent as ever.

The pattern. The Old Covenant mostly addressed outward actions: do not kill, do not steal, do not commit adultery. A person could keep the letter of these laws while their heart was full of hatred and lust. Christ goes to the heart. And He does not leave us to change our hearts by our own effort, which we could never do. Through the prophet Jeremiah, God promised a new covenant: “I will set My instruction deep inside them and write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). Through Ezekiel He promised, “I will give you a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). This is what the Holy Spirit does (see Chapter 4). He writes God’s law within us, so that we begin to want what God wants. The Sermon on the Mount is not a heavier law laid on tired backs. It is a description of the new heart the Spirit is creating.

Loving enemies: Martin Luther King Jr.

The last of Jesus’ six examples is the hardest of all:

“You have heard the saying, ‘Love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I tell you: love your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you, so that you will be children of your Father in heaven.” (Matthew 5:43–45)

In the twentieth century, few people put these words to a harder public test than an American Baptist pastor named Martin Luther King Jr.

In 1954, at the age of twenty-five, King became pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, Alabama. The southern United States was then ruled by segregation laws. Black citizens were forced to sit at the back of city buses and give up their seats to white passengers. In December 1955, a woman named Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat and was arrested. The Black community of Montgomery decided to stop riding the buses altogether, and they chose the young pastor King to lead them.

For more than a year, thousands of people walked to work, sometimes many miles a day, or shared cars. Their leaders were arrested and threatened. On the night of 30 January 1956, while King was speaking at a meeting, a bomb exploded on the porch of his home. His wife Coretta and their baby daughter were inside. By God’s mercy, no one was hurt.

When King reached home, a large and angry crowd had gathered. Some carried guns and knives. The police were nervous, and violence could have broken out at any moment. King stood on the damaged porch and spoke to the people. He told them that he wanted them to go home and put away their weapons. Violence, he said, could not solve the problem. They must meet hatred with love. He reminded them of Jesus’ command to love their enemies. The crowd slowly went home.

The boycott continued. In late 1956 the United States Supreme Court ruled that bus segregation was against the law, and the boycott ended in victory after more than a year. King went on to lead a wider movement for justice across the nation, always insisting that it must be nonviolent. His approach had many roots. He had studied the work of Mahatma Gandhi in India, whose own thinking had been shaped in part by the Sermon on the Mount and by the Russian writer Leo Tolstoy’s reflections on it. But King himself pointed above all to Jesus. In a sermon later published as Loving Your Enemies, he taught that love for enemies is not a weak sentiment but the only force that can turn an enemy into a friend. He was jailed many times. In 1968, at the age of thirty-nine, he was shot and killed in Memphis, Tennessee.

King’s life shows that the Sermon on the Mount is not only for private devotion. It speaks to how we respond to injustice, how we treat those who wrong us, and how we work for a better society without becoming what we oppose. Paul puts it this way: “Do not let evil defeat you; defeat evil with good” (Romans 12:21). In many of our nations, believers face tribal hatred, political violence or religious persecution. Jesus’ command remains the same: love, pray, do good, and leave judgment to God.

Sabbath fulfilled in Christ

Before we go on to Matthew 6, we must consider an important question: how does Jesus fulfil the Sabbath? This is the book’s main treatment of rest, and it matters for every worker, parent and leader.

The fourth commandment told Israel to rest on the seventh day, for “the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea and everything in them, in six days, and on the seventh day He rested” (Exodus 20:11). Jesus kept the Sabbath, but He also taught that “the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is Lord even over the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27–28).

Faithful Christians understand the Sabbath in different ways. Some hold that Sunday is the Christian Sabbath. Others see Sunday as the Lord’s Day, distinct from the Sabbath. Others keep the seventh day, Saturday. The Appendix sets out these views fairly. Here is this book’s view.

This book’s view: Jesus is our Sabbath rest. He said, “Come to Me, all of you who are worn out with work and weighed down with burdens, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The letter to the Hebrews explains that the rest God offered Israel pointed beyond itself:

“So a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God’s people. For whoever has entered God’s rest has come to rest from their own works too, just as God did from His.” (Hebrews 4:9–10)

We enter that rest by trusting Christ. We stop working to earn God’s favour, because Jesus has finished the work. So every day becomes a day of resting in Him: relying on God for everything, abiding in Christ (see Chapter 9), and laying down the anxious striving that tries to carry the world on our own shoulders. Paul writes that the Sabbath was “a shadow of what was coming; the substance is Christ” (Colossians 2:17).

At the same time, regular physical rest remains God’s good gift and a wise rhythm for workers and leaders alike. God made our bodies to need sleep and a regular day of rest. A farmer who never stops, a trader who opens her stall seven days a week, a pastor who never takes a day off, will sooner or later break down. Resting regularly is an act of trust. It says, “God, the world does not depend on me.” Chapters 20 and 24 will return to this rhythm of work and rest. And whatever view we hold, we gladly gather with God’s people on the Lord’s Day to worship the risen Christ, and we give each other freedom: “Each person must be fully convinced in their own mind” (Romans 14:5).

Secret devotion: before the Father who sees

In Matthew 6, Jesus turns to three practices of devotion: giving, prayer and fasting. He warns against doing them to impress people:

“Take care not to put your righteousness on show for others to see. If you do, your Father in heaven has no reward for you.” (Matthew 6:1)

When you give, He says, do it quietly. When you pray, go into an inner room and shut the door. When you fast, wash your face so no one can tell (see Chapter 10). Each time the promise is the same: “Your Father sees what is hidden, and He will repay you” (Matthew 6:6).

This is coram Deo in its purest form. The hypocrite lives before the faces of people, performing for their praise. The disciple lives before the face of the Father. What matters is not what others see, but what He sees. That frees us. We no longer need to look spiritual. We need only to be honest with God.

In the middle of this teaching, Jesus gives us the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13). It begins, not with our needs, but with our Father and His name, His Kingdom and His will. Chapter 7 looked at it as a model for our own praying.

Treasure in heaven and freedom from worry

Jesus then speaks about money and anxiety, two things that fill most people’s minds most days.

“Do not pile up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moths and rust ruin them and thieves dig through walls and steal them. Instead, pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where no moth or rust can ruin them and no thief can dig through and steal. Your heart will always be where your treasure is.” (Matthew 6:19–21)

He says, “You cannot serve both God and money” (Matthew 6:24). Money makes a good servant but a terrible master.

Then He speaks to the worried. Look at the birds, He says. They do not plant or harvest, “and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth far more than they are?” (Matthew 6:26). Worry cannot add a single hour to our lives. Instead:

“Above all, seek the kingdom and His righteousness, and you will be given all these things as well. So do not be troubled about tomorrow; tomorrow can take care of its own worries.” (Matthew 6:33–34)

Seeking the Kingdom first does not mean we stop working, planning or saving. It means God’s rule comes first in our decisions, and we trust Him for the rest. The mother worried about school fees, the young man anxious about finding work, the farmer watching the sky for rain: each is invited to bring that worry to the Father and seek His Kingdom first. Chapter 13 will show how this kind of trust grows.

Judging, asking and the narrow way

In Matthew 7, Jesus addresses how we treat others. “Stop passing judgment on others, so that you will not be judged” (Matthew 7:1). He pictures a man with a beam of wood in his own eye, trying to take a splinter out of his neighbour’s. This does not mean we never discern right from wrong. It means we deal honestly with our own sin first, and we never look down on others.

Then He invites us to pray boldly: “Keep asking, and you will receive. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and the door will be opened for you” (Matthew 7:7). If earthly parents give good gifts to their children, how much more will our Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him.

He sums up the whole law in one sentence, often called the Golden Rule: “So in everything, treat others the way you would want them to treat you” (Matthew 7:12).

And He warns us that this way is not the crowd’s way:

“Go in through the narrow gate. The gate that leads to destruction is wide and the road to it is easy, and many go in that way. But the gate that leads to life is narrow and the road is hard, and only a few find it.” (Matthew 7:13–14)

Building on the rock: hearing and doing

Jesus ends with a story every builder understands. Two men build houses. One builds on rock; the other on sand. From the outside the houses may look the same. Then the storm comes.

“So anyone who listens to what I have said here and acts on it will be like a sensible person who built a house on solid rock. The rain poured down, the floods rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house. But it did not fall, because its foundation was on rock.” (Matthew 7:24–25)

The difference between the two builders is not that one heard Jesus’ words and the other did not. Both heard. The difference is that one acted on them. It is possible to admire the Sermon on the Mount, preach it and even memorise it, and still build on sand. The storms of life, sickness, loss, temptation, persecution, will show which foundation we chose.

When Jesus finished, “the crowds were amazed at His teaching” (Matthew 7:28). The question for us is not whether we are amazed, but whether we will build.

This is a high calling, and no one keeps it by their own strength. It calls for faith: trust in the Father who feeds the birds, hears our prayers and sees in secret. That is where we turn next, in Chapter 13.

Questions for reflection

  • Which of the Beatitudes describes you most, and which least? What would it look like for that missing quality to grow in you?
  • Where is God calling you to be salt and light: at home, at work, in your community?
  • Jesus took the commands about murder and adultery to the heart. Where do anger, contempt or lust need His healing in your heart?
  • What did Martin Luther King Jr.’s response to the bombing of his home teach you about loving enemies? Who is your “enemy” today?
  • How can you rest in Christ every day, and how can you build a wise rhythm of physical rest into your week?
  • In what area of life have you been hearing Jesus’ words without acting on them?

A step for this week

Read the whole Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 5 to 7, once this week in a single sitting; it takes about twenty minutes. As you read, ask the Holy Spirit to show you one teaching you are not yet putting into practice. Write it down, and choose one specific action to obey it before the week ends: forgiving someone, giving in secret, praying for an enemy, or laying down a worry before your Father. Then take one evening or half-day this week to rest from work completely, and use part of it to thank God that He holds your life.

study_questions.question: What is the main message of the Sermon on the Mount?
study_questions.answer: In Matthew 5 to 7 Jesus gives the manifesto of the Kingdom of God: a portrait of the life He creates in His people, not a list of rules for earning heaven. It turns the world's ideas upside down, blessing the poor in spirit, the mourners and the gentle, and it calls us to live before the Father who "sees what is hidden" (Matthew 6:4). It ends with the call to build on rock by hearing Jesus' words and acting on them (Matthew 7:24).

study_questions.question: How did Jesus fulfil the law in the Sermon on the Mount?
study_questions.answer: Jesus said, "I have not come to do away with them but to fulfill them" (Matthew 5:17), and He took the commandments to the heart. Murder is not only the physical act, because anger and contempt break the commandment too; adultery is not only the physical act, because lust in the heart is adultery too (Matthew 5:21-22, 27-28). The Old Covenant addressed outward actions, but God promised, "I will set My instruction deep inside them and write it on their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:33), which the Holy Spirit now does.

study_questions.question: Do Christians still need to keep the Sabbath?
study_questions.answer: Christians hold several views, set out in the Appendix. This book's view is that Jesus is our Sabbath rest: "So a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God's people" (Hebrews 4:9), and we enter it by trusting Christ, so every day becomes a day of resting in Him and relying on God for everything. Regular physical rest remains God's good gift and a wise rhythm for workers and leaders, and we gladly gather on the Lord's Day while respecting each other's conscience (Romans 14:5).

fields.title: Faith and Trusting God
fields.body_html:
“And no one can please God without faith, since anyone who approaches God has to believe both that He exists and that He repays those who search for Him.”

— Hebrews 11:6 (OWB)

A tired woman walks into a village church and sits down on a wooden bench at the back. She does not first examine the bench, test its legs or ask who made it. She simply sits, and the bench holds her. She may know nothing about carpentry. Her faith is not in her knowledge, or in how strongly she feels about benches. It is in the bench. And because it holds, she can rest.

That simple picture tells us a great deal about faith. In the last chapter Jesus told His disciples not to worry, but to seek first the Kingdom of God and trust their Father for everything else (see Chapter 12). That is easy to say on a calm day. It is harder when the school fees are due, the harvest has failed, the diagnosis is frightening, or the job has gone. This chapter asks what faith really is, how it grows, and how we can trust God in the details of daily life. To live coram Deo, before the face of God, is to live by faith, because the God whose face we seek is unseen. “We make our way by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7).

What biblical faith is, and what it is not

The great chapter on faith in the Bible, Hebrews 11, begins with a definition:

“Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for, the proof of realities we do not see.” (Hebrews 11:1)

Faith is assurance. It is a settled confidence that God’s promises are true, even when we cannot yet see them fulfilled. It treats unseen things as real, because God has spoken.

Then comes our opening verse. Without faith it is impossible to please God, because “anyone who approaches God has to believe both that He exists and that He repays those who search for Him” (Hebrews 11:6). Notice the two parts. Faith believes that God is: that He is real, present and exactly who He says He is. And faith believes that God rewards those who seek Him: that He is good, that He cares, and that coming to Him is never wasted.

It also helps to say what faith is not.

  • Faith is not a feeling. Feelings rise and fall with our health, the weather and the news. Faith rests on God’s Word, not on our mood. Some days we feel full of faith and are not; other days we feel weak and are trusting God more than we know.
  • Faith is not positive thinking. Telling yourself that all will be well is not biblical faith. Faith is not confidence in our own minds; it is confidence in God.
  • Faith is not a force to make God do what we want. Some teachers suggest that if we believe hard enough, God must give us wealth or health. But faith does not control God. It trusts Him, even when His answer is “no” or “wait.”
  • Faith is not blind. It does not ignore facts. It sees the facts clearly and then sees something bigger: the faithfulness of God.

The strength of faith lies not in how much faith we have, but in whom we trust. Jesus said that faith even “the size of a mustard seed” (Matthew 17:20) can move mountains. A small faith in a great God achieves more than great faith in a small god. When a desperate father cried to Jesus, “I believe! Help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24), Jesus did not send him away. He healed his son.

Abraham, the father of faith

The Bible’s great example of faith is Abraham. When God called him, he was living comfortably in Mesopotamia. God told him to leave his country and go to a land He would show him. “By faith Abraham obeyed God’s call to leave for a land he would later be given as his own, and he set out without knowing where he was headed” (Hebrews 11:8).

Years passed, and Abraham and Sarah still had no child. One night God took him outside and told him to count the stars, if he could. God said, “Your descendants will be like that” (Genesis 15:5). And then comes one of the most important sentences in the whole Bible:

“Abram put his trust in the LORD, and the LORD counted it to his credit as righteousness.” (Genesis 15:6)

Abraham did not earn God’s approval by his good works. He believed God’s promise, and God counted him righteous. This is the gospel in seed form. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 4 to show that we too are made right with God through faith in Christ.

But Abraham’s faith did not stop at that first moment. It was tested for years. He was nearly a hundred years old, and Sarah was long past the age of having children. Paul writes:

“His faith did not weaken when he looked at his own body, as good as dead now that he was about a hundred years old, or at the deadness of Sarah’s womb. He did not doubt God’s promise or waver in unbelief. Instead he grew strong in faith and gave glory to God, fully convinced that God had the power to carry out what He had promised.” (Romans 4:19–21)

Abraham did not pretend the facts were different. He looked straight at them. Then he looked at God, and God was bigger.

Faith that grows through the Word and through testing

How does faith grow? The Bible gives two main answers.

Through hearing God’s Word. “So faith comes from hearing the message, and the message is heard through the word about Christ” (Romans 10:17). We cannot trust a God we do not know, and we come to know Him through His Word. Every promise we read, every story of His faithfulness, every revelation of His character, feeds our faith. That is why the daily reading of Scripture (see Chapter 6) is not just a religious duty. It is how trust is built.

Through testing. James writes something surprising:

“My brothers and sisters, whenever you find yourselves in trials of every sort, regard it as a reason for great joy, because you know that the testing your faith goes through produces endurance.” (James 1:2–3)

A muscle grows by being stretched under weight. A young tree sends its roots deeper when the wind blows. In the same way, faith grows strong when it is tested. Peter says that faith “once tested and shown to be genuine” (1 Peter 1:7) is worth far more than gold.

George Müller, whose story we tell below, wrote from long experience:

“Wherever God has given faith, it is given, among other reasons, for the very purpose of being tried.”

George Müller, The Life of Trust

He added that God tests us gently at first, little by little, as a wise teacher gives a pupil harder lessons only as they grow. If you are in a trial today, it does not mean God has forgotten you. It may mean He is strengthening you.

The orphan father of Bristol: George Müller

George Müller was born in 1805 in Prussia, in what is now Germany. As a young man he was a liar and a thief. He stole money from his own father, ran up debts at hotels he could not pay, and was once put in prison.
