He was studying theology at the University of Halle, but only because a pastor’s life seemed comfortable. Then, in 1825, a friend invited him to a small Bible study in a private home. He saw ordinary believers kneel and pray with sincerity, and something broke open in him. He gave his life to Christ.

Müller came to England as a young missionary and in 1832 settled in Bristol as a pastor. The city’s streets were full of orphaned children, many hungry and uncared for. Müller longed to help them. But he had a deeper reason for starting an orphan house. Many Christians he knew believed in God in theory but did not trust Him in practice. He wanted to give them visible proof that God still answers prayer. He wrote:

“Now, if I, a poor man, simply by prayer and faith, obtained, without asking any individual, the means for establishing and carrying on an orphan house, there would be something which, with the Lord’s blessing, might be instrumental in strengthening the faith of the children of God.”

George Müller, The Life of Trust

In April 1836 he opened his first orphan house in a rented building in Wilberforce Street. He made a firm decision: he would never ask anyone for money, never go into debt, and never make the needs known except to God. He would simply pray.

There were many hard days. His journal records one of them, in November 1838:

“Never were we so reduced in funds as to-day. There was not a single halfpenny in hand between the matrons of the three houses.”

George Müller, Answers to Prayer

That afternoon Müller prayed with his fellow workers and told them they must wait and see how the Lord would help. He felt cold and decided to walk home the long way. Twenty yards from his door, he met a believer who had twice called at his house while he was out. The man gave him money for the poor, and five pounds for the orphans. Had he come home half a minute later, Müller wrote, he would have missed him. “But the Lord knew our need, and therefore allowed me to meet him.”

The work grew far beyond anything he could have planned. From 1849 he built large orphan houses on Ashley Down, on the edge of Bristol. In the end five great houses cared for more than two thousand children at a time. Over his lifetime, more than ten thousand orphans were cared for, fed, clothed and taught. Every penny came in answer to prayer. Near the end of his life, Müller could write:

“Never since the Orphan work has been in existence have I asked one single human being for any help for this work; and yet, unasked for, simply in answer to prayer, from so many parts of the world, as has been stated, the donations have come in, and that very frequently at a time of the greatest need.”

George Müller, Answers to Prayer

Some people said Müller must have a special gift of faith that ordinary Christians do not have. He strongly denied it. The faith he exercised, he said, was “the self-same faith which is found in every believer,” and it had grown little by little over many years. His secret was not a special gift. It was a daily habit of reading the Bible, believing its promises and bringing every need to God. He died in 1898, at the age of ninety-two. He had lived his whole life before the face of a God he could not see, and he found Him faithful every single day.

Trusting God’s promises when circumstances say otherwise

There will be times when everything you see seems to contradict what God has said. The promise says, “My God will fill every need you have” (Philippians 4:19), but the bank account is empty. The promise says He works all things together for good (Romans 8:28), but the doctor’s report is bad.

The prophet Habakkuk faced such a time. He saw a terrible invasion coming on his people, and he could not understand why God would allow it. But at the end of his book he wrote one of the bravest songs of faith ever sung:

“Though the fig tree does not flower and the vines bear no grapes, though the olive harvest fails and the fields yield nothing to eat, though the sheep vanish from the pen and the stalls hold no cattle, yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will find joy in God, my Savior.” (Habakkuk 3:17–18)

Any farmer understands what Habakkuk is describing: total failure of every crop and every animal. Yet he says, “yet I will rejoice in the LORD” (Habakkuk 3:18). His joy is not in the harvest. It is in God.

Faith in hard times does not deny the pain. It holds on to God’s character. “God is not a human, who might lie, nor a mortal, who might change course” (Numbers 23:19). If He has promised, He will keep His word, in His way and in His time, which is always best. Sometimes the answer comes quickly, as it did for Müller on the cold walk home. Sometimes it comes after many years, as it did for Abraham. And sometimes, as Hebrews says of many faithful people, they “did not receive what was promised, but they saw it from far off and welcomed it” (Hebrews 11:13). Faith trusts God even with the promises that will only be fulfilled in eternity.

Living by faith in finances, decisions and calling

Faith is not only for great crises. It is for ordinary days.

In finances. Müller’s way of never asking for money was a special calling. Not everyone is called to run an orphanage without appeals or salary. But every believer is called to trust God with money. That means working honestly and diligently, giving generously, avoiding debts we cannot repay, and bringing our needs to God in prayer before we panic. Hudson Taylor, the pioneer missionary to China, learned this before he ever left England. As a young medical assistant, he decided not to remind his employer when his salary was due, but to ask God to remind him instead. He wrote that his aim was to learn:

“to move man, through God, by prayer alone.”

Hudson Taylor, A Retrospect

In decisions. Proverbs gives a promise many believers hold close:

“Trust the LORD with your whole heart, and do not rely on your own insight. Keep Him in mind in everything you do, and He will clear a straight road ahead of you.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

This does not mean we stop thinking. God gave us minds. It means we do not lean on our own understanding alone. We pray, seek His Word, ask counsel, and then step forward trusting Him to guide and correct us.

In calling. Sometimes faith means stepping into something God has called us to when the way ahead is not clear. Gladys Aylward was a parlourmaid in London, a servant who cleaned other people’s homes. She believed God was calling her to China, but a missionary society turned her down because they thought she could not learn the language. She did not give up. She saved her small wages, and in 1932 she set off alone, by train across Europe and Russia, with almost nothing. In China she worked with an older missionary at an inn for mule drivers, telling Bible stories to the travellers in the evenings. She learned the local language well, became a citizen of China, and took in orphaned children. During the war with Japan, in 1940, she led about a hundred children on a long and dangerous journey over the mountains to safety. An ordinary woman with an ordinary education trusted an extraordinary God.

Faith and works together

Some people worry that the Bible contradicts itself. Paul says we are saved by faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9). James says, “It is the same with faith: if it has no works, it is dead in itself” (James 2:17). Which is true?

Both are. Paul is speaking about how we are made right with God: not by our works, but by trusting Christ. James is speaking about what true faith looks like: it always produces a changed life. Paul himself says straight after, “For we are God’s own work. In Christ Jesus He created us for good works” (Ephesians 2:10). We are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone.

Think again of Abraham. He believed God’s promise, and that was counted as righteousness. But his faith also moved his feet. He left his home. Years later he obeyed God even when it seemed to cost him his son (Hebrews 11:17–19). His faith and his actions worked together.

Or think of Müller. He prayed and trusted God for every meal. But he also worked tirelessly, kept careful accounts, built houses, hired teachers and cared for each child. His faith was never lazy. Real faith works, and real works flow from faith. A tree is not made alive by its fruit, but a living tree will bear fruit.

Living before the unseen face

Faith, in the end, is how we live before the face of God while we cannot yet see Him. Abraham “set out without knowing where he was headed” (Hebrews 11:8), but he knew who was leading him. Müller did not know where tomorrow’s bread would come from, but he knew the Father who had promised daily bread. Gladys Aylward did not know the way over the mountains, but she knew the One who walked with her.

Faith says, “Lord, I cannot see You, but I know You are here. I cannot see the way, but I know You see it. I will trust You.” And God, who rewards those who seek Him, is pleased.

Trusting God also leads us into holiness. When we believe that God is truly good and truly present, we want to please Him, and sin loses its attraction. That is where we turn next, in Chapter 14.

Questions for reflection

  • How would you explain biblical faith to a new believer? What is faith not?
  • What part of Abraham’s story encourages you most in your own waiting?
  • What trial in your life right now might be God’s way of strengthening your faith?
  • What strikes you about George Müller’s story? Where do you need to bring a practical need to God in prayer rather than worry?
  • In which decision are you being tempted to lean on your own understanding alone?
  • How do faith and works fit together in your own life? Is there an act of obedience your faith is calling for?

A step for this week

Write down one practical need you are facing, such as money, work, health or a decision, and one promise of God from this chapter that speaks to it. Each morning this week, read that promise aloud and pray about the need specifically, telling no one else unless wisdom requires it. Then do the one practical thing that faith requires of you, whether a hard conversation, a job application or a budget. Keep a short record, as Müller did, of how God answers, and at the end of the week thank Him for what He has done and for what you are still trusting Him to do.

We are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone; it always produces a changed life.

fields.title: Holiness and Victory over Sin
fields.body_html:
“Be holy yourselves in all your conduct, just as the One who called you is holy, because it is written, ‘You are to be holy, because I am holy.’”

— 1 Peter 1:15–16 (OWB)

In Chapter 13 we learned to trust God: to take Him at His word when circumstances say otherwise. Now faith meets one of its hardest tests. Can God really change us? Not just forgive us, but change us, so that the sins we confessed last year are not still ruling us this year?

Many Christians quietly lose hope here. They believe God has forgiven them, but they have made a private peace with a temper that still flares or a habit that still wins in the dark. Holiness, they think, is for monks and missionaries, not for a trader with a family to feed or a nurse working night shifts.

The Bible will not let us settle there. God’s call is plain: “Be holy yourselves in all your conduct, just as the One who called you is holy” (1 Peter 1:15). And the God who calls us to holiness is the God who makes it possible. This chapter is about how He does it.

God’s call to be holy as He is holy

When Peter wrote those words, he was quoting the book of Leviticus. There God had told Israel, “You must be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). The word “holy” means set apart. A holy thing belongs to God and is kept for Him. The bowls in the tabernacle were holy, not because they were made of a special metal, but because they were set apart for God’s use and for nothing else.

So holiness begins with belonging: it is first a matter of whose we are. Paul could write to the church in Corinth, a church full of problems, and still say, “You have been washed clean; you have been made holy; you have been put right with God, in the name of the Lord Jesus and through the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

But belonging must show itself in living. A bride who has made her vows belongs to her husband on the wedding day. Over the years that follow, her love, her choices and her habits will show that she belongs to him. In the same way, God says to His people: you are Mine, now live like it. Peter says “in all your conduct”, which means in every part of life. Holiness is not only for Sunday. It reaches the market stall, the office computer, the conversation at the well and the thoughts we think lying awake at night.

This is where the theme of this whole book meets us again. To live coram Deo, before the face of God, is to live a holy life. We are not holy when people are watching and different when they are not. The writer of Hebrews puts it strongly: “Go after holiness, since apart from it no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14). The face we long to see is the face of the Holy One, and He is making us fit to see it.

What Christ did, and what He is doing

To understand holiness, we must hold two great Bible words side by side: justification and sanctification. They sound like long words for theologians, but they are simple and they are precious.

Justification is what God did for us, once for all, when we trusted Christ. He declared us righteous. He took our sin and laid it on His Son, and He took the righteousness of His Son and counted it as ours (see Chapter 3). A new believer who trusted Christ this morning is as fully justified as an old saint who has walked with God for sixty years.

Sanctification is what God is doing in us, day by day, for the rest of our lives. It is the work of making us actually holy, of shaping our desires, habits and character to look like Jesus. It grows, sometimes quickly and sometimes slowly.

The English bishop J. C. Ryle (1816–1900) wrote a famous book called Holiness, which is in the Ochorus library. He was worried that Christians in his day were mixing up these two things, and he set out the difference with great clarity. Here is part of what he wrote:

“Justification is the act of God about us, and is not easily discerned by others. Sanctification is the work of God within us, and cannot be hid in its outward manifestation from the eyes of men.”

J. C. Ryle, Holiness

Why does this matter? If we think our acceptance with God depends on how holy we have become, we will live in fear. But if we think that because we are justified, holiness does not matter, we will treat grace as permission to sin.

Ryle kept both truths together. Our standing with God rests entirely on Christ. And the same grace that forgives us also goes to work in us. As Paul wrote, “Keep working out your own salvation... For it is God who is at work in you, producing both the wanting and the doing, for His own good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). We work, because God works in us. Ryle also gave a definition worth memorising:

“Holiness is the habit of being of one mind with God, according as we find His mind described in Scripture.”

J. C. Ryle, Holiness

Notice the word “habit”. Holiness is not a feeling we have at a conference. It is a settled way of agreeing with God, of loving what He loves and hating what He hates, built up over years.

Dead to sin, alive to God

So how does God change us? Romans 6 is the great chapter on this question, and it begins with an objection. If grace is so generous, why not keep sinning and let grace keep covering it? Paul answers: “Certainly not! We are people who died to sin; how could we still be living in it?” (Romans 6:2).

Paul does not first tell us to try harder. He tells us something that has already happened. When we were joined to Christ by faith, we were joined to His death and His resurrection. “Our old self was nailed to the cross with Him, so that the body of sin would be stripped of its power and we would no longer serve sin as slaves” (Romans 6:6). The old “you”, the person who belonged to sin and could do nothing else, died with Christ. A new “you” has been raised with Him.

Think of a man who was once a slave on a farm. A law is passed that sets him free. The old master still shouts at him across the fence, and the old fear still rises in his chest, but the master has no more right to command him. He must learn to live as the free man he now is.

That is what Paul means when he says, “Count yourselves as dead to sin, and as living for God in Christ Jesus” (Romans 6:11). The word “count” is a word for accounts and money. It means to reckon something as true because it is true. We do not make ourselves dead to sin by counting. We count because God says it is so. Then Paul draws the practical conclusion: “Hand yourselves over to God, as people who were dead and are now alive” (Romans 6:13). And he gives a promise: “Sin will not be lord over you, for you do not live under the law but under grace” (Romans 6:14).

Paul says the same thing in his own testimony: “I am no longer the one who lives; Christ lives in me. Whatever life I still have in the flesh is a life lived by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and handed Himself over for my sake” (Galatians 2:20). Victory over sin is not mainly a technique. It is a Person living in us.

Watchman Nee: from struggling to seeing

Few people have helped believers understand Romans 6 as much as a young Chinese preacher named Watchman Nee.

Nee was born in 1903 and grew up in Fuzhou, on the south-east coast of China. In 1920, when he was seventeen, he heard the evangelist Dora Yu preach and gave his life to Christ. He threw himself into studying the Bible and preaching, helped greatly by an older English missionary, Margaret Barber, who lived simply and prayed much. Soon he was planting churches across China.

But Nee had a problem, and he was honest about it. He had been taught that the secret of victory was to “reckon” himself dead to sin, as Romans 6:11 says. So he tried. He tried for years. In The Normal Christian Life, a book drawn from talks he gave in the 1930s and now in the Ochorus library, he describes what happened:

“For years after my conversion I had been taught to reckon. I reckoned from 1920 until 1927. The more I reckoned that I was dead to sin, the more alive I clearly was. I simply could not believe myself dead and I could not produce the death.”

Watchman Nee, The Normal Christian Life

Perhaps you know that feeling. Nee describes believers who “begin to reckon furiously: ‘I am dead; I am dead; I am dead!’ but in the very act of reckoning they lose their temper.”

Nee became so troubled that he told the Lord he would stop preaching until he understood. For months he sought God, sometimes fasting. Then one morning, sitting at his desk upstairs, reading the Bible and praying, he cried out, “Lord, open my eyes!” He wrote:

“And then in a flash I saw it. I saw my oneness with Christ. I saw that I was in Him, and that when He died I died.”

Watchman Nee, The Normal Christian Life

What Nee saw was that Romans 6:11 rests on Romans 6:6. Counting ourselves dead does not make it true. We count it because it is already true. “Knowing” comes before “reckoning”. His death to sin was not something he had to produce by effort; it was a fact accomplished at the cross, to be received by faith. From that morning his whole Christian life changed. He did not become sinless, but he stopped fighting for a victory Christ had already won and began to live from it.

Nee’s later life was marked by suffering. Arrested in 1952 under the Communist government, he spent his last twenty years in prison and died in 1972, still a prisoner.

The soul under the Spirit’s rule

Nee had a second insight that many find helpful. In Chapter 4 we met his teaching that a human being is made of spirit, soul and body: the spirit is where we know God, the soul is our mind, will and emotions, and the body is our physical life. As we said there, many theologians see the human person as two parts rather than three, and both views are held by faithful believers. This book offers Nee’s picture as a helpful lens, not as a test of faith.

Through that lens, Nee taught that the problem in many Christians is not that the Spirit of God is absent. He lives in every believer. The problem is that the soul, our strong opinions, our stubborn will, our unruly feelings, stands in the way like a hard shell around a seed. In a later book, The Release of the Spirit, Nee wrote about the “breaking of the outer man”: God, in His love, uses the circumstances of life to break the hard shell of our self-will, so that the life of the Spirit within can flow out to others.

Jesus used a picture from the farm: “If a grain of wheat does not fall into the ground and die, it stays just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). A seed in a sack is safe and unchanged. Only when its hard outer case breaks open in the soil does life come out of it.

The Word of God plays a part in this too. “The word of God is alive and at work, and it has a keener edge than any two-edged sword. It reaches right in, cutting through soul and spirit” (Hebrews 4:12). When we read Scripture with open hearts, it shows us what comes from God and what comes from our own pride or fear. In The Normal Christian Life Nee tells of breaking a biscuit in half at a supper table and fitting the two halves back together. It looked whole, he said, but it was never quite the same again. In the same way, a believer whose self-will has been broken by God “will yield ever after to the slightest touch from God.”

This is not a call to crush our personalities. God wants our mind, will and emotions yielded to Him, so that we think His thoughts, choose His ways and feel what He feels. Chapter 15 will look more closely at how God heals and renews the soul.

Practical victory

Grace does not make us passive. The same Paul who said “count yourselves dead” also said, “If by the Spirit you keep putting the body’s practices to death, you will live” (Romans 8:13). The Puritan pastor John Owen (1616–1683) wrote a whole book on this verse, The Mortification of Sin, which is in the Ochorus library. “Mortification” is an old word that means putting to death. Owen did not soften the call:

“Do you mortify; do you make it your daily work; be always at it whilst you live; cease not a day from this work; be killing sin or it will be killing you.”

John Owen, The Mortification of Sin in Believers

Sin never stays small. Either we deal with it, or it slowly deals with us. Here are four ways God has given us to fight.

Confession. “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and righteous: He will forgive our sins and cleanse us from every kind of wrongdoing” (1 John 1:9). To confess is to agree with God about what we have done, calling it by its true name. Not “I was a bit short with my wife”, but “I was proud and cruel.” Sin loves the dark. Confession drags it into the light, where it loses its power. “Whoever hides their sins will not succeed, but whoever admits them and turns away from them will receive mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

Repentance. Confession names the sin; repentance turns from it. The Bible word means a change of mind that leads to a change of direction. If you have been cheating on your taxes, repentance means paying them. If you have been gossiping about a colleague, it means stopping, and perhaps apologising. Repentance is not a mood. It is a turn of the feet.

Accountability. God never meant us to fight alone. “Make it your practice to confess your sins to each other and to pray for each other, so that you may be healed” (James 5:16). One or two trusted friends who know your weak places, who will ask you hard questions and pray for you, are worth more than many good intentions. In the East African Revival, believers spoke of “walking in the light” with one another, drawing on 1 John 1:7. They found that sins brought into the open among loving brothers and sisters lost their grip.

Walking in the Spirit. “Walk by the Spirit, and you will never carry out what the flesh desires” (Galatians 5:16). Notice the order. Paul does not say, “Stop doing what the flesh desires, and then you will walk by the Spirit.” He says walk by the Spirit, and the desires of the flesh will lose their power. This means staying close to God through the day: a quick prayer before a hard meeting, a verse remembered in temptation. This is what Chapter 9 called abiding. Victory comes less from fighting sin directly than from being filled with something better.

God’s training

Sometimes holiness comes through hard things. Hebrews 12 calls these hard things discipline, the training a loving father gives his children. “God does it for what truly benefits us, so that we may come to share in His holiness” (Hebrews 12:10). Then the writer is honest: “At the time it is given, no discipline seems a matter for joy; it seems a matter for sorrow. But afterward it pays back those who have been trained by it with a harvest of peace: righteousness” (Hebrews 12:11).

A farmer prunes his coffee bushes and they look bare for a season, but they will bear more fruit. When God allows a loss or a long wait, He may be cutting away something that would choke our growth (see Chapter 17).

The same chapter of Hebrews gives us the secret of running the race: “Let us strip off every burden, and the sin that wraps itself around us so readily... Let us keep our eyes on Jesus” (Hebrews 12:1–2). Holiness is not mainly staring at our sins. It is fixing our eyes on Jesus. We become like what we look at.

Grace for when we fall

You will fall. Every believer does. John, who wrote so much about holiness, also wrote this: “I am writing this to you so that you will not sin. Yet if anyone does sin, we have an advocate in the Father’s presence, Jesus Christ, who is righteous” (1 John 2:1).

When you fall, the enemy will whisper that God is tired of you. Do not believe him. You are not condemned. “Those who are in Christ Jesus now face no sentence of condemnation. For in Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit who gives life has freed you from the law of sin and death” (Romans 8:1–2). Your standing before God’s face did not depend on your performance yesterday, and it does not depend on your failure today. It rests on Christ.

So get up quickly. Confess honestly. Make right what you can. Then go on, without wallowing. A child learning to walk falls many times a day, and a loving father simply picks the child up. Slowly, the falls become fewer.

Remember Nee’s lesson. The battle is real, but the decisive victory is already won. You are fighting from victory, not for it. Paul says that God sent His own Son “as an offering for sin, and in the flesh He passed sentence on sin. He did this so that the law’s righteous requirement would be fully met in us, who conduct our lives by the Spirit and not by the flesh” (Romans 8:3–4). What the law could not do, God has done.

To live coram Deo is to live as people already loved, already forgiven, already made holy in Christ, who are learning every day to become in practice what we already are in Him. In the next chapter we will see how this work reaches into the deepest places of the soul, including the wounds many of us carry from the past.

Questions for reflection

  • How would you explain the difference between justification and sanctification to a new believer? Why does it matter that we do not confuse them?
  • Is there a sin you have quietly made peace with, believing it will never change? What would it look like to bring it into the light?
  • Watchman Nee tried for seven years to “reckon” himself dead to sin before he saw that it was already true in Christ. How does knowing this change the way you fight temptation?
  • Where might God be using hard circumstances to break your self-will, as Nee described? How are you responding?
  • Do you have one or two people you can be fully honest with about your struggles? If not, who might you ask?
  • When you fall, what is your first response: hiding, despair, or running back to God? What does 1 John 2:1 say to you?

A step for this week

Choose one sin that keeps returning in your life, and fight it this week with the four weapons of this chapter. Each morning, read Romans 6:6–14 slowly and thank God that your old self was crucified with Christ. Each evening, confess honestly anything you have done, naming it plainly, and receive the promise of 1 John 1:9. Where you have wronged someone, put it right before the week ends. And before Sunday, tell one trusted, mature believer about this struggle and ask them to pray for you and to ask you about it again in a week’s time.

study_questions.question: What is the difference between justification and sanctification?
study_questions.answer: Justification is what God did for us once for all when we trusted Christ: He declared us righteous, counting the righteousness of His Son as ours. Sanctification is what God is doing in us day by day for the rest of our lives, making us actually holy. As J. C. Ryle wrote in Holiness, justification is the act of God about us, while sanctification is the work of God within us. Confusing the two leads either to fear or to carelessness.

study_questions.question: What does it mean to be dead to sin and alive to God?
study_questions.answer: When we were joined to Christ by faith, we were joined to His death and resurrection: "Our old self was nailed to the cross with Him, so that the body of sin would be stripped of its power and we would no longer serve sin as slaves" (Romans 6:6). So Paul tells us to "count yourselves as dead to sin, and as living for God in Christ Jesus" (Romans 6:11). Watchman Nee learned that we count it because it is already true, not to make it true. We fight sin from Christ's victory, not for it.

study_questions.question: How can a Christian overcome sin in practice?
study_questions.answer: God has given confession, repentance, accountability and walking in the Spirit. "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and righteous: He will forgive our sins and cleanse us from every kind of wrongdoing" (1 John 1:9), and James urges believers to confess their sins to each other and pray for each other. Above all, "walk by the Spirit, and you will never carry out what the flesh desires" (Galatians 5:16). When we fall, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, so we get up, confess and go on.

fields.title: Spirit, Soul and Body: Healing and Growing the Soul
fields.body_html:
“May the God of peace Himself make you holy in every part, and may your spirit, soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

— 1 Thessalonians 5:23 (OWB)

God does not save only a part of us. He does not rescue our souls for heaven and leave the rest of us to fend for itself. Paul’s prayer for the believers in Thessalonica reaches every corner of a human life: “May the God of peace Himself make you holy in every part, and may your spirit, soul and body be kept whole” (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

In Chapter 4 we met the idea that a human being can be described as spirit, soul and body. In Chapter 14 we saw how God makes us holy, breaking the hard shell of self-will so that His life can flow through us. This chapter brings those threads together. It asks a simple question: what is God doing with the whole of me, and when?

The answer has three tenses. God has made our spirit new. He is renewing our soul. And He will make our body new. Past, present and future. Seeing this pattern brings great peace, because it tells us where we are on the road, and it tells us that the God who started the journey will finish it.

The whole person

Christians have described the human person in two main ways. Some, like Watchman Nee in The Spiritual Man, see three parts: the spirit, by which we know God; the soul, which is our mind, will and emotions; and the body, by which we live in the physical world. They point to verses like 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and Hebrews 4:12, which speak of soul and spirit side by side. Many other theologians see two parts: an inner self, which the Bible sometimes calls soul and sometimes spirit, and an outer, bodily self. They point out that the Bible often uses “soul” and “spirit” for the same inner life.

Both views are held by faithful, Bible-loving Christians, and this is not a matter on which believers should divide (see the Appendix). This book uses the three-part picture as a helpful lens, as it did in Chapter 4. But if you hold the two-part view, you can follow every step of this chapter. Simply read “spirit” as the deepest part of the inner self, where we are joined to God, and “soul” as the inner self as it thinks, chooses and feels.

What matters most is what both views agree on. God made us whole persons. Sin damaged every part of us. And God’s salvation reaches every part of us too.

Spirit made new: what God has done

Before we came to Christ, the Bible says we were dead toward God. We could be very alive in every other way, clever at school, successful in business, warm to our families, and still be dead to Him. “But God is rich in mercy. Because of the great love He had for us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, He made us alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:4–5).

This is the new birth that Jesus described to Nicodemus: “Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh, and whatever is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6). At conversion something happened deep inside us that we could not do for ourselves. The Holy Spirit gave us new life and came to live in us. God had promised it long before through Ezekiel: “I will give you a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).

This is done. It is past tense. “If anyone is in Christ, that person is part of a new creation. The old things have gone, and look, new things have come into being” (2 Corinthians 5:17). On the day you trusted Christ, you were justified, declared righteous before God, and you were made alive to Him. “The Spirit Himself joins our own spirit in testifying that we are God’s children” (Romans 8:16). Nothing that happens to you later can undo this.

Soul being renewed: what God is doing

But if our spirit has been made new, why do we still struggle? Why does the believer still feel anxious, still lose his temper, still carry old fears? Because the renewing of the soul is a work in the present tense. It takes a lifetime.

Paul writes, “Do not let this present age press you into its mold, but be changed through and through as your mind is made new” (Romans 12:2). Notice the words “be changed” and “is made new”. This is something happening to us now, step by step. Our minds learn to think God’s thoughts. Our wills learn to choose God’s ways. Our emotions learn to rest in God’s love instead of being thrown about by every wind.

Think of a family that moves from a village into a new house in town. On the first day, the house is theirs. The keys are in their hand. But it takes months to feel at home: to learn which window lets in the morning light, to arrange the furniture, to stop reaching for a light switch where the old one used to be. In the same way, God has given us new life in our spirit, but our minds, wills and feelings still carry the habits of the old house. The Holy Spirit is patiently teaching us to live in the new one.

This is what the Bible calls sanctification, the work we looked at in Chapter 14. It is the slow, sure work of God in the present.

Augustine: a restless heart and a wounded soul

No one in the history of the Church has written more honestly about the inner life than Augustine, who was born in 354 in Thagaste, a small town in North Africa, in what is now Algeria. His father was a pagan, his mother Monica a praying Christian. He was brilliant and ambitious. He studied in Carthage, became a teacher of public speaking, and later moved to Rome and then Milan, where he won a respected post.

Outwardly he was a success. Inwardly he was in pieces. In his forties he wrote Confessions, which is in the Ochorus library. It is a long prayer to God, telling the story of his life. Its first paragraph holds the words we met in Chapter 2: God made us for Himself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in Him. Augustine knew that restlessness from the inside.

Augustine did not only write about sin. He wrote about wounds. As a young man in Thagaste he lost a close friend to fever, and the grief overwhelmed him. Everything he looked at reminded him of his friend. He wrote, “I became a great riddle to myself, and I asked my soul, why she was so sad, and why she disquieted me sorely: but she knew not what to answer me.” Many readers today know exactly that feeling: grief or pain so deep that we do not understand our own hearts.

For years Augustine tried to fill the emptiness with pleasure, success and clever ideas. Nothing healed it. He knew that the problem was not out there but within, and he could not fix it. Looking back, he wrote to God:

“Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee.”

Augustine, Confessions

The turning point came in a garden in Milan in 386. Augustine was weeping, torn between the life he wanted to leave and the God he could not yet trust. He heard a child’s voice from a nearby house chanting, “Take up and read.” He picked up a book of Paul’s letters and read words from Romans 13 telling him to put on the Lord Jesus Christ like clothing and stop making plans to satisfy the flesh (Romans 13:14). Light flooded his heart. He was baptised the following Easter.

That was the new birth, the spirit made alive. But the healing of his soul went on. Only months later his mother Monica died at Ostia, on the journey home to Africa. Augustine wrote that “my soul was wounded, and that life rent asunder as it were.” He did not pretend he was not hurting. He brought his grief to God in prayer and in the company of his friends, who sang a psalm together in the house.

Augustine returned to North Africa, and in 395 or 396 he became bishop of Hippo, the city he served until his death in 430. His books shaped the faith of the whole Western Church. Yet his greatest gift to ordinary believers may be his honesty. He shows us that a person can be truly converted and still need healing, and that God is patient with both.

Soul wounds and how God heals them

Many people come to Christ carrying deep hurts. A child who grew up with a father who drank and beat his mother. A woman abused by someone she trusted. A man who survived war or genocide and saw what no one should see. A young person crushed by years of being told they were worthless. Others carry wounds received inside the Church itself, from harsh words, betrayal or spiritual pressure.

These wounds are real. They shape how we see God, ourselves and others. A believer may know in her head that God is a loving Father, yet freeze inside every time she pictures Him, because the word “father” carries pain. Being born again does not erase memories in a moment. Sometimes God heals suddenly. More often He heals gently, layer by layer.

The good news is that healing the wounded is close to the heart of God. “He heals those whose hearts are crushed and bandages their injuries” (Psalm 147:3). When Jesus began His ministry, He read from Isaiah 61, which speaks of the Lord’s servant sent “to bandage hearts that are broken, to announce freedom for captives... to console all who grieve” and to give “the oil of rejoicing in place of grief, a cloak of praise in place of a spirit burning low” (Isaiah 61:1–3). Charles Spurgeon, preaching on Psalm 147:3, marvelled that the God who names the stars also cares for broken hearts:

“...the same mighty hand which rolls the stars along, puts liniments around the wounded heart.”

Charles Spurgeon, Healing for the Wounded

How does God heal the soul? The Bible and the experience of the Church point to several ways, which work together.

His presence. “He brings back my life and leads me in the tracks of what is right” (Psalm 23:3). Healing begins when we bring our pain into the light of God’s face instead of hiding it. Many of the psalms are wounded people telling God exactly how they feel. We can do the same. Jesus invites us: “Come to Me, all of you who are worn out with work and weighed down with burdens, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

His Word. Lies often lodge in wounded hearts: “I am unlovable”, “It was my fault”, “God has abandoned me.” Scripture replaces lies with truth. As we read, memorise and meditate on God’s Word (see Chapter 6), our minds are made new.

Forgiveness. Some of the deepest wounds come from what others have done to us, and some of the strongest chains are bitterness and the longing for revenge. Forgiving does not mean saying the wrong did not matter, or trusting a dangerous person again, or that justice should not be done. It means handing the debt to God and refusing to let the wrongdoer go on ruling our hearts. “Forgive each other freely, just as God has forgiven you in Christ” (Ephesians 4:32). It is often a process, not a single moment.

The Ugandan bishop Festo Kivengere knew this from the inside. When Idi Amin’s regime murdered Archbishop Janani Luwum in 1977, Kivengere himself had to flee the country. In exile he found bitterness rising in his own heart toward the man who had killed his friend and brought such suffering to his people. He came to see that he too needed the cross to heal him of hatred, and he wrote a short book with the startling title I Love Idi Amin. Forgiveness did not mean pretending evil was good. It meant refusing to let evil poison his soul.

The community of believers. God heals us in the company of His people. “Take up one another’s heavy loads, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). A small group that listens without judging, a mature friend who prays with us, a church that welcomes the broken: these are God’s hands.

Pastoral care, counselling and medical care. Some wounds go so deep that we need skilled help. A wise pastor, a qualified Christian counsellor, or a doctor may be part of God’s answer to our prayers. Depression, trauma and anxiety can have physical as well as spiritual causes, and seeking treatment is not a lack of faith. Luke, who wrote a Gospel, was a physician. Prayer and good care are not rivals. They work alongside each other, and God can use both.

Jesus once asked a man who had been lying by a pool for thirty-eight years, “Do you want to be well?” (John 5:6). It is a real question. Healing can be frightening, because it asks us to face what we have avoided. But the One who asks is gentle, and He does not hurry us.

Growing up in Christ

Healing is part of a larger journey: growing up. God does not want us to stay spiritual infants. Paul longs for the day when “we will be a mature adult, grown to the full measure of the stature that belongs to the fullness of Christ” so that “we will no longer be infants, thrown about by the waves” (Ephesians 4:13–14).

Maturity is not the same as age or knowledge. An old church elder can be spiritually childish, and a young believer can be wise. Maturity shows itself in steadiness, in love that does not depend on being loved back, in the ability to take correction, to forgive quickly and to trust God in the dark. It grows the way a tree grows: slowly, through seasons, with deep roots.

So be patient with yourself, and with others. You will not be finished in this life. But you are not stuck either. “The one who started a good work in you will keep working at it until it is finished on the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6). God does not abandon half-built houses.

Body made new: what God will do

Our bodies are also part of God’s plan. Right now they are tired, ageing and often sick. Some of us live with pain every day. Every one of us will grow weaker with the years, unless Christ returns first. Paul does not deny this: “Our outer self may be decaying, but our inner self is being made new day after day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

But decay is not the end of the story. On the day Christ returns, our bodies will be raised and transformed. “It is sown in decay; it is raised imperishable. In dishonor it is sown, in glory it is raised; in weakness it is sown, in power it is raised” (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). We are waiting for “a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will change these bodies of our humble state and give them the same form as His glorious body” (Philippians 3:20–21).

This matters for how we live now. God does not despise the body. We care for our bodies as gifts on loan from Him. And when we suffer in the body, we can groan with hope, as Paul says we do, “while we long for our adoption as children, when our body will be redeemed” (Romans 8:23). Chapter 28 will look more fully at that great day.

The pattern of salvation

Now we can see the whole pattern. Theologians use three words for it.

  1. Justification (past): God declared us righteous in Christ, and our spirit was made alive to Him. We have been saved.
  2. Sanctification (present): God is renewing our soul, making us holy and healing our wounds. We are being saved.
  3. Glorification (future): God will raise our bodies and make us perfectly like Christ. We will be saved.

Paul joins these together in one sentence: “Those He called, He also declared righteous. And those He declared righteous, He also glorified” (Romans 8:30). Notice he speaks of glorification as if it has already happened, because in God’s mind it is as sure as if it were done.

If you prefer the two-part view of the person, the pattern still holds. Our inner self was made alive at conversion, is being renewed day by day, and will be made perfect, and our body will be raised. Whichever way we describe the parts, the God who began the work will complete it.

To live coram Deo, before the face of God, is to live inside this pattern. We do not need to fear that God will give up on us halfway. We can bring our wounds to Him without shame, because He is already at work in us. And we can look at our ageing bodies without despair, because the same face we seek now will one day be seen with eyes made new.

The soul that is being healed is also a soul under attack. In the next chapter we turn to the unseen battle and to Christ’s victory over every power that would keep us bound.

Questions for reflection

  • In your own words, what has God already done in you, what is He doing now, and what will He do in the future?
  • Augustine wrote, “Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee.” Have there been seasons in your life when this was true of you?
  • Are there wounds from your past that still shape how you see God, yourself or others? Which of the ways of healing in this chapter might God want to use?
  • Is there someone you need to forgive? What would it mean to hand that debt to God, even if your feelings take time to follow?
  • Have you ever felt that seeking counselling or medical help showed a lack of faith? How does this chapter answer that fear?
  • How does the promise of a resurrection body change the way you think about sickness, ageing and death?

A step for this week

Set aside one quiet hour this week with your Bible and a notebook. Read Psalm 147:1–6 and Isaiah 61:1–3 slowly. Then ask God to show you one hurt from the past that still affects you today, and write down honestly what happened and how it made you feel. Pray about it in your own words, and write one truth from Scripture beside it that answers the lie the wound has taught you. Before the week ends, share what you wrote with one trusted believer or your pastor and ask them to pray with you. If the hurt is very deep, ask them to help you find a qualified Christian counsellor.

study_questions.question: What is the difference between spirit, soul and body?
study_questions.answer: Many Christians, like Watchman Nee, describe the spirit as the part by which we know God, the soul as our mind, will and emotions, and the body as our physical life; many other theologians see two parts, an inner self and an outer bodily self. Both views are held by faithful believers. Either way, God is at work in the whole person: "May the God of peace Himself make you holy in every part, and may your spirit, soul and body be kept whole" (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

study_questions.question: How does God heal emotional wounds and soul hurts?
study_questions.answer: God heals the soul through His presence, His Word, forgiveness, the community of believers and, where needed, pastoral care, qualified counselling and medical care, which work alongside prayer rather than against it. "He heals those whose hearts are crushed and bandages their injuries" (Psalm 147:3). Healing is often gradual, layer by layer, and God is patient with us.

study_questions.question: What are justification, sanctification and glorification?
study_questions.answer: They are the past, present and future of salvation. In justification God declared us righteous and made our spirit alive to Him; in sanctification He is renewing our soul day by day; in glorification He will raise our bodies and make us perfectly like Christ. Paul joins them together: "Those He called, He also declared righteous. And those He declared righteous, He also glorified" (Romans 8:30).

fields.title: Spiritual Warfare: Angels, Demons and Victory in Christ
fields.body_html:
“Finally, be made strong in the Lord and in His mighty strength. Clothe yourselves in God’s complete armor, so that you can hold your ground against the devil’s cunning plans. Our fight is not with flesh and blood.”

— Ephesians 6:10–12 (OWB)

In Chapter 15 we saw God healing and renewing the soul. But every believer soon discovers that this growth does not happen in peaceful surroundings. There is opposition. The Christian life is a walk with God, and it is also a battle.

Some Christians hardly think about this at all. Others see a demon behind every flat tyre and headache. The Bible avoids both mistakes. It tells us plainly that we have a real enemy, and it tells us even more plainly that Jesus Christ has defeated him. This chapter is about living coram Deo, before the face of God, in a world where the battle is real but the outcome is already settled.

The reality of the unseen realm

When the king of Aram sent an army by night to capture the prophet Elisha, Elisha’s servant woke to find the city surrounded by horses and chariots. He panicked. Elisha did not. “‘Do not be afraid,’ Elisha answered. ‘There are more with us than there are with them.’” Then he prayed for his servant’s eyes to be opened, “and he saw that the hill was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:16–17).

The servant’s eyes did not create the army of God. They only showed him what was already there. That is how the Bible speaks of the spiritual world. It is as real as the physical world, even when we cannot see it. In many parts of Africa, Asia and Latin America, believers need no persuading of this; they have grown up surrounded by talk of spirits, curses and powers. In much of the West, people have been taught to laugh at such things. The Bible corrects both. The unseen world is real, but it is not ruled by chance or by the spirits. It is ruled by God.

Angels: servants of God and of His people

Angels are created beings. They are not God, they are not to be worshipped, and they are not the spirits of people who have died. They are spirits made by God to serve Him. The book of Revelation pictures them around God’s throne, a number “beyond counting: ten thousands of ten thousands, and thousands of thousands” (Revelation 5:11), worshipping the Lamb.

Angels also serve God’s people. “Are not all the angels spirits in holy service, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are going to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14). In Scripture they bring messages, as Gabriel did to Mary. They protect, as when an angel shut the mouths of the lions for Daniel. They carry out God’s judgments and His rescues. “For He will give His angels orders about you, to protect you wherever you go” (Psalm 91:11).

We do not pray to angels or seek experiences of them; our eyes are on the Lord who sends them. But it is a comfort to know that, when we walk with God, we are never as alone as we feel.

Satan and demons: their origin, limits and tactics

The Bible does not tell us everything about where evil spirits came from, but it tells us enough. Satan and his demons are fallen angels. Jude speaks of “the angels who did not stay in the place of authority that was theirs, but abandoned their own dwelling” (Jude 6). Revelation describes “the great dragon, cast out: the serpent of old, the one called the devil and Satan, deceiver of the whole world” (Revelation 12:9). Jesus said, “I watched Satan fall from heaven like a flash of lightning” (Luke 10:18). Many Christians have also seen Satan’s pride and fall reflected in the prophecies against the kings of Babylon and Tyre (Isaiah 14; Ezekiel 28).

Satan is not God’s equal opposite. He is a creature, and his power has limits. In the book of Job he cannot touch Job without God’s permission, and he must stop where God tells him to stop. He is not everywhere at once, he does not know everything, and he cannot snatch a believer out of the Father’s hand.

Scripture shows three main tactics he uses.

Deception. Jesus called him “a liar and the father of lies” (John 8:44). His first words in the Bible twisted God’s word: “Did God really tell you not to eat from any tree in the garden?” (Genesis 3:1). He still works by lies: about God (“He does not really love you”), about ourselves (“You are worthless”) and about sin (“It will make you happy”).

Accusation. Revelation calls him “the one who accused our brothers and sisters, accusing them day and night before our God” (Revelation 12:10). He reminds us of our failures and tells us God could never accept us. Often his accusations contain some truth, which is what makes them so painful.

Temptation. In the wilderness he tempted Jesus to meet His own needs His own way, to test God, and to gain the world by bowing down to him (Matthew 4:1–11). He tempts us the same way: to grab what God has not given, to doubt God’s care, and to take short cuts around the cross.

Principalities and powers

Paul writes, “Our fight is not with flesh and blood. It is with the rulers, with the authorities, with the world rulers of this darkness, with the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12). Behind the visible evil of the world, behind cruel systems, wars, oppression and corruption, there are spiritual powers at work.

The book of Daniel gives a rare glimpse of this. Daniel had prayed and fasted for three weeks. Then an angel came to him and said, “From the first day that you set your mind to gain understanding and humbled yourself before your God, your words were heard, and it is in answer to them that I have come. But the prince of the kingdom of Persia stood in my way for twenty-one days, until Michael, one of the chief princes, came to my aid” (Daniel 10:12–13). Daniel’s prayer was heard at once, but there was a battle in the unseen world before the answer arrived.

This teaches us two things. First, our real enemy is never the neighbour, the politician or the relative who opposes us. People can be used by evil, but they are not the enemy; they are people for whom Christ died. Second, prayer matters far more than we think. When we pray, we take part in a battle we cannot see.

Christ’s victory and our authority in His name

The heart of this chapter is not the devil’s power but Christ’s victory. “This is why the Son of God was revealed: to undo the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8). At the cross, what looked like Satan’s greatest triumph became his defeat. “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and exposed them to public disgrace, leading them as captives in His victory procession by the cross” (Colossians 2:15). By His death Jesus stripped of power “the one who holds the power of death, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14).

The picture is of a Roman general leading defeated kings in chains through the streets. The enemy still fights, but the war has been decided.

Believers share in that victory. When Jesus sent out seventy-two disciples, they came back amazed: “Lord, when we use Your name, even the demons obey us!” Jesus answered, “I have given you authority to trample snakes and scorpions underfoot, and authority over all the enemy’s power” (Luke 10:17–19). Then He added a warning: “Do not be glad because the spirits obey you. Be glad instead that your names stand written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). Our authority is real, but our joy is in our relationship with God, not in our power.

“As for you, dear children, you belong to God, and you have already won the victory over them, because the One in you is greater than the one in the world” (1 John 4:4).

Martin Luther: a mighty fortress

Martin Luther, the German Reformer of the sixteenth century, took the devil seriously, perhaps more seriously than most Christians today. He had known terrible inner struggles as a young monk, seasons of fear, doubt and despair that he called his Anfechtungen, his attacks or assaults. After he stood before the emperor at Worms in 1521 and refused to take back his teaching, friends hid him for his safety in the Wartburg castle. There, lonely and often unwell, he felt these assaults sharply, and there he also translated the New Testament into German so that ordinary people could read it.

Luther learned to fight the devil not with his own strength but with the Word and with Christ. In his Table Talk, now in the Ochorus library, he described how the enemy attacked him with accusation, asking whether God could really be gracious to such a sinner. Luther knew it was useless to answer by pointing to his own love for God, because the devil would simply reply that he had not loved God with all his heart, and his conscience would agree. Instead, he said:

“...at such a time I must arm myself and encounter him with this text, namely: ‘That Jesus Christ died for me, and through him I have a gracious God and Father; Christ hath made an atonement for me.’”

Martin Luther, Table Talk

That is exactly how we answer accusation. Not “I am good enough”, but “Christ died for me.”

Luther also faced deception. He tells of a time when, praying, he saw what seemed to be a shining vision of Christ with His wounds. He was tempted to treat it as a special revelation. But he recalled that Christ comes to us in His Word, in a humbler form, and he spoke to the vision: “Avoid, thou confounded devil; I know no other Christ than he who was crucified, and who in his Word is pictured unto me.” The vision vanished. The Word of God was his test for every experience.

Luther’s best-known hymn, “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God”, is built on Psalm 46: “God is a shelter and a strength for us, a help always close at hand in times of distress” (Psalm 46:1). It admits that the world is full of devils and that the ancient foe is strong, but it insists that one champion, Christ Himself, fights for us and will win the field. For Luther, spiritual warfare was never mainly about the devil. It was about trusting Christ.

The armour of God

Paul gives us a picture of a Roman soldier, and invites us to put on God’s own armour (Ephesians 6:13–18). Notice that it is God’s armour. We do not make it; we put it on.

  • The belt of truth. “Tie truth around your waist as a belt” (Ephesians 6:14). A soldier’s belt held everything else in place. Truth, God’s truth believed and honesty lived out, holds the Christian life together. Lies, even small ones, open the door to the father of lies.
  • The breastplate of righteousness. This guards the heart. It is first the righteousness of Christ given to us, which answers every accusation, and then a life of integrity that gives the enemy no foothold.
  • Shoes of the gospel of peace. “Put on the readiness that the gospel of peace gives” (Ephesians 6:15). A soldier needs firm footing. The gospel gives us peace with God and makes us ready to carry that peace to others.
  • The shield of faith. “With it you will be able to put out all the burning arrows of the evil one” (Ephesians 6:16). Fear, doubt, lust and despair fly at us like burning arrows. Faith takes God at His word and puts them out.
  • The helmet of salvation. This guards the mind. Knowing that we are saved, kept and destined for glory protects us from the thoughts that would pull us down.
  • The sword of the Spirit. “The sword that the Spirit gives, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17). This is the one weapon for attack as well as defence.

Then Paul adds prayer: “Pray in the Spirit at every opportunity, with every kind of prayer and request” (Ephesians 6:18). The English Puritan William Gurnall wrote a huge book on these verses, The Christian in Complete Armour, published in the 1650s and 1660s. His great point was that a soldier must wear the whole armour, not just the pieces he likes, and must keep it on, because the enemy does not announce his attacks.

In The Pilgrim’s Progress, John Bunyan shows his pilgrim, Christian, meeting the monster Apollyon in the Valley of Humiliation. Christian wonders whether to run, but he remembers something about his armour:

“He considered again, that he had no armor for his back, and therefore thought that to turn the back to him might give him greater advantage with ease to pierce him with his darts; therefore he resolved to venture and stand his ground.”

John Bunyan, The Pilgrim’s Progress

God’s armour is made for facing the enemy, not for running.

How to fight our enemy

How, then, do we fight in daily life? Scripture gives us several weapons.

Truth and the Word. When Jesus was tempted, He answered every time with Scripture: “No one lives on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4), and finally, “Get away, Satan! ... You must worship the Lord your God and serve no one but Him” (Matthew 4:10). If the Son of God used the written Word, so must we. Know specific verses for your specific battles.

Taking thoughts captive. Much of the battle happens in the mind. “We capture every thought and lead it away to obey Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). When a lie comes, do not entertain it. Name it, and answer it with truth.

Prayer and fasting. Jesus said of one stubborn case, “This kind cannot be made to come out by any means except prayer” (Mark 9:29). Daniel prayed and fasted. Fasting (see Chapter 10) is a way of saying to God that we need Him more than food.

Praise. Worship lifts our eyes from the enemy to God. “Out of the mouths of children and babies ... You have built a stronghold against Your foes” (Psalm 8:2). Paul and Silas sang in prison at midnight. Praise is a declaration of whose side we are on.

The name of Jesus. God has given Jesus “the name that is above every name, so that every knee will bend before the name of Jesus” (Philippians 2:9–10). We pray and command in His name, not as a magic word, but as servants acting on His authority.

The blood of the Lamb and the word of our testimony. Of the believers who overcame the accuser, Revelation says: “They have overcome him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony; they did not hold their lives dear, even in the face of death” (Revelation 12:11). The blood of Jesus answers every accusation. Our testimony, speaking aloud what Christ has done for us, declares His victory.

Resisting and standing firm. “So place yourselves under God. Stand against the devil, and he will run from you” (James 4:7). The order matters: first we submit to God, then we resist the devil. Peter adds, “The devil, your opponent, roams about like a lion that roars, hunting for someone to swallow up. Stand up to him and hold firm in your faith” (1 Peter 5:8–9). Four times in Ephesians 6 Paul tells us to stand. Often victory simply means not giving way.

Hedges of protection

In the book of Job, Satan complains to God: “Have You not put a protective hedge around him and his household and everything he owns on every side?” (Job 1:10). God protects His people, and it is right to ask Him to.

Many believers pray daily for God’s protection over themselves, their children, their homes and their work, often using Psalm 91: “Whoever makes a home under the cover of the Most High will spend the night in the shade of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1). “The angel of the LORD pitches camp all around the people who fear Him, and sets them free” (Psalm 34:7). Luther’s Small Catechism includes an evening prayer that believers have prayed for centuries:

“I put myself in your care, body and soul and all that I have. Let Your holy angels be with me, so that the evil enemy will not gain power over me.”

Martin Luther, The Small Catechism

Praying for protection is not a guarantee that we will never suffer; Job himself suffered greatly, and Chapter 17 will look at that. But nothing reaches us except what God allows, and He sets the limits.

Deliverance and freedom

The Gospels show Jesus setting people free from evil spirits again and again. A man who had been possessed by a legion of demons was found “sitting there with clothes on and in his right mind” (Mark 5:15). The apostles did the same in Jesus’ name (Acts 16:18).

Christians hold different views about deliverance ministry today. Some churches practise it often and openly. Others believe it is needed only rarely and should be done quietly by mature leaders. Many also discuss whether a true believer, in whom the Holy Spirit lives, can be under the control of a demon, or only troubled and oppressed by one from outside. Sincere believers answer these questions differently.

But all agree on the most important thing: Jesus came “to announce freedom to the captives” (Luke 4:18), and He still sets captives free. Wise practice everywhere includes leading people to Christ and to repentance, renouncing any involvement with witchcraft, charms or occult powers, forgiving others, filling the life with the Word and prayer, and caring for the person in a loving church afterwards. Freedom is not only about driving something out. It is about bringing Christ in.

Staying balanced

C. S. Lewis, the British writer, wrote The Screwtape Letters in 1942, a clever book of imaginary letters from a senior devil to his young nephew, teaching him how to lead a man away from God. In its preface Lewis warned of two opposite errors about devils, both equally pleasing to them: to disbelieve in their existence, or to take an excessive and unhealthy interest in them.

Both errors are common. Some believers are spiritually asleep, unaware of the enemy’s schemes. “We know well enough what he has in mind” (2 Corinthians 2:11), Paul wrote; many today do not. Others are so fascinated with the devil that they talk more about him than about Jesus, blame every problem on demons, and live in fear.

The cure for both is the same: keep your eyes on Jesus. “Let us keep our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer who leads the way in faith and brings it to perfection” (Hebrews 12:2). We do not walk through life staring at the enemy. We walk before the face of God, under the shelter of the Almighty, in the victory of the Lamb. And from that place, standing firm, we are not afraid.

Questions for reflection

  • Are you more likely to ignore the spiritual battle or to be fearful and fascinated by it? Which correction from this chapter do you most need?
  • Which of the enemy’s tactics, deception, accusation or temptation, do you face most often? How will you answer it?
  • Luther answered accusation with “Christ died for me.” Which truths from Scripture can you use when you feel condemned?
  • Which piece of the armour of God do you most need to put on this week, and why?
  • How does knowing that Christ has already disarmed the powers change the way you pray?
  • Who in your family or community could you pray a hedge of protection around this week?

A step for this week

Each morning this week, read Ephesians 6:10–18 aloud and “put on” each piece of the armour in prayer, naming it and thanking God for it. Then choose one verse to be your sword for the week, a promise that answers the lie or temptation you face most often, write it on a card, and carry it with you. Whenever the lie or temptation comes, speak the verse aloud, as Jesus did in the wilderness. Each evening, pray for God’s protection over your household, using Psalm 91 or Luther’s evening prayer.

study_questions.question: What does the Bible teach about angels and demons?
study_questions.answer: Angels are created spirits who worship God and serve His people: "Are not all the angels spirits in holy service, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are going to inherit salvation?" (Hebrews 1:14). Satan and his demons are fallen angels whose power is limited by God. They work by deception, accusation and temptation, but Christ has defeated them.

study_questions.question: How do Christians fight spiritual warfare?
study_questions.answer: We put on the whole armour of God described in Ephesians 6 and fight with truth, the Word of God as the sword of the Spirit, prayer and fasting, praise, the name of Jesus, and the blood of the Lamb and the word of our testimony (Revelation 12:11). We submit to God and resist the devil: "Stand against the devil, and he will run from you" (James 4:7). Jesus Himself answered every temptation with Scripture.

study_questions.question: Has Jesus already defeated Satan?
study_questions.answer: Yes. At the cross Christ "disarmed the rulers and authorities and exposed them to public disgrace, leading them as captives in His victory procession by the cross" (Colossians 2:15). The enemy still fights, but the war has been decided, and believers share in that victory: "the One in you is greater than the one in the world" (1 John 4:4). So we keep our eyes on Jesus, neither ignoring the enemy nor obsessing over him.

fields.title: Suffering, Trials and the Sovereignty of God
fields.body_html:
“We know that, for people who love God, all things work together and lead to good. They are the ones called in keeping with His purpose.”

— Romans 8:28 (OWB)

Sooner or later, every believer meets suffering. A child falls sick and does not recover. A harvest fails. A job is lost, a marriage breaks, a body weakens, a church is closed by the authorities. Sometimes the pain comes suddenly, like a storm. Sometimes it settles in slowly and stays for years.

In Chapter 16 we saw that we have an enemy, and that Christ has defeated him. But victory over the enemy does not mean a life without pain. Some of the godliest men and women who ever lived suffered terribly. Jesus Himself, the Son of God, was “a man of pains, no stranger to sickness” (Isaiah 53:3). He told His disciples plainly, “In the world you have affliction. But have courage: I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

This chapter does not offer easy answers. Suffering is a mystery, and anyone who claims to explain it completely has not understood it. But the Bible does give us light to walk by in the dark, and above all it gives us a God who walks with us. To live coram Deo, before the face of God, is to discover that His face does not turn away when the night comes.

Why Christians suffer

The Bible gives several reasons why believers suffer. None of them explains every case, but together they help us.

We live in a fallen world. When sin entered the world, everything was damaged: our bodies, our relationships and the creation itself. “We know that all creation, to this very day, groans as one and suffers the pains of giving birth together” (Romans 8:22). Christians get malaria and cancer. Christian farmers face drought. Christian families are caught in war. Much suffering is not a punishment for any particular sin. It is simply part of living in a broken world that has not yet been made new.

God uses trials to refine us. James writes something that surprises us: “Whenever you find yourselves in trials of every sort, regard it as a reason for great joy, because you know that the testing your faith goes through produces endurance. Let endurance carry its work through to the end, so that you may be mature and whole, with nothing missing” (James 1:2–4). Gold is purified in fire. A goldsmith does not put gold in the furnace because he hates it, but because he values it. Paul says the same: “Trouble leads to endurance, endurance to proven character, and proven character to hope” (Romans 5:3–4).

We share in the sufferings of Christ. Some suffering comes precisely because we follow Jesus. Peter wrote to believers facing persecution: “Dear friends, the fire that is burning among you has come to test you; do not be taken aback by it, as though something alien to you were happening. No, the more you share in the sufferings of Christ, the more you should rejoice” (1 Peter 4:12–13). Paul longed “to know Him, to know the power of His resurrection and what it is to share in His sufferings” (Philippians 3:10). Millions of believers in our world today know this from experience.

God’s sovereignty and goodness in pain

Two truths hold the believer steady in suffering. God is sovereign: He rules over all things, and nothing happens outside His control. And God is good: He loves His children and intends their good. We need both. A God who was good but not in control would be kind but helpless. A God who was in control but not good would be frightening. The God of the Bible is both.

That is why Romans 8:28 is so precious: “We know that, for people who love God, all things work together and lead to good.” Notice what this verse does not say. It does not say all things are good. Cancer is not good. Betrayal is not good. It says that God works in all things, even the evil ones, to bring about good for those who love Him. The “good” is defined in the next verse: being shaped into the likeness of His Son.

Joseph is the great example. His brothers sold him as a slave. He was falsely accused and thrown into prison. Years later, when he stood before those same brothers as the ruler of Egypt, he said: “Evil was what you planned against me; good was what God planned by it, so as to bring about what you see today: the lives of a great many people saved” (Genesis 50:20). The evil was real. So was God’s purpose through it.

Sovereignty does not mean that God is the author of evil, or that He enjoys our pain. The brothers were guilty of what they did to Joseph; God did not make them sin. Nor does it mean we should accept every injustice without a word. Christians should fight disease, care for the poor and speak against cruelty. But it does mean that no suffering is meaningless, and that nothing has slipped out of God’s hands. A mother in a refugee camp, a farmer watching his crops wither, a pastor in a prison cell: none of them is forgotten, and none of their pain is wasted.

Job lost his children, his wealth and his health in a single season. His first response is one of the most astonishing in Scripture: “He fell to the ground and worshiped. He said, ‘I came naked from my mother’s womb, and naked I will go back there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; may the name of the LORD be blessed’” (Job 1:20–21). Job grieved deeply; he tore his robe. But he grieved toward God, not away from Him.

The missionary Hudson Taylor, who knew great loss in China, put it this way in a meditation in the Ochorus library:

“The believer does not need to wait until he sees the reason of GOD’S afflictive dealings with him ere he is satisfied; he knows that all things work together for good to them that love GOD.”

Hudson Taylor, Blessed Adversity

Wang Mingdao: faithful, fallen and restored

Few lives show the reality of suffering, and the honesty of faith under it, more clearly than that of Wang Mingdao, one of the most respected Chinese pastors of the twentieth century.

Wang was born in Beijing in 1900, the year of the Boxer uprising, when many Christians in northern China were killed. He came to faith as a young man and gave himself to preaching the Bible. In the 1920s he began a church in Beijing that grew into the Christian Tabernacle, and for decades he also published a magazine of Bible teaching that was read across China. He was known for his plain, fearless preaching and for his insistence that the church must belong to Christ alone.

That conviction cost him dearly. During the Japanese occupation he refused to join a church union controlled by the occupiers. After 1949 the new government set up the Three-Self Patriotic Movement to bring the Protestant churches under state control. Wang refused to join it, believing that the church could not be placed under any authority but Christ’s. In 1955 he and his wife were arrested.

Here his story becomes painfully honest. After months of pressure in prison, Wang signed a confession admitting to crimes he had not committed, and in 1956 he was released. But he found no peace. He was tormented by what he had done, and he compared himself to Peter, who had denied the Lord. He and his wife decided they could not live with the lie. They went to the authorities to take back his confession. In 1958 they were both arrested again, and Wang was sentenced to life in prison.

He spent more than twenty years in prison and labour camps. He was finally released in 1980, an old man, and spent his last years in Shanghai, where he died in 1991, still holding to the faith he had preached.

Wang Mingdao’s story teaches us several things. Suffering for Christ is real, and it can last a very long time. Even strong believers can stumble under pressure. But failure is not the end. Like Peter, Wang was restored, and he went on to finish with faith. The God who rules over all things also rules over our weakest moments, and He works all things together for good, even through our falls.

Honest questions

Sometimes our questions are not about why suffering exists, but about why God does not answer our prayers. We pray for healing, and it does not come. We pray for a son to return to the Lord, and he does not. We cry out for a sign, and heaven seems silent.

It is important to say clearly: God does heal, and we should pray for healing with faith. But God does not always heal in this life, and when He does not, it is not always because someone lacked faith. Paul prayed three times for his “thorn in the flesh” to be removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–8). The answer was no. Instead, the Lord said to him, “My grace is enough for you, for power comes to its fullness in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Paul went on: “That is why I am glad to have weaknesses, insults, calamities, persecutions and tight corners, for the sake of Christ. For it is when I am weak that I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

Joni Eareckson Tada knows this from the inside. In 1967, at the age of seventeen, she dived into shallow water in Chesapeake Bay in the United States, broke her neck, and was left paralysed from the shoulders down. In the months that followed she fell into deep despair and even wished she could die. She prayed earnestly to be healed, and she was not. Over time, through Scripture, friends and many honest struggles with God, she came to trust Him in her wheelchair. She learned to paint with a brush held in her teeth, wrote many books, and in 1979 founded a ministry, Joni and Friends, which has helped disabled people and their families around the world receive wheelchairs and hear the gospel.
