Later she also lived with chronic pain and cancer. Joni has often written that God may allow things He hates in order to accomplish things He loves.

Her story does not make suffering easy. But it shows that unanswered prayer is not the same as unloved prayer.

There are also seasons of doubt and of God’s silence. Faithful believers have walked through them: times when prayer feels like speaking into an empty room, when the Bible seems to say nothing, and when the joy of earlier years feels like a memory. If that is where you are, you are not alone, and you are not lost. God’s silence is not His absence.

What should you do in such a season? Keep doing the simple things. Keep reading Scripture, even a few verses. Keep gathering with God’s people, even when you feel nothing. Tell a trusted friend or pastor honestly how you feel, instead of pretending. Be careful, too, of anyone who offers a simple formula: “If you just had more faith, you would be healed”, or “You must have hidden sin.” Job’s friends said things like that, and at the end of the book God said they had not spoken rightly about Him. Some suffering has no explanation we can see in this life. We are asked to trust a Person, not to solve a puzzle.

Lament: faithful prayer in pain

The Bible gives us a language for suffering that many Christians have forgotten. It is called lament. A lament is a prayer that pours out pain, confusion and even complaint to God, while still holding on to Him.

Around a third of the psalms are laments. Listen to David: “How long, LORD? Will You go on forgetting me for good? How long will You turn Your face away from me? How long must I keep turning plans over in my mind, with grief in my heart all day long?” (Psalm 13:1–2). Notice the theme of this book appearing even here. David feels that God’s face is turned away, and he says so.

But lament does not end in despair. The same psalm ends: “But I trust in Your loyal love; my heart will be glad because You save. I will sing to the LORD, because He has been so generous to me” (Psalm 13:5). Lament moves from honest pain, through asking, to trust. Sometimes that journey takes a few verses. Sometimes it takes years.

On the cross Jesus Himself prayed a lament, the opening words of Psalm 22: “My God, My God, why have You abandoned Me?” (Psalm 22:1). If the Son of God could pray that, we may bring our hardest questions to the Father. Lament is not a lack of faith. It is faith that refuses to let go of God even when it does not understand Him.

Charles Spurgeon, who suffered from depression and painful illness for much of his life, preached a sermon called Songs in the Night, now in the Ochorus library. He wrote:

“Any man can sing in the day. When the cup is full, man draws inspiration from it... It is easy enough for an Aeolian harp to whisper music when the winds blow—the difficulty is for music to come when no wind blows.”

Charles Spurgeon, Songs in the Night

God gives songs in the night. Often the first of those songs is a lament.

Comfort received and comfort given

Suffering is never wasted in God’s hands. One of its purposes is to make us comforters. “Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the merciful Father and the God from whom all comfort comes. He comforts us in every hardship we face, so that we in turn can comfort people facing any hardship, passing on to them the same comfort God gives us” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4).

God’s comfort is real and near. “The LORD stays close to those whose hearts are broken, and rescues those whose spirits are crushed” (Psalm 34:18). Often He comforts us through His people. Job’s friends did best in the first week, when “they sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was” (Job 2:13). They did worst when they started to explain his suffering.

So when others suffer, be slow to explain and quick to be present. Bring food. Sit by the hospital bed. Pray with them, briefly. “Share the joy of those who are glad, and the tears of those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Jesus Himself, standing at the tomb of His friend Lazarus, knowing He was about to raise him, still wept (John 11:35).

Horatio Spafford was a lawyer in Chicago in the nineteenth century. He and his wife Anna had already lost a young son, and much of his property was destroyed in the great Chicago fire of 1871. In 1873 Anna and their four daughters sailed for Europe on the ship Ville du Havre. In the middle of the Atlantic it collided with another ship and sank within minutes. All four girls drowned. Anna was rescued, and when she reached land she sent her husband a telegram with two words: Saved alone. As Horatio sailed to join his grieving wife, he wrote the words of the hymn “It Is Well with My Soul”. The Spaffords later moved to Jerusalem, where they and their friends spent years caring for the poor and the sick. Their comfort became comfort for many.

The hope of glory

Finally, the Bible puts our suffering in the light of eternity. “I have weighed it up: what we suffer in this present time does not begin to balance the glory that is going to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18). Paul was not a man who had suffered little. He had been beaten, stoned, shipwrecked and imprisoned. Yet he wrote: “Our troubles are light and last only a moment, and they are bringing about for us an eternal glory, weighty beyond all measure. All the while, we look not at what can be seen but at what cannot be seen” (2 Corinthians 4:17–18).

Imagine a set of old market scales. On one side put every sorrow you have ever known. On the other side put the glory God has prepared for His children. The scale does not just tip; it crashes down. One day “every tear He will wipe from their eyes. Death will be no more, and no more mourning, no crying, no pain” (Revelation 21:4). Chapter 28 will look at that hope in full.

Until then we live before His face, sometimes with joy, sometimes through tears, always held. He is the God who rules all things and loves us still. The next part of this book turns to how we live as God’s people together, beginning with marriage in Chapter 18, where many of life’s joys and sorrows are shared.

Questions for reflection

  • Which of the reasons for suffering in this chapter, a fallen world, refining, or sharing Christ’s sufferings, helps you most in your own situation?
  • Why do we need to believe both that God is sovereign and that God is good? What happens if we hold only one?
  • How does Wang Mingdao’s story of failure and restoration encourage you?
  • Have you prayed for something, perhaps healing, that God has not granted? How do 2 Corinthians 12:9 and Joni Eareckson Tada’s story speak to you?
  • Have you ever prayed a lament? What might it look like to bring your hardest questions honestly to God?
  • Who around you is suffering now, and how could you share God’s comfort with them this week?

A step for this week

Write your own lament this week, following the shape of Psalm 13. Take a page and write four parts: first, tell God honestly what hurts (“How long, Lord…?”); second, ask Him plainly for what you need; third, write down one thing you know to be true about His character, such as His loyal love; and fourth, end with a sentence of trust, even if your feelings have not yet caught up. Then think of one person you know who is suffering, and visit, call or write to them before the week ends, simply to be present and to pray with them.

study_questions.question: Why do Christians suffer?
study_questions.answer: Christians suffer because we live in a fallen world, because God uses trials to refine us, and because we share in the sufferings of Christ. James says that "the testing your faith goes through produces endurance" so that we may be "mature and whole, with nothing missing" (James 1:3–4). Suffering is never wasted in God's hands.

study_questions.question: What does Romans 8:28 really mean?
study_questions.answer: "We know that, for people who love God, all things work together and lead to good" (Romans 8:28). It does not say that all things are good; cancer and betrayal are not good. It says that God, who is both sovereign and good, works in all things, even evil ones, to bring about good for those who love Him, above all shaping them into the likeness of His Son.

study_questions.question: Is it wrong for a Christian to question God in suffering?
study_questions.answer: No. The Bible gives us lament, prayer that pours out pain and questions to God while still holding on to Him. David prayed, "How long, LORD? Will You go on forgetting me for good?" (Psalm 13:1), and ended, "But I trust in Your loyal love" (Psalm 13:5). Lament is not a lack of faith; it is faith that refuses to let go of God even when it does not understand Him.

fields.title: Marriage: The First Divine Union
fields.body_html:
“Then the LORD God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be on his own. I will make him a helper who matches him.’”

— Genesis 2:18 (OWB)

Think of a wedding day. In a village, the families have gathered since early morning. There is singing, there is food cooking over open fires, and the elders have spoken words of blessing. In a city, the hall is decorated, the cars are hooting outside, and a choir is warming up. A man and a woman stand side by side and make promises that will shape the rest of their lives.

So far in this book we have looked at who God is (Part One), how we walk with Him day by day (Part Two), and how He makes us like Christ, even through warfare and suffering (Part Three). Now, in Part Four, we turn to life as God’s people. And we begin where the Bible begins, in the home.

Marriage is the place where living coram Deo, before the face of God, is tested most closely. In public we can wear a smile. At home, behind a closed door, the people who live with us see us as we really are. Yet even there, especially there, we are before the face of God. He was the first witness to the first marriage, and He is a witness to every marriage since. What we say to our husband or wife at the end of a hard day, how we spend money, how we speak about each other when the other is absent: all of it is lived in His sight. That is not a threat but an invitation.

God’s first institution

Before there was any government, before there was a temple, a priest or a church, there was a marriage. God made the man and the woman and joined them together in the garden. “So God created human beings in His image. In the image of God He created them; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). Then He blessed them and gave them their first task together: “Be fruitful and multiply. Fill the earth and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28).

Genesis 2 tells the same story more closely. Everything God made so far was good, but now God says something is “not good”: the man is alone. God brings the animals to Adam to be named, and Adam does his work well, but among all the creatures “no helper who matched him was found for the man” (Genesis 2:20). So God makes the woman and brings her to him, and Adam bursts into the first poem in the Bible: “At last, here is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh!” (Genesis 2:23).

Notice the word “helper”. In our languages a helper can sound like a junior servant. In the Old Testament the same Hebrew word is used of God Himself, who comes to the help of His people. So the word does not mean someone of lesser worth. It means someone who supplies what is missing. The woman matches the man. She is like him and yet different from him, and together they can do what neither could do alone.

Martin Luther, whose own marriage we will meet later in this chapter, saw that this order matters. Marriage is not a human invention that the Church later blessed. God gave it first. In The Large Catechism, explaining the commandment against adultery, he wrote:

“Therefore He also wishes us to honor it, and to maintain and conduct it as a divine and blessed estate; because, in the first place, He has instituted it before all others”

Martin Luther, The Large Catechism

Because marriage comes first, it is also the foundation of everything else. Families grow out of marriages. Villages and towns grow out of families. Nations are built from towns and villages. When marriages are strong, children grow up secure, the elderly are cared for, and communities hold together. Caring for your marriage is one of the most important things you will ever do for your children, your church and your nation.

Two become one: a covenant before God

The chapter that tells of the first marriage ends with a sentence that Jesus and Paul both quote: “This is why a man leaves his father and mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24).

There are three movements here. First, the man leaves. In many cultures a marriage joins two families, and that is a good thing. Parents and relatives are involved in the choice, gifts are exchanged, and the wider family promises to stand behind the couple. But Scripture says that something new begins on the wedding day. The husband and wife are no longer first of all a son and a daughter. They are a new household, and their first loyalty, after God, is now to each other.

Second, the man clings. The word speaks of holding fast, of glue that does not let go. Marriage is not a trial arrangement that lasts while the feelings are strong. It is a commitment to stay.

Third, the two become one flesh. This includes the physical union of husband and wife, which is God’s good gift for marriage. But it is more than that. Two lives, two sets of plans, two incomes and two histories are woven into one. When Jesus was asked about divorce, He went straight back to Genesis: “Have you never read that the Creator, at the beginning, made them male and female?” (Matthew 19:4). Then He added His own word: “So they are not two any longer; they are one flesh. What God has yoked together, then, no human being may pull apart” (Matthew 19:6).

That is why the Bible calls marriage a covenant. A contract is an agreement between two parties, each protecting their own interests; if one side fails, the contract ends. A covenant is a promise made before God, binding yourself to another person for their good. The prophet Malachi rebuked the men of his day who were abandoning their wives, and he gave the reason it mattered so much: “the LORD was a witness between you and the wife you married in your youth. You have broken faith with her, though she is your partner and your wife by covenant” (Malachi 2:14).

The LORD was a witness. He was there when the vows were spoken, whether in a cathedral, a mud-brick church or a registry office. And He remains a witness every day afterwards. This is marriage coram Deo.

The great mystery: a picture of Christ and His Church

Why did God design marriage this way? Paul gives the deepest answer in Ephesians 5. After quoting Genesis 2:24 again, he says something surprising: “There is a great mystery here, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32).

In the Bible a “mystery” is not a puzzle with no answer. It is something hidden for a long time and now made known. Paul is telling us that from the very beginning, marriage was meant to be a living picture of a greater love: the love between Christ and His people. The Old Testament prophets spoke of God as the husband of Israel. The New Testament calls the Church the bride of Christ, and the Bible ends with a wedding: “the Lamb’s wedding has come, and His bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7).

This means every Christian marriage is a kind of sermon. People around us who never open a Bible are watching how a believing husband treats his wife and how a believing wife treats her husband. When they see faithfulness, kindness and self-giving love, they are seeing a small picture of how Christ loves His Church. When they see bitterness and betrayal, the picture is spoiled. Your ordinary marriage, with its meals, quarrels and reconciliations, can point people to Jesus.

Husbands and wives: distinct callings

Paul’s teaching on marriage in Ephesians 5 begins with a verse for every believer: “And you will submit to one another in the reverent fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21). Christians are people who put others first. That sets the tone for what follows. Then Paul speaks to wives and to husbands in turn, and he gives each a different calling.

To wives he says: “Wives should submit to their own husbands, as to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:22). He sums it up at the end of the passage: “the wife must see to it that she respects her husband” (Ephesians 5:33). Peter says the same, adding that a wife’s godly way of life can win an unbelieving husband “even without your saying a word” (1 Peter 3:1). A wife’s calling is to respect and support her husband, to stand with him, to honour him in public and in private, and to help him lead the home in the ways of God. This is not the submission of an inferior to a superior. It is a free and willing choice made “as to the Lord”, by a woman who is equally made in God’s image.

To husbands Paul gives a calling that is, if anything, even heavier: “Husbands, love your wives the way Christ loved the church and handed Himself over for her” (Ephesians 5:25). How did Christ love the Church? He left heaven. He served. He washed feet. He went to the cross. Headship in the Bible is not a throne; it is a cross. A husband who is head of his home is the first to serve, the first to apologise, the first to pray, and the first to stand between his family and danger. He leads by laying down his life. Paul adds a plain warning: “Husbands, love your wives and never turn harsh or bitter against them” (Colossians 3:19). Peter tells husbands to live with their wives “with understanding”, to give them honour, and to remember that she is one “who will inherit the grace of life together with you, so that nothing stands in the way of your prayers” (1 Peter 3:7). A man who mistreats his wife should not expect his prayers to be heard.

Christians read these passages in different ways. Many, often called complementarians, understand them as teaching distinct and lasting roles for husbands and wives, with the husband carrying a loving, servant leadership in the home. Others, often called egalitarians, read the passages in the light of their first-century setting and stress the mutual submission of verse 21, so that husband and wife share leadership equally. This book teaches the distinct callings as Paul and Peter give them, while recognising that faithful believers differ here, and that this is not a matter that should divide us as brothers and sisters (see the Appendix). On the central things, all agree: husband and wife are equal in worth before God, both are heirs of grace, both are called to put the other first, and harshness or control has no place in a Christian home.

One word must be said clearly. Nothing in Scripture asks a wife to accept violence or abuse. Headship is never permission to harm. If you are in danger in your home, go to trusted leaders in your church and, where needed, to the authorities. Protecting the weak is what Christ, the true Head, would do.

Martin Luther and Katie: a marriage in the Reformation

In April 1523 a group of nuns escaped from a convent at Nimbschen in Germany. They had been reading the writings of Martin Luther and had become convinced that their vows were not what God required. With the help of a merchant who delivered goods to the convent, they were smuggled out in his wagon and brought to Wittenberg, where Luther lived.

Luther felt responsible for them and worked hard to find each woman a home or a husband. One of them, Katharina von Bora, was not easily placed. She was intelligent, strong-minded and of noble family. In the end, on 13 June 1525, the former monk married the former nun. He was forty-one; she was twenty-six. Luther said he married partly to please his father, partly to spite the Pope and the devil, and partly to show that he believed what he taught.

But it became one. The couple moved into the old monastery building in Wittenberg, which was soon full of children, relatives, students and guests. Katharina ran it all. She managed the farm, kept animals, brewed beer, tended a garden and fed the crowds who came to hear Luther talk at the table. He relied on her completely, and teased her by calling her my lord Katie because she ruled the household so well. They had six children. One daughter died as a baby, and their beloved Magdalena died at thirteen in her father’s arms. They wept together, and they held on to God together.

Their marriage was not perfect. Luther was famously stubborn, and Katie was no quiet mouse. Luther himself admitted it, with a smile, in one of the sayings collected in Table Talk:

“I, said Luther, must have patience with the Pope; I must have patience with heretics and seducers; I must have patience with the roaring courtiers; I must have patience with my servants: I must have patience with Kate my wife”

Martin Luther, Table Talk

Yet the same man wrote in The Large Catechism that husband and wife “must by all means live together in love and harmony, that one may cherish the other from the heart and with entire fidelity.” That is what he and Katie learned to do. Their home became a model for thousands of Protestant pastors’ families. For centuries before, many had thought that the holiest life was one without marriage. The Luthers showed that a home, with its noise and work and laughter and grief, can be a holy place where God is served.

Faithfulness, forgiveness and praying together

Three habits keep a marriage strong before the face of God.

The first is faithfulness. “All of you should treat marriage as precious and keep the marriage bed undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4). Unfaithfulness rarely begins with a single act. It begins with a glance, a secret message, a friendship that becomes too close, a habit of sharing your heart with someone who is not your spouse. Malachi’s counsel is wise: “So guard yourselves in your spirit, and let no one be unfaithful to the wife of his youth” (Malachi 2:15). Guard your eyes, your phone and your time. Speak well of your husband or wife when they are not there.

The second is forgiveness. Two sinners cannot live under one roof for long without hurting each other. The question is not whether you will be hurt, but what you will do when it happens. Paul’s command is for every home: “Be kind to one another and full of compassion. Forgive each other freely, just as God has forgiven you in Christ” (Ephesians 4:32). Forgiveness does not pretend that the wrong did not happen. It names it, and then it releases the debt, because God has released ours. Do not let the sun go down on your anger.

The third is praying together. Many couples have found that it is hard to stay angry with someone you have just knelt beside in prayer. The Preacher wrote, “a cord of three strands does not snap quickly” (Ecclesiastes 4:12), and Christians have long seen in that line a picture of a husband, a wife and God bound together. Praying together need not be long or eloquent. Five minutes at the end of the day, thanking God for one thing and bringing Him one concern, can change the climate of a home.

Jonathan Edwards, the eighteenth-century American pastor, and his wife Sarah were known for such a home. They married in 1727 and raised eleven children. When the evangelist George Whitefield stayed with them in 1740, he wrote in his journal how deeply their love for each other and for God had moved him, and it stirred him to pray about marriage himself. When Edwards lay dying in 1758, far from home, he sent a last message to Sarah, telling her that their uncommon union had been spiritual, and so would continue for ever. A marriage lived before the face of God does not end in dust.

No one in God’s family is single

Not every reader of this chapter is married. Some have never married. Some are widowed or divorced. Here is a truth for all of you: in God’s family, no one is single. You may not have a spouse, but you belong to a family, the household of God. “You are citizens together with God’s holy people, and you belong to God’s household” (Ephesians 2:19).

The Bible does not treat singleness as a failure or a waiting room. Jesus Himself never married, and He was the most complete human being who ever lived. Paul was unmarried when he wrote most of his letters, and he could even say, “I would like everyone to be as I am. Yet God gives each person a gift of their own, to one this way and to another that” (1 Corinthians 7:7). Marriage is a gift; singleness is also a gift. Paul points out one of its blessings: “The unmarried man gives his care to the things of the Lord, how he may please Him” (1 Corinthians 7:32). He wants all believers “to stay close beside the Lord with nothing to draw you away” (1 Corinthians 7:35). A single believer can often give time, energy and attention to God’s work in ways that a married person cannot.

Amy Carmichael, the Irish missionary who sailed to India in 1895, never married. In southern India she began rescuing children who were in danger, including girls who had been given to temples. Over the years hundreds of children came to live at Dohnavur, and they called her Amma, mother. She served there for over fifty years. She had no husband and no children of her own, and yet few women in history have had a larger family. In our own time, the English pastor and writer John Stott also remained unmarried, and gave his life to teaching the Bible and encouraging churches across Africa, Asia and Latin America.

God’s promise is that He “gives the lonely a home to live in” (Psalm 68:6). Often He keeps that promise through His people. Jesus promised that those who leave home and family for His sake will receive “a hundred times as much now, in this present time: homes, brothers, sisters, mothers, children and land, together with persecutions” (Mark 10:30). Where do those homes and families come from? From the Church. That means the Church has work to do. Married believers should open their homes and tables to single brothers and sisters, include them in holidays and celebrations, and stop asking, “When will you marry?” as if their life has not yet begun. Single believers, in turn, can be aunts and uncles, mothers and fathers in the faith, to the children and young people around them.

Married or single, every believer is called to the deepest union of all, union with Christ. Earthly marriage is the picture; He is the reality.

In the next chapter we turn to the fruit that so often comes from marriage: children, and the great calling of passing on the faith to the next generation.

Questions for reflection

  • Why does it matter that God established marriage before government or the Church? How does that change the way you see marriage?
  • What is the difference between a contract and a covenant? Where do you see a “contract” attitude creeping into marriages around you?
  • Read Ephesians 5:21–33. If you are married, which part of your calling as a husband or wife do you find hardest? Why?
  • Luther and Katie’s marriage began without much romance but grew into deep love. What helps love grow over the years?
  • Which of the three habits (faithfulness, forgiveness, praying together) most needs attention in your home, or in the homes you care about?
  • How could your church become more of a family to those who are single, widowed or divorced?

A step for this week

If you are married, set aside five minutes each night this week to pray with your husband or wife before you sleep. Each of you thank God for one thing about the other, and bring Him one concern you share. Keep it short and simple, and do it even on the nights you do not feel like it. If you are single, invite one married couple or family from your church to share a meal with you this week, or accept such an invitation, and pray for their marriage by name each day.

study_questions.question: Why is marriage called the first divine institution?
study_questions.answer: Before there was any government, temple or church, God made the man and the woman and joined them together in Eden. He saw that "It is not good for the man to be on his own" and made "a helper who matches him" (Genesis 2:18). Because marriage comes first, it is the foundation of families, villages and nations, and caring for it is one of the most important things we can do for our children, our church and our society.

study_questions.question: What does the Bible teach about the roles of husbands and wives?
study_questions.answer: Paul begins with mutual submission, "in the reverent fear of Christ" (Ephesians 5:21), then gives distinct callings. Wives are called to respect and support their husbands, and husbands to "love your wives the way Christ loved the church and handed Himself over for her" (Ephesians 5:25), leading by serving and never turning harsh. Complementarian and egalitarian Christians read these passages differently, but all agree that husband and wife are equal in worth and heirs of grace together, and nothing in Scripture asks a wife to accept abuse.

study_questions.question: What does the Bible say to Christians who are single?
study_questions.answer: In God's family no one is single: every believer belongs to the household of God (Ephesians 2:19). Jesus never married, and Paul called singleness a gift, saying "God gives each person a gift of their own, to one this way and to another that" (1 Corinthians 7:7). God "gives the lonely a home to live in" (Psalm 68:6), often through the Church, which is called to be a real family to single, widowed and divorced believers.

fields.title: Raising Children in the Faith
fields.body_html:
“Keep these words that I am commanding you today close to your heart. Teach them carefully to your children, and speak of them as you sit in your house and as you go on your way, as you lie down and as you rise.”

— Deuteronomy 6:6–7 (OWB)

In many villages the old stories are told in the evening. The fire is lit, the meal is finished, and the children gather round a grandmother or an uncle. They hear where the family came from, who their ancestors were, and what it means to belong to this people. Nobody writes it down. It passes from mouth to ear, from one generation to the next.

In the cities of today that circle around the fire has often disappeared. Parents leave home before dawn and return after dark. Children spend hours with screens, with teachers, with friends, with whoever is minding them. And so a question presses on every Christian parent: who is telling our children the story of God?

In the last chapter we saw that marriage is God’s first institution, a covenant lived before His face. Very often marriage bears fruit in children. This chapter is about the great privilege and responsibility of raising them in the faith. It is written for mothers and fathers, but also for grandparents, aunts, uncles, teachers, and every believer who loves a child. Because in God’s family, as we shall see, the whole Church shares this work.

Children: a gift and a heritage

The Bible’s view of children is warm and clear. “Children are a gift handed down from the LORD; the fruit of the womb is a reward” (Psalm 127:3). The psalmist goes on: “Children born to the young are like arrows in a fighter’s hand” (Psalm 127:4). An arrow is not made to stay in the quiver for ever. It is shaped, straightened and then sent out towards a target. Parents have the children God gives them for a season, to shape them and then to send them out into the world for His purposes.

This means children are not a burden to be endured or a possession to be used. They are not a retirement plan, a source of family pride, or a way to fulfil our own unfinished dreams. They belong first to God. We are stewards of them, entrusted with their care before His face.

Jesus Himself showed how God sees children. When parents brought little ones to Him and the disciples tried to send them away, He was angry. “Allow the children to come to Me. Do not try to stop them, because it is to people like them that the kingdom of God belongs” (Mark 10:14). Charles Spurgeon, the great London preacher, wrote a whole book about that scene. In Come Ye Children he gave this warning to the Church:

“Anything we do to hinder a dear child from coming to Jesus greatly displeases our dear Lord.”

Charles Spurgeon, Come Ye Children

A word here to those who long for children and have none. Your worth before God does not depend on the size of your family. Some of the greatest servants of God had no children of their own. As we will see at the end of this chapter, there is a spiritual parenthood open to every believer.

Parents: the first disciple-makers

Jesus told His Church to make disciples of all nations. For Christian parents, the first nation is the one at their own table.

Deuteronomy 6 is one of the most important passages in the Bible on raising children. Moses was preparing Israel to enter the promised land, and he gave them the great confession of faith: “Hear, Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Then came the great command: “You are to love the LORD your God with your whole heart, with your whole being, and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:5).

Notice the order. Before Moses says a word about teaching children, he speaks to the parents. “Keep these words that I am commanding you today close to your heart” (Deuteronomy 6:6). We cannot pass on what we do not have. A father who never opens his Bible cannot expect his son to love it. A mother who never prays cannot expect her daughter to treasure prayer. The first step in raising children in the faith is for the parents themselves to live coram Deo, before the face of God. Children learn far more from what they see than from what they are told.

Only then does Moses say, “Teach them carefully to your children” (Deuteronomy 6:7). God gave this task to parents, not first to priests, schools or Sunday school teachers. Church and school can help, and we thank God for them. But they cannot replace a mother and father. A child spends perhaps one or two hours a week in church. The rest of the week is spent at home and in the world. Long before God spoke to Moses, He had said of Abraham, “I have singled him out so that he will charge his children and his family after him to walk in the way of the LORD” (Genesis 18:19). The home is God’s first school.

Words, example and daily life

How are parents to teach? Deuteronomy gives a picture of ordinary life: “as you sit in your house and as you go on your way, as you lie down and as you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7). In other words, all the time. Faith is passed on in the kitchen, on the road to school, in the field, at bedtime and at breakfast.

This takes some of the pressure off. You do not need to be a skilled preacher to teach your children about God. You need to bring God into the ordinary moments. When you plant seeds together, talk about the God who makes them grow. When a neighbour is sick, pray for her together, and visit her together. When your child is afraid of the dark, teach him that God watches over him at night. When money is short, let your children see you trust God and give thanks when He provides. When you lose your temper, let them hear you apologise, and see you ask God for forgiveness.

Deuteronomy expects children to ask questions: “Some day your son will ask you, ‘What do they mean, these decrees, statutes and rulings that the LORD our God has commanded you?’” (Deuteronomy 6:20). And the answer Moses gives is not a list of rules but a story: we were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD brought us out with a mighty hand. When our children ask why we go to church, why we pray, why we do not lie, the best answer begins with the story of what God has done, in the Bible and in our own lives.

Psalm 78 shows the chain of generations that God intends. “We will not conceal them from their children; we will pass on to those who come after us the deeds for which the LORD is praised, His strength, and the marvels He has worked” (Psalm 78:4). Why? “So that those born later, children not yet born, would know them, and would grow up and tell them to their own children, so that they would rest their hope on God” (Psalm 78:6–7). Each generation is a link in the chain. Our task is to make sure the chain does not break with us.

What about the famous promise in Proverbs? “Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not leave it” (Proverbs 22:6). This is a proverb, a wise saying about how life usually works, not a guarantee that every child of faithful parents will follow Christ. Children are real people who make their own choices. Some wander for years. If that is your story, do not despair and do not stop praying. The seeds you sowed are still in the ground, and God is still at work. Many prodigals have come home.

Susanna Wesley: a school in the rectory

Few mothers in church history have had a greater influence than Susanna Wesley. She was born in London in 1669, the youngest of many children of a Puritan pastor. She married Samuel Wesley, a clergyman, and they moved to the poor country parish of Epworth in Lincolnshire. She gave birth to nineteen children, and only about half of them lived beyond infancy. The family was often in debt. Her husband was frequently away, and he was not always easy to live with. In 1709 the rectory burned down, and five-year-old John was rescued from an upstairs window moments before the roof fell in.

In the middle of all this, Susanna made her home a school. She taught her children herself for six hours a day. And she taught them to pray almost from the time they could talk. Years later she described her method in a letter to her son John:

“Our children were taught as soon as they could speak the Lord’s prayer, which they were made to say at rising and at bedtime constantly, to which, as they grew bigger, were added a short prayer for their parents, and some collects, a short catechism, and some portion of Scripture as their memories could bear.”

Susanna Wesley, quoted in Susanna Wesley

“At rising and at bedtime”: she was living out Deuteronomy 6:7. But the most striking part of her method was the personal time she gave each child. With so many children, it would have been easy to treat them as a crowd. Instead, during a winter when her husband was away in London, she resolved to do more for the souls around her. “I resolved to begin with my own children,” she wrote, and she described what she did:

“I take such a proportion of time as I can best spare every night to discourse with each child by itself”

Susanna Wesley, quoted in Susanna Wesley

Each evening of the week belonged to a different child. Thursday evening was for John. Those quiet talks shaped a boy who would one day ride across England preaching the gospel, while his brother Charles wrote thousands of hymns that are still sung around the world. The revival that followed reached far beyond Britain.

We should be honest about Susanna. She lived three hundred years ago, and some of her methods were very strict, even harsh, by the standards of Scripture’s own warnings to parents, which we will look at next. She wrote of “conquering” a child’s will. We need not copy everything she did. But we can learn from what mattered most: her own life of prayer, her steady teaching of Scripture, her consistency, and her determination to know each child’s heart. You do not need nineteen children or six hours a day. You need a little time, given regularly, with each child, before the face of God.

Discipline and instruction with love

Children need boundaries. Scripture is clear that loving parents correct their children, just as God corrects His. “For the LORD corrects the one He loves, as a father corrects the son who is his joy” (Proverbs 3:12). A parent who never says no is not being kind. He is leaving his child unprotected.

But the Bible also gives a strong warning to parents, and especially to fathers. “Fathers, do not drive your children to anger. Instead, bring them up with the Lord’s training and correction” (Ephesians 6:4). And again: “Fathers, do not keep provoking your children, or they will lose heart” (Colossians 3:21). In Paul’s day fathers had almost unlimited power over their children. Paul limits that power. A Christian father must not crush his children.

How do parents provoke children to anger? By correcting in a rage. By punishing harshly or unfairly. By mocking, shaming or comparing them with their brothers and sisters. By making promises and breaking them. By never listening. By demanding a holiness from them that the parents do not show themselves. A child treated this way may obey for a time, but inside he loses heart, and often loses interest in his parents’ God as well.

So discipline must be given with love. The word “discipline” is close to the word “disciple”. The goal is not punishment but training: to help a child grow in wisdom and self-control. Explain why a rule matters. Correct calmly, and never in anger. Keep your word. Praise what is good, often and specifically. And after any correction, hold your child close, so that he knows your love has not changed. “At the time it is given, no discipline seems a matter for joy... But afterward it pays back those who have been trained by it with a harvest of peace” (Hebrews 12:11).

Children too have their calling: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, because this is right” (Ephesians 6:1). Parents can help their children obey by making obedience a joy and not a fear.

Worship, prayer and Scripture in the home

One of the simplest ways to pass on the faith is to worship God together as a family. Joshua stood before the whole nation and declared, “My household and I will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15). That decision is made again in every home that gathers to pray.

Family worship does not need to be long or formal. Ten minutes after the evening meal is enough. Sing a song, perhaps one the children can choose. Read a short passage of Scripture, or a Bible story for little ones. Ask one question about it. Then pray, letting each person who wishes say a short prayer. With small children, keep it short and lively. With teenagers, let them lead sometimes, and welcome their hard questions. There will be evenings when the baby cries, the teenager sulks and nothing seems to happen. Keep going. The fruit of family worship is not seen in a single evening but over many years.

Hudson Taylor, who later took the gospel deep into inland China, grew up in such a home in Yorkshire. As a teenager he drifted from the faith of his parents. His mother and sister did not stop praying. One afternoon, while his mother was away from home, she felt a strong burden to pray for her son’s conversion, and she prayed until she was sure God had heard her. At that very time, the boy picked up a gospel tract in his father’s library and came to faith in Christ. He wrote in A Retrospect:

“Thus while my dear mother was praising God on her knees in her chamber, I was praising Him in the old warehouse to which I had gone alone to read at my leisure this little book.”

Hudson Taylor, A Retrospect

Never underestimate the prayers of a parent. They may be the most important thing you do for your children.

Lois, Eunice and the whole Church

When Paul wrote to his young friend Timothy, he remembered where Timothy’s faith began: “I recall your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice, and which I am sure now lives in you” (2 Timothy 1:5). Timothy’s father was a Greek and, it seems, not a believer (Acts 16:1). The faith came through a grandmother and a mother. Paul goes on: “from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15).

This is an encouragement to every mother raising children with an unbelieving husband, and to every grandmother who prays for her grandchildren. Your faithfulness is not wasted. A Lois and a Eunice prepared the way for one of the great leaders of the early Church.

Paul himself had no children, yet he called Timothy his son in the faith. He could write to a church, “For it was I who fathered you in Christ Jesus, through the gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). In God’s family, everyone can be a spiritual parent or grandparent. Paul tells Titus to teach the older women so that “they can train the younger women to love their husbands and children” (Titus 2:4). The old psalmist prayed that God would not abandon him “until I have told the generation after me what Your arm has done” (Psalm 71:18).

So the whole Church helps raise the next generation. The Sunday school teacher who prepares carefully each week. The youth leader who answers messages late at night. The single brother who becomes an uncle to a fatherless boy. The widow who knows every child in the congregation by name and prays for them. Charles Spurgeon often spoke of how much he owed to his mother, who prayed with her children and pleaded with them to come to Christ. But he was also shaped by his grandfather, a pastor, in whose home he spent much of his early childhood. It truly takes a family, and in Christ that family is the Church.

Do you know the children in your church by name? Do you pray for them? Could you be a Lois or a Eunice to a child whose own home is not a place of faith? This is how the chain of Psalm 78 holds firm: not only through parents, but through a whole people who live before God’s face and will not let the next generation forget Him.

In the next chapter we leave the home and step into the world of work, where most of us spend the greater part of our waking hours, and where we are just as surely before the face of God.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Deuteronomy 6:4–9. Why do you think Moses speaks to the parents’ own hearts before he speaks about teaching children?
  • What ordinary moments in your family’s day could become opportunities to speak about God?
  • Susanna Wesley set aside time for each child individually. What would that look like in your home or among the children you care for?
  • In what ways can parents “drive their children to anger”? Which of these do you most need to guard against?
  • Who were the Lois and Eunice of your own life, the people who first showed you faith in God?
  • Which child, outside your own family, could you begin to pray for and encourage?

A step for this week

Begin a simple family worship time on at least three evenings this week. Choose a fixed time, perhaps straight after the evening meal, and keep it to ten minutes: one song, one short Bible passage (a story from the Gospel of Mark works well), one question, and a time of prayer in which each person who wishes can pray. If you do not have children at home, choose one child or young person in your church or neighbourhood, pray for them by name every day this week, and find one way to encourage them, such as a kind word after church or a short message.

study_questions.question: Who is responsible for teaching children about God?
study_questions.answer: God gave this task first to parents. Moses told Israel, "Teach them carefully to your children, and speak of them as you sit in your house and as you go on your way, as you lie down and as you rise" (Deuteronomy 6:7). Church and school can help, but they cannot replace a mother and father, and parents must first keep God's words close to their own hearts, because children learn more from what they see than from what they are told.

study_questions.question: Does Proverbs 22:6 guarantee that children will follow God?
study_questions.answer: "Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not leave it" (Proverbs 22:6) is a proverb, a wise saying about how life usually works, not a guarantee. Children are real people who make their own choices, and some wander for years. Parents should not despair or stop praying, because the seeds they sowed are still in the ground and many prodigals have come home.

study_questions.question: How should Christian parents discipline their children?
study_questions.answer: Loving parents correct their children, as "the LORD corrects the one He loves" (Proverbs 3:12). But Paul warns, "Fathers, do not drive your children to anger. Instead, bring them up with the Lord's training and correction" (Ephesians 6:4). Discipline should be training, not rage: explain the rules, correct calmly, keep your word, praise what is good, and reassure your child afterwards that your love has not changed.

fields.title: Work and Workers: Serving as unto the Lord
fields.body_html:
“Whatever you are doing, put your whole self into the work, as for the Lord and not for people, knowing that you will receive from the Lord the inheritance as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you serve as slaves.”

— Colossians 3:23–24 (OWB)

Before the sun rises, a woman in a market town is already setting out her tomatoes and onions in neat piles. A farmer is walking to his field with a hoe on his shoulder. A nurse is finishing a long night shift. A young man in a city office is opening his laptop, already tired at the thought of the week ahead. A mother is preparing breakfast for four children while planning how to stretch the money until the end of the month.

Most of us spend the greater part of our waking lives working, whether for wages, on our own land, in our own small business, or in the unpaid work of caring for a home and family. And many Christians quietly believe that this part of life does not really count with God. Sunday is for God; Monday is for survival.

This chapter says the opposite. Living coram Deo, before the face of God, does not stop at the church door or the front door of the home. The Lord who sees us at prayer sees us at the market stall, the office desk and the kitchen sink. In the last two chapters we looked at marriage and the raising of children. Now we step out into the world of work, where God is just as present and just as interested.

Work was God’s idea

Work is not a result of the fall. Before sin ever entered the world, “The LORD God took the man and settled him in the garden of Eden to work it and take care of it” (Genesis 2:15). Adam was a gardener before he was a sinner. God Himself is a worker: the Bible opens with six days of creating, and it describes God resting from “all the work” He had done. We are made in the image of a working God, and so we were made to work.

What the fall did was to make work painful. After Adam’s sin God said, “Through painful work you will eat from it all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:17), and “You will eat bread by the sweat of your brow” (Genesis 3:19). That is why work is so often frustrating: weeds in the field, broken machines, unfair bosses, effort that comes to nothing. But the frustration is the curse; work itself remains a gift.

Jesus spent most of His earthly life not preaching but working with His hands. The people of Nazareth asked, “Is He not the carpenter, the son of Mary?” (Mark 6:3). For years the Son of God made doors, tables and ploughs, and every one of them was done to please His Father. Paul too, the greatest missionary of the early Church, earned his living by making tents (Acts 18:3). He told the believers in Thessalonica to “live calmly, look after your own affairs and earn your living with your hands” (1 Thessalonians 4:11).

Scripture honours good work. “Do you see someone who is skilled at their work? They will serve kings, not people of no account” (Proverbs 22:29). The carpenter who joins wood carefully, the teacher who prepares her lessons well, the driver who keeps his vehicle safe, the accountant who keeps honest books: all of them are doing something God values.

Work also gives us something to share. Paul told former thieves, “Instead they must work hard, doing something good with their own hands, so that they have something to share with anyone in need” (Ephesians 4:28). We work not only to feed ourselves but to bless others: to support our families, to help a neighbour in trouble, and to give to God’s work. The money you earn honestly at the market or the office can become food for a widow, school fees for an orphan or support for a missionary. Seen this way, even the most ordinary job becomes a channel of God’s care for the world (we return to this in Chapter 26).

Martin Luther saw this clearly in the sixteenth century. In his day many believed that monks and nuns lived a higher kind of life, while ordinary people with ordinary jobs served God less. Luther taught that every honest calling, or vocation, is a way of serving God and neighbour. The maid, the farmer and the shoemaker please God as much as any priest, when they do their work in faith. In The Large Catechism he imagined what would happen if a servant girl understood this:

“If this truth, then, could be impressed upon the poor people, a servant-girl would leap and praise and thank God; and with her tidy work for which she receives support and wages she would acquire such a treasure as all that are esteemed the greatest saints have not obtained.”

Martin Luther, The Large Catechism

Your work, done for God, is not second-class service. It is part of your worship.

Servants and masters: reading these passages honestly

The main New Testament passages on work are addressed to “slaves” and “masters” (Ephesians 6:5–9; Colossians 3:22–4:1). Many readers, especially in Africa and among people whose ancestors were enslaved, find these passages painful. We must read them honestly.

In the Roman world of the first century, slavery was everywhere. A large part of the population of many cities was enslaved. People became slaves through war, debt, kidnapping or being born to enslaved parents. Some were educated and held responsible posts in households; many others laboured in fields and mines under brutal conditions. All of them were legally owned by another person. The early churches were small, poor and often persecuted, and many of their members were slaves. The apostles did not call for an armed uprising, which would have been crushed. Instead they taught enslaved believers how to live faithfully where they were, and they taught masters a way of thinking that would, in time, undermine the whole system.

Look at what the New Testament actually says. In Christ, “there is no slave or free person” (Galatians 3:28); all are one family. Paul tells slaves who have the chance of freedom, “make the most of it” (1 Corinthians 7:21). He names “slave traders” among the lawbreakers whom God’s law condemns (1 Timothy 1:10), echoing the Law of Moses, which said that whoever kidnaps and sells a person must die (Exodus 21:16). He tells masters that they and their slaves have the same Master in heaven, who “does not show favoritism” (Ephesians 6:9). And in his letter to Philemon, he sends the runaway slave Onesimus back to his master asking him to receive him “no longer as a slave but as more than a slave, a dear brother” (Philemon 1:16). Once a master sees his slave as a dear brother, slavery has lost its foundation.

So let it be said plainly: this book does not endorse slavery. The buying and selling of human beings, whether in the Roman Empire, in the Atlantic slave trade that carried millions of Africans across the ocean, or in the trafficking, forced labour and debt bondage that still exist today, is sin against God and against people made in His image. Those who once used these verses to defend slavery twisted them.

What, then, do these passages say to us? The principles God gave to slaves and masters in their hard situation apply with even greater force to employees and employers, who meet as free people. That is how most Christians have always applied them, and it is how we will apply them now.

William Wilberforce: a statesman before the face of God

William Wilberforce was born in 1759 in Hull, in the north of England, to a wealthy merchant family. He was clever, charming and witty, and at twenty-one he was elected to Parliament. He loved society, cards and late nights. Then, in 1784 and 1785, during long journeys with a Christian friend, he read the New Testament and was converted. It changed the whole direction of his life.

His first thought was that he should leave politics and become a clergyman, because surely that was the way to serve God properly. He went to see John Newton, a pastor who had once been a slave-ship captain and had become a Christian and the writer of the hymn “Amazing Grace”. Newton urged him to stay in Parliament. God, he believed, could use Wilberforce right where he was.

Wilberforce stayed. In 1787 he wrote in his diary that God had set before him two great tasks: ending the slave trade, and the reformation of the morals of his country. For twenty years he brought the matter before Parliament again and again. He was mocked, threatened and defeated many times. He worked alongside others, among them Olaudah Equiano, a man born in what is now Nigeria, kidnapped as a child and enslaved, who later bought his freedom, became a Christian, and wrote a book telling his story that moved thousands of readers. At last, in 1807, Parliament abolished the British slave trade. Wilberforce kept working for the freedom of all enslaved people in the British Empire, and the law ending slavery passed in 1833, just days before he died.

Wilberforce did not think his work in Parliament was less spiritual than preaching. In his book A Practical View of Christianity he noted that some early Christians had thought they should give up their ordinary affairs, and that the apostle corrected them:

“But the Apostle most pointedly guarded them against so gross an error, and expressly and repeatedly enjoined them to perform the particular duties of their several stations with increased alacrity and fidelity, that they might thereby do credit to their Christian profession.”

William Wilberforce, A Practical View of Christianity

“Their several stations” means wherever God has placed each of us. Wilberforce’s station was Parliament. Yours may be a farm, a classroom, a hospital, a shop or a home. The call is the same: serve there with energy and faithfulness, as unto the Lord. Elsewhere in the same book Wilberforce described the true Christian as one who desires to please God in all his thoughts, words and actions, and then added: “No calling is proscribed, no pursuit is forbidden, no science or art, no pleasure is disallowed, which is reconcilable with this principle.”

Employees: serving with integrity

Here is what Paul told slaves, and what he tells every worker today: “Do not work only while they are watching, to win their favor, but with an undivided heart, out of reverence for the Lord” (Colossians 3:22). That is a description of coram Deo at work. Most of us work differently when the boss is in the room. We look busy. We speak politely. When the boss leaves, we slow down, or spend the afternoon on our phones. But the Christian worker has another Master who never leaves the room. “Whatever you are doing, put your whole self into the work, as for the Lord and not for people” (Colossians 3:23).

What does this look like on Monday morning?

  • Honesty. Paul tells workers not to steal from their employers, “but to show that they can be fully trusted” (Titus 2:10). Do not take what belongs to the company, whether money, supplies or time. Record your hours truthfully. Refuse bribes, even when “everyone does it”.
  • Diligence. Do your work well, even the parts no one will check. Arrive on time. Finish what you start.
  • A good attitude. Do not join in the constant complaining about the boss. Speak respectfully, even when you disagree.
  • Trustworthiness. When Daniel’s enemies tried to find something to accuse him of in his government work, “they could find no grounds and no corruption, because he was trustworthy” (Daniel 6:4). Could that be said of you?

Not every job is pleasant. Brother Lawrence, the seventeenth-century French monk, was assigned to the kitchen of his monastery, and he did not like it. But he learned to do it all for God. In The Practice of the Presence of God we read that:

“in his business in the kitchen (to which he had naturally a great aversion), having accustomed himself to do everything there for the love of God, and with prayer, upon all occasions, for His grace to do his work well, he had found everything easy, during fifteen years that he had been employed there.”

Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God

If you are in a job you did not choose and do not enjoy, you are not outside God’s care. Ask Him for grace to do this day’s work well, for His sake. And if you are without paid work, or your work is unpaid caring for children, the sick or the elderly, remember that God sees and values that labour too. “It is the Lord Christ you serve” (Colossians 3:24).

Employers and leaders: a Master in heaven

Paul did not speak only to those at the bottom. “Masters, give your slaves what is right and fair, because you know that you too have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1). In Ephesians he adds, “Stop threatening them” (Ephesians 6:9).

If you employ others, manage a team, run a farm with hired workers, or lead in any organisation, you also live before the face of God. You will give account to Him for how you treated the people under you. The Law of Moses said, “When you hire a laborer, the pay must not stay in your hands overnight until morning” (Leviticus 19:13). James warned rich landowners, “The pay you held back from the laborers who mowed your fields is crying out” (James 5:4). God hears the cry of the worker who is cheated.

So a Christian employer pays fair wages, and pays them on time. He keeps his workers safe. He does not shout, threaten or humiliate. He does not favour his own tribe or relatives in hiring and promotion. He keeps his promises. He treats the cleaner with the same respect as the manager, remembering that both are made in God’s image, and that there is “no favoritism with the Lord” (Colossians 3:25).

Witness in the workplace

The workplace is one of the main places where unbelievers meet Christians. Paul wanted believers to work quietly and well “so that outsiders will see you live rightly” (1 Thessalonians 4:12). Jesus said, “your light must shine where people can see it, so that they will see your good deeds and give glory to your Father in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Witness at work begins with the quality of your work and the quality of your character. A Christian who preaches to colleagues but arrives late and leaves early does more harm than good. A Christian who is honest, reliable, kind and calm under pressure earns the right to be heard. Then, when a colleague is sick, grieving or asking big questions, you will have opportunities to pray for them and to speak of Christ. Do not use your employer’s time to preach, but do not hide your faith either. Be ready, at the right moment, to explain the hope you have.

Rest alongside work

God designed us not only to work but also to rest. The fourth commandment gave Israel a rhythm: “You have six days to labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath for the LORD your God” (Exodus 20:9–10). Notice that the command protected servants, foreigners and even animals. Rest was a gift for the weakest, not only for the powerful.

In Chapter 12 we saw this book’s view: Jesus Himself is our Sabbath rest. He calls, “Come to Me, all of you who are worn out with work and weighed down with burdens, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Every day, then, becomes a day of resting in Him, relying on God for everything rather than on our own striving. Christians hold different views about how the Sabbath command applies to Sunday or Saturday (see the Appendix), but all agree that regular physical rest remains God’s good gift and a wise rhythm for workers and leaders alike.

Luther, explaining the commandment about the holy day in The Large Catechism, said that one of its purposes was simply the rest of tired workers: it was given “for the common people, man-servants and maid-servants, who have been attending to their work and trade the whole week, that for a day they may retire in order to rest and be refreshed.” Many of us need to hear that. “It does you no good to get up early and stay up late, eating food earned by anxious work; He gives sleep to the one He loves” (Psalm 127:2). Working seven days a week is not a sign of great faith. It may be a sign that we trust our own effort more than God’s provision. Rest is an act of trust.

In the next chapter we turn from the workplace to the place where God’s people gather to rest, worship and grow together: the Church, God’s family.

Questions for reflection

  • Do you tend to think of your daily work as “spiritual” or “unspiritual”? How does Genesis 2:15 change that?
  • How would you explain to a friend why the New Testament passages on slaves and masters do not endorse slavery?
  • Wilberforce thought of leaving politics to serve God, but was encouraged to stay. Where has God placed you, and how could you serve Him there?
  • Colossians 3:22 speaks of working “not only while they are watching”. In what areas of your work is this hardest for you?
  • If you lead or employ others, which part of Colossians 4:1 or Leviticus 19:13 challenges you most?
  • What does your weekly pattern of work and rest say about where your trust lies?

A step for this week

Each working day this week, before you begin your work (whether at a job, on the farm, in a business or at home), pray this short prayer: “Lord Jesus, I do this work for You today. Help me to do it well and honestly, and to treat everyone I meet as You would.” At the end of each day, take two minutes to look back: where did you work as for the Lord, and where did you work only for people? Thank God for the first, and ask His forgiveness and help for the second.

study_questions.question: What does it mean to work as unto the Lord?
study_questions.answer: It means doing every task for Christ, who sees us at work as surely as at prayer. Paul wrote, "Whatever you are doing, put your whole self into the work, as for the Lord and not for people" (Colossians 3:23), and warned against working "only while they are watching" (Colossians 3:22). In practice it means honesty, diligence, a good attitude and trustworthiness, even in jobs we did not choose.

study_questions.question: Does the Bible endorse slavery?
study_questions.answer: No. The New Testament spoke to slaves and masters in the Roman world, but it undermined slavery: in Christ "there is no slave or free person" (Galatians 3:28), it condemns "slave traders" (1 Timothy 1:10), and Paul asked Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave but as more than a slave, a dear brother" (Philemon 1:16). This book does not endorse slavery; buying and selling human beings, past or present, is sin, and the principles of these passages now apply to employees and employers.

study_questions.question: Is work a result of the fall?
study_questions.answer: No. Before sin entered the world, "The LORD God took the man and settled him in the garden of Eden to work it and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15). The fall made work painful and frustrating, but work itself remains God's gift. Jesus worked as a carpenter and Paul as a tentmaker, and every honest calling can be a way of serving God and neighbour.

fields.title: The Church: God’s Family Together
fields.body_html:
“They gave themselves fully to the apostles’ teaching and to the shared life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers.”

— Acts 2:42 (OWB)

On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came, Peter preached, and about three thousand people were baptised. What happened next? They did not simply go home with a warm feeling. They became a community. Luke describes it in a few unforgettable sentences: they learned together, shared their lives and their possessions, ate together in their homes, prayed together and praised God together. “And each day the Lord brought into their company more people who were being saved” (Acts 2:47).

Two thousand years later, that same family meets under a mango tree in a village, in a rented school hall in a busy city, in a cathedral of ancient stone, in a house church whose members whisper their songs for fear of the police, and in a tin-roofed building where the drums can be heard three streets away. The Church is the most widespread family on earth.

So far in Part Four we have looked at marriage, children and work. Now we come to the family that holds all the others: the Church. Living coram Deo is never a private matter between me and God alone. We stand before His face together, as His people. In this chapter we will look at what the Church is, why we need one another, what the Church does when it gathers, how it holds together across its many differences, and how each of us can serve in it. The next chapter will look at how the Church is organised and led.

The body and the bride of Christ

The New Testament uses many pictures for the Church. Two of the most important are the body and the bride.

First, the Church is the body of Christ. “You are Christ’s body, and each of you individually is one of its parts” (1 Corinthians 12:27). Christ is the head: God “has given Him to the church to be head over all things. The church is His body” (Ephesians 1:22–23). A body is alive. It is not an organisation that people join like a club, but a living thing in which every part is connected to the head and to every other part. Through the Church, the risen Jesus still has hands to heal, feet to go, and a voice to speak in the world.

Second, the Church is the bride of Christ. We saw in Chapter 18 that marriage is a picture of “Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). Christ “loved the church and handed Himself over for her” (Ephesians 5:25). The Bible ends with the new Jerusalem “descending out of heaven from God, ready like a bride who has adorned herself for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). The Church is loved. Whatever her faults today, and they are many, she is the one Jesus died for, and He is making her beautiful.

Notice that in both pictures, the Church is people, not a building. We say “I am going to church”, but in the Bible’s language, you do not go to church: you are the Church. The building is only where the Church meets.

Why we need each other: no solo Christians

Many people today say, “I love Jesus, but I do not need the Church.” Some have been hurt by Christians. Some find church services dull. Some simply prefer to watch a sermon on their phone at home. These are real struggles, and churches often do need to repent of the hurt they have caused. But the Bible knows nothing of a Christian who belongs to Christ and not to His people.

Paul puts it this way: “So the eye cannot tell the hand, ‘I can do without you,’ and the head cannot tell the feet, ‘I can do without you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21). A hand cut off from the body does not become free; it dies. In the same way, a believer cut off from other believers grows cold. A burning coal taken out of the fire soon turns grey. Put it back among the others, and it glows again.

So the letter to the Hebrews urges, “Let us also keep one another in mind, so as to rouse each other to love and good works. Let us not walk away from our own gatherings, as some have made it their practice, but keep urging one another on” (Hebrews 10:24–25). We need others to encourage us when we are weak, to correct us when we wander, to pray for us when we cannot pray, and to rejoice with us when God is good. And others need us. “If one part is in pain, all the parts share its pain; if one part is honored, all the parts share its joy” (1 Corinthians 12:26).

There is a promise here too. Jesus said, “For whenever two or three come together in My name, I am there among them” (Matthew 18:20). We rightly think of meeting God’s face in our private prayer (see Chapters 7 and 8). But Christ is present in a particular way when His people gather. When a few believers kneel together in a crowded city flat, or a congregation sings under a village tree, He is in the midst. Living before the face of God includes seeking His face together.

The Church is also where we learn to carry one another. “Take up one another’s heavy loads, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). In a family, no one carries a heavy load alone. When a father loses his job, when a child is sick, when a widow cannot pay her rent, the family gathers round. The Church is meant to be that kind of family: “Love one another warmly, as brothers and sisters in one family; take the lead in honoring one another” (Romans 12:10). Jesus Himself said, “anyone who does the will of My Father in heaven is a brother and sister and mother to Me” (Matthew 12:50).

Cyprian of Carthage: a bishop who held the family together

In the city of Carthage, on the coast of North Africa in what is now Tunisia, lived a wealthy and gifted teacher of public speaking named Cyprian. Around the year 246 he came to faith in Christ as an adult. He gave much of his wealth to the poor, gave himself to the study of Scripture, and within a few years the Christians of Carthage chose him as their bishop.

He led the church through some of its hardest years. In 250 the Roman emperor Decius ordered everyone in the empire to offer sacrifice to the gods. Many Christians were imprisoned or killed. Many others gave in to fear and sacrificed, or bought false certificates saying they had. Cyprian went into hiding and led his people through letters. When the persecution eased, the church faced a painful question: what should be done with those who had denied Christ and now wanted to return? Some said they should never be received back. Others said they should be welcomed at once, without any repentance. The church was in danger of breaking apart.

Cyprian called for real repentance and also a real welcome back, and he worked tirelessly to keep the church united. He wrote a short book, On the Unity of the Church, which has been read ever since. In it he used pictures from nature to show how one Church can be spread over many places:

“As there are many rays of the sun, but one light; and many branches of a tree, but one strength based in its tenacious root; and since from one spring flow many streams, although the multiplicity seems diffused in the liberality of an overflowing abundance, yet the unity is still preserved in the source.”

Cyprian of Carthage, The Treatises of Cyprian

In the same book he wrote his most famous line: “He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother.” Christians of different traditions apply those words in different ways, and Cyprian himself was thinking of people who had broken away into rival groups. But the heart of what he said is true for all of us: God does not give us Himself as Father without also giving us His family.

A few years later a terrible plague swept through Carthage. People abandoned their sick relatives in the streets. Cyprian urged the Christians to care for the sick and bury the dead, not only their fellow believers but their pagan neighbours too. In his treatise On the Mortality (found in The Treatises of Cyprian) he said that the plague was testing everyone, to see “whether they who are in health tend the sick; whether relations affectionately love their kindred; whether masters pity their languishing servants”. The Church was to be a family whose love spilled over its walls.

In 258, under the emperor Valerian, Cyprian was arrested and beheaded outside Carthage, with his people around him. Like Augustine after him, he is one of the great Christian leaders of Africa, and a reminder to African readers that the Church in their continent is not a recent arrival. It is as old as almost any church on earth.

What the Church does together

Acts 2:42 gives four marks of the first church: “They gave themselves fully to the apostles’ teaching and to the shared life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers.” These are still the heart of church life.

Teaching. The first Christians gave themselves to the apostles’ teaching, which we now have in the New Testament. A healthy church is fed on the Word of God, explained clearly and applied to real life (see Chapter 6).

The shared life. The word often translated “fellowship” means sharing something in common. It is more than tea after the service. “Everyone who believed kept together and treated all they had as shared” (Acts 2:44). They sold land and goods to help anyone in need. Today that may mean bringing food when a family has a new baby, helping a brother find work, or paying a sister’s hospital bill.

The breaking of bread. This includes ordinary meals in one another’s homes, where “at home they broke bread, eating their food with joyful and simple hearts” (Acts 2:46), and it includes the Lord’s Supper, which Jesus gave on the night He was betrayed. Jesus gave His Church two sacraments, outward signs of His grace: baptism and the Lord’s Supper. In baptism we are marked as His, “buried with Him into death, in order that, as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might live a life that is new” (Romans 6:4). In the Supper we remember His death and are fed by Him: “For each time you eat this bread and drink the cup, you are announcing the Lord’s death, until He comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). Christians hold different convictions about who should be baptised and how, and about how Christ is present in the Supper. These are important matters, but they are secondary ones that should not break our fellowship as believers (see the Appendix). All agree that Christ commanded both, and that both point us to His death and resurrection.

The prayers. The first church prayed together, regularly and often. A praying church is a living church. Many of the great revivals in history began with a few believers who met to pray.

Out of these four flowed worship. They were “praising God and well regarded by all the people” (Acts 2:47). When the Church gathers, we come before the face of God together, to sing His praise, hear His Word and offer Him our lives.

Unity in diversity across traditions and cultures

The Church is one, and yet it is wonderfully varied. It includes Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant believers; Anglicans and Baptists, Lutherans and Pentecostals, Methodists and Presbyterians and many independent churches. It includes every tribe and tongue. John saw the final picture: “a crowd so vast that no one could number it. They came from every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9).

Paul tells us how to hold this family together: “Be humble and gentle in every way, and be patient, putting up with one another in love. Spare no effort to keep the unity the Spirit gives, with peace as the bond that holds you together” (Ephesians 4:2–3). Notice that we do not create this unity; the Spirit gives it. Our task is to keep it. And it rests on what we share: “There is one body and one Spirit... one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Ephesians 4:4–6).

John Wesley, the eighteenth-century evangelist, had strong views and was not afraid to state them. Yet in his sermon “Catholic Spirit” (the word catholic here means universal, for the whole Church) he asked whether Christians who cannot think alike may still love alike (a question the Appendix returns to). He answered that they can:
