“Herein all the children of God may unite, notwithstanding these smaller differences. These remaining as they are, they may forward one another in love and in good works.”

John Wesley, Sermons on Several Occasions

Unity across cultures can be even harder than unity across traditions. In many places the deepest divisions in the Church are not about doctrine but about tribe, caste, class, race or language. Yet Peter writes to a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles: “At one time you were no people at all; now you are God’s people” (1 Peter 2:10). In Christ we become a new people, “a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9), with a new family identity that runs deeper than our earthly ones.

Bakht Singh of India showed what this can look like. Born into a Sikh family in the Punjab in 1903, he came to faith in Christ while studying in Canada, and returned to India in the 1930s as an evangelist. He planted congregations that were led by Indians and supported by Indian believers, simple in worship and devoted to prayer and the Word. At the large gatherings he led in Hyderabad, thousands of believers came together for days of worship and teaching, and people of different castes, languages and backgrounds sat together and ate together as one family. In a land where caste divided people at every meal, that shared table was itself a sermon.

The German pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who led an underground seminary for the Confessing Church in the 1930s, wrote a small book called Life Together about the community he shared with his students. One of his warnings is worth remembering. Christian community, he said, is a gift God has already given us in Christ, not an ideal we must build. Those who fall in love with their dream of the perfect church end up despising the real one. The church you belong to will disappoint you. Love it anyway, because Christ does.

Serving in the local church

The universal Church is made real in local churches, ordinary congregations with names, addresses and imperfect members. That is where we are called to belong and to serve.

“We have many parts in a single body, and the parts do not all have the same task. In the same way, many as we are, we are one body in Christ, and each of us is a part that belongs to all the others” (Romans 12:4–5). Every believer has a part to play. The church grows, Paul says, “as each part does its own work” (Ephesians 4:16). It is not meant to be a few leaders doing everything while the rest watch.

Begin by committing yourself to one local church. Some believers drift from congregation to congregation, always looking for better music or a better preacher, and never put down roots. But a tree that is moved every season never bears fruit. Find a church that teaches the Bible faithfully, join it, and stay long enough to love its people and to be known by them.

You do not need a title to serve. Arrive early and welcome newcomers at the door. Learn the names of the children. Visit the sick member nobody else has visited. Help clean the building, set out chairs, cook for a funeral, drive an elderly widow to the service. Join a small group where people know each other well enough to pray honestly. Give faithfully. Use the gifts God has given you, which we will explore in Chapter 23. And honour those who lead, while remembering that leaders exist to equip all of God’s people for service, as we will see in Chapter 22.

When you serve in this way, you are not serving a human institution. You are serving Christ in His body, before His face. “So welcome one another, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God” (Romans 15:7).

Questions for reflection

  • Which picture of the Church means most to you: the body or the bride? Why?
  • Have you ever been tempted to follow Christ without His Church? What drew you away, and what might draw you back?
  • Cyprian worked to hold together a church divided by fear and failure. Where is your church in danger of division, and how could you help keep “the unity the Spirit gives”?
  • Look at the four marks in Acts 2:42. Which is strongest in your church, and which is weakest?
  • What divisions of tribe, class, language or background does your church need to overcome? What could a shared table look like for you?
  • What is one way you could serve in your local church that you are not doing now?

A step for this week

This week, do one thing to strengthen the family of your local church beyond attending the main service. Invite someone from church, preferably someone from a different background, age or tribe from yours, to share a meal in your home. Or visit or call a member who has been sick or absent. Before you go, pray Ephesians 4:2–3 for your church by name, asking God to help you keep the unity His Spirit gives.

study_questions.question: Why do Christians need to belong to a church?
study_questions.answer: The Bible knows nothing of a Christian who belongs to Christ but not to His people. "The eye cannot tell the hand, 'I can do without you'" (1 Corinthians 12:21), and Hebrews urges, "Let us not walk away from our own gatherings" (Hebrews 10:25). We need others to encourage, correct and pray for us, and they need us, just as a coal taken out of the fire soon goes cold.

study_questions.question: What are the marks of a healthy church in Acts 2:42?
study_questions.answer: The first believers "gave themselves fully to the apostles' teaching and to the shared life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers" (Acts 2:42). These four marks, teaching, shared life, the breaking of bread (including the Lord's Supper) and prayer, are still the heart of church life, and worship flows out of them.

study_questions.question: How can Christians from different churches and cultures be united?
study_questions.answer: We do not create unity; the Spirit gives it, and our task is to "keep the unity the Spirit gives, with peace as the bond that holds you together" (Ephesians 4:3). It rests on what all believers share: "one Lord, one faith, one baptism" (Ephesians 4:5). Differences over baptism or the Lord's Supper are secondary, and in Christ people of every tribe, caste and language become one people, "a royal priesthood, a holy nation" (1 Peter 2:9).

fields.title: The Organisation of the Church: Ministries and Offices
fields.body_html:
“It was He who gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some shepherds and teachers. He gave them to equip God’s holy people for the work of serving, so that the body of Christ would be built up.”

— Ephesians 4:11–12 (OWB)

Think of a house being built in a growing town. There are stones, timber, iron sheets and cement, and many willing hands. But if no one knows where the walls should stand, and no one checks that the foundation is level, the house will not survive the first rains. Willing hands are not enough. A building needs a plan, and people who serve the plan.

In Chapter 21 we saw that the Church is God’s family, the body and bride of Christ. A body needs joints and ligaments as well as eyes and hands. So Christ, who loves His Church, has given it a shape. He gives some people to lead, teach and shepherd, and He gives every believer a part to play.

This chapter is about that shape: the ministries Christ gives, the offices of elder and deacon, how men and women serve together, and the truth that every Christian is a priest and a minister. This is not only church business for committee meetings. How a church is led shapes how its people grow. And all of it is done coram Deo, before the face of God, who sees the preacher in the pulpit and the deacon carrying chairs with the same eyes.

Christ, the Head who gives leaders

Before we speak of any human leader, we begin with the true Head. God “has given Him to the church to be head over all things” (Ephesians 1:22). Christ “is also the head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18). No pastor, bishop or elder owns the Church. It belongs to Jesus, who won it “through His own blood” (Acts 20:28).

So leaders are not owners but stewards, under-shepherds serving the Chief Shepherd. And they are His gifts: “It was He who gave” (Ephesians 4:11). Why did He give them? “To equip God’s holy people for the work of serving” (Ephesians 4:12). The leaders do not do all the work. They equip the saints, and the saints do the work. The goal is maturity, “until all of us arrive at the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God” (Ephesians 4:13).

The measure of a good leader, then, is not how busy he is or how many come to hear him. It is whether the people around him are growing up into Christ. A coach is judged not by how well he plays, but by how well his team plays. Christ gives leaders so that His whole body “grows and builds itself up in love” (Ephesians 4:16).

The equipping ministries of Ephesians 4

Paul names apostles, prophets, evangelists, and shepherds and teachers. Many readers take “shepherds and teachers” as one ministry, the pastor-teacher.

Faithful Christians differ on whether apostles and prophets continue today. Some believe these belonged to the founding of the Church, which is “built on the apostles and prophets as your foundation” (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Others believe that, while the first apostles were unique, God still sends apostolic pioneers and still gives prophetic words. Many stand in between, preferring words such as “missionary” and “church planter”.

Yet the common ground is wide. All agree that the Twelve and Paul were unique witnesses of the risen Christ, that no one today adds to Scripture, and that every word claiming to come from God must be tested by it. And all agree that the work these ministries describe is still needed.

Apostles are “sent ones”. The first apostles laid the foundation of the Church with the teaching we now hold in the New Testament. In a wider sense, the church at Antioch sent out Barnabas and Saul after the Holy Spirit said, “Set Barnabas and Saul apart for Me, for the work I have called them to do” (Acts 13:2). Such people pioneer: they go where Christ is not known, plant churches and lay foundations.

Prophets hear and speak God’s word to strengthen His people: “someone who prophesies speaks to people, and the words build them up, encourage them and comfort them” (1 Corinthians 14:3). This is not a new Bible, but a word in season, often bringing Scripture home to a particular people at a particular time. It must always be tested: “do not look down on prophecy. Test everything; keep hold of what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21).

Evangelists proclaim the good news, like “Philip the evangelist” (Acts 21:8), who explained Isaiah to an Ethiopian official on a desert road. They also equip the whole Church to share the gospel. Paul told Timothy, a pastor, to “do the work of an evangelist” (2 Timothy 4:5). We return to this in Chapter 25.

Pastor-teachers shepherd, feed and protect the flock. God promised, “I will give you shepherds who are after My own heart, and they will shepherd you with knowledge and insight” (Jeremiah 3:15). A shepherd leads the sheep to good pasture, which for God’s people is His Word, and guards them from wolves, which means guarding them from false teaching.

The pastor’s heart for soul care

One part of a pastor’s work is easy to forget in a busy church: the care of souls. Through Ezekiel, God rebuked the leaders who fed themselves but not the flock: “You have not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bandaged the injured. You have not brought back the strays or gone looking for the lost” (Ezekiel 34:4). Then He promised to do it Himself: “I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bandage the injured and strengthen the sick” (Ezekiel 34:16).

That is the heart of the Good Shepherd, and it should be the heart of every pastor. In Chapter 15 we saw that many people come to Christ carrying deep wounds: rejection, grief, abuse, shame. Their spirit has been made new, but their soul still needs healing and growth. A central calling of pastors is to teach, help and heal believers, so that they grow to maturity in Christ. The Lord “heals those whose hearts are crushed and bandages their injuries” (Psalm 147:3), and He often does it through shepherds who sit with the wounded, listen, pray and open the Word. Wise pastors also know when to involve others, as Chapter 15 explained. But the sheep need to be known.

In the seventeenth century, Richard Baxter was pastor in the English town of Kidderminster. He decided that Sunday preaching was not enough. With his assistant he gave Monday and Tuesday each week to meeting families in their homes, about fifteen or sixteen households a week, to teach them the faith and speak with each person about their soul. Over the years the town was changed. In The Reformed Pastor he urged other ministers to do the same, but first to watch over their own hearts:

“Take heed to yourselves, lest your example contradict your doctrine, and lest you lay such stumbling-blocks before the blind, as may be the occasion of their ruin; lest you unsay with your lives, what you say with your tongues.”

Richard Baxter, The Reformed Pastor

A pastor who helps heal others must himself live close to the Healer.

Elders: shepherds who watch over souls

The New Testament gives the Church two lasting offices: elders and deacons. Elders are also called overseers, and the two words describe the same people (compare Titus 1:5 and 1:7). “Elder” speaks of maturity; “overseer” speaks of watching over the flock.

From the beginning, the apostles made sure each church had elders. Paul and Barnabas “appointed elders for the believers, and after praying and fasting, they placed them in the care of the Lord in whom they had believed” (Acts 14:23). Notice the plural: churches were led by a group of elders, not one person alone.

Elders shepherd, teach, guard sound doctrine and give spiritual oversight. Paul told the elders of Ephesus, “Be on your guard, for yourselves and for the whole flock” (Acts 20:28). Peter wrote: “Tend God’s flock among you as shepherds do. Take care of it freely, the way God would have it, not because you are forced to; not to make money for yourselves, but gladly and readily. Do not rule harshly over the people given into your charge; set an example for the flock instead” (1 Peter 5:2–3). An elder “must hold firmly to the trustworthy message as it has been taught, so that he can encourage others with sound teaching and correct those who oppose it” (Titus 1:9).

Most striking is the list of qualifications in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1. Almost all of it is about character. An overseer must be “someone no one can fairly criticize: faithful to his one wife, clear-headed, self-controlled, respected, welcoming to guests, able to teach” (1 Timothy 3:2). He must not be a heavy drinker, violent, quarrelsome or a lover of money. He must manage his household well, must not be a recent convert, and must have a good name among outsiders. Only “able to teach” is a skill. The Church does not first ask, “Can he preach?” It asks, “Is he faithful at home? Is he honest in the market? Do his neighbours respect him?”

The flock, in turn, honours such leaders: “Follow your leaders and yield to them. They stay awake watching over your souls, as people who will have to answer for them” (Hebrews 13:17).

Deacons: serving so the Word is not neglected

The second office grew out of a practical problem. In Jerusalem, the Greek-speaking widows “were being passed over when food was given out each day” (Acts 6:1). The apostles said, “It is not fitting for us to leave aside the word of God in order to serve at tables” (Acts 6:2). So the church chose seven men “of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom” (Acts 6:3), while the apostles would “hold fast to prayer and to the service of the word” (Acts 6:4). The result: “So God’s word went on spreading” (Acts 6:7).

Deacons serve the practical needs of the body: caring for the poor, managing money and property, organising, visiting, mending. This is not lesser work. Among the first seven were Stephen, the first martyr, and Philip the evangelist. Paul’s standard is high: “deacons must be worthy of respect, sincere in what they say, not heavy drinkers, and not greedy for money. They must hold on to the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience” (1 Timothy 3:8–9).

Churches arrange these offices differently: some have bishops, some are led by elders joined in a presbytery, some are governed by the congregation. The Appendix treats these as secondary matters, important but not reasons to break fellowship. What matters most is that every church has godly shepherds and godly servants, both under Christ.

Men and women in the Church

Scripture begins with a clear truth: “So God created human beings in His image. In the image of God He created them; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). Men and women are equal in worth and dignity. In Christ, “there is no male and female, for all of you are one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). Both receive the Spirit, both are heirs of grace, both are called to serve.

This book’s view is that men and women, equal in worth, have complementary roles in the Church that mirror those of husbands and wives in the family, which we explored in Chapter 18. Paul writes that “Christ is the head of every man, man is the head of woman, and God is the head of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:3). The Son is fully equal with the Father, yet He gladly honours the Father’s headship, so headship and equality are not enemies. The passages on elders describe the overseer as a husband, and Paul gives instructions about teaching and authority in the gathered church in 1 Timothy 2:11–15. On this reading, the office of elder is entrusted to qualified men, while women serve in a wide range of vital ministries.

And that range is wide. Paul commends “our sister Phoebe, a deacon of the church in Cenchreae” (Romans 16:1), who was “a patron to many” (Romans 16:2). When the gifted preacher Apollos needed fuller teaching, “Priscilla and Aquila heard him there, and they took him in and taught him the way of God more precisely” (Acts 18:26). Paul greets Mary, “who has worked hard for you” (Romans 16:6). And it was women who stayed at the cross, and women who first found the tomb empty and carried the news of the resurrection to the apostles (Luke 24:1–10; John 20:17–18). Many churches in Africa, Asia and Latin America would hardly exist without praying mothers, Bible women and faithful sisters. A church that overlooks its women has not understood the New Testament.

We should also say honestly that many faithful Christians, called egalitarians, read these passages differently. They believe 1 Timothy 2 addressed a particular situation in Ephesus, and that all ministries and offices are open to both men and women. As the Appendix explains, this is a secondary issue. It may shape which church we join, but it should not break our fellowship as brothers and sisters in the same Lord.

Character before gifting

A gifted leader with a crooked heart is one of the most dangerous people in any church. Gifts can draw crowds; only character carries weight over many years. Charles Spurgeon, who trained hundreds of young men at his Pastors’ College in London, urged his students:

“We must live as under the more immediate eye of God, and as in the blaze of the great all-revealing day. Holiness in a minister is at once his chief necessity and his goodliest ornament.”

Charles Spurgeon, Lectures to My Students

That is coram Deo in the life of a leader: in the study, at home, and when no one in the congregation is watching. Scripture adds three safeguards. Leadership is servant leadership, for “whoever among you wants to become great must be your servant” (Mark 10:43), as Chapter 24 explores. It is plural: a team of elders shares the load, combines gifts and guards against pride. And it is accountable: a leader who answers to no one is in great danger, and so is his flock.

Bakht Singh: a church that belonged to its people

Bakht Singh was born in 1903 into a Sikh family in the Punjab, in a region now part of Pakistan. As a young man he went abroad to study engineering, first in England and then in Canada. He had no interest in Christianity. But in Canada, around 1929, he began reading the New Testament, and the Lord Jesus became real to him.

In 1933 he returned to India. His family found his new faith very hard to accept, and following Jesus cost him dearly. He gave himself to preaching, often in the open air, and many came to faith. But he soon saw a problem. New believers had nowhere to grow, and many churches of the time felt foreign to ordinary Indians, with leaders, money and ways of worship from overseas.

So Bakht Singh went back to the book of Acts. He became convinced that each local church should be led by its own elders, chosen from its own people, supported by its own members’ giving and dependent on God rather than on foreign funds. In the 1940s an assembly began in Madras, now Chennai, and later the fellowship called Hebron in Hyderabad became a centre of the work. Prayer was at the heart of it. Believers gathered for long times of prayer and worship and studied the Bible with great seriousness. Each year thousands came to gatherings called Holy Convocations, living simply together for days of prayer, teaching and praise.

Over the following decades, hundreds of these assemblies sprang up across India and beyond. Bakht Singh trained local brothers to shepherd them, and he expected ordinary believers to witness, pray and serve. He died in 2000. His story shows this chapter’s lessons at work: Christ, not a foreign board or a single strong man, is the Head; local elders can shepherd their own people; and when leaders equip believers rather than doing everything themselves, the Church grows.

The priesthood of all believers

In the Old Testament, only priests from the tribe of Levi could offer sacrifices, and ordinary Israelites came to God through them. But when Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn, and the way into God’s presence was opened to all who trust in Him.

Peter writes to ordinary believers, many of them poor: “you yourselves, as living stones, are being built up as a house for the Spirit, to serve as a holy priesthood and to offer, through Jesus Christ, spiritual sacrifices that God gladly accepts” (1 Peter 2:5). And again: “you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people God has claimed as His own” (1 Peter 2:9). Christ “made us a kingdom, priests in the service of His God and Father” (Revelation 1:6).

This means two wonderful things. First, every Christian has direct access to God through Christ. You may come before His face yourself, at any hour, in your own words. That is the heart of this whole book.

Second, every Christian is a minister. We often use “minister” for the pastor, but in Scripture every believer has a ministry. Leaders equip God’s people “for the work of serving” (Ephesians 4:12). The pastor is not the only player while the congregation watches from the stands. The pastor is the coach; the whole church is the team.

A central part of this priesthood is prayer. Like the priests of old, who carried the names of the tribes before God, we bring people to God in intercession and bring God to people through our witness. “First of all, then, I urge that requests, prayers, intercessions and thanks be offered for everyone” (1 Timothy 2:1), because God “wants everyone to be saved and to come to know the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). The grandmother who prays each morning for her neighbours by name is doing priestly work. So is the trader who tells a customer about Jesus. You need no title to serve as a priest. You need only to stand before God’s face for others, and before others for God.

This leads into Chapter 23, where we ask what gifts the Spirit gives each believer for this ministry, and how we discover God’s calling.

Questions for reflection

  • Ephesians 4:12 says leaders are given to equip God’s people for the work of serving. Do you see yourself as someone being equipped, or as someone watching others do the work?
  • Why do you think almost every qualification for elders and deacons is about character rather than skill?
  • How have you seen a pastor or leader care for wounded souls? What made that care helpful?
  • How can your church honour the ministry of women, as Paul honoured Phoebe, Priscilla and Mary?
  • What does it mean to you that you have direct access to God through Christ, with no one standing in between?
  • Who has God placed on your heart to carry to Him in prayer, as a priest carries others before God?

A step for this week

Choose one leader in your church, a pastor, elder or deacon. Pray for them by name every day this week, using 1 Peter 5:2–3 as your guide, and send them a short message thanking them for one specific way they have served you. Then, as a priest yourself, write down three people outside the church whom you will carry before God each morning, and ask Him to open a door for you to serve one of them before the week ends.

study_questions.question: What are the five ministries in Ephesians 4:11 and what are they for?
study_questions.answer: Paul names apostles, prophets, evangelists, and shepherds and teachers, often read together as the pastor-teacher. Christ gave them "to equip God's holy people for the work of serving, so that the body of Christ would be built up" (Ephesians 4:12). Leaders do not do all the work themselves; they equip every believer to serve, so the whole church grows to maturity. Christians differ on whether apostles and prophets continue today, but all agree that no one adds to Scripture and every word must be tested by it.

study_questions.question: What is the difference between elders and deacons in the church?
study_questions.answer: Elders, also called overseers, shepherd the flock, teach, guard sound doctrine and give spiritual oversight, as Peter says: "Tend God's flock among you as shepherds do" (1 Peter 5:2). Deacons serve the practical needs of the body, as the seven in Acts 6 did, so that leaders can "hold fast to prayer and to the service of the word" (Acts 6:4). For both offices, the qualifications in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 are almost all about character rather than skill.

study_questions.question: What does the priesthood of all believers mean?
study_questions.answer: It means every Christian has direct access to God through Christ and every Christian is a minister. Peter tells ordinary believers, "you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation" (1 Peter 2:9). A central part of this priesthood is prayer: we bring people to God in intercession and bring God to people through our witness, offering "requests, prayers, intercessions and thanks" for everyone (1 Timothy 2:1).

fields.title: The Gifts of the Spirit and Calling
fields.body_html:
“Each of you has received a gift; use it to serve one another, as good managers of the richly varied grace of God.”

— 1 Peter 4:10 (OWB)

Imagine a family gathering at a grandmother’s home. Each grandchild arrives with something: one brings bread, another brings a goat, a third brings music, a fourth simply comes ready to wash the pots. No one brings everything, and no one comes with nothing. The meal is rich because everyone shares what they have been given.

That is a picture of the Church. In Chapter 22 we saw that every believer is a priest and a minister. Now we ask how God equips us for that ministry. Peter’s answer is simple: “Each of you has received a gift” (1 Peter 4:10). Not some of you. Each of you.

Everything is a gift

Before we speak of spiritual gifts, we need to see that everything we have is a gift. God “gives life and breath and all things to everyone” (Acts 17:25). Your next breath, your family, your abilities, your salvation: all of it came from His hand. James writes, “Every good act of giving and every perfect gift is from above. It comes down from the Father of the lights in the sky” (James 1:17).

This guards us against two errors. The first is pride. Paul asked the proud Corinthians, “What do you have that was not given to you? And if it was given to you, why do you take pride in it as though it were not a gift?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). The gifted singer, the able preacher and the successful farmer have nothing to boast of. They have only something to thank God for.

The second error is false humility, the feeling that “I have nothing to offer”. That is not true either. If you belong to Christ, the Spirit lives in you, and He does not live in anyone without giving them something to share. We receive our gifts with gratitude and humility, and we use them before the face of the Giver.

What the gifts are for

Spiritual gifts are not trophies or badges of rank. Paul says, “Each person is given a way in which the Spirit is openly at work, and it is given for the good of all” (1 Corinthians 12:7). Gifts exist to build up the Church, to glorify Christ and to serve others in love. Peter adds that whoever speaks or serves should do it “in the strength God supplies. Then in everything God will be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4:11).

That is why Paul places his great chapter on love right in the middle of his teaching on gifts. “Suppose I speak in the tongues of human beings, and of angels too. If I do not have love, I am no more than booming bronze or a clashing cymbal. I may be able to prophesy, and know every mystery and everything there is to know; I may have all the faith there is, enough to move mountains; but if I do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:1–2). A gift used without love is noise. A small gift used with love builds the house of God. As Chapter 5 taught, love is the mark of a Christian.

The gifts of the Spirit in 1 Corinthians 12

In 1 Corinthians 12:8–10, Paul lists nine ways the Spirit works. Many teachers group them in three sets of three.

Revelation gifts help believers know what God is showing.

  • A message of wisdom is Spirit-given insight into how to act in a situation, applying God’s truth to a hard problem.
  • A message of knowledge is understanding given by the Spirit, whether into the truths of Scripture or into a situation that the speaker could not otherwise know.
  • The ability to tell spirits apart, often called discernment, is the gift of recognising whether something comes from God, from the human heart or from an evil spirit (compare 1 John 4:1).

Power gifts show God’s strength at work.

  • Faith here is not saving faith, which every believer has, but a special confidence that God will act in a particular situation.
  • Gifts of healing are God’s healing of the sick through a believer’s prayer. Paul says “gifts”, plural, perhaps because healings come in many kinds.
  • The power to work miracles is God’s intervention beyond nature, for His glory and the good of His people.

Speaking gifts bring God’s word to people, or people’s praise to God.

  • Prophecy is speaking a word from God whose words “build them up, encourage them and comfort them” (1 Corinthians 14:3), always tested by Scripture.
  • Different kinds of tongues is speaking by the Spirit in a language the speaker has not learned.
  • The interpretation of tongues makes the meaning of a tongue known, so that the church is built up.

And over all of these Paul writes: “One and the same Spirit is at work in all of these, giving to each person separately as He chooses” (1 Corinthians 12:11). The Spirit decides. We do not choose our gifts like goods in a market.

Romans 12 and Ephesians 4

Paul gives other lists too, which shows that no single list is complete. In Romans 12 he describes gifts that shape how a person naturally serves, which some call motivational gifts: “We have gifts that differ, according to the grace given to us” (Romans 12:6). He names prophesying, serving, teaching and encouraging, then adds: “The one who shares should share generously; the one who leads, with eagerness; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness” (Romans 12:8).

You may recognise yourself here. Some people notice a broken chair and fix it before anyone asks: that is serving. Some cannot rest until a hard passage is explained clearly: that is teaching. Some always find the discouraged person at the back of the room. Some give quietly and gladly. Some organise. Some weep with the grieving. Each is a gift of grace.

Then there are the ministry gifts of Ephesians 4:11, the apostles, prophets, evangelists and pastor-teachers we met in Chapter 22. These are people given to the Church to equip all the others.

Praying in tongues and the gift of tongues

Few subjects have caused more debate than speaking in tongues. In Acts, believers spoke in tongues when the Spirit came on them at Pentecost (Acts 2:4), in the house of Cornelius (Acts 10:44–46) and at Ephesus (Acts 19:6). In 1 Corinthians 14, Paul gives careful teaching about tongues in the life of the church.

Many continuationists, those who believe all the gifts continue today, draw a distinction between two uses of tongues. That distinction is the view this book teaches, and the Appendix sets out other readings fairly.

Praying in tongues is a personal prayer language for building oneself up and praying in the Spirit. Paul writes, “Someone who speaks in a tongue is speaking not to people but to God” (1 Corinthians 14:2), and “Those who speak in a tongue build up themselves” (1 Corinthians 14:4). He describes his own practice: “When I pray in a tongue, it is my spirit that prays, while my mind bears no fruit. What follows, then? I will pray in the spirit, and I will pray with my mind as well” (1 Corinthians 14:14–15). He even says, “I am thankful to God that, more than every one of you, I speak in tongues” (1 Corinthians 14:18). Jude urges believers to keep “praying in the Holy Spirit” (Jude 20), and Paul tells us that when we do not know how to pray, “the Spirit Himself pleads on our behalf, with groans that no words carry” (Romans 8:26). On this view, praying in tongues is available to many believers as a gift for private prayer.

The gift of tongues is a public utterance in the gathered church, and it must be interpreted so that all are built up. Paul asks, “Does everyone speak in tongues? Does everyone interpret?” (1 Corinthians 12:30), expecting the answer no. In public worship, “anyone who speaks in a tongue should ask God for the power to interpret it as well” (1 Corinthians 14:13). Paul would be “glad for all of you to speak in tongues, but gladder still for you to prophesy” (1 Corinthians 14:5), because prophecy in a known language builds up the church.

Paul’s guidance for public worship is about order, love and edification. “Whenever you gather, each of you has something: a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, an interpretation. Everything should be done to build up the church” (1 Corinthians 14:26). Tongues should be spoken by two or three at most, in turn, with interpretation. “If there is no one to interpret, the speaker should keep silent in the church, speaking only to themselves and to God” (1 Corinthians 14:28). Prophecies are to be weighed. And the chapter ends with a balance every church needs: “do not stop anyone from speaking in tongues. But let everything be done properly and in good order” (1 Corinthians 14:39–40).

Where Christians differ

Sincere, Bible-believing Christians hold a wide range of views on these gifts. It is a secondary issue, and it should not divide us.

  • Continuationists, including Pentecostals and charismatics, believe all the gifts continue today. Many distinguish praying in tongues from the public gift, as above. Some Pentecostals also teach that tongues is the first evidence of baptism in the Spirit.
  • The open but cautious believe the gifts may continue today, but should be tested carefully and practised in order and love. They do not hold that tongues is required as evidence of the Spirit.
  • Cessationists believe the miraculous sign gifts, such as tongues, prophecy and healing, served to confirm the apostles’ message and ceased with the apostles. They gladly affirm that God still heals and works wonders in answer to prayer.

Some also read 1 Corinthians 14 as describing private prayer in tongues, while others believe it refers only to the public gift.

Here is the common ground. The Spirit gives gifts to every believer for the good of the body. Love is greater than any gift. And everything must be done to build up the Church. Whatever your tradition, seek the Spirit eagerly, test everything by Scripture, honour believers who see it differently, and walk in love.

Catherine Booth: a timid woman who became a fool for Christ

Catherine Booth was born in England in 1829. She was a serious, sickly girl who read the whole Bible through several times while still a girl. In 1855 she married William Booth, a young Methodist preacher, and together they would later found The Salvation Army.

Catherine had deep convictions, and in 1859 she wrote a pamphlet defending the right of women to preach. Yet for years she did not speak in public herself. She was shy, and the thought of standing before a crowd filled her with dread. During an illness she promised the Lord that if He would stir her again, she would obey Him.

In 1860, at the chapel in Gateshead where William was minister, she sat in the minister’s pew with her four-year-old son while about a thousand people listened to testimonies. She later told what happened in her address Witnessing for Christ. She felt the Spirit come upon her and urge her to speak, and she said in her heart that she could not do it. Then a thought came, which she recognised as the devil’s voice, telling her she would look like a fool and have nothing to say. That word settled it. She wrote:

“I have never yet been willing to be a fool for Christ, now I will be one.”

Catherine Booth, Witnessing for Christ

She rose, walked up the chapel and spoke. The congregation, who knew her “timid, bashful nature”, were astonished. From that day she became one of the most powerful preachers of her generation, speaking to crowds of rich and poor while raising eight children. She was clear about where the power came from: “It was not I that did this, but the Holy Ghost, the Holy Spirit of God” (Witnessing for Christ).

Christians hold different views on women preaching, as Chapter 22 and the Appendix explain. But every reader can learn from her story how gifts are discovered. Catherine’s gift lay hidden for years under fear. It came to life not through a test or a course, but through obedience in a single moment. She stepped out, and God met her. Many gifts are found that way: in the doing.

Discovering and growing in your gifts

How do you find your gifts? There is no magic formula, but Scripture and experience point to four companions.

  1. Scripture. Read the lists in Romans 12, 1 Corinthians 12, Ephesians 4 and 1 Peter 4. Let God’s Word stir your imagination about what He might do through you.
  2. Prayer. Ask the Giver. Paul says, “set your hearts on spiritual gifts” (1 Corinthians 14:1). It is right to desire gifts that build up others.
  3. Community. Other believers often see your gifts before you do. Ask mature Christians, “Where have you seen God use me?” Paul reminded Timothy “to stir up into flame the gift God gave you when I laid my hands on you” (2 Timothy 1:6). Gifts are recognised and encouraged in the body.
  4. Serving. Most of all, start serving. Visit the sick, teach the children, pray for the troubled, welcome the stranger. You will discover what brings fruit and joy, and what others confirm.

Do not wait until you are sure of your gift before you serve. Serve, and your gift will become clear.

Gifts also grow. A young man who stammers through his first Bible reading in a home group may, ten years later, be teaching with clarity and warmth. A woman who first prays aloud in a trembling voice may become the intercessor her whole church leans on. Like a seed in good soil, a gift grows when it is watered with prayer, exercised in love and corrected by wise friends. And like a hoe left in the rain, a gift that is never used grows rusty. Paul’s word to Timothy was to stir the gift up, not to wait for it to stir itself.

Calling in everyday work

The word “calling” is often used only for pastors and missionaries. But Scripture gives every believer a calling. “We are God’s own work. In Christ Jesus He created us for good works, which God made ready in advance so that we would live our lives doing them” (Ephesians 2:10).

Martin Luther helped recover this truth in the sixteenth century. In his day many believed that monks and priests had a holy calling, while farmers, shoemakers and mothers had merely worldly work. Luther taught that God calls people to every honest kind of work, and that a servant sweeping a floor or a mother caring for her child can please God as truly as a priest at the altar. In our own time, Os Guinness has written about this in The Call, reminding us that we are called first to Someone, Christ, and only then to something.

Paul says, “Whatever you are doing, put your whole self into the work, as for the Lord and not for people” (Colossians 3:23). As Chapter 20 showed, the teacher, the nurse, the driver and the shopkeeper all work coram Deo. Think of a bus driver in Nairobi who prays for his passengers as they climb aboard, or an accountant in Manila who refuses to falsify the figures when her manager asks. Think of a mother in a mountain village in Peru who teaches her children to read using the Gospel of Mark. None of them stands in a pulpit, yet each is answering God’s call. God may call some to leave their nets and serve full-time in the Church. He calls all of us to serve Him wherever we are.

Faithfulness in small things

Brother Lawrence spent many years as cook in a Paris monastery, a job he naturally disliked. He learned to do it for the love of God. Those who knew him recorded his counsel:

“We ought not to be weary of doing little things for the love of God, who regards not the greatness of the work, but the love with which it is performed.”

Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God

Jesus taught the same: “Someone who is faithful in the smallest matter is faithful in large matters too” (Luke 16:10). In His parable, the master says, “Well done! You are a good and faithful servant. You proved faithful in small matters; I will put you in charge of great ones” (Matthew 25:21).

Many people want a large gift for a large platform. God looks for faithful people with whatever He has given. Setting out chairs, praying for one neighbour, teaching five children: these are not small before His face. This leads into Chapter 24, where we see that the greatest gift is to serve as Jesus served.

Questions for reflection

  • Read 1 Corinthians 4:7. Which of your abilities or possessions do you most easily treat as your own rather than as a gift?
  • Looking at Romans 12:6–8, which of these gifts do you see in yourself? Which have others noticed in you?
  • How does 1 Corinthians 13:1–3 change the way you think about spiritual gifts?
  • What is your church’s view on the gifts and tongues? How can you honour believers who see it differently?
  • Catherine Booth’s gift came to life through one act of obedience. Is there a step God has been urging you to take that fear has held back?
  • How does it change your daily work to see it as a calling from God?

A step for this week

Ask two mature Christians who know you well this simple question: “Where have you seen God use me to help others?” Write down their answers. Then choose one small, practical way to serve in your church or neighbourhood this week that fits what they said, and do it as before the face of God. Before you begin, pray, “Lord, everything I have is Your gift. Use it for the good of others.”

fields.title: Servant Ministry
fields.body_html:
“The Son of Man Himself came, not so that others would serve Him, but to serve them and to give His life as the ransom price for many.”

— Mark 10:45 (OWB)

In many parts of the world, when an important visitor comes to a home, someone brings water to wash the guest’s hands or feet. It is a kindness, but it is usually done by the youngest or the lowest in the household. No one expects the head of the family to kneel with the basin. And no one would ever expect the important visitor to do it.

Yet on the night before He died, the Son of God got up from the table, took a towel and a basin, and knelt before His friends. Everything we will say about ministry in this chapter flows from that scene.

In Chapter 22 we saw how Christ organises His Church, and in Chapter 23 how He gifts every believer. Now we ask: in what spirit should we use those offices and gifts? Jesus’ answer is clear. We use them as servants.

The basin and the towel

John tells the story with great care. He begins with what Jesus knew: “Jesus knew that the Father had put everything into His hands. He knew too that He had come out from God and was on His way back to God” (John 13:3). Then he tells what Jesus did: “He got up from the meal, put aside His outer garments, took a towel and tied it around His waist. Next He poured water into the basin and began washing the disciples’ feet” (John 13:4–5).

Notice the order. Jesus did not wash feet in order to discover who He was. He washed feet because He already knew who He was. He was secure in the Father’s love, sure of where He had come from and where He was going. Because He had nothing to prove, He was free to take the lowest place.

This is the secret of servant ministry. People who are insecure need titles, seats at the front and praise from others. People who know they are loved by the Father before His face can kneel with a basin without losing anything.

Then Jesus explained what He had done: “So if I, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, then you too have a duty to wash each other’s feet. What I gave you was an example, so that you also would do as I have done for you” (John 13:14–15). And He added a promise: “Now you know these things; you are blessed if you act on them” (John 13:17). The blessing is not in knowing about service. It is in doing it.

Leadership in the Kingdom

The disciples found this lesson very hard. Not long before, James and John had asked for the best seats in Jesus’ coming Kingdom, and the other ten were angry with them, probably because they wanted those seats too. Jesus called them together and showed them two kinds of leadership.

The first is the world’s kind: “You know that those who are thought of as rulers of the nations lord it over their people, and their important men use their power over them” (Mark 10:42). We have all seen this kind. A manager who shouts at workers. A politician who grows rich while the people grow poor. Sadly, even a church leader who expects to be served and is quick to remind others of his position.

The second is the Kingdom’s kind: “That is not how it is among you. Instead, whoever among you wants to become great must be your servant, and whoever among you wants to be first must serve everyone as a slave” (Mark 10:43–44). And the reason is Jesus Himself: “The Son of Man Himself came, not so that others would serve Him, but to serve them” (Mark 10:45).

Kingdom leadership turns the pyramid upside down. The leader is not at the top with everyone serving him. He is at the bottom, holding others up. Paul says that Christ, though He was in the form of God, “emptied Himself, taking on the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), and that we should “think in the way that Christ Jesus also thought” (Philippians 2:5).

This does not mean leaders never lead. Jesus led His disciples firmly. He corrected them, taught them and sent them out. But He led for their good, not for His own comfort. A servant leader still makes decisions, still says hard things and still carries authority. The difference is in the heart: he uses his authority to lift others up, not to lift himself up.

Andrew Murray, the South African pastor, wrote a small book called Humility that has helped many leaders. He saw that our humility before God is tested in how we treat people:

“Humility before God is nothing if not proved in humility before men.”

Andrew Murray, Humility

And he described what this looks like in daily life:

“The spirit of Him who washed the disciples’ feet makes it a joy to us to be indeed the least, to be servants of one another. The humble man feels no jealousy or envy. He can praise God when others are preferred and blessed before him.”

Andrew Murray, Humility

Can you praise God when someone else is chosen for the role you wanted? That is a good test of a servant’s heart.

Serving the poor, the widow, the orphan and the stranger

Servant ministry is not only for the church building. Throughout Scripture, God shows special care for four kinds of people who were often forgotten: the poor, the widow, the orphan and the stranger. God “sees that orphans and widows get justice, and He loves the outsider living among you and gives them food and clothing” (Deuteronomy 10:18).

Through Isaiah, God told His people that religious fasting meant little if they ignored the needy. The fast He wanted was this: “to break your bread with someone who is hungry, to take the wandering poor into your home, to clothe the naked person you meet, and never to turn your back on your own kin” (Isaiah 58:7). And He promised: “if you give of yourself to the hungry and meet the needs of those who suffer, then your light will dawn in the darkness” (Isaiah 58:10).

The prophet Micah summed it up: “And what does the LORD ask of you except to do justice, to love loyalty, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). James echoes the same truth in the New Testament: “To God the Father, religion that is pure and untainted looks like this: going to the help of orphans and widows in their trouble, and keeping yourself unstained by the world” (James 1:27).

Then Jesus said something that should change how we see every needy person. In His picture of the final judgment, the King says, “For when I was hungry, you gave Me food; when I was thirsty, you gave Me a drink; when I was a stranger, you took Me into your home” (Matthew 25:35). The righteous are surprised, and the King explains: “each time you did it for one of these My brothers and sisters, even the least of them, you did it for Me” (Matthew 25:40).

This is coram Deo in its most practical form. When you carry a meal to a widow, you are not only before her face. You are before Christ’s face. When you welcome a refugee family or sit with a prisoner, you are serving the King Himself.

Christians in Latin America such as René Padilla of Ecuador have called the Church to what they named integral mission: proclaiming Christ in word and serving the whole person in deed, never setting one against the other. Jesus did both. He preached the Kingdom and He fed the hungry. The Church at its best has always done the same, through hospitals, schools, orphanages and countless kitchens. In the nineteenth century, William and Catherine Booth (whom we met in Chapter 23) took the gospel into the poorest streets of East London. The Salvation Army they founded preached Christ to drunkards and thieves, and also opened shelters, served food and found work for the jobless. Today its officers serve in many nations, including across East Africa, often in places others avoid.

Toyohiko Kagawa: a servant in the slums of Kobe

One of the most remarkable servants of the twentieth century came from Japan. Toyohiko Kagawa was born in Kobe in 1888. He lost both his parents when he was a small child and grew up a lonely boy in the home of his father’s family. As a teenager he went to American missionaries to learn English, and there he met Jesus Christ. He became a Christian, and his family cut him off.

Kagawa studied for the ministry, but his health was poor and he became seriously ill with tuberculosis. He nearly died. When he recovered, he made a decision that shocked those who knew him. On Christmas Eve 1909, when he was twenty-one, he moved into Shinkawa, one of the worst slums in Kobe. He lived in a tiny room, only a few paces across, among thieves, beggars, gamblers, the sick and the dying.

He did not visit the poor from a distance. He lived among them. He shared his small room and his food with people who had nowhere else to go. He preached in the streets, cared for the sick and buried the dead. He caught trachoma, an eye disease that damaged his sight for the rest of his life. He married Haru, a young factory worker, and she joined him in the work.

Kagawa came to see that serving the poor meant more than giving bread. It also meant asking why so many were poor. He worked to help labourers organise for fair wages, started cooperatives so that poor families could buy and sell together, and was arrested more than once. In 1920 he published a novel drawn from his life in the slums, Before the Dawn, which sold widely across Japan, and he gave much of its income to his work among the poor. After the great earthquake that destroyed much of Tokyo in 1923, he led relief work among the homeless. Later he travelled the country preaching in what he called the Kingdom of God movement, calling his nation to Christ. He died in 1960.

Kagawa was not perfect, and like every servant of God he had his limits. But his life shows that the call of Mark 10:45 is not only for missionaries far away. It can be lived out by a sick young man in his own city, who decides that the face of Christ is to be found among the poorest of his neighbours.

Ministry flowing from intimacy, not striving

There is a danger in all this. We can become so busy serving that we forget the One we serve. We can work for God while drifting far from God.

Martha welcomed Jesus into her home and worked hard to prepare a meal. Her sister Mary sat at Jesus’ feet and listened. When Martha complained, Jesus answered gently: “Martha, Martha, you are fretting and in a stir about so many things. Yet there is need of few things, or only of one. Mary has picked the good share” (Luke 10:41–42). Jesus did not despise Martha’s service. But He knew that service which does not flow from His presence soon becomes anxious, resentful and tired.

As we saw in Chapter 9, Jesus said, “Whoever remains in Me, with Me remaining in them, is the one who bears much fruit, because you can do nothing apart from Me” (John 15:5). Ministry is meant to be fruit, not factory work. Fruit grows from a branch that stays joined to the vine.

Andrew Murray put it plainly in his book Working for God!:

“As waiting on God lies at the root of all true working for God, so working for God must be the fruit of all true waiting on Him.”

Andrew Murray, Working for God!

He also warned that the Church suffers “because so much working for God is done without waiting on God” (Working for God!).

Francis of Assisi understood this. Born in Italy around 1181 to a wealthy cloth merchant, he gave up his comfortable life to follow Christ in poverty. He served lepers, whom he had once found hard even to look at, and he later wrote that the Lord Himself led him among them. Francis and his brothers worked and begged among the poor, but they also withdrew often to lonely places to pray. His service was strong because his prayer was deep.

The same is true for us. The nurse who begins her shift with a few quiet minutes before God, the youth leader who prays over each name before the meeting, the farmer who gives thanks in the field before lending his ox to a neighbour: their service carries a fragrance that busy activity alone cannot produce. The first service we owe is to sit at Jesus’ feet.

Avoiding burnout: rest and healthy boundaries

Many faithful servants of God burn out. A pastor works seven days a week for years and then collapses. A mother cares for everyone but herself until she is empty. A church volunteer says yes to every request until she can no longer bear to enter the building.

Scripture takes this seriously. When Moses tried to judge every dispute among the people alone, his father-in-law Jethro said: “This way of doing things is not good. You are sure to wear out, both you and the people who are with you. The load is too heavy for you; you cannot carry it by yourself” (Exodus 18:17–18). So Moses shared the work with others, which is exactly the pattern of plural leadership we saw in Chapter 22.

When Elijah was exhausted and wanted to die, God did not scold him. He let him sleep, and then an angel touched him and said, “Get up and eat” (1 Kings 19:5). Sometimes the most spiritual thing a tired servant can do is rest and eat a good meal.

Jesus Himself cared for His tired disciples. When crowds pressed on them so that “they could not even find time for a meal”, He said, “Come away on your own, to a place without people, and get a little rest” (Mark 6:31). Jesus regularly withdrew to pray, even when many still needed Him (Mark 1:35).

As Chapter 12 explained, Jesus is our Sabbath rest. He invites us: “Come to Me, all of you who are worn out with work and weighed down with burdens, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Every day we can serve from a place of resting in Him, relying on God rather than our own strength. Regular physical rest also remains God’s good gift and a wise rhythm for servants and leaders alike.

Here are a few healthy boundaries for those who serve:

  • Remember you are not the Saviour. Jesus is. You are His servant. The needs of the world are endless, but you are not called to meet them all.
  • Share the load. Train others, delegate, and let the whole body serve, as Chapters 22 and 23 taught.
  • Guard your time with God. Ministry that eats up your prayer life will soon have nothing left to give.
  • Guard your family. Your spouse and children are your first ministry, not your last.
  • Take regular rest. A day each week, and seasons of refreshment, are not laziness but obedience.

Paul encourages us: “We must not tire of doing good. When the right time comes we will bring in the harvest, as long as we do not slacken” (Galatians 6:9). The way not to grow weary over a lifetime is to keep returning to the One who gives strength.

Serving before His face

Servant ministry is not about grand titles or famous projects. It is about a basin and a towel, and a heart that knows it is loved. It is the deacon fixing a leaking roof, the teenager reading to a blind neighbour, the mother of five who still finds room for one more child at her table, and the pastor who visits a dying man at midnight.

Paul adds: “So whenever we have the chance, we should do good to everyone, and above all to those who belong to the family of faith” (Galatians 6:10). Every day brings such chances. Most of them are small and easy to miss: a colleague who is struggling after a death in the family, a child at church who sits alone, a neighbour whose crops failed this season, a stranger at the bus stop who does not know the city. Servants learn to notice. They ask the Lord each morning, “Whom will You put in my path today?” and then they keep their eyes open. And every time we take one, we do it before the face of God, for Christ Himself.

This leads into Part Five and Chapter 25, where we see that the greatest service of all is to carry the good news of Jesus to those who have never heard.

Questions for reflection

  • Jesus washed feet because He knew who He was and where He was going (John 13:3). How does being secure in God’s love free you to serve?
  • Where have you seen the world’s kind of leadership, and where have you seen Kingdom leadership? What made the difference?
  • Who are the “least of these” in your neighbourhood or city? How might you serve Christ by serving them?
  • What can you learn from Toyohiko Kagawa’s decision to live among the people he served?
  • Are you more like Martha or Mary at the moment? What would help your service flow from time with Jesus?
  • Which of the healthy boundaries listed above do you most need to practise?

A step for this week

Do one act of hidden service this week for someone who cannot repay you: a widow, an orphan, a stranger, a sick neighbour or a prisoner’s family. Cook a meal, mend something, pay a bill, or simply sit and listen. Tell no one about it. Before you go, spend fifteen minutes alone with Jesus, reading John 13:1–17 slowly, and ask Him to give you His servant heart. Afterwards, thank Him that what you did for the least, you did for Him.

study_questions.question: What does it mean that Jesus came to serve?
study_questions.answer: Jesus said, "The Son of Man Himself came, not so that others would serve Him, but to serve them and to give His life as the ransom price for many" (Mark 10:45). He showed this when He washed His disciples' feet, and then told them, "What I gave you was an example, so that you also would do as I have done for you" (John 13:15). Because He was secure in the Father's love, He was free to take the lowest place, and so are we.

study_questions.question: What does the Bible say about serving the poor, widows and orphans?
study_questions.answer: God shows special care for the poor, the widow, the orphan and the stranger, and calls His people to do the same. James writes that pure religion means "going to the help of orphans and widows in their trouble" (James 1:27). Jesus taught that whatever we do for the least of His brothers and sisters, "you did it for Me" (Matthew 25:40).

study_questions.question: How can Christians avoid burnout in ministry?
study_questions.answer: Ministry should flow from time with Jesus, not from striving, for He said, "you can do nothing apart from Me" (John 15:5). Scripture also teaches sharing the load, as Jethro told Moses, "you cannot carry it by yourself" (Exodus 18:18), and taking rest, as Jesus told His tired disciples to "get a little rest" (Mark 6:31). Guarding time with God, caring for your family and taking regular rest are acts of obedience, not laziness.

fields.title: The Great Commission: Evangelism and Missions
fields.body_html:
“Go, then, and make disciples of all the nations: baptize them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teach them to keep everything I have commanded you. And remember this: I Myself am with you every day, until the close of the age.”

— Matthew 28:19–20 (OWB)

When a family receives wonderful news, such as the birth of a child, a healing, or a son’s safe return from a long journey, they cannot keep it to themselves. They phone their relatives, they tell the neighbours, they stop friends in the market. Good news wants to travel.

The gospel is the best news the world has ever heard. In Chapter 24 we saw that the greatest service is to serve as Jesus served. Now, as we begin Part Five, we look at the greatest service of all: carrying the good news of Jesus to those who have never heard it, near and far.

A command for every believer

Before Jesus returned to the Father, He gathered His disciples on a mountain in Galilee. He began with a claim: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been placed in My hands” (Matthew 28:18). Then He gave a command, which we call the Great Commission: “Go, then, and make disciples of all the nations” (Matthew 28:19). And He closed with a promise: “I Myself am with you every day, until the close of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Some think this command was only for the apostles, or only for pastors and missionaries. But look at what it says. The disciples were to teach new believers “to keep everything I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:20). That includes this very command. Each new disciple is to make disciples, and so on, down every generation until the end of the age. The Great Commission has come all the way to you.

Charles Spurgeon, the London preacher, said this plainly in The Soul-Winner, speaking of the honour of leading people to Christ:

“The honour does not belong to ministers only; they may take their full share of it, but it belongs to every one of you who have devoted yourselves to Christ.”

Charles Spurgeon, The Soul-Winner

And he added: “There is no man placed by God’s providence where he cannot do some good” (The Soul-Winner). The office worker, the student, the grandmother and the motorbike taxi driver are all placed where they are by God, among people who need to hear.

God’s heart for all nations

Mission did not begin with the Great Commission. It runs through the whole Bible, because it flows from the heart of God.

When God called Abram, He promised: “I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing ... and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:2–3). From the start, God chose one family in order to bless every family. The psalmist sang, “Tell the nations of His glory, and all the peoples of the wonders He has done” (Psalm 96:3). Through Isaiah, God spoke of His Servant: “I will make you a light for the nations as well, so that you may be My salvation to the farthest edge of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6).

Even the reluctant prophet Jonah, who ran the other way rather than preach to Israel’s enemies in Nineveh, learned that God’s mercy reaches people we would rather leave out.

Then Jesus came as that light. After His resurrection He told His disciples, “when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, you will receive power, and you will bear witness to Me in Jerusalem, through all Judea and Samaria, and out to the farthest end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). The rest of Acts tells how the gospel crossed one border after another: from Jews to Samaritans, to an Ethiopian official, to a Roman soldier, to the cities of Asia and Europe.

And the story ends with a vision of the goal: “I saw a crowd so vast that no one could number it. They came from every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages, and they stood before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9). That crowd will include Maasai and Malay, Quechua and Korean, Yoruba and Ukrainian, all crying, “To our God, seated on the throne, and to the Lamb, salvation belongs!” (Revelation 7:10). Mission is simply joining God in filling that crowd. To live coram Deo is to share His heart for every face He has made.

What the gospel is

To share the gospel, we must be clear about what it is. Many people have heard about church but have never heard the good news itself. Paul summed it up as “the first and chief thing”: “that Christ died for our sins, in keeping with the Scriptures; that He was buried; that He has been raised on the third day, in keeping with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

Here is a simple way to explain it.

  1. God made us to know Him. We were created to live before His face, in His love.
  2. We have turned away. “Everyone has sinned, and all come short of God’s glory” (Romans 3:23). Sin separates us from God and leads to death: “The wages sin pays are death” (Romans 6:23).
  3. God has come to rescue us. Jesus, God’s Son, lived the life we should have lived and died the death we deserved. He rose again, defeating sin and death. “God’s free gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23).
  4. We receive Him by faith. “All who call on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). We turn from sin, trust in Christ, and begin to follow Him.

Paul was proud of this message: “I am not ashamed of the gospel. It is God’s own power at work to save everyone who believes” (Romans 1:16). The gospel is not good advice about how to improve ourselves. It is good news about what God has done for us in Christ.

Sharing your own story of grace

You do not need to be a preacher to share the gospel. One of the most powerful tools you have is your own story of what God has done.

When Jesus set free a man tormented by demons, the man begged to travel with Him. But Jesus said, “Go home to your own people, and let them know all that the Lord has done for you, and the mercy He has shown you” (Mark 5:19). The Samaritan woman at the well had a poor reputation and no training. Yet “many of the Samaritans from that town believed in Him because of the woman’s word” (John 4:39). She simply told them about the man who knew everything about her.

Your story need not be dramatic. Think about three parts: what your life was like before you knew Christ, how you came to trust Him, and what difference He has made since. Practise telling it in two or three minutes, in plain words, without church language. Then end by pointing to Jesus, not to yourself.

Peter tells us to be ready: “in your hearts set Christ apart as the holy Lord. Be ready at all times to make your defense to anyone who asks you for the reason behind the hope you hold” (1 Peter 3:15). Notice where it starts: in our hearts, before the face of Christ. Witness flows from worship.

Evangelism empowered by the Spirit and backed by prayer

The disciples were not sent out the moment Jesus gave the command. He told them to wait for the Spirit’s power (Acts 1:8). Evangelism is not a sales technique. It is the work of God, who opens blind eyes and gives new birth (see Chapter 4).

That is why prayer comes first. When the early church was threatened, they did not pray for safety. They prayed, “Let Your slaves speak Your word with complete boldness” (Acts 4:29). And “every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit, and they went on proclaiming God’s word fearlessly” (Acts 4:31). Paul, the greatest missionary of all, asked others to pray for him “that when I open my mouth I will be given the words to make known with boldness the mystery of the gospel” (Ephesians 6:19).

So pray for the people you hope will come to Christ. Pray by name, daily, for open hearts. Pray for open doors and the right words. Pray for workers to be sent to unreached peoples. Every great movement of the gospel in history has been carried on the shoulders of praying people.

Love, courage and wisdom in conversations

Paul gives practical advice: “Live wisely with those outside the church, making the most of every opportunity. Let your conversation always be gracious and seasoned with salt, so that you know how to answer each person” (Colossians 4:5–6).

Love means we care for the person, not just their decision. Listen to their story. Ask questions. Respect their dignity. People can tell whether we see them as a project or as someone made in God’s image.

Courage means we speak when it would be easier to stay silent. Fear of rejection keeps many believers quiet. But we are “ambassadors who speak for Christ, and it is God Himself who makes His appeal through us” (2 Corinthians 5:20). An ambassador does not speak in his own name, and he does not carry the result on his own shoulders.

Wisdom means we choose the right time and the right words. A grieving neighbour may need a meal and a prayer before a sermon. A curious colleague may welcome a Gospel of John and an invitation to read it together. “Seasoned with salt” means our words have flavour: they are honest, gracious and interesting, never harsh or dull.

Alexander Mackay of Uganda: the engineer missionary

For many readers in East Africa, the story of the gospel in Uganda is part of their own family history. One of the first to bring it was a Scottish engineer named Alexander Mackay.

Mackay was born in 1849 in Rhynie, in the north-east of Scotland, the son of a minister. He trained as an engineer and worked for a time in Germany. In 1875 the explorer Henry Morton Stanley published a letter in a British newspaper saying that Mutesa, the Kabaka (king) of Buganda, would welcome Christian teachers. The Church Missionary Society answered the call, and Mackay offered himself.

The journey inland was terribly hard. Some of the first party died, and others turned back. Mackay reached Buganda in 1878. He did not only preach. He used his engineering skills, working with wood and iron, building and repairing, which drew the curiosity and respect of the people. He learned Luganda, translated parts of Scripture, including the Gospel of Matthew, and printed portions with his own hands so that people could read God’s Word in their own language. Many young men at the royal court learned to read, and some came to faith in Christ.

Then came the cost. After Mutesa died in 1884, his son Mwanga became Kabaka and turned against the Christians. In 1885 Bishop James Hannington, travelling to Buganda, was killed on Mwanga’s orders. In 1886 many young believers, both Anglican and Catholic, were put to death, many of them burned at Namugongo. They are remembered today as the Uganda Martyrs. Mackay stayed as long as he could, encouraging the believers and continuing his translation work, until he was forced to leave in 1887. He moved to Usambiro, at the southern end of Lake Victoria, and kept working on the Scriptures. He died there of fever in 1890, at the age of forty.

Mackay did not live to see the harvest. But the seed sown with his translations, his prayers and the blood of the martyrs grew. Within a generation the church in Uganda was spreading, carried largely by Ugandan evangelists, and later it became one of the centres of the East African Revival that touched many nations. Mackay’s life reminds us that mission is costly, that it often means planting seeds others will harvest, and that faithful witness before God’s face is never wasted.

The history and cost of missions

Mackay was one among many. In the late eighteenth century William Carey, an English shoemaker, sailed to India and spent his life translating the Bible. In the nineteenth century Hudson Taylor founded the China Inland Mission and dressed as the Chinese did so that the gospel would not seem foreign. Mary Slessor, a Scottish mill girl, served for decades in Calabar, in what is now Nigeria.

And mission has never only flowed from the West. Samuel Ajayi Crowther was a Yoruba boy captured by slave raiders around 1821 and sold onto a slave ship. The ship was stopped by the British navy, and he was set free in Sierra Leone. There he came to Christ and was baptised. He became a teacher, then a minister, translated the Bible into Yoruba, and travelled up the Niger River on missionary expeditions. In 1864 he was consecrated as the first African bishop of the Anglican Church. His journal of one of those voyages records his simple prayer after preaching: “May the Spirit of God apply the word to each and all our hearts” (Samuel Ajayi Crowther, Journal of an Expedition up the Niger).

Many missionaries buried children, suffered disease and faced violence. Some, like the Uganda Martyrs, gave their lives. Their sacrifice should humble us, and it should also stir us. The task is not finished. Many peoples still have no church among them and no Bible in their own language.

Going, sending, praying and giving

Not everyone is called to cross an ocean. But everyone has a part. Paul asks: “How, then, are they to call on Him if they have not believed in Him? And how are they to believe in Him if they have never heard Him? And how are they to hear without someone proclaiming? And how are people to proclaim it unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:14–15). Then he quotes Isaiah: “How lovely are the feet of those who bring the good news of good things!” (Romans 10:15).

There are four ways to take part:

  • Going. Some are called to go: across the street, to another town, to another tribe or nation. Is God calling you?
  • Sending. Churches send by choosing, training and laying hands on workers, as Antioch did (Acts 13:2–3, see Chapter 22).
  • Praying. Every believer can pray for missionaries by name and for unreached peoples.
  • Giving. John praised believers who supported travelling missionaries: “It is our duty, then, to take in and support such people, and so become fellow workers with the truth” (3 John 8). Your gift makes you a partner in their work.

Partnership with the global Church

The centre of world Christianity has moved. A century ago, most Christians lived in Europe and North America. Today, most live in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Churches in Kenya, Nigeria, Korea, Brazil and India now send missionaries across the world. Latin American thinkers such as Samuel Escobar of Peru have described this as mission from everywhere to everywhere.

This calls for cross-cultural humility. Missionaries from any land can carry their own culture along with the gospel, and mistake one for the other. The gospel belongs to no single culture. It speaks every language and judges every culture, including our own. So we serve as partners, not masters. We listen before we speak, learn local languages, honour local leaders and remember that the Spirit was at work before we arrived.

For believers in East Africa this is a great opportunity. The churches that once received missionaries now send them, to neighbouring nations, to unreached peoples in the north and east, and to cities across the world. The circle of blessing promised to Abraham keeps widening.

Before His face, for every face

The Great Commission ends with the words “I Myself am with you every day” (Matthew 28:20). We never witness alone. The One who sends us goes with us. That promise has carried believers into prisons and palaces, into refugee camps and university halls, into remote villages reached only on foot. It will carry you into your office, your classroom and your neighbour’s home. You may feel weak, untrained or afraid. So did many of the witnesses in this book: Catherine Booth, as Chapter 23 told, was so timid that for years she dared not speak in public at all. What matters is not our strength but His presence. When we speak to a neighbour about Jesus, we do it before His face and in His company.

This leads into Chapter 26, where we consider how we manage the time, talents and treasure God has entrusted to us, including how we use them for His mission in the world.

Questions for reflection

  • Do you see the Great Commission as a command for you personally, or mainly for pastors and missionaries? Why?
  • How would you explain the gospel in two minutes to a friend who has never heard it?
  • What are the three parts of your own story of grace: before Christ, coming to Christ, and life since?
  • What holds you back most from sharing your faith: lack of love, lack of courage or lack of wisdom?
  • What does the story of Alexander Mackay and the Uganda Martyrs teach you about the cost and fruit of mission?
  • In which of the four ways, going, sending, praying or giving, is God calling you to take part more fully?

A step for this week

Write down the names of three people in your life who do not yet know Christ, and pray for each of them by name every day this week, asking God for open hearts and open doors. Then write out your own story of grace in three short parts and practise telling it aloud in under three minutes. Before the week ends, ask God for one natural opportunity to share it, or to invite one of the three to read a Gospel with you, and take it when it comes.

study_questions.question: Is the Great Commission for every Christian?
study_questions.answer: Yes. Jesus told His disciples to "make disciples of all the nations" and to teach them "to keep everything I have commanded you" (Matthew 28:19–20), which includes the command to make disciples. So the commission passes from each generation of believers to the next. Not everyone is called to go overseas, but everyone can take part by going, sending, praying and giving.

study_questions.question: What is the gospel in simple words?
