study_questions.answer: God made us to know Him, but "Everyone has sinned, and all come short of God's glory" (Romans 3:23). Jesus, God's Son, died for our sins, was buried and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). We receive Him by faith, for "all who call on the name of the Lord will be saved" (Romans 10:13).

study_questions.question: How do I share my faith with friends and family?
study_questions.answer: Start with your own story: what your life was like before Christ, how you came to trust Him, and what difference He has made, just as Jesus told one man to "Go home to your own people, and let them know all that the Lord has done for you" (Mark 5:19). Pray for the people you hope will come to Christ by name. Speak with love, courage and wisdom, letting your conversation be "gracious and seasoned with salt" (Colossians 4:6).

fields.title: Stewardship: God’s Managers of Time, Talents and Treasure
fields.body_html:
“The earth is the LORD’s, and all that fills it, the world and everyone who lives there.”

— Psalm 24:1 (OWB)

Imagine a man who manages a large tea estate in the hills. He drives the estate lorry, holds the keys to the store and hires the pickers. To the village below, he looks like a wealthy man. But he knows that the lorry, the land and the keys are not his. At the end of every month the owner’s accountant sits down with him and goes through the books, line by line.

A good manager is not crushed by this. He is proud to be trusted, and he looks after the estate carefully precisely because it is not his. A bad manager forgets whose estate it is, sells a few sacks from the store, and tells himself that nobody will notice.

The Bible’s word for the good manager is a steward: someone who looks after what belongs to another. Every one of us is a steward. Our money, our time, our abilities, our bodies, our families, our influence and even the gospel itself have been placed in our hands by God. We do not own them. We manage them, and we manage them before His face.

That is what it means to live coram Deo with our possessions. The question is not only, “What do I have?” but, “Whose is it, and what does He want done with it?”

Everything belongs to God

The psalmist begins with a sweeping claim: “The earth is the LORD’s, and all that fills it, the world and everyone who lives there” (Psalm 24:1). Not most of the earth, nor the parts we give to church. All of it.

God owns everything because He made everything. So every field, shop, bank account and pair of hands belongs to Him first. Gathering an offering for the temple, King David prayed, “Everything comes from You; what we have given You came from Your own hand” (1 Chronicles 29:14). Even a king’s gift only gives God back what was already His.

This truth is both humbling and freeing. It removes our right to say, “This is mine, and I will do what I like with it.” And it lifts a heavy weight: the owner is responsible for the estate; the manager is responsible only to be faithful. Stewardship does not remove the need for careful planning, but it changes the centre of our trust. The Owner does not abandon His own.

Managers, not owners

This calling goes back to the very beginning. When God made the man and the woman, He gave them a task: “Be fruitful and multiply. Fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish in the sea, the birds in the sky, and every living creature that moves along the ground” (Genesis 1:28). Then we read that “The LORD God took the man and settled him in the garden of Eden to work it and take care of it” (Genesis 2:15).

Those two verses belong together. Humanity was given authority, but on God’s behalf. Adam was not the landlord of Eden. He was its gardener.

Sin turned this upside down. The fall was, among other things, a manager deciding he would rather be the owner. Much of the world’s misery flows from that grab: land taken by force, workers cheated, rivers poisoned, families divided over inheritance.

In Christ, God restores us to our first calling. Paul describes Christian leaders in exactly these terms: “as assistants of Christ and as household managers put in charge of the mysteries of God” (1 Corinthians 4:1). Peter widens it to every believer: “Each of you has received a gift; use it to serve one another, as good managers of the richly varied grace of God” (1 Peter 4:10).

What Jesus taught: faithful in little

In the parable of the talents, a man going on a journey “summoned his own servants and handed his property over to them” (Matthew 25:14). He gave five bags of silver to one, two to another and one to a third, “according to what each could manage” (Matthew 25:15). The first two servants went to work and doubled what they were given. The third dug a hole and buried his bag in the ground. When the master returned, he praised the first two with the same words: “Well done! You are a good and faithful servant. You proved faithful in small matters; I will put you in charge of great ones. Come in and share the joy of your master” (Matthew 25:21).

Notice three things. The servants received different amounts, and we are not judged by what someone else was given. The servant with two bags received exactly the same praise as the servant with five: faithfulness, not size, is what counts. And the servant who failed did not steal. He simply did nothing, out of fear. Jesus treats that burying as a serious failure.

Luke records a similar story, the parable of the minas, in which each servant receives the same amount and they produce different results. To the faithful one the king says, “Excellent, good servant!... You have been trustworthy in a very small matter, so you will have authority over ten cities” (Luke 19:17). A very small matter, and ten cities. The proportion is wildly generous. God takes our small faithfulness and answers it with a reward far beyond it.

In the parable of the shrewd manager (Luke 16:1–13), Jesus praises not a dishonest man’s cheating but his foresight, and then draws the lesson: “Someone who is faithful in the smallest matter is faithful in large matters too, and someone who is dishonest in the smallest matter is dishonest in large matters too” (Luke 16:10). He ends with a warning that cuts through every excuse: “You cannot serve both God and wealth” (Luke 16:13).

Money is a small matter compared to eternal things, but it is a revealing one. A shopkeeper who gives short weight on a kilo of sugar would not be safer with a million shillings. Faithful in little, faithful in much.

The day of accounting

Every one of these parables ends with the master’s return and a reckoning. “A long time afterward the master of those servants returned and went over the accounts with them” (Matthew 25:19). Paul says: “So each of us will have to give an account of ourselves” (Romans 14:12). And he names the one thing that is required of a manager: “Now what is looked for in household managers is this: that each one proves trustworthy” (1 Corinthians 4:2).

For a believer, this accounting is not about whether we are saved. That was settled at the cross, as Chapter 28 explains. It is about how we used what was placed in our hands. It should not terrify a child of God, but it gives weight to ordinary choices: how you spend your evening, treat your workers or use your salary.

And there is a joy waiting in it. The highest hope of a manager is not a payment but a word from the owner’s mouth: “Well done! You are a good and faithful servant.” To hear those words from the One whose face we have sought all our lives will be worth every sacrifice. Living coram Deo means living now with that day in view.

John Wesley: gain, save, give

Few people in Christian history took stewardship more seriously than John Wesley. Born in 1703 in the small town of Epworth in England, he became a scholar and fellow at Oxford University. In 1738, at a meeting in Aldersgate Street in London, he came to trust in Christ alone for salvation, and for the next half century he travelled Britain on horseback, preaching in fields, market squares and mining villages.

Wesley watched the poor working people who came to faith under his preaching stop drinking away their wages and work hard and honestly. Many became far better off. And he noticed a danger: their new prosperity was cooling their love for God.

So Wesley preached a famous sermon on the subject, now in the Ochorus library as The Use of Money. He boiled the teaching down to three rules, each of which he explained with care. First, “Gain all you can,” by honest work and without harming your own body or soul or your neighbour’s. Second, “Save all you can,” by refusing to waste money on vanity, show and the desires of the flesh. Third, and this was the whole point of the first two, “give all you can.” He explained why:

“When the Possessor of heaven and earth brought you into being, and placed you in this world, he placed you here not as a proprietor, but a steward: As such he entrusted you, for a season, with goods of various kinds; but the sole property of these still rests in him, nor can be alienated from him.”

John Wesley, The Use of Money

Wesley practised what he preached. As a young man at Oxford he fixed the sum he needed to live on, and when his income rose he went on living on about the same amount and gave the rest away. Later in life his books sold widely and brought in large sums. He used the money for the poor, for schools, for medicine and for the spread of the gospel. When he died in 1791, at the age of eighty-seven, he left very little money behind. What he had managed, he had passed on.

Wesley even gave his hearers questions to ask before spending, among them: “Am I acting herein, not as a proprietor, but as a steward of my Lord’s goods?” (from The Use of Money). That question is as useful in a market today as it was in eighteenth-century England.

From the tithe to total surrender

How much should a Christian give? Here it helps to see how the Bible’s teaching unfolds.

In the Old Testament, Israel was commanded to give a tenth. “All the tithe of the land belongs to the LORD, both grain from what is sown and fruit from the trees. It is holy to the LORD” (Leviticus 27:30). When the people neglected this, the prophet Malachi called them back: “Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, so that there will be food in My house. Put Me to the test in this, says the LORD of Armies, and see if I do not open the windows of heaven for you and pour out on you a blessing until you have more than enough” (Malachi 3:10). The book of Proverbs adds a call to give God the first share, not the leftovers: “Honor the LORD with what you own, with the first and best of everything your land produces” (Proverbs 3:9).

In the New Testament, the standard is not lowered but raised: all we are and all we have belongs to God. Paul urges us to “offer your bodies to God as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to Him” (Romans 12:1). If our very bodies are offered to God, then a tenth is not the ceiling of our giving. Everything is His.

That is why the New Testament sets no fixed percentage. It points us to the cross. “After all, you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: rich as He was, He became poor for your sake, so that His poverty might make you rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Christian giving is a response to that grace. And Paul is clear that it should be free and glad, not forced: “Each of you should give the amount you have settled on in your own heart, not with regret and not because you feel you must. God loves a giver who gives gladly” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

So what of the tithe? This book’s view is this: tithing, and giving beyond it, are good and worthy practices. Many believers find that setting aside a tenth, from the first of their income, is a wise and joyful discipline, and many are led to give far more. But giving is guided by the Spirit and flows from grace and gratitude, not from rules or obligation. A tenth is a fine place to start, but it is neither a fee for God’s favour nor a limit on love. Wesley himself put it strongly: give “not a tenth, not a third, not half, but all that is God’s, be it more or less” (from The Use of Money), meaning that every coin is to be used for God, whether given away or spent wisely on our families and needs.

Two warnings follow. Beware of anyone who promises that if you give to them, God is bound to make you rich. Paul says the blessing of generous giving is that “you will have everything you need, with plenty to spare for every good work” (2 Corinthians 9:8): the plenty is for more good works, not more luxury. And beware of the opposite error: “Since there is no fixed rule, I will give whatever is left over.” Freedom in grace should make us more generous than the law, not less.

Generosity and contentment

Generosity and contentment are twins. You rarely find one without the other.

Paul wrote to Timothy: “Godliness is indeed great gain, when it comes with contentment. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. If we have food and clothing, we will be content with that” (1 Timothy 6:6–8). Then: “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs” (1 Timothy 6:10). Money itself is not called evil; the love of it is, and a poor man can love it as fiercely as a rich one.

To those who do have more, Paul gives a different instruction. They are not to be proud, nor to put their hope in wealth, “but in God, who richly gives us everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). Then: “Tell them to do good, to be rich in good deeds, to give generously and to share. In this way they will store up treasure for themselves as a firm foundation for the age to come, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life” (1 Timothy 6:18–19).

Jesus said the same: “Do not pile up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moths and rust ruin them and thieves dig through walls and steal them. Instead, pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Matthew 6:19–20). And He told us why it matters so much: “Your heart will always be where your treasure is” (Matthew 6:21). If you want your heart to move towards God, move your treasure towards His purposes.

Contentment is not laziness. It is the quiet confidence that God is enough. A mother in a rented room who shares her food with a hungry neighbour may be far richer in God’s eyes than a businessman lying awake over his investments.

Stewarding all of life

Money is only one of the things we hold in trust. Think of the whole estate God has placed in your care.

Time. Each of us is given a limited number of days. Moses prayed, “Teach us, then, to reckon our days rightly, so that our hearts may grow wise” (Psalm 90:12). Time wasted is part of our stewardship too. Chapter 8’s morning watch is, among other things, a way of giving God the first of our time, as the tithe gave Him the first of the harvest.

Talents. Every gift, whether teaching, building, caring for the sick or fixing engines, is a bag of silver placed in our hands. Chapter 23 explores spiritual gifts more fully.

Our bodies. Paul writes, “your body is a temple where the Holy Spirit lives... You do not belong to yourselves. You were bought, and a price was paid for you. So bring glory to God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Rest, food and sexual purity are matters of stewardship.

Relationships and influence. Our families, friendships and whatever influence we have are also entrusted to us. William Wilberforce, the English politician who spent decades fighting to end the British slave trade, saw his place in Parliament in exactly this light. In his book A Practical View of Christianity, now in the Ochorus library, he wrote that the Christian “is diligently to cultivate the talents with which God has entrusted him, and assiduously to employ them in doing justice and shewing mercy.” The slave trade was abolished by Britain in 1807, and slavery itself in the British colonies just after his death in 1833.

The gospel and creation. We have been entrusted with the best news in the world, and keeping it to ourselves would be the worst kind of burying (see Chapter 25). And the command to care for the garden still stands: a farmer who protects his land from erosion for his grandchildren is a good steward.

Work as worship

All of this brings us to our daily work. Chapter 20 showed that work is a calling from God. Stewardship adds that our work is also a form of worship. Paul tells even slaves, “Whatever you are doing, put your whole self into the work, as for the Lord and not for people, knowing that you will receive from the Lord the inheritance as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you serve” (Colossians 3:23–24).

The Dutch theologian Abraham Kuyper, who was a pastor, a newspaper editor, the founder of the Free University of Amsterdam and, for a time, prime minister of the Netherlands, is remembered for insisting that there is no corner of human life over which Christ does not claim lordship. Science, art, politics, business, education and farming all belong to Him. Kuyper’s conviction is simply Psalm 24:1 applied to Monday morning.

So the nurse turning a patient at night, the trader keeping honest scales and the mother washing clothes by the river are doing holy work when they do it for Christ, not because it happens in a church, but because it is done before the face of the Owner, for His glory.

Living as stewards before His face

A careless manager sweeps the yard only on the day the owner visits. A faithful one works the same every day, because he wants to please him. That is the steward’s life coram Deo. God is not a distant owner who visits once a year. He is present in every transaction, every hour and every choice. And He is not a harsh master, as the fearful servant imagined. He is the Father who gave His own Son for us, who “richly gives us everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17), and who longs to say to each of His children, “Come in and share the joy of your master.”

Faithful stewardship is not finished in a day or a year. It is the work of a whole lifetime, which leads us into Chapter 27 and the question of how we can run the race to the end and finish well.

Questions for reflection

  • If someone looked only at your bank statements and your diary for the last month, what would they conclude you treasure most?
  • Which of your gifts, abilities or opportunities are you most tempted to “bury in the ground”, and why?
  • How do you respond to the teaching that the tithe is a good practice but not a fixed rule? Does it make you want to give more or less?
  • Wesley asked, “Am I acting herein, not as a proprietor, but as a steward of my Lord’s goods?” Where in your spending would that question make the biggest difference?
  • What area of stewardship (time, body, relationships, influence, creation) have you thought about least, and what would faithfulness look like there?
  • How does knowing that you will one day give an account to a loving Father change the way you see ordinary work?

A step for this week

This week, sit down with a notebook and write two lists. In the first, list the main things God has placed in your care: your income, your time, your skills, your relationships, your influence and anything you own. In the second, write what you actually did with each of them over the past seven days. Then pray over both lists, thanking God as the Owner of everything. Choose one specific change: perhaps setting aside a first portion of your next income before anything else is spent, giving an hour of your time to someone in need, or using one skill you have neglected. Write it down, do it, and at the end of the week thank God for the joy of being His manager.

study_questions.question: What does it mean that Christians are stewards?
study_questions.answer: A steward is someone who looks after what belongs to another. Because "The earth is the LORD's, and all that fills it, the world and everyone who lives there" (Psalm 24:1), our money, time, abilities, bodies, relationships and even the gospel are placed in our hands by God. From the beginning humanity was told to work the garden "and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15): we are managers, not owners, and we manage before His face.

study_questions.question: Do Christians have to tithe ten percent?
study_questions.answer: In the Old Testament Israel gave a tenth: "All the tithe of the land belongs to the LORD" (Leviticus 27:30). In the New Testament all we are and all we have belongs to God, so it sets no fixed percentage. This book's view is that tithing and giving beyond it are good and worthy practices, but giving is guided by the Spirit and flows from grace and gratitude, not rules: "God loves a giver who gives gladly" (2 Corinthians 9:7).

study_questions.question: What did Jesus teach in the parable of the talents?
study_questions.answer: A master handed his property to his servants "according to what each could manage" (Matthew 25:15), and on his return praised the faithful ones with the same words: "Well done! You are a good and faithful servant. You proved faithful in small matters; I will put you in charge of great ones" (Matthew 25:21). Faithfulness, not the size of the gift, is what counts, and the servant who buried his silver out of fear is treated as a serious failure. Each of us "will have to give an account of ourselves" (Romans 14:12).

fields.title: Finishing Well: Perseverance and Legacy
fields.body_html:
“I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Now there is waiting for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day.”

— 2 Timothy 4:7–8 (OWB)

Anyone who has watched a long-distance race knows that the start is easy to watch and the finish is hard to run. At the starting line everyone is fresh. The crowd cheers, the runners bounce on their toes and the first lap feels light. But somewhere in the middle of the race the legs grow heavy, the crowd thins and the finish line is still out of sight. That is where races are won and lost.

The Christian life is like that. Many begin with great joy. Fewer finish with the same fire. Some fall away openly. More simply drift: they do not deny Christ, but they slowly stop seeking His face. Prayer becomes a habit without warmth, Scripture a book on a shelf, church a duty.

Paul wrote the words above from a Roman prison, near the end of his life. He knew he was about to die, and he could look back without regret. He had not been perfect, but he had been faithful. He had fought, he had finished, he had kept the faith.

This chapter asks how we can do the same. How can we keep running when the legs are heavy, bear fruit when the body is weak, and pass the faith on to those who come after us? The answer is not a new technique. It is the same truth that runs through this whole book: we live before the face of God, and He is the one who holds us to the end.

Running the race with perseverance

The letter to the Hebrews gives the clearest picture: “So then, since we too have so vast a cloud of witnesses all around us, let us strip off every burden, and the sin that wraps itself around us so readily, and let us run the race laid out ahead of us, and run it with endurance” (Hebrews 12:1).

Notice four things in this verse and the one that follows.

First, we are not alone. The “cloud of witnesses” are the men and women of faith in Hebrews 11, and all who have run before us. They are like a stadium full of former champions, not watching to judge us but showing by their lives that the race can be finished.

Second, we must travel light. A runner does not carry a sack of maize on his back. Some burdens are not sinful in themselves, but they slow us down: too many commitments, love of comfort, the endless pull of the phone. Other weights are plainly sin, the kind that “wraps itself around us so readily,” like a long cloth catching around a runner’s legs. Both must be stripped off.

Third, the race is “laid out ahead of us.” We do not choose the course. God marks it out, with its hills and its straight roads, its seasons of plenty and of loss. Our task is to run the course He has set, not the one we wish for.

Fourth, and most important: “Let us keep our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer who leads the way in faith and brings it to perfection. For the sake of the joy that lay ahead of Him, He endured a cross and counted its shame as nothing” (Hebrews 12:2). Jesus is both the one who has run ahead of us and the one who will bring us home. When we look at our own strength, we will grow tired. When we look at Him, we find strength to continue: “Weigh up what He endured... Then you will not wear out and let your spirits give way” (Hebrews 12:3).

Paul knew this kind of running. To the elders of Ephesus he said: “All I want is to run my course to the end and carry out the ministry I received from the Lord Jesus: to bear full witness to the gospel of the grace of God” (Acts 20:24). And to the Philippians he wrote: “I put out of mind what is behind me and stretch out for what is in front of me, and I run straight for the goal to win the prize promised by God’s upward call in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:13–14). Even near the end of his life, Paul did not think he had arrived. He kept pressing on.

Polycarp: eighty-six years of faithfulness

Some time in the middle of the second century, in the city of Smyrna on the coast of what is now western Turkey, an old man was hunted by the authorities. His name was Polycarp, and he was the bishop of the church there. Irenaeus, who knew him as a young man, later wrote that Polycarp had been taught by apostles and had known John, the beloved disciple. He was a living link between the first generation of believers and the growing church of the second century. Smyrna is one of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, and the risen Christ had said to it: “Stay faithful even to death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10).

The account of what happened next is one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament, and it is in the Ochorus library as The Epistle and Martyrdom of Polycarp. Friends persuaded Polycarp to leave the city, and he stayed at a country house nearby, where, the account says, he spent night and day praying for all people and for the churches throughout the world. But when the soldiers finally came to the house where he was staying, he refused to escape, saying, “The will of God be done.” Then he did something remarkable. He ordered food and drink to be set before the men who had come to arrest him, and asked only for an hour to pray. The account says that “he stood and prayed, being full of the grace of God, so that he could not cease for two full hours, to the astonishment of them that heard him.”

He was taken into the city and brought before the Roman governor in the crowded stadium. The governor tried to spare the old man. “Have respect to thy old age,” he said. All Polycarp had to do was swear by the emperor’s fortune and curse Christ, and he would be set free. Polycarp’s answer has been remembered for nearly two thousand years:

“Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?”

The Epistle and Martyrdom of Polycarp

The governor threatened wild beasts, then fire. Polycarp replied that the governor’s fire “burneth for an hour, and after a little is extinguished,” but that there is a judgment to come that matters far more. He was put to death in the stadium that day.

What strikes us most about Polycarp’s last hours is not a sudden burst of courage. It is that his death matched his life. A man who had prayed for eighty-six years prayed for two hours before his arrest. A man who had served Christ for eighty-six years would not betray Him at the end. Faithfulness at the finish line was the fruit of faithfulness on every ordinary day before it. That is the secret of finishing well. We do not suddenly become faithful in the last lap. We become faithful in the thousand small choices of the middle of the race.

In his own letter to the church at Philippi, also in that library volume, Polycarp had urged believers: “Let us then continually persevere in our hope, and the earnest of our righteousness, which is Jesus Christ... Let us then be imitators of His patience.” He lived what he wrote.

Growing in faithfulness through every season

Life comes in seasons. There is the fresh zeal of new faith, the busy years of building a family or a career, the middle years when responsibilities pile high, and the later years when strength begins to fade. Each season has its own dangers.

The young believer may be tempted to think that early enthusiasm will carry him all the way. It will not. Feelings rise and fall. What carries us is the daily habit of meeting God, which Part Two of this book described: Scripture, prayer, the morning watch and abiding in Christ.

The person in the middle years faces a different danger: busyness and drift. Work, children, school fees, church responsibilities and aging parents crowd every hour. Many believers do not fall in a dramatic sin but in a slow cooling. They are too busy to pray and too tired to read. The cure is not to add more activity but to guard the centre. Five quiet minutes before the face of God each morning can keep a heart alive through years of pressure.

And what if you have already stumbled badly? Finishing well does not require a perfect record. Peter denied Jesus three times on the night of His arrest, yet the risen Lord met him by the lake, asked him three times, “Do you love Me?” and gave him work to do (John 21:15–19). Peter went on to feed Christ’s sheep for the rest of his life. A race can be resumed. If you have fallen, do not lie on the track. Confess your sin, receive His forgiveness, get up and run again. God is far more interested in where you finish than in how many times you fell.

Success brings its own temptation. Some of the saddest falls in church history have come not in times of trouble but at the height of influence, when a leader stopped being accountable and began to believe his own reputation. Finishing well requires humility and honest friends who will ask hard questions.

Paul gives a word for every season: “So then, my dear brothers and sisters, be firm and unshakable, always doing more and more in the work of the Lord, since you know that in the Lord your hard work is never wasted” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Never wasted. Not the prayers that seemed unanswered, not the Sunday school class that seemed restless, not the years of caring for a sick relative. Nothing done for Christ is lost.

Some are called to be faithful under great pressure. Janani Luwum grew up in the Acholi region of northern Uganda, became a teacher, and came to living faith through the East African Revival. He rose to become Archbishop of the Church of Uganda in the dark years of Idi Amin’s rule. When soldiers and agents of the government were killing ordinary Ugandans, Luwum and other bishops spoke out and protested to the president. In February 1977 he was arrested, and he was killed in custody. The government claimed he had died in a car accident, but few believed it. Luwum did not seek death, but he would not keep quiet to save his life. Like Polycarp, he finished faithful, and his witness has strengthened believers across East Africa ever since.

Bearing fruit in old age, illness and decline

One of the most beautiful promises in the Psalms is for those whose strength is fading: “The righteous will thrive like the palm tree and rise tall as a cedar on Lebanon. Rooted in the LORD’s house, they will bloom in the courtyards of our God. Even when they are old they will still bear fruit; they will stay rich with sap and green” (Psalm 92:12–14).

Many cultures honour the old, and many of our readers come from places where grandparents are respected. Yet even there, the elderly can feel useless when they can no longer farm, work or travel. Illness can bring the same feeling at any age. A person who once led a choir or ran a business may now spend most days in a chair.

But God’s Word says the righteous “will still bear fruit.” The fruit may look different. It may be prayer instead of preaching, wisdom instead of labour, patience instead of activity. An old woman who prays daily for each of her grandchildren by name is bearing fruit. A sick man who receives visitors with peace and speaks of Christ’s faithfulness is bearing fruit. Paul knew that “Our outer self may be decaying, but our inner self is being made new day after day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

God also gives a promise to carry us when we cannot carry ourselves: “Until you are old I am He, and until your hair turns gray I am the one who will carry you” (Isaiah 46:4). The same God who held us as newborn believers will hold us at the end. Perseverance is not only our holding on to Him. It is first His holding on to us.

Leaving a spiritual legacy

Finishing well is not only about our own race. It is also about the runners who come after us. In a relay race, the most important moment is the passing of the baton. A team can run brilliantly and still lose if the baton is dropped.

Paul’s final letter, written to his young friend Timothy, is full of this concern. “And what you heard from me before many witnesses, pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). Count the generations in that one verse: Paul, Timothy, trustworthy people, and others. Four links in a chain. That chain has continued for two thousand years, and it has reached you.

Polycarp himself shows how this works. He learned from apostles. He taught Irenaeus, who went on to serve the church in Gaul, in what is now France, and to write against the false teachings of his day. The faith passed from John to Polycarp to Irenaeus, and onwards to us. The psalmist prayed for the same thing: “Now that I am old and gray, God, do not abandon me, not until I have told the generation after me what Your arm has done” (Psalm 71:18).

John Bunyan, the tinker and preacher who spent twelve years in prison for his faith, painted this in the second part of The Pilgrim’s Progress. When the old warrior Mr. Valiant-for-truth receives his summons to cross the river of death, he gathers his friends and says:

“My sword I give to him that shall succeed me in my pilgrimage, and my courage and skill to him that can get it. My marks and scars I carry with me, to be a witness for me that I have fought His battles who will now be my rewarder.”

John Bunyan, The Pilgrim’s Progress

His sword and his skill he leaves behind for others. His scars he takes with him. That is a picture of a spiritual legacy.

What will you hand on? Most of us will not leave large sums of money or famous books. But every one of us can leave something more lasting: a faith that has been seen, tested and shared. Parents can pass on a daily habit of prayer and Scripture to their children (see Chapter 19). Older believers can take a younger believer under their wing, meet regularly, open the Bible together and pray. A farmer can teach a young neighbour both how to plant and how to trust God for the rain. A teacher can model honesty that students remember for life.

A legacy is built less by grand plans than by consistent presence. The young watch how we handle money, how we speak of our spouses, how we respond to disappointment, whether we still pray when life is hard. They learn more from a lifetime of quiet faithfulness than from any sermon.

Looking ahead: the hope that keeps us running

Why do runners keep going when every muscle cries out to stop? Because they can see the finish line, or at least they know it is there.

Paul could face death calmly because he knew what lay beyond it: “Now there is waiting for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have longed for His appearing” (2 Timothy 4:8). Notice the last words. The crown is not only for apostles. It is for all who long for Christ’s appearing. If you love Him and long to see Him, that crown is waiting for you too.

This hope is not escapism. It is fuel. A runner who knows the prize is real will train harder, not less. A believer who knows that heaven is real will live more faithfully on earth. Polycarp could face the fire because he knew a greater judgment and a greater glory were coming. Luwum could face the soldiers because he knew whose face he would see next.

What exactly is that hope? What happens when we die, what will the judgment be like, and what will the new heavens and new earth hold? Those are the questions of Chapter 28, which explores the hope of glory fully. For now it is enough to know that the race has a finish line, and at the finish line is a Person. The One whose face we have sought every morning will be the One who welcomes us home.

Questions for reflection

  • Which season of life are you in now, and what particular danger to faithfulness does it bring?
  • What “burdens” or entangling sins slow you down in your race, and which one could you strip off this month?
  • Polycarp’s faithful death grew out of eighty-six years of faithful days. What small daily habits are shaping how you will finish?
  • If you are older or unwell, what fruit might God want you to bear in this season? If you are younger, which older believer could you learn from?
  • Who has passed the faith on to you? Who are you passing it on to now?
  • How does the hope of “the crown of righteousness” change the way you face hardship today?

A step for this week

This week, choose one person younger in the faith than you, whether a child, a new believer, a student or a colleague, and arrange to meet with them. Open a passage such as Hebrews 12:1–3 or 2 Timothy 2:1–2 together, talk honestly about how you keep going in your walk with God, and pray for each other. If you are the younger believer, do the opposite: seek out an older Christian whose faithfulness you admire and ask them to tell you how they have kept running. Either way, before the week ends, write down the name of that person and commit to praying for them by name every day for the next month.

study_questions.question: How can a Christian finish well?
study_questions.answer: Hebrews tells us to "strip off every burden, and the sin that wraps itself around us so readily, and let us run the race laid out ahead of us, and run it with endurance" (Hebrews 12:1), keeping our eyes on Jesus. Faithfulness at the finish line grows out of faithfulness in the thousand small choices of ordinary days, as Polycarp's eighty-six years of service show. Above all, perseverance is first God holding on to us: "Until you are old I am He, and until your hair turns gray I am the one who will carry you" (Isaiah 46:4).

study_questions.question: Can older or sick believers still bear fruit for God?
study_questions.answer: Yes. The psalm promises that the righteous "Even when they are old they will still bear fruit; they will stay rich with sap and green" (Psalm 92:14). The fruit may look different: prayer instead of preaching, wisdom instead of labour, patience instead of activity. "Our outer self may be decaying, but our inner self is being made new day after day" (2 Corinthians 4:16).

study_questions.question: What does it mean to leave a spiritual legacy?
study_questions.answer: It means passing the faith on, like a baton in a relay race: "what you heard from me before many witnesses, pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well" (2 Timothy 2:2). The faith passed from the apostle John to Polycarp to Irenaeus and onwards to us. Most of us will not leave money or famous books, but we can leave a faith that has been seen, tested and shared with children, younger believers and neighbours.

fields.title: Judgment, Paradise and the New Heavens and New Earth
fields.body_html:
“See, God’s dwelling is with human beings! He will make His home with them, and they will be His peoples; God Himself will be with them. Every tear He will wipe from their eyes. Death will be no more, and no more mourning, no crying, no pain.”

— Revelation 21:3–4 (OWB)

Every story needs an ending. A farmer plants with the harvest in mind; a builder lays a foundation with the finished house in mind. The end gives meaning to everything before it.

The same is true of the Christian life. This book began with the face of God: the man and the woman hiding from His face in the garden, Moses speaking with Him face to face, and the promise of Revelation that “they will look upon His face” (Revelation 22:4). We have spent twenty-six chapters learning to live before that face now, in prayer, work, family, suffering and mission. This chapter looks at where the story ends. What happens when we die? What will the return of Christ bring? What is the judgment, and what will the new creation be like?

These questions shape how we live today. Chapter 27 spoke of the hope that keeps us running. Here we look more closely at that hope, and at the sober truths that stand beside it.

Death and paradise

Death is the one appointment none of us can cancel. Yet for the believer, death has lost its terror. One of the two criminals crucified beside Jesus turned to Him in his last hours and asked to be remembered. Jesus answered, “Truly I tell you, this very day you will be with Me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Not after a long wait. Not after paying for his sins. This very day.

Paul agrees: “We have courage, then, and we would much rather move out of the body and make our home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8). Writing from prison, he could not decide whether he preferred to live or to die: “My desire is to leave this life and be with Christ, for that is far, far better” (Philippians 1:23).

So when a believer dies, the body is laid in the ground, but the person is at home with the Lord, conscious and at rest. This is far better than anything here. Yet it is not the final ending. The Bible’s great hope is not only that our souls go to heaven but that our bodies will be raised and the whole creation renewed.

At a graveside we grieve, as Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus, but not as those without hope. The believer we bury has simply gone ahead into the presence we have been seeking all our lives.

The return of Christ and the resurrection of the dead

The Christian hope centres on a Person and an event: Jesus Christ will come again. When He ascended, the angels told the disciples, “This Jesus has been taken up from you into heaven, and He will come in the very way you saw Him leave for heaven” (Acts 1:11). Paul describes the moment: “The Lord Himself will come down from heaven at a shout of command, at an archangel’s call and the sound of God’s trumpet, and the dead who belong to Christ will rise first. Then those of us still living, who are left, will be swept up with them into the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. From then on we will be with the Lord always” (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17).

At His coming the dead will be raised. “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised, never again to decay, and we who are alive will be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52). Our resurrection bodies will be real bodies, like the risen body of Jesus, but free from sickness, weakness and death.

Jesus taught that this resurrection includes everyone: “An hour is coming when everyone in the tombs will hear His voice and come out” (John 5:28–29).

Faithful Christians differ on many details of the end times, such as the order of events, the thousand years of Revelation 20 and the timing of the gathering of believers. This book treats these as matters on which we may freely differ (see the Appendix). But all the historic creeds confess together that Christ “will come again to judge the living and the dead.” That is the common ground, and it is enough to live by.

The final judgment

Scripture is plain that judgment is coming. “It is in store for human beings to die once and after that to be judged” (Hebrews 9:27). John saw the scene in a vision: “Next I saw a great white throne, and the one who sat on it; from His face earth and sky ran away, and no place could be found for them. I saw the dead, the great and the lowly, standing in front of the throne. Books were opened, and so was another book, the book of life” (Revelation 20:11–12).

Notice “the great and the lowly.” Presidents and herdsmen will stand on the same level ground. No bribe will work there. For people who have suffered under corrupt officials, cruel employers or violent men, this is good news: every hidden injustice will be brought into the light.

Jesus pictured the same day as a shepherd separating sheep from goats: “The Son of Man will come in His glory, and all the angels with Him. Then He will take His seat on the throne of His glory. Every nation will be brought together before Him” (Matthew 25:31–32). Every nation. Every person. Every life laid open before the face of God.

This is the ultimate meaning of coram Deo. Today we may forget that we live before God’s face; on that day no one will. The only question will be whether we meet that face as a judge to be feared or as a Father we have longed to see.

No condemnation for those in Christ

Here is the heart of the gospel. If judgment were based only on our record, none of us could stand. But God has done something astonishing. At the cross, Jesus bore the wrath of God against our sin. “God put Him forward as the means of atonement, by His blood, to be received through faith” (Romans 3:25). Because of this, Paul says, “Since we have now been declared righteous by His blood, it is all the more certain that we will be saved through Him from God’s wrath” (Romans 5:9).

So the believer can face the judgment without fear. “So then, those who are in Christ Jesus now face no sentence of condemnation” (Romans 8:1). Jesus Himself promised: “Truly, truly, I tell you, anyone who hears My word and believes the One who sent Me has eternal life. Such a person does not come under condemnation, but has already moved out of death into life” (John 5:24).

Notice the tense: “has already moved.” The verdict for those in Christ has been spoken. The sentence we deserved has been carried by another. We are fully forgiven, and we will never face condemnation.

Yet we will give an account

This does not mean that how we live makes no difference. Paul, who taught so clearly that we are saved by grace alone, also wrote: “For all of us must be laid open before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what matches the things done in the body, whether good or worthless” (2 Corinthians 5:10). And again: “We will all stand before God’s judgment seat... So each of us will have to give an account of ourselves” (Romans 14:10, 12).

Every believer will stand before Christ and be judged individually for how we lived and what we did with His great sacrifice. This judgment is not to decide our salvation. That was settled at the cross. It is for reward or loss.

Paul gives a vivid picture. Jesus Christ is the only foundation. On that foundation each of us builds with our lives, some with “gold, silver, costly stones,” others with “wood, hay or straw.” Then “the fire itself will prove what kind of work each one has done. If what someone has built on the foundation survives, that builder will receive a reward. If someone’s work burns up, that person will suffer loss. The builder will still be saved, but only as one who comes out through the fire” (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

Imagine two houses after a bush fire. One was built of stone and still stands; the other was grass and sticks, and only ashes remain. Both families escaped alive, but only one has something to show for years of labour. A believer can be saved and yet see much of a life’s work burn away, because it was done for self or for show. This is why Chapter 26 spoke of faithful stewardship. What we do with our time, money and gifts matters to Christ.

Rewards, crowns and “well done”

The New Testament is not shy about rewards. It speaks of “the crown of righteousness” for all who long for Christ’s appearing (2 Timothy 4:8), “the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him” (James 1:12), and “a crown of glory that will never wither” for faithful shepherds of God’s flock (1 Peter 5:4).

Is it selfish to serve God for a reward? No. The rewards of Scripture are not wages that we earn. They are gifts of a generous Father, who delights to honour what His children did for love of Him. And notice what the elders in heaven do with their crowns: “They throw down their crowns in front of the throne” (Revelation 4:10). Our crowns will be things to give back to Him in worship.

The greatest reward of all will be a word. To the faithful servant, the master says, “Well done! You are a good and faithful servant... Come in and share the joy of your master” (Matthew 25:21). To hear those words from the lips of Jesus, to see His face and know that He is pleased, will be worth every hidden sacrifice and every unseen act of love.

The reality of judgment for those who reject Christ

We must also speak, soberly and with tears, about those who reject Christ. Jesus Himself taught about it more than anyone. At the end of the sheep and goats He said, “These will depart to eternal punishment, and the righteous will go to eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). Paul writes that those who refuse the gospel “will pay the penalty of eternal destruction, cut off from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of His power” (2 Thessalonians 1:9).

The whole Bible is the story of God’s face. To be cut off from that face for ever is the deepest loss a human being can know.

Christians have held differing views on the nature of hell. The view held by most Christians through history, including Augustine and Jonathan Edwards, is that the lost will experience conscious punishment that has no end. They point to Jesus’ words setting “eternal punishment” beside “eternal life” in the same sentence. Other Bible-believing teachers, among them the respected English pastor John Stott, have suggested more tentatively that the lost, after a just judgment, will finally be destroyed and cease to exist. They point to words such as “destruction,” to Jesus’ warning about the One “who can destroy soul and body alike in hell” (Matthew 10:28), and to Revelation’s “second death.” Christians also differ on how far the Bible’s pictures of fire and darkness are literal or are images of a reality worse than words.

Yet all these views agree on what matters most. Judgment is real. It is just. It is final. It means being shut out from the presence of God, the source of all life, love and joy. And God takes no pleasure in it: “As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, the death of the wicked gives Me no pleasure. I would rather that they turn from their ways and live” (Ezekiel 33:11). Peter tells us why the end has not yet come: “He does not want anyone to be destroyed, but wants all people to turn back in repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).

C. S. Lewis explored this in his short book The Great Divorce, a story he was careful to call a dream and not a map of the afterlife. In it, ghosts from a grey, dreary town take a bus ride to the edge of heaven. Heaven is so solid and real that the grass hurts their feet. Each is invited to stay, and most turn back, because they will not let go of their pride, their grievances or their self-pity. Lewis’s point was that the lost are not people who longed for God and were refused. They are people who, in the end, would rather have themselves than Him.

This truth should never make us proud or cold. It should break our hearts and move our feet, and it is one of the deepest reasons for the urgency of the Great Commission (see Chapter 25). If judgment is real, then the gospel is the best news anyone can hear, and we must share it with love while there is time.

The new heavens and new earth

The Bible does not end with souls floating in the clouds. It ends with a renewed creation. Long ago God promised through Isaiah, “Look, I am about to create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). In that world, “They will build houses and settle in them, plant vineyards and enjoy their grapes” (Isaiah 65:21), and “None will hurt and none will destroy anywhere on My holy mountain” (Isaiah 65:25).

Paul says the whole creation is waiting for that day: “The created world cranes its neck in longing, waiting for God’s children to be revealed... creation itself will also be released from its slavery to decay and will enter the freedom that comes with the glory of God’s children” (Romans 8:19, 21). The droughts, floods, diseases and decay of this world are not the last word. Peter adds, “we are looking forward to what He promised: new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home” (2 Peter 3:13).

And then John sees it: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth; the first heaven and the first earth had gone, and the sea was no more” (Revelation 21:1). God comes to live with His people. Every tear is wiped away. Death, mourning, crying and pain are gone. The One on the throne says, “See, I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5).

In the final chapter of the Bible we are back in a garden, now a garden city. A river of the water of life flows from the throne, and the tree of life grows on its banks, “and its leaves bring healing to the nations” (Revelation 22:2). Then comes the line this whole book has been moving towards: “His servants will offer Him worship; they will look upon His face, and His name will be written on their foreheads” (Revelation 22:3–4). The hiding that began in Eden is over for ever. We will live coram Deo, before the face of God, in perfect joy.

Augustine of Hippo, the great North African bishop, wrote The City of God after Rome was sacked in 410, when the world seemed to be falling apart. Its last pages look past every earthly city to the one that will never fall:

“There we shall rest and see, see and love, love and praise. This is what shall be in the end without end.”

Augustine, The City of God

Jonathan Edwards: a world of love

Few people have thought more deeply about heaven than Jonathan Edwards. Born in 1703 in Connecticut, in the American colonies, he became pastor of the church in Northampton, Massachusetts, and was one of the leading preachers of the revival known as the Great Awakening. Many people know him only for one fierce sermon about judgment, Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God. But Edwards’s deepest love was for the beauty of God, and the joy of knowing Him for ever.

His life was not easy. In 1750, after more than twenty years of ministry, his own congregation dismissed him after a painful dispute. He moved his large family to the frontier town of Stockbridge, serving as a missionary pastor to Native American families and writing some of his greatest books. In 1758 he was called to be president of the college at Princeton. Within weeks of arriving, he died after an inoculation against smallpox. He was fifty-four.

Edwards preached a series of sermons on 1 Corinthians 13, ending with one that described heaven as a world of love. On earth, he said in effect, love is mixed with selfishness and misunderstanding. In heaven, love flows perfectly from God to His people and between all His people, with nothing to spoil it, and it never ends.

In another sermon, The Christian Pilgrim, now in the Ochorus library, Edwards urged his hearers to see this life as a journey towards that world. He compared every earthly joy to the joy of God Himself:

“Fathers and mothers, husbands, wives, or children, or the company of earthly friends, are but shadows; but the enjoyment of God is the substance. These are but scattered beams; but God is the sun. These are but streams; but God is the fountain. These are but drops; but God is the ocean.”

Jonathan Edwards, The Christian Pilgrim

Edwards loved his wife Sarah and his children deeply. But he knew that every good thing on earth is a small stream that flows from a great fountain. In the new creation we will have the fountain itself.

Living now in the light of eternity

How then should we live? Peter answers directly: “Since everything is to be dissolved in this way, think what sort of people you ought to be! Live holy and godly lives, as you wait for the coming of the day of God” (2 Peter 3:11–12). John adds, “when He is revealed, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He truly is. Everyone whose hope is set on Him in this way makes themselves pure, just as He is pure” (1 John 3:2–3).

The hope of eternity produces three things in us.

Holiness. If we will one day see God’s face, we want to be ready, as a bride prepares for her wedding day.

Hope. The grief, injustice and pain of this world are real, but they are not final. A widow in a village, a refugee in a camp, a patient in a hospital ward can lift their heads. “Every tear He will wipe from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4).

Faithful service. Because judgment and reward are real, our daily work matters. Because hell is real, the gospel is urgent. Because the new creation is coming, nothing done for Christ is ever wasted.

The Bible’s last prayer is “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20), the cry of every heart that has learned to seek God’s face. One day He will answer it, and we will see Him.

Questions for reflection

  • How does knowing that believers go at once to be with Christ change the way you think about your own death, or the death of someone you love?
  • Why is the promise of “no sentence of condemnation” (Romans 8:1) such good news when we think about the final judgment?
  • What in your life right now might be “wood, hay or straw,” and what might be “gold, silver, costly stones”?
  • How do you respond to the different Christian views on the nature of hell? What common ground do they share, and how should it affect the way you speak to others about Christ?
  • What part of the picture of the new heavens and new earth gives you the most hope, and why?
  • Edwards said earthly joys are streams and God is the fountain. Which “streams” are you most tempted to love more than the fountain?

A step for this week

This week, set aside one evening to read Revelation 21:1–22:5 slowly, out loud if you can, alone or with your family. As you read, note every promise that touches a particular sorrow in your own life or in your community, and turn each one into a prayer of thanks. Then think of one person you know who does not yet know Christ. Pray for them by name each day this week, and look for one opportunity before the week ends to tell them, simply and kindly, why you have hope beyond death.

study_questions.question: What happens to a Christian when they die?
study_questions.answer: The believer goes at once to be with Christ. Jesus told the dying criminal, "Truly I tell you, this very day you will be with Me in paradise" (Luke 23:43), and Paul wrote that he would "much rather move out of the body and make our home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). This is far better than anything here, yet it is not the final ending: at Christ's return the dead will be raised and creation renewed.

study_questions.question: Will Christians be judged if they are already forgiven?
study_questions.answer: Those in Christ will never face condemnation: "those who are in Christ Jesus now face no sentence of condemnation" (Romans 8:1), because Jesus bore God's wrath against sin on the cross. Yet every believer will stand before the judgment seat of Christ, "so that each one may receive what matches the things done in the body, whether good or worthless" (2 Corinthians 5:10). This judgment does not decide salvation; it is for reward or loss (1 Corinthians 3:10–15).

study_questions.question: What will the new heavens and new earth be like?
study_questions.answer: The Bible ends not with souls in the clouds but with a renewed creation: "Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth" (Revelation 21:1). God will live with His people, and "Every tear He will wipe from their eyes. Death will be no more, and no more mourning, no crying, no pain" (Revelation 21:4). Above all, His servants "will look upon His face" (Revelation 22:4), living coram Deo in perfect joy.

fields.title: Conclusion: Moving Forward with God
fields.body_html:
“Of this I am convinced: the One who started a good work in you will keep working at it until it is finished on the day of Christ Jesus.”

— Philippians 1:6 (OWB)

When a traveller reaches the top of a long hill, she often stops and turns round. Below her lies the whole road: the river she crossed at dawn, the market town where she rested, the steep places where she nearly turned back. On the road it was one step after another. From the hilltop it looks like a journey.

We have come to that kind of place. This book began with a face. In the Introduction we heard David’s prayer: “My heart says to You what You have said: ‘Seek My face.’ So I will seek Your face, LORD” (Psalm 27:8). We saw that every one of us lives before someone’s face, and that the Reformers named a better way: coram Deo, living before the face of God. Since then we have walked a long road together.

So let us stop on the hilltop, look back, and then look ahead. This is not the end of anything. As the Introduction said, this is not a book to finish, but a life to begin.

Looking back on the journey

Part One, Foundations, asked the first question of all: whose face are we seeking? We met Almighty God, our Father, holy and sovereign and yet near enough to be called Abba (Chapter 2); Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, who died and rose so that the hiding that began in Eden could end (Chapter 3); and the Holy Spirit, our Helper, who gives new birth, lives within us and empowers us (Chapter 4).

Part Two, Walking with God, showed how we meet this God day by day. Love stands at the heart of it all (Chapter 5). We hear Him in His Word (Chapter 6), answer Him in prayer (Chapter 7), give Him the first moments of the day in the morning watch (Chapter 8), bear fruit by abiding in the vine (Chapter 9), and keep near to Him through the spiritual disciplines (Chapter 10).

Part Three, Becoming Like Christ, explored how God changes us. We learned what it means to be a disciple (Chapter 11) and how to live the upside-down life of the Kingdom from the Sermon on the Mount (Chapter 12). We learned to trust God (Chapter 13), to walk in holiness and victory over sin (Chapter 14), and to let Him heal and grow the soul (Chapter 15). We faced the reality of spiritual warfare and Christ’s victory (Chapter 16), and we stood with believers in their suffering under the sovereign hand of God (Chapter 17).

Part Four, Living as God’s People, carried all of this into marriage and family, work, the Church, its ministries, spiritual gifts and servant ministry (Chapters 18 to 24). Part Five, Living for God’s Purposes, lifted our eyes to mission, stewardship, finishing well and the new heavens and new earth (Chapters 25 to 28).

That is a lot of road. If you have not yet put half of it into practice, you are in good company. The point of looking back is not to grade yourself. It is to see that every part of the road leads to the same place: the face of God.

The thread that runs through it all

If you pulled one thread through every chapter of this book, it would be this: we were created for relationship with God, restored to it through Christ, and empowered for it by the Spirit.

We were created for it. God did not make us because He needed servants. He made us out of the overflow of His love, to know Him and enjoy Him. Jesus said, “And eternal life is this: that they know You, the only true God, and the one You sent, Jesus Christ” (John 17:3). Not knowing about Him, but knowing Him.

We were restored to it through Christ. Sin sent us into hiding, but God came looking for us, and in the fullness of time He came in person. Paul says that God “is the one who shone in our hearts, to bring the light of the knowledge of God’s glory, the glory seen in the face of Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). In Christ we can stand before God’s face without shame.

We are empowered for it by the Spirit. We could never keep this relationship alive by our own strength. “Since our life comes from the Spirit, let us also follow the Spirit’s lead in each step we take” (Galatians 5:25). The Spirit cries “Abba, Father” in our hearts (Romans 8:15), opens the Word to us and slowly changes us. “But all of us, our faces uncovered, look upon the Lord’s glory as in a mirror, and we are being changed into the same image we see, from glory to ever greater glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Created, restored, empowered. Everything else in this book, from the morning watch to the way we manage money, hangs on that thread.

Building a rule of life

How do you carry all of this forward without being crushed by it? Christians down the centuries have found help in what they called a rule of life. Rule here does not mean a list of laws. Think of a trellis, the frame a farmer builds so that a vine can climb towards the sun. The trellis does not make the vine grow. Only life does that. But it gives the life a shape.

A rule of life is a written pattern of the few practices that keep you near to God, in a rhythm you can actually live. A rule that works only on your best week is a wish.

From the chapters of this book, five strands belong in almost every rule of life:

  1. Scripture. A daily portion of God’s Word, read slowly and with a listening heart (Chapter 6).
  2. Prayer. Talking with God and listening to Him, through the day as well as at set times (Chapter 7).
  3. The morning watch. A first meeting with God before the day’s demands rush in (Chapter 8). Jesus Himself did this: “Long before daylight, He got up and went out. He went off to a lonely place and spent time there in prayer” (Mark 1:35).
  4. Community. Regular worship and fellowship with a local church, and at least one or two friends who know you well (Chapter 21). The first believers “gave themselves fully to the apostles’ teaching and to the shared life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers” (Acts 2:42).
  5. Service. Some regular way of using your gifts to serve others, in the church and beyond it (Chapters 23 and 24).

Andrew Murray, the South African pastor who guided us in Chapter 9, warned that reading good books about Christ is not enough. We need time with Him:

“No, it needs day by day time with Jesus and with God. We all know the need of time for our meals each day, — every workman claims his hour for dinner; the hurried eating of so much food is not enough.”

Andrew Murray, Abide in Christ

A farmer in western Kenya may meet God before he walks to his fields, and pray as he weeds. A nurse in Manila on night shifts may keep her morning watch in the afternoon, when her day begins. A mother of small children may have ten quiet minutes before the house wakes, and a verse on a card above the cooking fire. The shape changes. The strands stay the same.

Write yours on one page. Micah gives a good test for any rule: does it help you live out what God asks? “And what does the LORD ask of you except to do justice, to love loyalty, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8).

Next steps for new believers

Perhaps you came to faith recently. If so, welcome. You do not need to do everything in these pages at once. Here are four first steps.

Be baptized. Baptism is the first step of obedience Jesus gave His followers, a public sign that you belong to Him. On the day of Pentecost Peter told the crowd, “Repent, and every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, so that your sins may be forgiven; and you will receive the Holy Spirit as a gift” (Acts 2:38). Christians practise baptism in different ways (see the Appendix), but all agree that Jesus commands it. Speak to a pastor about it.

Join a local church. A coal taken out of the fire soon grows cold. Find a church where the Bible is taught and love is real, and do not only attend; belong.

Find a mentor. Ask a mature believer whose life you respect to read the Bible and pray with you regularly. Most will be glad to be asked.

Begin a daily time with God. Start small: one chapter of a Gospel each morning, a prayer about what you read, thanks for one thing. Ten faithful minutes a day will do more than two hours once a month.

Behind all four is a simple decision, the one Joshua set before Israel: “Whom will you serve? ... My household and I will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15). Make that choice today, and make it again tomorrow.

Next steps for mature believers

Perhaps you have walked with God for many years. What does moving forward look like for you?

Go deeper, not just wider. We can know more about God while praying less. Return to first love (Chapter 5).

Let God keep healing your soul. Old wounds and fears do not always disappear with age, and God heals and grows the soul through the whole of life (Chapter 15).

Disciple others. Paul wrote to Timothy, “And what you heard from me before many witnesses, pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). Count the generations: Paul, Timothy, trustworthy people, others. Who is your Timothy?

Leave a legacy. Legacy is not mainly about buildings or reputation, but about people who know God because you walked with them (Chapter 27).

And keep running. Even the apostle Paul wrote: “I do not mean that I already have all this, or that I have already been made perfect. But I keep pursuing it ... I put out of mind what is behind me and stretch out for what is in front of me, and I run straight for the goal to win the prize promised by God’s upward call in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:12-14).

Corrie ten Boom is a picture of this. She was in her fifties when she came out of Ravensbrück concentration camp at the end of 1944, having lost her father and her sister Betsie because the family had hidden Jewish people in their home in Haarlem. Instead of retiring, she spent more than thirty years travelling the world, telling of God’s love and of the forgiveness He gives us power to offer. Even when they are old, the psalmist says, the righteous “will still bear fruit; they will stay rich with sap and green” (Psalm 92:14).

Living on mission

Whether you are new or mature, every follower of Jesus is sent: “But when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, you will receive power, and you will bear witness to Me in Jerusalem, through all Judea and Samaria, and out to the farthest end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Jesus said to His disciples, “You did not choose Me; I chose you. I appointed you for this: to go and bear fruit, and for your fruit to remain” (John 15:16).

Think of it as four circles moving outwards: your home, where people see your faith at breakfast; your work, whether office, shop, field or ward; your church, where your gifts build up the body; and the nations, which you can pray for, give to and, if God sends you, go to (Chapters 18 to 25).

The East African Revival, which began in the 1930s, shows how this spreads. Ordinary men and women who had met Jesus walked in the light with one another, confessed their sins openly, and told their neighbours what Christ had done. It crossed tribe and church boundaries. Festo Kivengere, the Ugandan evangelist and bishop, was one of its fruits, and carried its simple message of Jesus and His cross from Kigezi to many nations. John wrote, “But if we walk in the light, just as He is in the light, we share fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, His Son, goes on cleansing us from every sin” (1 John 1:7).

And we do not go alone. The Great Commission ends with a promise: “And remember this: I Myself am with you every day, until the close of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Every day. That is coram Deo carried into the world.

Grace for the journey: Hudson Taylor

Perhaps you look ahead with fear, because you have started well before and faltered. Then Hudson Taylor’s story is for you.

James Hudson Taylor was born in 1832 in Barnsley, Yorkshire, the son of a chemist who was also a Methodist lay preacher. At seventeen, reading a gospel tract in his father’s library, he was struck by the words “The finished work of Christ.” If the whole work was finished, what was left for him to do but kneel and accept the Saviour? He reached Shanghai in 1854, in the middle of a civil war, and in 1865, on the beach at Brighton, he gave himself to God for inland China, and the China Inland Mission was born.

Outwardly a hero of faith, by the late 1860s he was inwardly close to despair. He had buried a daughter, seen his workers attacked by a mob, and been criticised in Parliament. Worse, he felt his own heart was failing:

“I was painfully conscious that I was not living all that I was trying to teach the Chinese. Struggling for victory, too often I found myself defeated, until I asked myself whether I ought not to cease to preach, and to retire from missionary work.”

Hudson Taylor, Unfailing Springs

Then, in about 1869, the change came. His biographers connect it with a letter from a younger colleague, John McCarthy, about resting on the Faithful One instead of straining after faith. In Taylor’s own telling, it came one afternoon in his ordinary Bible reading, when Jesus’ words in John 4 became a present message to his soul: “But no one who drinks the water I will give will ever be thirsty again” (John 4:14). He took Jesus at His word. He received the living water, he wrote, “believing from His own Word that my thirsty days were all passed, not from any present feeling, but because of His promise.”

That was the secret of the rest of his life. He stopped trying to hold on to Christ by effort and rested in the fact that Christ was holding him. The years that followed brought his deepest sorrows: in 1870 two of their young sons died, and then his wife Maria. Yet he went on. The mission grew far beyond anything he had asked, and when he died at Changsha in 1905, hundreds of missionaries were serving across China.

Looking back in A Retrospect on times his own trust had been weak, Taylor wrote: “He is wholly true whether we trust or not.” That is the grace that carries us forward. Paul says the same: “If we are unfaithful, He remains faithful, for He cannot be false to Himself” (2 Timothy 2:13).

This is why the opening verse of this chapter matters. The One who started a good work in you will keep working at it until it is finished. Your growth does not finally rest on your discipline or your rule of life, good as those are. It rests on Him. Andrew Murray wrote that believers who grieve over their ups and downs need one thing above all:

“What they need is the simple faith that the stablishing in Christ, day by day, is God’s work, — a work that He delights to do, in spite of all our weakness and unfaithfulness, if we will but trust Him for it.”

Andrew Murray, Abide in Christ

“Let us run the race laid out ahead of us, and run it with endurance. Let us keep our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer who leads the way in faith and brings it to perfection” (Hebrews 12:1-2). And when you fall, remember who is keeping you: “Now to the One who is able to guard you from stumbling, and to bring you into the presence of His glory without blemish and rejoicing greatly, to God alone, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, might, and authority, before time began, now, and for all the ages to come. Amen” (Jude 24-25).

A prayer of commitment

Sixteen centuries ago in North Africa, Augustine spent years searching for happiness in pleasure, success and clever ideas, and found none of them enough. When at last he came home to God, he began his Confessions with words that sum up this whole book:

“Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.”

Augustine, Confessions

If you want to answer God’s call to seek His face, you may pray in your own words, or use this prayer:

Father, You made me for Yourself, and my heart is restless until it rests in You. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for Your cross and Your empty tomb, for taking away my sin and bringing me near. Holy Spirit, fill me afresh today. I give You my mornings and my evenings, my home and my work, my money and my time, my gifts and my weaknesses. Teach me to walk before Your face every day. Make me like Jesus. Use me to bring others to You, near and far. When I stumble, lift me up; when I wander, call me back. You began this good work in me; I trust You to finish it. My household and I will serve the LORD. In the name of Jesus, Amen.

The face that shines

The Introduction ended with a blessing: may the LORD make His face shine toward you. So this book ends there too, with the words God gave the priests of Israel to speak over His people. They are words to receive, not to earn. Read them slowly, as spoken to you:

“May the LORD bless you and watch over you. May the LORD make His face shine toward you and show you favor. May the LORD lift up His face to look on you and grant you peace.” (Numbers 6:24-26)

The face that Adam and Eve hid from now turns towards you in favour. The face that Moses longed to see has shone on us in Jesus Christ. And one day, the Bible promises, the hiding and the longing will both be over: “They will look upon His face, and His name will be written on their foreheads” (Revelation 22:4).

Until that day, seek His face. Live before Him. Walk with Him. And may the LORD make His face shine toward you.

Questions for reflection

  • Looking back over the five parts of this book, which chapter has meant the most to you, and why? Which one do you most need to return to?
  • How would you explain, in your own words, the thread that runs through it all: created for relationship with God, restored through Christ, empowered by the Spirit?
  • What would the five strands of a rule of life (Scripture, prayer, the morning watch, community and service) look like in your present season of life?
  • Are you at the beginning of your walk with God, or further along? Which of the next steps in this chapter is God asking you to take now?
  • Hudson Taylor found rest when he stopped straining and trusted Christ to hold him. Where are you still trying to live the Christian life in your own strength?

A step for this week

This week, write your own rule of life on a single sheet of paper. Under five headings (Scripture, prayer, the morning watch, community and service) write one simple, realistic practice for each, the kind you could keep even on a hard week. Share it with one Christian friend. Then, each morning this week, before you begin your day, read Numbers 6:24-26 aloud over yourself and your household, and receive it as God’s word to you: that He sees you, that His face shines toward you, and that you live this day before Him.

study_questions.question: What is a Christian rule of life and how do I make one?
study_questions.answer: A rule of life is not a list of laws but a written pattern of the few practices that keep you near to God, in a rhythm you can actually live, like a trellis that gives a vine's life a shape. Five strands belong in almost every rule: Scripture, prayer, the morning watch, community and service. Write yours on one page, keep each practice realistic enough for a hard week, and test it by Micah 6:8: "And what does the LORD ask of you except to do justice, to love loyalty, and to walk humbly with your God?"

study_questions.question: What should a new Christian do first?
